puertomadryn.bestTime: June to December is the southern right whale season in the Golfo Nuevo, when the animals come into the bay to calve and can be watched from the shore as well as from boats, and September and October are the peak. That overlaps with cold weather: winter here is windy and around ten degrees by day. Summer from December to February is warm, dry and windy, with temperatures in the mid twenties, and is when the penguin colony at Punta Tombo is at its fullest. The wind is a constant across every season.
puertomadryn.prosCons: Puerto Madryn is the base for one of the great marine wildlife concentrations on earth: right whales in the bay, elephant seals, sea lions and orcas on Peninsula Valdes, and half a million penguins at Punta Tombo. The town is safe, calm and cheap by international standards. Against that, the Patagonian wind is relentless, the town itself is functional rather than attractive, there is no foreign community, and Argentina's economic instability makes financial planning genuinely difficult in a way that no other country in this batch does. The town also grew around an aluminium smelter rather than tourism, which is why it looks more industrial than a wildlife destination usually does.
puertomadryn.whoFor: Puerto Madryn suits wildlife travellers, divers and photographers who want a base on the Patagonian coast during the whale season, and anyone crossing Patagonia who needs somewhere to stop and work. It works for people comfortable with Argentine practicalities and with Spanish. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an international community, a reliable financial environment, or shelter from wind, and for those expecting a scenic town, since the appeal here is entirely what lies outside it. It also suits divers specifically, since the shipwrecks and sea lion colonies in the gulf are among the better cold-water diving in South America.

laserena.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month as a solo remote worker in La Serena, which is good value for Chile and below Santiago or Valparaiso. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $350 to $550, rising through the January and February holiday season when Chilean families fill the coast. Groceries are moderate by Chilean standards, which are the highest in South America, and wine and produce are cheap. Utilities are low because the climate is mild year-round and neither heating nor cooling is much needed. Eating out is reasonable and the seafood along the coast is excellent value.
laserena.whereToWork: Chile leads South America on connectivity and La Serena is well served, with fast fibre available across the city at reasonable prices and reliable mobile coverage. A small coworking presence exists, and the Universidad de La Serena and the astronomy sector give the city a professional population unusual for its size. The observatory operations in the Elqui valley bring an international scientific community that has been here for decades. Power is reliable. For remote work this is one of the more dependable options in South America. The observatory sector also means the region has better technical infrastructure than a coastal town of this size would otherwise justify.
laserena.gettingAround: La Serena's colonial centre is compact and walkable, and the long beach connects it to Coquimbo four kilometres south along an avenue lined with the city's lighthouse and promenade. Local buses and colectivo shared taxis cover both cities cheaply. La Florida airport has domestic connections to Santiago. Long-distance buses run north to the Atacama and south to the capital in about six hours. The Elqui valley, the observatories and the pisco distilleries all lie inland and need a car or a tour. Cycling along the seafront is practical. Coquimbo next door has the fishing port and a rougher character, and the two cities function as one for most practical purposes.
laserena.visas: Chile grants most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once for a further ninety days. There is no dedicated Chilean digital nomad visa, though a temporary residence permit exists for people with independent income and Chile has generally been open to longer stays. Peru is a long way north and Argentina over the Andes, so an overland reset is a substantial journey. Chile's agricultural import controls are enforced strictly at every border and airport, and undeclared food attracts a large fine regardless of intent. Anyone driving in from Argentina should expect the Andean passes to close in winter, sometimes for days at a time.
laserena.bestTime: La Serena has one of the most even climates in this dataset, with warm dry summers around twenty-four and mild winters around fifteen, so the season matters less here than almost anywhere. January and February are the Chilean holidays, when the beach fills and prices rise. March to May and September to November are the quiet and comfortable months. The coastal camanchaca fog rolls in on many mornings and burns off by midday. Inland in the Elqui valley the skies are famously clear, which is why the observatories are there.
laserena.prosCons: La Serena combines a colonial centre, a long beach, a genuinely mild year-round climate and the Elqui valley inland, where the clearest skies in the world support a cluster of international observatories and a pisco industry. Chilean infrastructure and connectivity are the best in South America. Against that, Chile is expensive by regional standards, English is limited and Chilean Spanish is difficult, street crime has risen across the country in recent years, and the town is quiet outside the summer season. The camanchaca fog also means that mornings are frequently grey even in summer, which surprises people who booked on the sunshine figures.
laserena.whoFor: La Serena suits people who want a mild coastal base with reliable infrastructure and are willing to pay Chilean prices for it, particularly anyone drawn to astronomy, since the Elqui observatories are a genuine draw rather than a curiosity. It works for those with Spanish. It is a poor fit for budget travellers who would get far more for their money in Peru or Bolivia, for anyone needing a large international community, and for people who want a lively city rather than a coastal town. It also suits anyone who wants a base within reach of the Atacama without committing to living in the desert itself.

cagliari.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Cagliari, which is cheaper than mainland Italian cities of comparable size and well below Rome or Milan. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $550 to $850, with the Castello and Marina districts at the upper end. Food is good value: the markets are excellent and a full meal in an ordinary trattoria is reasonable. Sardinian wine and produce are cheap. Utilities are moderate, with hot summers needing cooling. Ferry and flight connections to the mainland are an ongoing cost that island living adds.
cagliari.whereToWork: Cagliari has a modest coworking scene, supported by the university and a small technology and services sector, with desks at reasonable rates. Italian fibre has reached the city and offers decent speeds at ordinary European prices, and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the urban area. Quality varies by building, as it does throughout Italy, and the older stone properties in Castello can be awkward to service. For ordinary remote work the connectivity is entirely adequate, and better than much of southern Italy. Anyone taking a flat in the Castello should ask specifically about the connection, since the medieval walls defeat a lot of domestic wifi hardware.
cagliari.gettingAround: Cagliari climbs from the port to the walled Castello district and the centre is walkable if you accept the hills and the lifts that help with them. Buses and a light rail line cover the wider city cheaply. Poetto beach runs eight kilometres along the eastern side and is reachable by bus in fifteen minutes. The airport at Elmas is ten minutes out by train with connections across Europe. Ferries leave for the Italian mainland. A car is needed for the rest of Sardinia, where public transport is thin and the interior is empty.
cagliari.visas: Italy is in the Schengen area, so most non-EU nationals get ninety days within any 180-day period and EU citizens face no restriction. Italy's digital nomad visa, in force since 2024, is open to highly qualified remote workers meeting income, insurance and accommodation requirements, applied for at an Italian consulate before travel. Processing is slow and consulate practice varies considerably, so allow months rather than weeks. The elective residence visa is an alternative for those with sufficient passive income who will not work. Anyone applying for the nomad visa should also budget for the appointment backlog, which in some consulates has run to many months.
cagliari.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, with warm dry days, sea temperatures that are comfortable from late spring into autumn, and none of the August crowds. Summer from July to August is hot, regularly above thirty, and the island fills with Italian holidaymakers, which is when accommodation is most expensive and hardest to find. Winter is mild by any northern standard, with highs around fifteen, and it is the wettest season, though the totals are modest. The mistral wind blows hard through parts of the year. The mistral is also what makes the sailing here good, so the same wind that empties the beach fills the bay with boats.
cagliari.prosCons: Cagliari gives you a genuine Italian city with a walled medieval quarter, an eight-kilometre city beach, flamingos in the salt pans at the edge of the built-up area, and Sardinian food and wine, at prices below the mainland. The airport is ten minutes from the centre. Against that, English is limited, island logistics add cost and time to anything involving the mainland, the interior of Sardinia requires a car, and the city is quiet outside the summer in a way that suits some people and not others. Flight connections are also seasonal: the routes that make the airport feel well connected in July thin considerably by November.
cagliari.whoFor: Cagliari suits people who want Mediterranean island living with a real city attached rather than a resort, particularly those with some Italian or the willingness to learn. It works well for anyone who swims, sails or wants a beach in the same municipality as a medieval quarter. It is a poor fit for anyone needing English throughout, for those who find island logistics frustrating, and for people who want a large international community, which Sardinia does not have outside the Costa Smeralda in season. It also suits anyone who wants a Mediterranean island that is genuinely lived in year-round rather than one that closes in October.

maribor.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Maribor, which is meaningfully cheaper than Ljubljana and among the better value cities in the eurozone. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $450 to $650, kept reasonable by a large student population. Groceries are ordinary central European prices and eating out is good value, with the local wine particularly cheap given the region produces it. Utilities include real winter heating. Ski passes at Pohorje and the transport to reach the surrounding hills are the discretionary costs that add up. Prices also rise noticeably during the ski season for anything close to the Pohorje cable car.
maribor.whereToWork: Slovenia has good digital infrastructure and Maribor is fully covered, with fast fibre at reasonable prices and reliable mobile data. The University of Maribor is the city's largest institution and supports a small coworking scene and a technology sector that has grown steadily. English is widely spoken among younger Slovenes and in the professional world, which removes most of the administrative friction. Power is reliable. For remote work this is a straightforward, well-connected European city at a price well below the western half of the continent. Graz, an hour and a half away by train, is the nearest city with a larger professional network if that becomes necessary.
maribor.gettingAround: Maribor is compact and the old town, the main square and the Lent riverside are all walkable, with the Drava running through the middle. Local buses cover the city cheaply and cycling is practical on the flat riverside. The Pohorje cable car leaves from the edge of town and reaches the ski and hiking area in a few minutes, which is the single most useful transport link here. Trains connect to Ljubljana in about two hours and to Graz in Austria in under an hour and a half. Vienna and Zagreb are both close.
maribor.visas: Slovenia is in the Schengen area and the eurozone, so most non-EU nationals get ninety days within any 180-day period and EU citizens face no restriction. Slovenia introduced a digital nomad permit in 2025 allowing up to a year for remote workers employed outside the country, without the right to renew immediately, which is a genuine new option worth checking the current terms of. Longer stays otherwise run through employment or business registration. Croatia and Austria are both Schengen, so neither offers a reset. Anyone considering the new permit should read the current terms directly, since it was introduced recently and the practice around it is still settling.
maribor.bestTime: May, June, September and early October are the most comfortable months, with warm days, long evenings and the wine country at its best around the September and October harvest. Summer from July to August is warm, into the high twenties, and the Lent Festival fills the riverside in late June and early July. Winter from December to February is cold, grey and often damp in the city, with proper snow up on Pohorje, which is the point for anyone here to ski. Rain is spread through the year with an early summer peak.
maribor.prosCons: Maribor puts a ski area at the end of a cable car from the city, the world's oldest producing vine on a house by the river, a university that keeps the place young, and Austria, Croatia and Hungary all within a couple of hours, at a cost well below Ljubljana. Slovenia is safe, clean and well organised. Against that, the city is small and quiet, the winter is grey, there is no nomad community, and air quality scores a 6 because of winter inversions and domestic heating in the Drava valley.
maribor.whoFor: Maribor suits people who want a Schengen base at a price that makes a longer stay affordable, particularly skiers and cyclists who will use Pohorje and the wine roads. It works for anyone who wants central Europe with quick access to Austria and Croatia. It is a poor fit for those who need a large city, an international community or a nightlife beyond the student circuit, and for anyone whose Schengen days are already committed elsewhere, since Slovenia offers no escape from that clock. It also suits anyone who wants to be inside the eurozone without the banking and currency friction that the neighbouring non-euro countries add.

almeria.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Almeria, which is among the cheapest coastal cities in Spain and well below Malaga, Valencia or Barcelona. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $450 to $700, with the centre and the seafront at the upper end. Food is inexpensive, helped by the enormous agricultural sector immediately west that supplies much of Europe's winter vegetables. Eating out is good value and the tapa that comes free with a drink is a genuine local custom here. Utilities are low given the mild winters and dry heat.
almeria.whereToWork: Spain has one of the best fibre networks in Europe and Almeria is comprehensively covered, with fast, inexpensive home connections and reliable mobile data. A small coworking scene exists, and the University of Almeria supports a modest professional population. The city has not attracted the nomad numbers that Malaga and Valencia have, which means fewer dedicated spaces but also none of the pressure on housing that those cities now have. Power is reliable. For remote work the infrastructure is a genuine strength at a price well below the rest of the Spanish coast.
almeria.gettingAround: Almeria's centre is compact and walkable, running from the port and the seafront promenade up to the Alcazaba on its ridge. Local buses cover the city cheaply and cycling along the flat seafront is practical. Trains and buses connect to Granada, Malaga and Madrid, though the rail links are slower than elsewhere in Spain and the high-speed line has been under construction for years. The airport is fifteen minutes out with European connections. A car matters for Cabo de Gata, the Tabernas desert and the Alpujarras, none of which are well served by bus.
almeria.visas: Spain is in the Schengen area, so most non-EU nationals get ninety days within any 180-day period and EU citizens face no restriction. Spain's digital nomad visa, created under the 2023 startups law, is among the more accessible in Europe: it covers remote workers for foreign companies, has an income threshold tied to the minimum wage, runs for up to three years and can be applied for from inside Spain after entering as a tourist. It also carries a favourable tax regime for qualifying applicants, which is a substantial part of its appeal.
almeria.bestTime: Almeria has the mildest winter in mainland Europe and that is the argument for it: December to February sits around eighteen or nineteen by day with abundant sun, which is why it fills with northern European long-stay visitors. April to June and September to October are close to ideal, warm and dry with swimmable sea from late spring. Summer from July to August is hot, above thirty-two, though the humidity is lower than the Mediterranean average. Rain is almost absent, with an annual total among the lowest in Europe. The lack of rain is also why the region grows so much of the winter produce that reaches northern Europe, which is visible as soon as you drive west.
almeria.prosCons: Almeria offers the driest, sunniest and mildest climate in mainland Europe, a hilltop Moorish alcazaba, the empty beaches and volcanic coast of Cabo de Gata half an hour east, and Spanish city living at prices the rest of the coast left behind years ago. The free tapas custom is real. Against that, English is limited outside tourism, the city is quiet compared with Malaga or Valencia, rail connections are poor, and the vast plastic greenhouse sea west of the city is an environmental and social issue worth understanding. The greenhouses are also visible from space and cover a substantial part of the coastal plain, which is worth seeing rather than reading about.
almeria.whoFor: Almeria suits people who want winter sun in the eurozone at a price that makes months rather than weeks affordable, particularly those on Spain's digital nomad visa. It works for hikers and divers drawn to Cabo de Gata, and for anyone who wants a working Spanish city rather than an expat coastal strip. It is a poor fit for anyone needing English, for those who want a large nomad community, and for people who would find a provincial city short on things to do after the first month. It also suits film enthusiasts, since the Tabernas desert north of the city is where a great many westerns were shot and the sets survive.

napier.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Napier, which is cheaper than Auckland or Wellington and about average for provincial New Zealand. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $850 to $1,200, with the Art Deco centre and the Marine Parade seafront at the upper end and Taradale and Onekawa considerably cheaper. New Zealand grocery prices are high and imported goods higher still, which is the adjustment most arrivals find hardest. Hawke's Bay wine is one of the few things that costs less here than elsewhere in the country. Eating out is expensive by any measure outside the region.
napier.whereToWork: Napier has a small coworking presence serving the wine, horticulture and port industries that dominate the local economy, with desks at modest rates. Fibre is widely available across the town at reliable speeds and typical New Zealand pricing, and mobile coverage is comprehensive in the built-up area. The port is one of the country's larger ones and brings a professional layer that a town this size would not otherwise have. Connections are arranged per property, so confirm what a lease includes before arriving rather than assuming the landlord has done it.
napier.gettingAround: Napier is flat along the seafront and the Art Deco centre is compact enough to cross on foot in fifteen minutes. A local bus network connects to Hastings twenty minutes south, and the two towns function as one urban area for most purposes. The Hawke's Bay cycle trails run for over two hundred kilometres through vineyards and along the coast, which makes cycling genuinely practical rather than recreational. The airport is five minutes from the centre with domestic connections. A car matters for the wineries and the Cape Kidnappers gannet colony.
napier.visas: New Zealand clarified in 2025 that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer while on a visitor visa, which changed the practical position for nomads considerably. Most Western nationals obtain an NZeTA and receive up to three months on arrival, extendable in some circumstances to a maximum of nine months within an eighteen-month period. Working Holiday visas cover a defined list of nationalities and ages with twelve months of full work rights. Longer stays run through the accredited employer route or the skilled residence pathway, and settings change often enough to warrant checking directly.
napier.bestTime: November to April is the warm half, with daytime temperatures in the low to mid twenties and Hawke's Bay recording among the highest sunshine hours in the country. February and March are the best months: the vintage is under way, the sea is at its warmest and the summer crowds have thinned. The Art Deco Festival in February fills the town for a week with vintage cars and period dress and is worth timing around or avoiding depending on temperament. Winter is mild with highs around fourteen and considerably drier than the west coast.
napier.prosCons: Napier is the most concentrated Art Deco townscape outside Miami Beach, rebuilt in a single style after the 1931 earthquake flattened it, and it sits in New Zealand's largest wine region with a gannet colony down the coast. Costs are below the main centres and the weather is among the country's best. Against that, it is a small town with no nomad community, the international presence is essentially nil, and New Zealand's distance from everywhere and its grocery prices are permanent conditions rather than temporary ones. The town also sits at the northern end of Hawke's Bay, so the region's other centre, Hastings, is twenty minutes away and the two share most services between them.
napier.whoFor: Napier suits people with New Zealand work rights or on a working holiday who want a warm, dry, small coastal town with good wine and a cycling network. It works for anyone interested in architecture, since the Art Deco concentration is genuinely unusual. It is a poor fit for those who need an international community, a nightlife or a large professional network, all of which mean Auckland or Wellington. Anyone arriving in winter should know the town is quiet and the tourist economy largely pauses. Anyone arriving for the February Art Deco Festival should book months ahead, since the town's entire accommodation stock fills for that week.

wollongong.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker in Wollongong, and the cost score of 4 is an honest reflection of Australian prices rather than anything unusual about the city. A one-bedroom apartment near the beach or in the centre runs roughly $1,000 to $1,400, meaningfully below Sydney for a comparable coastal life. Groceries and eating out are expensive by European or Asian measure. The university keeps some prices honest around the campus. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data, so treat it as a working budget.
wollongong.whereToWork: Wollongong has a genuine coworking scene for its size, helped by the University of Wollongong and a growing technology and engineering sector that grew partly out of the steelworks. Desks run from roughly $250 a month. The NBN reaches most of the inner suburbs with reliable speeds, and mobile coverage across the city is comprehensive. The consistent Australian complaint applies: home internet is expensive relative to what it delivers and plans vary enormously by address, so check what a specific lease includes. Sydney is ninety minutes by train if a day in a larger professional network is worth the trip, which is a genuine option here rather than a theoretical one.
wollongong.gettingAround: Wollongong is strung along a narrow coastal strip between the escarpment and the sea, which makes it long rather than wide and reasonably walkable within each part. A free shuttle bus circles the centre and the university. The train to Sydney takes about ninety minutes along a scenic coastal line and is the reason many people live here rather than in the city. The Grand Pacific Drive and the Sea Cliff Bridge run south along the coast. Cycling on the coastal shared path is genuinely practical. Parking near the beaches fills early on any warm weekend, and the day-tripper traffic from Sydney is a real factor in how the city feels from Friday evening.
wollongong.visas: Australia has no dedicated digital nomad visa. Most Western nationals get an eVisitor or Electronic Travel Authority allowing three months per entry within a twelve-month period, which does not permit work for an Australian employer and leaves remote work for a foreign one in a grey area the government has not clarified. Working Holiday visas cover under-thirties or under-thirty-fives depending on nationality and allow twelve months with work rights. Longer stays require employer sponsorship or the skilled migration points system, neither of which is undertaken casually. Anyone hoping to complete the regional work requirement for a second-year working holiday extension should check whether Wollongong itself qualifies, since the eligible postcodes have changed.
wollongong.bestTime: October to April is the comfortable half of the year, with warm days, swimmable ocean and long light evenings. Summer from December to February runs into the high twenties with humidity that the sea breeze usually handles, and it is when the beaches fill with day visitors from Sydney. March and April are the best combination of warm water and thinner crowds. Winter from June to August is mild by northern standards, with daytime highs around seventeen, and the surf is at its most consistent through those months. The escarpment also creates its own weather, so the hills behind the city can be in cloud while the beach is in full sun.
wollongong.prosCons: Wollongong puts a sandstone escarpment on one side and seventeen beaches on the other, with Sydney ninety minutes up a coastal railway. It has a real university, a growing technology sector and rents well below the capital. Against that, Australia is expensive across the board, the visa position is the genuine obstacle for a non-Australian rather than anything about the city, the international community is thin, and the city is long and thin enough that a car helps more than the walkability suggests. The steelworks at Port Kembla still operates and dominates the southern end of the city, which is part of the character rather than a blemish but is worth knowing before choosing a suburb.
wollongong.whoFor: Wollongong suits remote workers with an existing right to be in Australia, particularly people leaving Sydney for the coast and those on working holiday visas. It works well for surfers, climbers drawn to the escarpment, and anyone connected to the university. It is a poor fit for anyone arriving without a visa pathway, for budget travellers, and for those who need a large international community, since the foreign population here is students rather than a settled scene. It also suits anyone who wants to be within a train ride of Sydney's job market while paying substantially less for a place to live, which is the calculation most residents here have made.

geelong.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker in Geelong, which is below Melbourne for a comparable standard and is the main financial argument for the city. A one-bedroom apartment near the waterfront runs roughly $1,000 to $1,400, with the suburbs considerably cheaper. Groceries and eating out are ordinary Australian prices, which are high. The Melbourne train is an ongoing cost for anyone commuting. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget rather than a measurement.
geelong.whereToWork: Geelong has a small coworking scene and a professional base built on Deakin University, the health sector and a manufacturing economy that has been reinventing itself since the Ford plant closed in 2016. Desks run from roughly $250 a month. The NBN reaches most of the city with reliable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive. The waterfront redevelopment has brought newer office space and the cafes along it are used to people working from them. Australian home internet remains expensive for what it delivers. Melbourne is an hour by train for anything the local network cannot supply, which is how most people here treat the professional gap.
geelong.gettingAround: Geelong's centre and waterfront are flat and walkable, and the Baywalk Bollards run along the promenade as a public art trail. A local bus network covers the suburbs. The train to Melbourne takes about an hour and runs frequently, which is what makes the city viable as a cheaper alternative to living there. Avalon airport is twenty minutes away with domestic and some international flights. The Great Ocean Road starts west of the city and Bells Beach is half an hour down the coast. The Bellarine Peninsula with its wineries and beach towns is half an hour east, and the rail trail out to Queenscliff is a good day on a bicycle.
geelong.visas: Australia has no digital nomad visa. Most Western nationals get an eVisitor or Electronic Travel Authority allowing three months per entry within twelve months, with no right to work for an Australian employer and remote work for a foreign one legally unclear. Working Holiday visas are open to under-thirties or under-thirty-fives depending on nationality and allow twelve months with work rights. Longer stays run through employer sponsorship or skilled migration, both substantial processes requiring a skills assessment and considerable time. Avalon airport nearby handles some international flights, which matters for anyone whose visa runs on repeated entries rather than a single long stay.
geelong.bestTime: December to March is the summer window, with daytime temperatures in the mid twenties and the bay warm enough to swim. Melbourne's reputation for four seasons in a day applies here too, and a February day can swing from thirty-five to eighteen when a cool change comes through. Autumn in March and April is the most settled weather of the year. Winter from June to August is cold and grey by Australian standards, with highs around fourteen, though it rarely freezes. Rain is spread across the year. Anyone planning around the Great Ocean Road should know it is busiest between December and February and considerably more pleasant in autumn.
geelong.prosCons: Geelong combines a rebuilt waterfront on Corio Bay, a university, an hour's train to Melbourne and the start of the Great Ocean Road, at rents meaningfully below the capital. Bells Beach and the Otways are close. Against that, Australian costs are high, the visa position rules the city out for most non-Australians, the weather is unreliable, and the city is still working through the closure of the industries that built it, which shows in parts of it. The bay itself is shallow and calm rather than surf coast, so anyone expecting waves needs to drive to Torquay or Bells, half an hour south.
geelong.whoFor: Geelong suits people with Australian work rights who want coastal living within reach of Melbourne without paying Melbourne rents, and surfers drawn to the Surf Coast. It works for anyone connected to Deakin. It is a poor fit for non-Australians without a visa route, for travellers on a budget, and for anyone who wants reliable warm weather, which this stretch of coast does not offer even in summer. It also suits families, since the city has the schools, hospitals and space that inner Melbourne makes expensive, and anyone whose work is in Melbourne but only two or three days a week.

newplymouth.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,650 a month as a solo remote worker in New Plymouth, which is among the cheaper options in New Zealand while keeping a full range of services. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $800 to $1,150. New Zealand grocery prices are high and imported goods carry a premium that surprises arrivals from Europe or Asia. The region's economy rests on dairy and on oil and gas, which keeps wages and some prices higher than a town this size would otherwise support. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
newplymouth.whereToWork: New Plymouth has limited formal coworking, with a small number of spaces serving the energy sector that dominates local professional employment. Fibre is widely available at reliable speeds and typical New Zealand pricing, and mobile coverage is comprehensive in town and patchy on the mountain and around the coast. The Len Lye Centre and the town's arts programme give the place a creative layer unusual for its size. As everywhere in New Zealand, confirm the connection at a specific property rather than assuming it is in place. Anyone whose work depends on being seen in person should understand that the nearest city of any size is four hours away by road.
newplymouth.gettingAround: New Plymouth is compact and the Coastal Walkway runs thirteen kilometres along the shore from the port to Bell Block, which functions as the town's main artery for walking and cycling rather than as a recreational path. A local bus network covers the suburbs. Egmont National Park and the trailheads onto Mount Taranaki are half an hour inland. The airport has domestic connections. Everything beyond the town, the Surf Highway, the Forgotten World Highway and the mountain, needs a car. The Surf Highway 45 runs around the coast from the town and is the route to almost every break in the region, which is what most people here use a car for.
newplymouth.visas: New Zealand's 2025 clarification that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer changed the practical position considerably. Most Western nationals get an NZeTA and up to three months on arrival, extendable in some cases to a maximum of nine months within eighteen. Working Holiday visas cover a defined list of nationalities and ages with twelve months of work rights. Longer stays go through the accredited employer route or the skilled residence pathway. Immigration settings change frequently, so verify the current rules directly rather than relying on a guide. The region's oil and gas sector has historically sponsored skilled workers, which is one of the few employer-led routes into New Zealand outside the main centres.
newplymouth.bestTime: December to March is the warm half, with daytime temperatures around twenty-two and the sea swimmable. Taranaki is wet: the mountain catches weather off the Tasman and rain falls in every month, so a dry spell is luck rather than season. February is the most settled month. Winter from June to August is mild at sea level, with highs around thirteen, while the mountain holds snow and the ski field operates. The famous view of a symmetrical volcanic cone depends entirely on the cloud lifting. Locals will tell you the mountain is visible about one day in three, which is worth knowing before booking a trip around the view.
newplymouth.prosCons: New Plymouth has one of the most striking settings of any town in this dataset: a near-perfect volcanic cone thirty minutes inland, a thirteen-kilometre coastal walkway through the middle, and consistent surf along the Surf Highway. The Len Lye Centre is a serious gallery for a town this size. Against that, it is remote even by New Zealand standards, the weather is genuinely wet, there is no international community, and the local economy's dependence on oil and gas makes its future a live local question. The town is also on the wrong side of the island for most itineraries, so it is rarely somewhere people pass through by accident.
newplymouth.whoFor: New Plymouth suits people with New Zealand work rights who organise their life around the mountain and the surf, and who want a small town with real services and an unexpectedly good arts scene. It works for climbers and trampers, since Mount Taranaki is a serious objective rather than a walk. It is a poor fit for anyone needing an international community, dependable sunshine, or a professional network beyond the energy sector. It also suits anyone drawn to the Len Lye Centre and the WOMAD festival in March, which together give the town a cultural life well beyond its size. It is not a place to arrive expecting company.

nadi.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Nadi, which is moderate for the Pacific and reflects an island economy where almost everything imported carries freight and duty. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $450 to $750. Local produce from the market is cheap and Indo-Fijian food costs very little, while anything Western-facing, particularly in the resort areas at Denarau, is priced for tourists. Alcohol and electronics are expensive. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a planning figure.
nadi.whereToWork: Connectivity is the weakest part of the case. Fiji has fibre in the main towns and Nadi has usable connections, but speeds are modest by international standards, reliability is inconsistent and data costs more than in Asia or Europe. Mobile coverage is reasonable along the western corridor and patchy elsewhere. There is minimal coworking. Power cuts occur, and cyclone season can take infrastructure down for days. Anyone with a demanding video schedule should test a specific connection carefully rather than assume the resort wifi is representative. Suva, four hours away, has the country's better infrastructure if a stretch of reliable work becomes necessary.
nadi.gettingAround: Nadi is small and the main town along Queens Road is walkable, though the airport, Denarau and the port are spread along a corridor that needs transport. Local buses are very cheap and taxis are inexpensive and metered in town. Denarau, where the marina and the boats to the Mamanuca and Yasawa islands leave from, is fifteen minutes west. The Coral Coast runs southeast and Suva is about four hours by road. The airport is the Pacific's main hub for onward connections. Driving is on the left and the Queens Road carries most of the island's traffic, with standards that require attention rather than confidence.
nadi.visas: Fiji grants most Western nationals four months visa-free on arrival, which is unusually generous and extendable to six months in total. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa, though Fiji has actively courted remote workers and offers a longer-stay option through its investor and work permit routes. The four-month entry alone makes an extended stay straightforward without paperwork. Fiji is outside every regional visa bloc, so time here counts against nothing else. Check requirements close to travel, since Pacific entry rules change with little notice. Anyone island-hopping onward through the Pacific should note that Fiji is the regional aviation hub, so most routings pass back through Nadi.
nadi.bestTime: May to October is the dry season and the reason to come: warm days around twenty-nine, lower humidity, reliable sun and calm seas for the island boats. That is also peak season, when accommodation prices rise. The wet season from November to April brings heavy afternoon rain, high humidity and the cyclone season, which runs to the end of April and is a genuine planning consideration rather than a formality, since Fiji is hit regularly and severely. Nadi itself sits on the drier western side of Viti Levu. Anyone planning around the island boats should also know the Yasawa transfers are weather-dependent and cancel in a strong swell.
nadi.prosCons: Nadi is the arrival point for Fiji and the base for the Mamanuca and Yasawa islands, which are the reason most people come, with a four-month visa-free entry that makes a long stay easy. Fijian and Indo-Fijian cultures sit side by side and the hospitality is genuine. Against that, connectivity is weak, the town itself is functional rather than attractive, Pacific costs are higher than the tropics elsewhere, and the cyclone season is a real risk from November to April. The town is also a place most visitors pass through in a day on the way to the islands, which means the services are built for transit rather than for residents.
nadi.whoFor: Nadi suits divers, sailors and anyone whose plan is the islands rather than the town, and travellers who value the generous visa entry. It works for people whose work can tolerate an unreliable connection. It is a poor fit for anyone with a demanding remote schedule, for those wanting a nomad community, which Fiji does not have, and for budget travellers, since Pacific island economics are not the same as Southeast Asian ones. It also suits anyone who wants a Pacific base with straightforward flights onward to Australia, New Zealand and the smaller island states, which Nadi provides better than anywhere else in the region.

portvila.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Port Vila, and understand that Vanuatu imports nearly everything, so supermarket prices are startling relative to local wages. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $500 to $850. The market produce is excellent and cheap, and eating at the market food stalls costs very little, but anything packaged or imported is expensive. There is no personal income tax in Vanuatu, which is a genuine part of the arithmetic. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Rent for anything aimed at expatriates is quoted in a different bracket from local housing, which is worth understanding before assuming a listed price is the going rate.
portvila.whereToWork: Connectivity is the weakest score in this batch. Vanuatu is connected by a single submarine cable and outages have taken the whole country offline for days. Speeds in Port Vila are usable for email and light work, less so for anything demanding, and mobile data is expensive. There is essentially no coworking. Power is unreliable enough that a backup matters. The 2023 twin cyclones and the December 2024 earthquake both damaged infrastructure. Nobody should plan deadline-driven work here without a satellite fallback. Starlink has become the practical answer for anyone here who cannot afford to be offline, and is now common among businesses that depend on connectivity.
portvila.gettingAround: Port Vila is small and the seafront, the market and the centre are walkable. Minibuses circulate constantly and cost a dollar or two, flagged down anywhere and taking a roundabout route to wherever the other passengers are going, which is the normal way to move. Taxis are available. The airport is ten minutes out with connections to Australia, New Zealand and Fiji. Efate has a sealed ring road that circles the island in about three hours, and the other islands are reached by small aircraft or ferry. Driving is on the right, unusually for the region, and the ring road is sealed while most side roads are not.
portvila.visas: Vanuatu grants most Western nationals thirty days visa-free on arrival, extendable in country up to four months. There is no digital nomad visa, though Vanuatu is well known for a citizenship-by-investment programme that has attracted scrutiny and led several countries, including the European Union, to suspend visa-free access for Vanuatu passport holders. That is worth understanding as context rather than as a route. For a visitor the entry is simple. Vanuatu levies no income tax, which is the country's more legitimate financial draw. Anyone considering the investment programme should read the current international position on it carefully rather than the promotional material, since the restrictions on the passport have real consequences.
portvila.bestTime: April to October is the dry season and the best window, with warm days around twenty-eight, lower humidity and calmer seas. The wet season from November to March brings heavy rain, high humidity and the cyclone season, which in Vanuatu is not a formality: the country is among the most exposed to natural disaster on earth by most risk indices, and Cyclone Pam in 2015 and the twin cyclones of 2023 both caused severe damage. Plan around that window rather than through it. The volcano on Tanna, one of the most accessible active craters anywhere, is reachable year-round but the flights are more reliable in the dry months.
portvila.prosCons: Port Vila offers a genuine Pacific capital with no income tax, some of the best wreck diving in the world at the SS President Coolidge on nearby Espiritu Santo, accessible active volcanoes, and a small but real expatriate community. Bislama makes communication easy for English speakers. Against that, connectivity is poor and occasionally absent, costs are high for what you get, the cyclone and earthquake exposure is genuinely serious, and medical facilities are limited enough that evacuation insurance is essential rather than advisable. Bislama, the national creole, is close enough to English that a visitor can follow a conversation within days, which makes the country unusually easy to be in.
portvila.whoFor: Port Vila suits divers, sailors and people connected to the region's development or maritime sectors, and anyone whose income is flexible enough to survive a week offline. It works for those attracted by the tax position who understand what they are giving up in infrastructure. It is a poor fit for anyone with a demanding video schedule, for travellers who need reliable healthcare nearby, and for anyone unwilling to plan around a serious cyclone season. It also suits anyone drawn to the outer islands, since Efate is the gateway to Tanna's volcano and Espiritu Santo's wrecks and blue holes rather than the destination itself.

alula.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Al Ula, which is high for the region and reflects a place built around premium tourism rather than around residents. Accommodation is the problem: the valley's stock runs from a handful of mid-range guesthouses to Banyan Tree and Habitas at resort rates, and long-term rentals aimed at outsiders barely exist outside the staff housing attached to the Royal Commission's projects. Food is far cheaper than the room, with local restaurants at ordinary Saudi prices and imported goods marked up for the distance. There is no alcohol anywhere in the country, which removes a line most budgets carry. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
alula.whereToWork: Al Ula has no coworking scene in any meaningful sense. The hotels are where remote work actually happens, and the better ones have business-grade connections because the destination is built for international visitors. Saudi mobile data is fast and cheap by any standard, with 5G across the built-up parts of the valley and the main tourist sites, and a local SIM is the practical answer for anyone not staying somewhere with reliable fibre. Coverage thins quickly in the desert beyond the oasis, which matters if the plan involves working from the rock formations. The town is small enough that the same handful of cafes serve everybody, so expect familiarity rather than choice.
alula.gettingAround: Al Ula is a strip of oasis along a valley, and the distances between the old town, the modern centre and the archaeological sites are too great to walk in the heat. A car is close to essential, though the destination runs a shuttle between the main sites and hotels that covers most visitor needs. Hegra itself can only be entered on a guided tour using the site's own transport, which is a rule rather than a suggestion. AlUla airport sits twenty minutes from the centre with connections to Riyadh and Jeddah and a seasonal handful of international routes. Taxis exist but thin out considerably outside the winter season.
alula.visas: Saudi Arabia has no digital nomad visa. The eVisa covers around sixty nationalities, is valid a year for multiple entries and allows ninety days per stay up to a hundred and eighty in the year, which is the route almost every visitor uses. It is a tourist permission and does not authorise work for a Saudi employer; remote work for a foreign one sits in the same unaddressed space it does across the Gulf. Longer stays run through employer sponsorship or the Premium Residency programme, which carries a substantial fee. Rules here have changed quickly and repeatedly since the country opened to tourism, so check the current position directly rather than trusting a secondhand account.
alula.bestTime: October to April is the only sensible window. Winter days sit in the low twenties with cold desert nights that drop close to freezing in January, which is exactly the weather the destination was built around. The Winter at Tantora season and the concert programme at the Maraya mirrored hall fall in these months and are when the valley is busiest and priciest. Summer from June to September pushes past forty degrees and the archaeological sites become genuinely unpleasant by mid-morning, which is why most of the tourism infrastructure quietens down. February and March are the best balance of open sites and thinner crowds.
alula.prosCons: Al Ula holds Hegra, the Nabataean city that became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage site, with more than a hundred tombs carved into sandstone outcrops and almost none of the crowds that Petra carries three hundred kilometres north. The landscape around it is extraordinary and the air is clean. Against that, this is a managed destination rather than a city: there is no nomad community, no nightlife of any kind, no alcohol, and the cost of staying is set by hotels rather than by a rental market. Everything is a drive away. It is a place to spend a remarkable few weeks, not a base.
alula.whoFor: Al Ula suits someone who wants a stretch of desert quiet with genuinely world-class archaeology outside the door and has the budget to absorb resort pricing. It works well for a short concentrated block of work between site visits, particularly in the winter season when the cultural programming is running. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs company, nightlife, a rental market or a walkable city, and anyone travelling on a tight budget will find the accommodation maths does not work at all. Women travelling alone find it easier than the country's reputation suggests, though local norms still apply.

abha.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Abha, which makes it one of the cheaper places to sit in Saudi Arabia and a fraction of what the Gulf coast cities cost. A furnished one-bedroom flat runs roughly $400 to $650, with the higher end for something new near the centre or with a view over the escarpment. Food is inexpensive if eaten locally, and the Asir region grows much of its own produce, which shows in the markets. Fuel costs almost nothing and there is no alcohol spend anywhere in the country. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
abha.whereToWork: Abha has almost no coworking provision, and the cafes around the centre and the newer developments are where remote work happens in practice. Saudi mobile data is fast and inexpensive with strong 5G across the city, which is the reliable option; fixed connections in older buildings vary considerably by address. The city's summer role as the country's domestic hill station means hotels here are used to guests who stay for weeks, and the better ones have connections to match. Power is stable. English is limited outside the university and the tourism sector, so expect Arabic to be the working language of daily errands.
abha.gettingAround: Abha sits at around 2,200 metres and is built across ridges and valleys, which makes it hilly rather than walkable in any continuous sense. A car is the normal way to move around, and fuel costs almost nothing by international standards. Ride-hailing works in the city and is the usual answer for anyone without a vehicle. The cable cars down the escarpment are tourist infrastructure rather than transport but are worth taking once. Abha airport has frequent domestic connections to Riyadh and Jeddah and a small number of regional routes. The mountain roads down to the Tihamah plain are spectacular and demand real attention.
abha.visas: Saudi Arabia has no digital nomad visa. Most visitors arrive on the eVisa, which covers around sixty nationalities, runs for a year with multiple entries and allows ninety days per stay to a maximum of a hundred and eighty days in the year. It permits tourism, not employment by a Saudi entity, and remote work for a foreign employer is not addressed in the rules either way. Anyone wanting to stay longer needs employer sponsorship or the Premium Residency scheme and its fee. The country's visa policy has changed repeatedly since it opened to tourism in 2019, so confirm current conditions before planning a long stay.
abha.bestTime: Abha's altitude gives it the mildest climate in Saudi Arabia and the reason the rest of the country arrives here in July. Summer highs sit around the high twenties while Riyadh is above forty, and the monsoon fringe brings afternoon cloud and mist that rolls over the escarpment. That makes June to September the busiest and most expensive months, with domestic tourism filling the hotels. Spring and autumn are quieter and just as pleasant. Winter nights get genuinely cold for the region and can approach freezing at this elevation, and heating is not something every building here takes seriously.
abha.prosCons: Abha has weather no other Saudi city can offer, sitting high in the Asir mountains with green terraced slopes, cool summers and clean air, along with the stone tower houses at Rijal Almaa and the country's highest peaks nearby. Costs are low and the landscape is genuinely unusual. Against that, there is no nomad presence at all, English is thin, there is no nightlife or alcohol, and the region is conservative even by Saudi standards. Getting anywhere outside the kingdom means a domestic connection first. It is a place with real character and almost no international infrastructure to support a long stay.
abha.whoFor: Abha suits someone already working in Saudi Arabia who wants a cooler base than the coast or the capital, or a traveller drawn to mountain landscapes and heritage architecture that almost no outsiders see. It rewards anyone with some Arabic and patience for a place that has not organised itself around foreign visitors. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an international community, a bar or a nightlife of any kind, and anyone whose work depends on face-to-face meetings will find the professional network essentially absent. Summer arrivals should book early against the domestic holiday season.

fujairah.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Fujairah, which is well below Dubai and Abu Dhabi while still being the UAE. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $600 to $950 depending on how close it sits to the corniche, and the gap against Dubai rents is the main reason anyone chooses to live on this coast. Groceries are broadly Gulf standard, meaning imported goods carry a premium and local produce does not. Alcohol is available in hotels and licensed outlets and is expensive everywhere in the country. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
fujairah.whereToWork: Fujairah has a small coworking presence relative to Dubai's, mostly attached to the free zone and serving the port and shipping businesses that drive the local economy. Internet across the UAE is fast and well built, with fibre widely available and comprehensive 5G, though prices are high and the country's blocking of most voice-over-internet services still catches people out; a VPN is standard practice among remote workers here. The port at Fujairah is one of the world's largest bunkering hubs, which gives the emirate a professional layer beyond its size. Dubai is ninety minutes away for anything the local network cannot supply.
fujairah.gettingAround: Fujairah is spread along the coast between the Hajar mountains and the Gulf of Oman, and like most of the UAE it assumes a car. The corniche and the area immediately around it are walkable, but everything else, including the dive sites north towards Dibba and the mountain roads inland, needs driving. There is no metro and the bus network is limited. Taxis and ride-hailing work in town. Dubai is about ninety minutes by road through the mountains, which is a genuinely good drive, and Fujairah has its own small international airport with a handful of regional routes.
fujairah.visas: The UAE has one of the region's few real remote work visas: a one-year permit for people employed outside the country, requiring proof of around $3,500 a month in income, an employment contract of at least a year and health insurance valid in the country. It is renewable and can be applied for from abroad. Short visits run on visa on arrival for most Western nationalities, typically thirty or ninety days depending on passport. There is also the Golden Visa for longer horizons and defined categories. The remote work route is administratively straightforward by regional standards, which is a real point in the country's favour.
fujairah.bestTime: November to March is the comfortable half of the year, with daytime temperatures in the mid twenties, warm sea and the conditions that make the east coast diving worth the trip. This is also when the mountain wadis are at their best. Summer from June to September pushes past forty degrees with heavy humidity on the coast, and outdoor life effectively stops between mid-morning and evening. The east coast is marginally cooler and less humid than Dubai on the other side of the mountains, which is a difference locals notice, but it is still a Gulf summer and not somewhere to arrive unprepared.
fujairah.prosCons: Fujairah is the only emirate entirely on the Gulf of Oman, which gives it mountains directly behind the beach, the best diving in the country around Snoopy Island and Dibba, and the oldest mosque in the UAE at Al Bidyah. It costs meaningfully less than Dubai while keeping the same infrastructure, safety and visa options. Against that, there is essentially no nomad community, the town is quiet to the point of dullness for anyone used to a city, and the summer is brutal. Most social and professional life still happens ninety minutes away on the other coast.
fujairah.whoFor: Fujairah suits someone who wants the UAE's remote work visa, safety and connectivity without Dubai's rents, and who values a beach with mountains behind it over a skyline. Divers in particular get more here than anywhere else in the country. It works as a winter block rather than a full year, given what the summer does to the coast. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a community, a scene or a professional network within walking distance, all of which mean Dubai instead. Anyone without a car will find the emirate hard work from the first day.

amasra.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Amasra, which is inexpensive even by Turkish standards and reflects a small Black Sea town rather than a city. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $200 to $350, with the peninsula and the two harbours at the top of that range and anything a short walk inland at the bottom. Fish is the local staple and cheap in season, and the region's produce keeps grocery costs low. Turkish inflation makes any figure here a moving target, so treat this as a working budget rather than a fixed one. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
amasra.whereToWork: Amasra has no coworking spaces. This is a town of a few thousand people that fills with domestic tourists in summer and empties in winter, and remote work happens from apartments and a handful of cafes along the harbour. Turkish fibre reaches the town and mobile coverage is good, with data cheap by European standards, but connection quality varies by building and the older stock on the peninsula is the weakest of it. Anyone dependent on being online should test before signing anything longer than a month. Bartin, the provincial centre, is twenty minutes inland and has the services the town lacks.
amasra.gettingAround: Amasra is built on a small peninsula between two bays and is completely walkable, which is much of its appeal; the castle, both harbours and the museum all sit within fifteen minutes of each other on foot. Buses run to Bartin and on to Safranbolu and Ankara, and the coastal road east towards Sinop is one of the better drives in the country. Istanbul is around six hours away by bus. There is no airport nearby, with the nearest useful connections at Zonguldak or a longer trip to Ankara. A car opens up the Black Sea coast but is not needed in the town itself.
amasra.visas: Turkey allows most Western nationals ninety days within any hundred and eighty on arrival or through a straightforward e-visa, which covers a season comfortably. There is no digital nomad visa in the sense that other countries use the phrase, though Turkey introduced a Digital Nomad Identification Card in 2024 for citizens of a defined list of countries with a university degree and a minimum monthly income, which eases the residence permit process rather than replacing it. Short-term residence permits are the traditional longer route and have become notably harder to obtain in recent years, with many neighbourhoods closed to new foreign registrations.
amasra.bestTime: June to September is the season, with warm days, a swimmable Black Sea and a town that fills with Turkish holidaymakers who have known about it for generations. July and August are genuinely crowded and prices rise accordingly. May and September are the better months if the point is to work rather than to holiday. Winter on this coast is grey, wet and windy, with temperatures around eight degrees and much of the tourist infrastructure closed; the Black Sea gets far more rain than the Aegean or Mediterranean coasts and that is the defining fact of the off season.
amasra.prosCons: Amasra is one of the prettiest small towns on the Turkish coast, a Roman and then Genoese harbour settlement on a peninsula with a castle around it, cheap fish and a beach on each side. Costs are very low and the setting is unusual. Against that, it is tiny, has no international presence, English is barely spoken, and the winter is long, wet and empty. The 2022 mine disaster in the wider Bartin coalfield is part of the region's recent history and its economy is not only tourism. Anyone imagining a Mediterranean summer should understand this is a different and much wetter sea.
amasra.whoFor: Amasra suits someone who wants a genuinely cheap and genuinely quiet Turkish base with a working harbour and a walkable centre, and who is happy to be the only foreigner in the room. It works best as a summer or shoulder-season stay of a few weeks rather than a year, given what winter does to the place. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a nomad community, enterprise-grade internet or English-speaking services. Anyone considering a longer stay should look at Bartin or Safranbolu for the practicalities and keep Amasra for the weekends.

sanliurfa.costOfLiving: Budget around $600 a month as a solo remote worker in Sanliurfa, which is among the cheapest figures anywhere on this site and reflects a large southeastern Turkish city with almost no international demand on its housing. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $150 to $300 depending on the district, and the newer developments away from the old centre are the better value. Food is remarkably cheap and remarkably good, built on the local kebab tradition and the isot pepper that defines it. Turkish inflation moves these numbers constantly, so treat the figure as a working budget. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
sanliurfa.whereToWork: Sanliurfa has no coworking scene aimed at foreigners, though the city is large enough to have business centres and university facilities serving its own economy. Fibre reaches most of the modern districts and Turkish mobile data is fast and cheap, which is the practical answer for most people. English is very limited outside the archaeological tourism around Gobekli Tepe, and Arabic is widely spoken given the city's large Syrian population. Anyone working here should expect to do daily business in Turkish. Power and water are reliable, though summer demand on air conditioning is heavy across the whole region.
sanliurfa.gettingAround: Sanliurfa is a spread-out city of two million and the old centre around Balikligol is the only genuinely walkable part, which is where most visitors spend their time anyway. City buses and dolmus minibuses cover the rest cheaply, and taxis are inexpensive by any standard. Gobekli Tepe is about twenty minutes out by road and needs a taxi or a tour; Karahan Tepe, the newer excavation, is further out and harder to reach. Sanliurfa airport has domestic flights to Istanbul and Ankara. Summer heat makes walking anywhere in the middle of the day genuinely unpleasant from June onwards.
sanliurfa.visas: Turkey gives most Western nationals ninety days in any hundred and eighty, either visa-free or through a quick e-visa. The Digital Nomad Identification Card introduced in 2024 is open to citizens of a defined list of countries who hold a degree and meet a monthly income threshold, and it smooths the short-term residence permit process rather than being a visa in itself. Residence permits have become considerably harder to obtain, with many districts closed to new foreign registration once a quota is reached. Anyone planning to stay past the visa-free window should research the specific district rather than the country as a whole.
sanliurfa.bestTime: March to May and October to November are the only comfortable windows. Sanliurfa sits on the edge of the Mesopotamian plain and summer is severe, regularly above forty degrees through July and August with nights that stay warm, and it shapes everything about how the city runs in those months. Spring brings the plain briefly green and is the best time to see the archaeological sites without suffering for it. Winter is cool and can be wet, with daytime temperatures around ten degrees, and it is a perfectly workable season for anyone who does not mind grey.
sanliurfa.prosCons: Sanliurfa is next door to Gobekli Tepe, the eleven-thousand-year-old site that rewrote the timeline of monumental building, with Karahan Tepe and a dozen related excavations across the same plain. The old city around the Pool of Abraham is one of the most atmospheric places in Turkey, the food is exceptional and the cost of living is extraordinarily low. Against that, it is conservative, very hot, has essentially no international community, and English is rare. The Syrian border is around fifty kilometres away, which is worth understanding in context rather than as an alarm, and government travel advice for the region should be read directly.
sanliurfa.whoFor: Sanliurfa suits someone with a serious interest in archaeology or the ancient Near East, who wants to be near the sites rather than visiting them on a tour, and who can operate in a city that has not adapted itself for outsiders. The cost of living makes a long research stay unusually affordable. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a foreign community, a drink at the end of the day or a liberal social environment. Anyone sensitive to heat should not consider the summer months here at all, whatever else the trip has going for it.

oudtshoorn.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Oudtshoorn, which is inexpensive for South Africa outside the big cities and very cheap by the standards of anywhere with this much English spoken. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $500, and houses with land are within reach at figures that would be impossible on the coast. Groceries are cheap and local produce is excellent, with the Klein Karoo's wine and olive farms nearby. Budget separately for a vehicle and for power backup, both of which are practical necessities here. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
oudtshoorn.whereToWork: Oudtshoorn has no coworking provision to speak of, and remote work happens from homes and a few cafes on the main street. Fibre has reached much of the town and is reasonably priced, and mobile data on the main networks is workable though South African data costs remain high relative to local income. The real planning issue is electricity: load shedding has eased from its worst but has not gone away, and anyone whose work cannot pause needs an inverter and battery or a property that already has one. Most established rentals here now include some form of backup as standard.
oudtshoorn.gettingAround: Oudtshoorn is a small grid town that can be crossed on foot, but everything that makes the region worth being in, the Cango Caves, the Swartberg Pass, the ostrich farms and Route 62, needs a car. Public transport between towns is limited to minibus taxis, which serve a different market. George is about an hour away over the Outeniqua Pass and has the nearest airport with domestic connections to Johannesburg and Cape Town. Cape Town itself is around five hours by road. Driving is on the left and the mountain passes demand attention rather than speed.
oudtshoorn.visas: South Africa introduced a remote work visa in 2024, open to people employed by a foreign company earning above roughly $36,000 a year, initially for up to three years, and the regulations around tax registration for longer stays have been clarified since. Before that, most visitors used the ninety-day visitor visa that many Western nationalities receive on arrival, which remains the simplest option for a short stay and is extendable once. The remote work route is a genuine improvement on what the country offered previously, though processing times through South African missions abroad vary considerably by country.
oudtshoorn.bestTime: September to April covers the warm half, with hot dry summers that push into the mid thirties in January and February. The Klein Karoo is semi-arid and the heat is dry rather than oppressive, which makes it more bearable than the number suggests. Spring, from September to November, is the best combination of comfortable temperatures and green after the winter rain. The KKNK Afrikaans arts festival fills the town for a week each autumn. Winter nights get genuinely cold at this altitude and inland position, dropping close to freezing, and few older houses here are built for it.
oudtshoorn.prosCons: Oudtshoorn sits in the Klein Karoo with the Cango Caves and the Swartberg Pass on its doorstep, one of the most dramatic mountain roads in Africa, and it is the centre of the ostrich industry that gave the town its Victorian feather-boom architecture. Costs are low, English is universal and the air and space are exceptional. Against that, there is no nomad community, load shedding is a real planning constraint, a car is not optional, and South Africa's crime statistics call for the ordinary situational awareness the country demands everywhere. The town is quiet in a way some find restorative and others find limiting.
oudtshoorn.whoFor: Oudtshoorn suits someone who wants space, dry air and dramatic landscape at a low cost, with the whole Garden Route and Route 62 within a day's drive. It works well for anyone with a vehicle and a tolerance for small-town rhythms, and unusually well for people travelling with animals or family given how much house the money buys. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an international community, public transport or a nightlife. Anyone whose work cannot survive an outage should sort out power backup before the first week rather than after it.

ifrane.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Ifrane, which is cheap by any international measure but not by Moroccan ones, since the university and the summer visitors keep local prices above what a town this size would otherwise charge. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $250 to $400, with the chalets near the centre at the top of that and Hay Riad and the outer streets below it. Food is inexpensive and the Middle Atlas produce is good. Heating is a real winter line item here in a way it is nowhere else in Morocco. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
ifrane.whereToWork: Ifrane has no dedicated coworking, but Al Akhawayn University dominates the town and its presence changes what is available: the cafes around the campus are used to people working, English is spoken far more widely than in comparable Moroccan towns, and the general standard of infrastructure is higher. Moroccan fibre reaches the built-up area and mobile data on the main networks is fast and cheap. Power is stable. Anyone needing more than the town can offer has Fes about an hour and a quarter away, which has both coworking and the flight connections Ifrane lacks entirely.
ifrane.gettingAround: Ifrane is small, laid out on a grid of wide streets and completely walkable, which is unusual enough in Morocco to be worth saying. Grand taxis run to Azrou fifteen minutes away and on to Fes and Meknes, and buses cover the same routes for less. The cedar forest with its Barbary macaques starts just outside town and the Michlifen ski area is twenty minutes up the road, both of which are easier with a car. Fes is the nearest airport at around ninety minutes. Winter snow occasionally closes the higher passes, which is a genuine consideration between December and February.
ifrane.visas: Morocco gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, which is generous and simple. There is no digital nomad visa despite periodic announcements, so anyone wanting longer works through the carte de sejour residence card, which requires a local sponsor, a lease or property, and proof of means, and is processed through the local prefecture rather than centrally. A common informal approach is a short exit to Spain or Ceuta and a fresh ninety days on return, though this is tolerance rather than entitlement and border officials have discretion. Anyone planning a year here should start the residence process early.
ifrane.bestTime: May to October is the comfortable window, with warm dry days that rarely feel hot at this altitude and cool evenings that require a layer. July and August are when Moroccans arrive from Fes, Casablanca and Rabat to escape the lowland heat, and the town is at its busiest and most expensive. Winter is the other reason to come: Ifrane sits above 1,600 metres, gets real snow, and holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Africa. Skiing at Michlifen is modest by Alpine standards but genuinely exists, which surprises most visitors.
ifrane.prosCons: Ifrane is unlike anywhere else in Morocco, an alpine town of pitched roofs and cedar forest built by the French in the 1930s, exceptionally clean, cool in summer and snowy in winter, with an English-language American-curriculum university at its centre. Air quality is among the best in the country. Against that, it is small and quiet, there is no nomad community, prices are high relative to the surrounding region, and much of the town's life follows the university calendar and empties in the holidays. Anyone coming to Morocco for medinas and coastline will find none of it here.
ifrane.whoFor: Ifrane suits someone who wants clean mountain air, forest on the doorstep and a genuinely cool summer within reach of Fes, and who is happy in a small, orderly town rather than a Moroccan city. The university connection makes it unusually workable for anyone in academia or education. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a beach, a nightlife or a nomad scene, and anyone arriving in July should expect the domestic holiday crowd. It works best as a summer base or a winter curiosity rather than a year-round home.

djerba.costOfLiving: Budget around $750 a month as a solo remote worker in Djerba, which is low even by Tunisian standards outside the capital and reflects an island whose economy runs on package tourism rather than on residents. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with Houmt Souk and the beach strip at Sidi Mahrez costing more than anywhere inland. Food is very cheap if bought locally, and the island produces its own olives, dates and fish. The dinar is a closed currency, so bring the means to pay for things rather than assuming a card works. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
djerba.whereToWork: Djerba has almost no coworking provision, and remote work happens from apartments, hotel lobbies and the cafes of Houmt Souk. Tunisian fibre reaches the main towns and mobile data is inexpensive with reasonable coverage across the island, though speeds are modest by European standards and evening congestion is noticeable in the resort areas. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. French is the practical second language for anything administrative, with English limited to the tourism trade, so anyone here for a stretch will get further with some French than without it.
djerba.gettingAround: Djerba is flat, about five hundred square kilometres, and connected to the mainland by a Roman causeway that still carries the road, with a ferry at the other end of the island. Houmt Souk, the main town, is walkable, but the beaches, the synagogue at Erriadh and the villages are spread out and need transport. Scooters and rental cars are the usual answer and both are cheap. Louage shared taxis cover the longer routes. Djerba-Zarzis airport handles charter flights from across Europe in season, which is what makes the island unusually easy to reach for its size.
djerba.visas: Tunisia allows most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, which is straightforward and rarely questioned. There is no digital nomad visa. Staying beyond ninety days means either leaving and returning, which is generally tolerated, or applying for a residence permit through the local authorities, a process that requires local sponsorship and patience.
