Anyone overstaying should know that a fine is levied at departure, calculated by the length of the overstay, which is an administrative matter rather than a serious one but is easily avoided. Rules are applied more consistently at the airport than at the land borders.
djerba.bestTime: April to June and September to November are the best months, with warm days, a swimmable sea and none of the summer crowds. July and August are hot, above thirty most days, and the island fills with European package tourists, which pushes prices to their annual peak. Winter is mild by any northern measure, with daytime temperatures around seventeen and very little rain, and it is a genuinely pleasant time to work here even though much of the resort infrastructure closes. The El Ghriba pilgrimage falls in spring and brings a security presence with it.
djerba.prosCons: Djerba is a flat island of whitewashed courtyard houses, palm groves and one of the oldest synagogues in the world at El Ghriba, with a settlement pattern UNESCO listed in 2023 and a street art project at Erriadh that brought artists from thirty countries to paint the village. It is cheap, warm and easy to reach from Europe. Against that, the island is dominated by all-inclusive resorts that keep their guests inside, there is no nomad community, English is thin, and anything beyond the tourist economy runs slowly. It is a place to be quiet in rather than to network.
djerba.whoFor: Djerba suits someone who wants Mediterranean warmth, very low costs and a short flight back to Europe, and who is content with their own company. It works particularly well in the shoulder seasons, when the weather holds and the resorts have emptied. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a professional community, fast reliable internet or a city. Anyone with French will find the island far easier to live in than anyone without. It rewards a month or two rather than a year, unless the appeal is precisely how little happens.

nanyuki.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Nanyuki, which buys considerably more here than the same figure does in Nairobi. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, and houses with gardens are within reach at figures that would be impossible in the capital, which is why the town has attracted a long-standing settler and expatriate farming community. Food is cheap and the produce from the Mount Kenya slopes is excellent. Budget separately for a vehicle and for a backup power arrangement. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
nanyuki.whereToWork: Nanyuki has a small but real coworking presence, unusual for a Kenyan town this size, driven by the conservation organisations, the tourism operators and the resident expatriate community rather than by nomads. Fibre has reached parts of the town and Safaricom's mobile data is the reliable fallback almost everywhere, with 4G across the built-up area. Power cuts happen and anyone whose work cannot pause should assume an inverter or a generator. English is an official language and universally spoken, which removes the friction that a comparable town elsewhere in the region would carry. Nairobi is four hours by road.
nanyuki.gettingAround: Nanyuki is a small town straddling the equator at around 1,950 metres, and the centre is walkable while everything that draws people here is not. Ol Pejeta and Lewa conservancies, the Mount Kenya trailheads and the surrounding farms all need a vehicle, and most residents have one. Matatu minibuses and boda boda motorcycle taxis cover local trips cheaply. The road to Nairobi takes around four hours and is in reasonable condition. Nanyuki has an airstrip with light aircraft connections to Nairobi and the northern conservancies, which is how most safari traffic arrives.
nanyuki.visas: Kenya replaced its visa system with an Electronic Travel Authorisation in January 2024, required of almost all arrivals and granting stays of up to ninety days. In late 2024 the government announced a digital nomad work permit for remote workers employed outside Kenya, with an income threshold reported at around $55,000 a year and an initial validity of one year. Implementation details have moved since the announcement, so confirm the current requirements with a Kenyan mission rather than relying on secondary reporting. The older route, a class of work permit tied to an employer or a business, remains available and remains slow.
nanyuki.bestTime: Nanyuki sits high enough that the equator does not translate into heat, with daytime temperatures around the low twenties year-round and nights that get genuinely cold. The dry seasons, January to March and July to October, are the best for the mountain and the conservancies, and July to October is when Mount Kenya climbing is most reliable. The long rains from late March into May and the short rains in November bring afternoon storms rather than continuous wet, and the landscape is at its greenest immediately after. There is no bad season here, only a muddier one.
nanyuki.prosCons: Nanyuki sits on the equator at the foot of Mount Kenya, with Ol Pejeta and Lewa conservancies on the doorstep and some of the best air and light in East Africa. English is universal, costs are low, and there is a long-established resident community with the services that come with it. Against that, it is a small town with limited professional depth, internet reliability depends on the arrangement rather than the address, power cuts are routine, and a vehicle is not optional. The wider region's security situation varies by area, so travel advice north of the town should be read directly.
nanyuki.whoFor: Nanyuki suits someone who wants mountains, wildlife and a temperate climate at low cost with English spoken everywhere, and who is set up to work through occasional outages. It is unusually good for anyone in conservation, agriculture or field research, where the local network is genuinely deep. It works well for families given the space and the schools the expatriate community supports. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a city, a nightlife or a nomad scene, and anyone without a vehicle will find the surrounding landscape effectively out of reach.

lome.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Lome, which is low for a West African capital and reflects a city that has never had the oil or mining money that inflated some of its neighbours. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with the beachfront and the diplomatic quarter well above that and the inland neighbourhoods well below. Street food is very cheap and the markets are excellent. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes the currency volatility that complicates budgets elsewhere in the region. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
lome.whereToWork: Lome has a small startup and coworking scene, concentrated in a handful of spaces serving the city's technology and logistics sectors, and it is more developed than the country's size would suggest thanks to the port. Fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data on the main networks is workable, though West African internet pricing remains high relative to speed and evening congestion is real. Power cuts happen and most serious workplaces have a generator. French is the working language of everything administrative and English is limited, so operating here without French is genuinely difficult.
lome.gettingAround: Lome runs along the Gulf of Guinea coast with the Ghanaian border at its western edge, close enough that the frontier is effectively part of the city. Zemidjan motorcycle taxis are the dominant way to move and cost very little, though they demand a helmet and some nerve. Shared taxis cover the longer routes. The coastal road is the main axis and the Grand Marche sits at the centre of everything. Lome airport is a regional hub with connections across West Africa and to Europe, which makes the city considerably easier to reach than its profile suggests.
lome.visas: Togo offers an eVisa and visa on arrival at Lome airport for most nationalities, typically for stays of seven to thirty days and extendable at the immigration office in the city, which is the normal route rather than an exception. There is no digital nomad visa. Anyone planning a longer stay applies for a residence permit locally, a process that requires documentation, patience and generally some French. Togo is part of ECOWAS, so overland travel to Ghana, Benin and beyond is straightforward for citizens of the bloc and requires separate consideration for everyone else. Yellow fever vaccination is required on entry.
lome.bestTime: November to February is the dry season and the best time to be here, with less humidity than the rest of the year and daytime temperatures around thirty. The harmattan can bring dust down from the Sahara in December and January, which drops visibility and irritates anyone with a respiratory sensitivity. The long rains run from April to July and the short rains return in September and October, both bringing heavy downpours rather than continuous grey. Coastal humidity is a constant regardless of season and is the thing most arrivals underestimate about the climate here.
lome.prosCons: Lome is a genuinely underrated West African capital, with a long beach through the middle of the city, the vast Grand Marche, the Akodessewa fetish market that is unlike anything else on the continent, and an airport that connects across the region and to Europe. Costs are low and the port gives the city a commercial energy. Against that, there is no nomad community whatsoever, French is close to mandatory, power and internet are both unreliable, and the city demands more situational awareness than most places on this site. It is a place for the experienced rather than the first trip.
lome.whoFor: Lome suits someone who already works in West Africa or wants to, speaks French, and values a low-cost coastal capital with excellent regional flight connections. It works well as a base for anyone covering the region rather than as a destination in itself. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs reliable infrastructure, an English-speaking environment or any kind of nomad community, none of which exist here in usable form. Anyone new to the region would be better served starting in Accra, two hours west, and coming to Lome from there.

tofo.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Tofo, which is low for the diving it buys but not as low as the surrounding country, since everything on this beach is priced for visitors. A room or a simple one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450 depending on how close it sits to the sand and whether it is high season. Food is cheap if bought at the market in Inhambane and considerably less so at the beach restaurants. Diving is the real budget line here. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
tofo.whereToWork: Tofo has no coworking and its internet is the honest weak point of the place, which is why the connectivity score here is low rather than average. Mobile data on Vodacom or Tmcel is the primary connection for most people and speeds vary by hour and by weather. Fixed lines exist in a few of the better guesthouses and lodges. Power cuts are routine and most established places run on an inverter or a generator. Anyone whose work involves video calls should test thoroughly before committing to a month, and anyone who cannot tolerate an outage should look elsewhere on this coast.
tofo.gettingAround: Tofo is a beach village and everything in it is within a fifteen-minute walk, which is a large part of why people stay longer than they planned. Inhambane, the provincial town with the market, the bank and the ferry, is about twenty-five minutes inland by chapa minibus or taxi. Inhambane airport has flights to Maputo and Johannesburg, which is the practical way in. The road from Maputo takes seven or eight hours by bus. Sand tracks lead to the quieter beaches at Barra and Tofinho, and a four-wheel drive or a walk are the only ways along them.
tofo.visas: Mozambique removed visa requirements in 2023 for citizens of a long list of countries including most of Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia, allowing visits of up to thirty days, which transformed the practicality of getting here. Everyone else can obtain a visa on arrival at the main entry points or apply in advance. Extensions are handled at immigration offices in the provincial capitals, meaning Inhambane rather than the beach. There is no digital nomad visa. The policy shift was recent enough that some airlines and border posts have been slower than the rules, so carry the documentation anyway.
tofo.bestTime: Tofo works year-round, which is unusual, because the whale sharks and manta rays that draw divers here are resident rather than seasonal. April to September is the dry half, cooler and clearer, with humpback whales passing through between roughly June and October and the best visibility for diving. October to March is hotter and wetter, with the warmest water and the highest chance of a cyclone, most likely between January and March. The Mozambique Channel has produced serious storms in recent years, and anyone booking in that window should follow the forecasts.
tofo.prosCons: Tofo is one of the few places on earth where whale sharks and giant manta rays are present all year, on a wide arc of beach with a diving community that has been here for decades and a research presence studying both species. It is warm, cheap by the standards of what it offers, and small enough to know within a week. Against that, the internet is genuinely poor, power cuts are routine, medical facilities are limited and the nearest real hospital is a long way off, and the village has almost nothing beyond diving and the beach.
tofo.whoFor: Tofo suits a diver first and a remote worker second. Anyone whose work tolerates an unreliable connection and who wants to be in the water most days will find few better places at this price. It works well for a month or a season rather than a year. It is a poor fit for anyone with a demanding call schedule, anyone who needs medical infrastructure nearby, or anyone looking for a professional community; there is none. Bring a local SIM, a power bank and a tolerance for things happening slowly, and it repays all three.

boise.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Boise, which no longer makes it the bargain it was before 2020, when a wave of arrivals from the west coast reset the housing market permanently. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $1,100 to $1,500, with the North End and downtown at the top and the Bench and Garden City cheaper. Idaho has no local sales tax surprises beyond the state rate and utilities are reasonable. Health insurance is the line item that dominates any American budget and sits outside this figure. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
boise.whereToWork: Boise has a real coworking market for a city its size, built on a technology sector anchored by Micron and a startup scene that grew through the last decade. Desks run from roughly $200 a month. Fibre reaches most of the city at competitive American prices and mobile coverage is comprehensive. The professional network here is genuine rather than nominal, which distinguishes Boise from most of the smaller American cities on this site, and the state capital and university both add layers to it. Remote workers are common enough that no one finds the arrangement unusual.
boise.gettingAround: Boise is flat where it matters and the downtown grid is walkable, though the city sprawls into the valley beyond it and most residents drive. The Boise River Greenbelt runs about forty kilometres along the water and is the spine of the city for cycling and walking, which is the single best thing about moving around here. Valley Regional Transit buses cover the main corridors and little else. The Ridge to Rivers trail network starts at the edge of the foothills within reach of downtown. Boise airport is fifteen minutes out with direct flights across the western United States.
boise.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa and no intention of creating one. Most Western nationals enter under the Visa Waiver Programme with an ESTA, which allows ninety days per visit for tourism or business meetings but explicitly not productive work, and remote work for a foreign employer sits in a grey area that the government has never resolved and border officers judge individually. The B1 and B2 visitor visas allow up to six months for those who need them. Anything longer requires a work visa tied to an employer, an investor category or family sponsorship, none of which is quick.
boise.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, with warm dry days and cool nights that suit the trails and the river. Summer from July into August is hot and dry, regularly above thirty-five degrees, and wildfire smoke from the wider region has become a recurring feature of late summer that visibly affects air quality for days at a time. Winter is cold but not severe by northern American standards, with daytime temperatures around freezing and enough snow for Bogus Basin thirty minutes up the mountain, which is the reason many people here tolerate January.
boise.prosCons: Boise gives outdoor access that few American cities can match, with a forty-kilometre riverside greenbelt through the middle, foothill trails from the edge of downtown, a ski area half an hour away and whitewater within reach. It has a genuine technology employment base, a walkable centre and the largest Basque community in the United States with the food and festival culture to show for it. Against that, costs have risen sharply, the summer brings heat and wildfire smoke, and the city is a long way from anywhere, with Salt Lake City and Portland both a serious drive.
boise.whoFor: Boise suits an American remote worker who wants trails, river and a real professional network without a coastal price, and who is happy to drive for anything the city cannot supply itself. It is unusually good for anyone who skis, rides or paddles, since all three are within thirty minutes. It is a poor fit for anyone without the right to work in the United States, given how little the visa system offers, and for anyone who needs a large international community. Late-summer arrivals should know what the smoke season does to the air here.

spokane.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Spokane, which is one of the cheaper mid-sized cities in the American west and roughly half what the same life costs in Seattle. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $900 to $1,300, with downtown and the South Hill at the top of that and the north side and Spokane Valley below it. Washington has no state income tax, which is a meaningful difference for anyone earning here rather than abroad. Health insurance sits outside this figure and dominates any American budget. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
spokane.whereToWork: Spokane has a modest coworking market serving a healthcare, education and aerospace economy, with desks from roughly $150 a month and several spaces clustered downtown. Gonzaga University and the medical school give the city a professional layer beyond its size. Fibre is widely available at ordinary American prices and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the valley. Seattle is about an hour by air or four and a half hours by road, which is how most people here handle anything the local network cannot supply. Remote work is common enough in the city that it needs no explanation.
spokane.gettingAround: Spokane is built around a river gorge with waterfalls running through the middle of downtown, which makes the centre unusually walkable for an American city of this size. Riverfront Park sits at the heart of it and the Centennial Trail runs sixty kilometres along the river towards Idaho, which is the best cycling here by a distance. The bus network covers the main corridors adequately and little else, so most residents drive. Spokane airport is fifteen minutes from downtown with direct flights across the west. Coeur d'Alene and its lake are forty minutes east over the state line.
spokane.visas: The United States offers no digital nomad visa. Most Western nationals enter under the Visa Waiver Programme with an ESTA, which permits ninety days for tourism or business meetings but not productive work, and remote work for a foreign employer occupies a grey area that has never been formally resolved and is judged individually at the border. B1 and B2 visitor visas allow up to six months for nationalities outside the waiver programme. Anything longer requires employer sponsorship, an investor category or family, and none of those routes is quick or cheap.
spokane.bestTime: June, September and early October are the best months, with warm dry days, cool nights and the river at its most usable. July and August are hot and dry, often above thirty-two degrees, and wildfire smoke from the interior northwest has become a regular feature of late summer that can hold air quality down for a week at a time. Winter is cold and grey with real snow, daytime temperatures around freezing, and three ski areas within an hour and a half including Mount Spokane and Schweitzer over in Idaho. Spring comes late and wet.
spokane.prosCons: Spokane has a waterfall in the middle of downtown, sixty kilometres of riverside trail, three ski areas within ninety minutes and lakes across the Idaho border, all at costs that make Seattle look absurd. Hoopfest and Bloomsday give the city two of the largest events of their kind anywhere. Against that, there is no international community to speak of, the summer smoke season is a genuine health consideration, winters are long and grey, and the city is isolated enough that most trips involve a flight. The professional network is real but shallow outside healthcare and education.
spokane.whoFor: Spokane suits an American remote worker who wants outdoor access and a walkable downtown at a price the coast cannot match, and who does not mind a real winter. It is unusually good for anyone who skis, since three areas sit within easy reach and none of them carries resort pricing. It is a poor fit for anyone without the right to work in the United States, and for anyone who needs an international scene or a deep professional network. Anyone with a respiratory condition should look closely at what late summer does to the air here.

burlington.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Burlington, which is expensive for a city of forty-five thousand people and reflects a tight housing market squeezed by the university and by very limited new construction. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $1,300 to $1,700, and finding one at all is harder than affording one, particularly around the start of the academic year. Vermont's grocery prices run above the national average. Health insurance sits outside this figure as it does everywhere in the country. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
burlington.whereToWork: Burlington has a coworking scene disproportionate to its size, built on a startup community, the University of Vermont and a long-standing culture of small independent business. Desks run from roughly $200 a month and several spaces sit within walking distance of Church Street. Burlington Electric has run the city on entirely renewable sources since 2014, which is a genuine distinction rather than a marketing line, and the grid is reliable. Fibre is available across most of the city. Montreal is under two hours by road for anything the local network cannot supply.
burlington.gettingAround: Burlington is small enough to cross on foot, with the Church Street Marketplace as a genuine pedestrian centre rather than a token block, and the lakefront a few minutes downhill from it. The Island Line Trail runs north along Lake Champlain on an old causeway, with a seasonal bike ferry across the gap, and is one of the best rides in the northeast. Green Mountain Transit covers the county. Burlington airport is fifteen minutes out with connections through the eastern hubs. Stowe and Sugarbush are both under an hour, and Montreal is a straightforward drive north.
burlington.visas: The United States has no digital nomad visa. Visa Waiver Programme nationals enter with an ESTA for up to ninety days, which permits tourism and business meetings but not productive work, and remote employment for a foreign company sits in the unresolved grey area that American immigration policy has never addressed. Longer visits run on B1 or B2 visitor visas of up to six months. Anything beyond that requires an employer-sponsored category, an investor route or family sponsorship. The Canadian border is forty-five minutes away, which is convenient but is not a reset mechanism for status.
burlington.bestTime: September and early October are the reason people come, with clear cool days and foliage across the Green Mountains that draws visitors from across the country. Summer from June to August is warm, humid and the best time for the lake, and the city is at its most alive. Winter is long and genuinely cold, with January averages below freezing and heavy snow, which is excellent for the ski areas and hard on anyone unprepared for four months of it. Spring is the mud season locals warn about, wet and unattractive, and April is the month to skip.
burlington.prosCons: Burlington is a small city with the amenities of a much larger one: a real pedestrian centre, a lake with the Adirondacks on the far shore, a startup and food culture well beyond its size, and an electricity supply that has been fully renewable for over a decade. Skiing is under an hour and Montreal under two. Against that, it is expensive for what it is, housing is genuinely scarce, the winter is long, and the city is small enough that anyone looking for scale will exhaust it. There is no meaningful international community.
burlington.whoFor: Burlington suits an American remote worker who wants a walkable small city with mountains, a lake and a strong independent culture, and who actively likes winter rather than tolerating it. It works well for anyone in food, outdoor industry or climate work, where the local network is unusually deep. It is a poor fit for anyone without United States work rights, anyone who needs a large city, and anyone arriving in late August, when the student housing rush makes finding a place close to impossible. Anyone weighing it against Portland, Maine should note that Burlington trades the ocean for the mountains and gets closer to Montreal in the bargain.

nanaimo.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Nanaimo, which is meaningfully cheaper than Victoria and dramatically cheaper than Vancouver while sitting on the same coast. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $1,100 to $1,500, with the harbour and the north end at the top of that range. British Columbia's grocery and fuel prices are high by North American standards. The saving against the mainland is the entire reason the city has grown, and it has been narrowing steadily. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
nanaimo.whereToWork: Nanaimo has a small coworking presence serving a local economy of healthcare, education, forestry and the growing population of people who left Vancouver. Vancouver Island University keeps a professional layer in the city. Fibre is widely available at Canadian prices, which are high, and mobile coverage is good in the built-up area and patchy once the island road heads inland. The float plane to downtown Vancouver takes about twenty minutes, which makes a meeting on the mainland a morning rather than a day and is the single most useful piece of infrastructure here.
nanaimo.gettingAround: Nanaimo is strung along the coast and the downtown core near the harbour is walkable, but the city sprawls north and south along the highway and most residents drive. Two ferry routes cross to the mainland, at Departure Bay and Duke Point, taking around two hours to Horseshoe Bay and Tsawwassen respectively. Float planes and a passenger ferry serve downtown Vancouver directly. Victoria is ninety minutes south by road and Tofino around three hours west across the island. Saysutshun, the island in the harbour, is a ten-minute foot passenger ferry and a good afternoon.
nanaimo.visas: Canada has no digital nomad visa, but its 2023 tech talent strategy confirmed what had been ambiguous: visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer during a standard visitor stay, normally up to six months. That is the practical route for most people and it requires only an eTA for visa-exempt nationalities. The International Experience Canada working holiday covers under-thirties or under-thirty-fives depending on country and gives full work rights for one or two years. Permanent routes run through Express Entry and the provincial nominee programmes, both of which are competitive and slow.
nanaimo.bestTime: May to September is the dry half and the reason people put up with the rest, with warm days rarely above twenty-five, long light evenings and the water at its most usable. July and August are the busiest and the driest. October to April is the wet season, and the total rainfall is the defining fact of life on this coast: not cold, rarely below freezing, but grey and wet for weeks. The island's east coast, where Nanaimo sits, is considerably drier than the west, which is a difference worth understanding before choosing a town.
nanaimo.prosCons: Nanaimo gives access to Vancouver Island at a price the island's better-known towns no longer offer, with a working harbour, a twenty-minute float plane to downtown Vancouver, forest and coast in every direction and Tofino across the island. English is universal and the city is safe and easy. Against that, the winter is relentlessly grey and wet, there is essentially no nomad community, the city itself is functional rather than beautiful outside the harbour, and Canadian internet and grocery costs are high. Everything beyond the island involves a ferry or a flight.
nanaimo.whoFor: Nanaimo suits someone with Canadian work rights or a working holiday who wants the Pacific northwest coast without Vancouver's housing market, and who is set up for a wet winter. It works well for anyone who paddles, hikes or rides, with all three immediately accessible. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an international community, a nightlife or a dense professional network, all of which mean Vancouver. Anyone weighing it against Victoria should visit both, since the price gap has narrowed and the character of the two is not the same.

stjohns.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in St John's, which is the cheapest provincial capital in Canada and a real saving against anywhere on the mainland's populated coasts. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $900 to $1,300, and the colourful row houses downtown that appear in every photograph are within reach rather than aspirational. Groceries cost more than the Canadian average because everything arrives by ship or plane, which is the permanent condition of an island economy. Heating is a serious winter line item. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
stjohns.whereToWork: St John's has a small but real coworking and startup scene, built on an ocean technology sector, Memorial University and the offshore energy industry that shaped the city's last forty years. Fibre reaches most of the city at Canadian prices and mobile coverage is good in the built-up area. The time zone is the practical quirk: Newfoundland runs half an hour ahead of Atlantic time, which puts the city three and a half hours ahead of the American west coast and closer to European hours than anywhere else in North America, an advantage for anyone working with Europe.
stjohns.gettingAround: St John's is built on steep hills around a narrow harbour, and downtown is walkable if the gradients are acceptable; Signal Hill above the harbour entrance is a climb rather than a stroll. Metrobus covers the city adequately and most residents drive. The East Coast Trail runs for over three hundred kilometres along the coast south and north of the city, starting close enough to reach on a bus, and is the best thing about being here. St John's airport is fifteen minutes out with connections through the Canadian hubs and seasonal transatlantic service.
stjohns.visas: Canada has no digital nomad visa. The 2023 tech talent strategy clarified that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer during a normal visitor stay of up to six months, which is the route most people use and requires only an eTA for visa-exempt nationalities. The International Experience Canada working holiday covers a defined list of countries and age ranges with full work rights. Newfoundland and Labrador runs its own provincial nominee stream and has actively recruited remote workers and skilled migrants, which makes it a more realistic permanent route than the competition elsewhere in the country.
stjohns.bestTime: June to September is the season and it is short, with daytime temperatures rarely above twenty, long evenings and the whales and puffins offshore. Icebergs drift down what locals call Iceberg Alley between roughly April and June, which is the single best reason to time a visit. Fog is a defining feature and St John's is among the foggiest cities in Canada. Winter runs long, wet and windy rather than deeply cold, with heavy snow and the occasional storm that closes everything for a day. Anyone considering a year should visit in February first.
stjohns.prosCons: St John's is the oldest European-founded city in North America, built in tiers of painted houses around a harbour with the open Atlantic beyond it, three hundred kilometres of coastal trail, icebergs in spring, and a music and pub culture that punches far above the city's size. It is the cheapest provincial capital in the country and its time zone suits European work. Against that, the weather is genuinely hard, the fog and wind are constant, the island is remote and flights are expensive, and there is no international nomad presence at all.
stjohns.whoFor: St John's suits someone who wants a small, characterful, walkable city on the edge of the Atlantic and who is genuinely unbothered by weather, which is not a small requirement here. The time zone makes it unusually good for anyone working European hours from North America. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs sunshine, a large professional network or cheap flights. Anyone with Canadian ambitions should look at the provincial nominee stream, which has been more open to remote workers than most of its counterparts. It also suits anyone drawn to the music, since the traditional scene here is a living one rather than a heritage performance put on for visitors.

manta.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Manta, and the useful thing about Ecuador is that the figure needs no conversion, since the country has used the United States dollar as its currency since 2000. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with the Murcielago beachfront and Barbasquillo at the top of that and the inland neighbourhoods well below. Fish is exceptional and cheap in a city built on the tuna fleet. Imported goods carry a premium. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
manta.whereToWork: Manta has a small coworking presence, mostly serving the port, the fishing and canning industry and the local university rather than visitors. Fibre has reached the better neighbourhoods and mobile data is inexpensive with reasonable coverage, though speeds and reliability both sit below what a nomad would expect from the larger Latin American cities. Power is generally stable, but Ecuador has had scheduled outages during drought years when the hydroelectric system runs short, which is a real planning consideration. Spanish is essential; English is limited outside the university and a few businesses.
manta.gettingAround: Manta runs along the coast and the Malecon and the Murcielago beach form the walkable spine of it, with the port and the fish market at one end. City buses are cheap and cover the rest, and taxis are inexpensive. Montecristi, where the hats the world calls Panamas are actually woven, is twenty minutes inland and worth the trip. Manta has its own airport with domestic connections to Quito and Guayaquil, the latter about three hours away by road. The coastal route north towards Canoa and Pedernales is the way to the quieter beaches.
manta.visas: Ecuador gives most nationalities ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable to a hundred and eighty within a twelve-month period, which is generous by regional standards. The country also has a remote work visa introduced in 2022 for people employed or contracted outside Ecuador, requiring proof of a monthly income of around three times the national basic salary and granting two years with a path to renewal. The application runs through a consulate abroad or through the foreign ministry locally. Documentation requirements are specific and apostilles are involved, so allow considerably more time than the process appears to need.
manta.bestTime: December to May is the warm and wetter half, with hot humid days, the best sea temperatures and short heavy afternoon showers that pass quickly. June to November is drier and noticeably cooler, with grey overcast mornings that locals call garua and highs around twenty-five, and it is the more comfortable half for working even if it is the less attractive one for the beach. Humpback whales pass the coast between roughly June and September and are visible on day trips from the port, which is the strongest single reason to time a visit.
manta.prosCons: Manta is a working port city with a long city beach, Ecuador's tuna fleet, whale watching in season and prices that make it one of the cheapest coastal places in the Americas, all denominated in dollars. Montecristi and the quieter beaches to the north are close. Against that, this is an industrial city rather than a resort, the 2016 earthquake did serious damage to the region and its effects are still visible, Spanish is essential, and Ecuador's security situation has deteriorated in recent years, particularly in the coastal provinces. Read current government travel advice directly.
manta.whoFor: Manta suits a Spanish speaker who wants a genuinely inexpensive dollar-denominated coastal base with a real city behind the beach rather than a resort strip. It works well for anyone drawn to the ocean and to a place that is not organised around visitors. It is a poor fit for anyone without Spanish, anyone who needs strong infrastructure, and anyone uncomfortable with the security picture on this coast, which is materially different from what it was a decade ago and should be researched rather than assumed. It also suits anyone weighing a longer stay under the remote work visa, since two years in a dollar economy at these prices is a rare combination.

belem.costOfLiving: Budget around $850 a month as a solo remote worker in Belem, which is low for a Brazilian state capital of two million people and reflects a city that sits a long way from the country's economic centre. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with Nazare and Umarizal at the top of that and the outer bairros well below it. Food is the bargain here, with the market at Ver-o-Peso supplying produce from across the Amazon basin at prices that make eating well trivially cheap. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
belem.whereToWork: Belem has a coworking scene appropriate to a capital of its size, concentrated in the newer commercial districts and around the federal university, and it grew considerably in the run-up to the thirtieth United Nations climate conference the city hosted in November 2025, which brought infrastructure investment the region had been waiting decades for. Fibre reaches the central neighbourhoods and Brazilian mobile data is cheap and fast. Power cuts happen in the heavy rain season. Portuguese is essential; English is rare outside the university and the hotel trade. Anyone working European hours will find the city sits three or four hours behind depending on the season, which is a workable overlap.
belem.gettingAround: Belem sits where the Amazon meets the Atlantic and its historic core around Ver-o-Peso, the Estacao das Docas and the Theatro da Paz is walkable, shaded by the mango trees that give the city its nickname. Buses cover the rest and are cheap, and ride-hailing is widely used and the safer default at night. Boats leave the docks for Ilha do Marajo, the river island larger than Switzerland, and for the smaller communities upriver, which is the reason many people come. Belem airport has domestic connections and a small number of international routes.
belem.visas: Brazil launched a digital nomad visa in January 2022, open to remote workers employed or contracted outside the country who can show around $1,500 a month in income or $18,000 in savings, valid for a year and renewable for a second. It is one of the more accessible schemes in the region. Note that Brazil reinstated visitor visa requirements for citizens of the United States, Canada and Australia in April 2025 through an eVisa system, reversing the previous waiver, so travellers from those countries should not rely on older guidance about arriving visa-free.
belem.bestTime: Belem is equatorial and hot all year, with daytime temperatures around thirty-two and humidity that never really drops. The practical division is between the wetter months from December to May and the drier ones from June to November, though drier here means the afternoon rain is less certain rather than absent. The famous local habit of setting appointments around the daily downpour is real. The Cirio de Nazare procession in October is one of the largest religious gatherings on earth and fills the city entirely, which is either the best or worst time to arrive.
belem.prosCons: Belem is the gateway to the Amazon, with Ver-o-Peso, the largest open-air market in Latin America, a Belle Epoque centre built on the rubber boom, the best food in northern Brazil and a river system that starts at the docks. Hosting the thirtieth United Nations climate conference in 2025 brought the city visibility and infrastructure it had long lacked. Against that, the heat and humidity are unrelenting, English is rare, the safety picture requires real attention and is worse than the southern Brazilian cities, and there is no nomad community at all. The river itself is the compensation for all of it, since almost nowhere else puts the Amazon at the end of a city street.
belem.whoFor: Belem suits a Portuguese speaker with a serious interest in the Amazon, its food or its music, who wants a large Brazilian city that almost no foreign remote worker has considered. The cost of living and the quality of the eating make it exceptional value. It is a poor fit for anyone without Portuguese, anyone sensitive to heat and humidity, and anyone who needs a foreign community. Anyone coming should read current safety guidance for the city rather than generalising from Rio or Sao Paulo, since the conditions are not the same.

bucaramanga.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Bucaramanga, which is cheaper than Medellin and considerably cheaper than Bogota for a city with much the same climate advantages. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $250 to $450, with Cabecera and the newer developments in Floridablanca at the top of that range and the areas north of the centre well below it. Food is inexpensive and Santander's cooking is among the more distinctive in the country. The metro area spreads across four municipalities, so the neighbourhood matters more than the city average. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
bucaramanga.whereToWork: Bucaramanga has a small coworking market serving a local economy of health services, engineering and the oil sector in the wider department, with desks from roughly $80 a month. The Universidad Industrial de Santander gives the city a technical base that shows in the workforce. Fibre is widely available in the newer neighbourhoods at low prices and Colombian mobile data is cheap with good 4G coverage. Power is reliable. Spanish is essential, with English limited to the university and a handful of businesses, which is the main practical difference from Medellin.
bucaramanga.gettingAround: Bucaramanga sits on a plateau at around a thousand metres with the metro area spilling down the slopes into Floridablanca, Giron and Piedecuesta, which makes it larger on the ground than it appears. The Metrolinea bus rapid transit runs the main corridors and city buses cover the rest cheaply. Ride-hailing is widely used. Giron, a preserved colonial town, is fifteen minutes away and worth choosing as a base. Palonegro airport sits on a plateau across the canyon about forty minutes out. San Gil and Barichara are two hours south on a spectacular road.
bucaramanga.visas: Colombia gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once to a hundred and eighty days within a calendar year, which is straightforward and widely used. The country also introduced a dedicated digital nomad visa in late 2022, open to remote workers and freelancers employed outside Colombia who can show a monthly income of around three times the local minimum wage, valid for up to two years. The application is handled online through the foreign ministry and is one of the more accessible schemes in the region. Health insurance covering the full stay is required.
bucaramanga.bestTime: Bucaramanga is called the city of eternal spring by people who have not been to the other four cities that claim the title, and the climate genuinely is steady, sitting around twenty-three degrees most of the year with little seasonal variation. The distinction that matters is rain: April to May and October to November are the wetter months, with heavy afternoon storms, while December to March and July to August are drier and better for the paragliding and the canyon. Nothing about the calendar makes a month unworkable here, which is much of the appeal.
bucaramanga.prosCons: Bucaramanga has a climate that barely moves, more parks than a city its size has any right to, and the Chicamocha canyon half an hour away with a cable car crossing it and some of the best paragliding in South America off the Ruitoque mesa. It costs less than Medellin and has a strong university culture. Against that, there is almost no international community, English is rare, the city is functional rather than beautiful outside the parks, and Colombia requires the ordinary urban caution that the country's reputation still earns in places.
bucaramanga.whoFor: Bucaramanga suits a Spanish speaker who wants Medellin's climate at a lower price and without the crowd of foreign remote workers that has changed Medellin's character and its rents. It is exceptional for anyone who paraglides or climbs, with the canyon and San Gil both close. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an English-speaking environment or an established nomad scene, neither of which exists here. Anyone using the digital nomad visa will find the paperwork easier than the flight connections, which mostly route through Bogota. It also suits anyone wanting a Colombian base that has not been reshaped by foreign demand, which is increasingly hard to find in the better-known cities.

campogrande.costOfLiving: Budget around $850 a month as a solo remote worker in Campo Grande, which is inexpensive for a Brazilian state capital and reflects a city in the centre of the country rather than on the coast. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with the areas around Afonso Pena and the Parque dos Poderes at the upper end. Beef is exceptional and cheap here, which follows from the cattle economy the whole state runs on. Fuel and internal flights are the two lines that cost more than the coast. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
campogrande.whereToWork: Campo Grande has a modest coworking market serving agribusiness, logistics and a growing services sector, with desks at low prices by any international measure. The federal university and the state government both keep professional depth in the city. Fibre reaches most of the central neighbourhoods and Brazilian mobile data is cheap and fast, with good 4G and increasing 5G coverage. Power is reliable. Portuguese is essential and English is rare outside the university, which is the usual position in Brazilian cities away from the tourist coast. Anyone working with Europe should note the city sits five hours behind central European time, which makes a morning here a late afternoon there.
campogrande.gettingAround: Campo Grande is laid out on a wide grid with Avenida Afonso Pena running through the middle as one of the broadest urban avenues in the country, tree-lined and genuinely pleasant to walk. The city is flat and cycling works, though most residents drive. Buses cover the metro area and ride-hailing is cheap and widely used. The Parque das Nacoes Indigenas is one of the largest urban parks anywhere and sits inside the city. The airport has domestic connections, and the Pantanal, Bonito and the Bolivian border all lie a long drive west.
campogrande.visas: Brazil introduced a digital nomad visa in January 2022 for remote workers employed or contracted abroad, requiring proof of around $1,500 a month in income or $18,000 in savings, valid a year and renewable once. It is among the more accessible schemes anywhere. Travellers from the United States, Canada and Australia should note that Brazil reinstated visitor visa requirements for those three nationalities in April 2025 through an eVisa system, reversing an earlier waiver, so any guidance written before that date is out of step with the current rules. Anyone applying from within Brazil should expect the federal police appointment system to be the slow part of the process rather than the paperwork itself.
campogrande.bestTime: April to September is the dry season and the better half for anything outdoors, with warm days, cool nights and the Pantanal at its most accessible as the floodwaters recede and the wildlife concentrates around what water remains. July can be genuinely cold at night by Brazilian standards. October to March is the wet season, hot and humid with heavy afternoon storms, and the Pantanal floods, which changes the region from a wildlife destination into a waterscape. The city itself is workable year-round; the region around it is not. Anyone here specifically for wildlife should plan the Pantanal trip for July or August, when the animals are most concentrated and the tracks are passable.
campogrande.prosCons: Campo Grande is the gateway to the Pantanal, the largest tropical wetland on earth, with Bonito's crystal rivers a few hours southwest and one of the world's biggest freshwater aquariums in the city itself. There is a substantial Okinawan community whose soba at the central market is a genuinely local dish found nowhere else in Brazil. Against that, the city is a long way from anywhere, there is no international community, English is rare, and the summer heat and humidity are heavy. It is a base for the region rather than a destination.
campogrande.whoFor: Campo Grande suits a Portuguese speaker who wants a cheap, functional and safe Brazilian city as a base for the Pantanal and Bonito, and who values space and low costs over coastline. It works well for anyone in agriculture, conservation or wildlife work, where the regional network is deep. It is a poor fit for anyone without Portuguese, anyone who needs a beach or a foreign community, and anyone whose plans depend on cheap international flights, since almost everything routes through Sao Paulo first. It also suits anyone travelling overland between Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay, since the city is the natural stop on that route and has the connections to prove it.

hakodate.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Hakodate, which is low for Japan and reflects a regional city that has been losing population for decades rather than gaining it. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $400 to $650, which is a fraction of Tokyo for considerably more space. Food is the bargain: this is a fishing port and the seafood at the morning market costs a fraction of what the same thing does further south. Heating through a Hokkaido winter is a serious line item. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
hakodate.whereToWork: Hakodate has very little coworking provision and remote work happens from apartments and the cafes of the Motomachi and Goryokaku districts. Japanese fibre is excellent, widely available and cheap relative to speed, and mobile coverage is comprehensive; the practical obstacle is the paperwork rather than the infrastructure, since contracts generally require residency and a Japanese bank account. Pocket wifi rental is the standard workaround for shorter stays. English is limited outside the tourism trade, and anything administrative will require Japanese or a translation app and patience. Anyone working with Europe will find the time difference awkward, since a European morning lands in the Japanese evening.
hakodate.gettingAround: Hakodate is compact and its tram line, one of the oldest in Japan, runs from the station past the morning market to the foot of the Motomachi slopes, which covers most of what a visitor wants. The city is walkable in its historic core, though the hills are real. The ropeway up Mount Hakodate serves the night view that draws most visitors. The Hokkaido Shinkansen reaches Shin-Hakodate-Hokuto, about twenty minutes from the city, putting Tokyo around four hours away. Onuma Quasi-National Park is half an hour by train and worth the trip.
hakodate.visas: Japan launched a digital nomad visa in 2024, granting six months to remote workers who are citizens of countries with the relevant tax or visa agreements and who can show an annual income of around ten million yen, which is a high bar by international standards. It is not renewable in place and carries a waiting period before reapplying. Most visitors instead use the visa waiver, which gives ninety days to citizens of around seventy countries, extendable to a hundred and eighty for some nationalities. Longer stays run through work, study or spouse categories.
hakodate.bestTime: May to October is the comfortable window, with mild summers that rarely pass twenty-six degrees and make Hakodate a refuge for Japanese escaping the heat further south. May brings the cherry blossom to Goryokaku's star fort, about a month later than Tokyo, and it is one of the best hanami sites in the country. Winter is long, snowy and cold, with the city under snow from December to March, which is spectacular from the mountain viewpoint and hard work at street level. Autumn colour in October is excellent and the crowds are thin.
hakodate.prosCons: Hakodate has one of the most celebrated night views in Japan from the mountain above the harbour, a Western-influenced hillside quarter left over from its years as one of the first ports opened to foreign trade, a star-shaped fort, and a morning market where the squid is pulled from the tank in front of you. It is cheap by Japanese standards. Against that, the winter is severe, the population is shrinking, English is limited, and there is no international community. Everything administrative in Japan assumes residency and rewards patience. The city also sits at the end of the Shinkansen line rather than on it, so the four hours to Tokyo is the practical floor for getting anywhere else.
hakodate.whoFor: Hakodate suits someone who wants a small, safe, beautiful Japanese city with excellent food and none of the crowding of the main corridor, and who either speaks some Japanese or is content to muddle through. It is unusually good in summer, when the rest of the country is unbearable and this city is not. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a foreign community or a professional network, and the digital nomad visa's income threshold puts the formal route out of reach for many. Winter arrivals should understand what Hokkaido snow means.

kagoshima.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,350 a month as a solo remote worker in Kagoshima, which is inexpensive for a Japanese city of six hundred thousand and well below anything on the Tokyo to Osaka corridor. A one-bedroom apartment runs roughly $400 to $700 depending on the district and the distance from the tram line. Food is very good value, built on Kurobuta pork, Satsuma sweet potato and the shochu that the prefecture produces more of than anywhere else in Japan. Onsen bathing is genuinely cheap here. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
kagoshima.whereToWork: Kagoshima has a small coworking presence serving the prefectural economy and the university, and remote work otherwise happens from apartments and cafes around Tenmonkan, the central arcade district. Japanese internet is excellent and inexpensive relative to speed, with fibre widely available and comprehensive mobile coverage. The obstacle is administrative rather than technical: fixed contracts assume residency and a Japanese bank account, so short stays generally run on rented pocket wifi or a data SIM. English is limited, and the local dialect is difficult enough that other Japanese speakers struggle with it.
kagoshima.gettingAround: Kagoshima is built along a bay with the volcano directly opposite, and its tram network covers the central districts cheaply and frequently, which makes the city easy to move around without a car. The ferry to Sakurajima runs around the clock and takes fifteen minutes. The Kyushu Shinkansen puts Fukuoka about ninety minutes away and Osaka around four hours. Ferries leave for Yakushima and the Amami islands from the port, which is the reason many visitors come. Ash from the volcano falls on the city regularly and residents keep the bags the city provides for it.
kagoshima.visas: Japan's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2024, offers six months to citizens of countries with the relevant agreements who can demonstrate an annual income of about ten million yen. The threshold is high and the permit cannot be renewed without a break, which limits its usefulness. The visa waiver remains the practical route for most: ninety days for citizens of roughly seventy countries, extendable to a hundred and eighty for a subset of them. Anything longer means a work, study or family category, all of which require a sponsor in Japan.
kagoshima.bestTime: October to November and March to April are the best months, with mild dry weather and either autumn colour or blossom. Kagoshima is subtropical and its summers are hot and humid, running through July and August with the rainy season immediately before them in June. Typhoons reach this coast between roughly August and October and are a genuine planning factor rather than a remote possibility. Winter is mild, rarely near freezing, which makes it one of the more comfortable winters in Japan. Ash fall depends on the wind rather than the season.
kagoshima.prosCons: Kagoshima has an active volcano four kilometres across the bay that erupts hundreds of times a year and is simply part of daily life, an onsen culture including the sand baths at Ibusuki, Sengan-en garden, and ferries to Yakushima's ancient cedar forest. It is warm, cheap by Japanese standards and easy to move around by tram. Against that, the ash is real and coats cars and washing, typhoons hit this coast, English is scarce, and there is no international community. The city is a long way from Tokyo in every sense.
kagoshima.whoFor: Kagoshima suits someone who wants a warm, walkable Japanese city with hot springs, good food and an active volcano as a neighbour, and who is prepared to operate largely in Japanese. It is an excellent base for the southern islands, with Yakushima and Amami both reachable by ferry. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs an English-speaking environment or a foreign professional network. Anyone considering the formal nomad visa should check the income threshold first, since it excludes a large share of the people the scheme nominally targets.

vizag.costOfLiving: Budget around $600 a month as a solo remote worker in Visakhapatnam, which makes it one of the cheapest coastal cities anywhere with this level of infrastructure. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $150 to $300, with the beach road and MVP Colony at the top of that range and the inland areas well below it. Food is extremely cheap and Andhra cooking is among the spiciest and best regarded in India. The city is expanding fast as the state builds it up, and rents in the newer IT areas have moved accordingly. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
vizag.whereToWork: Visakhapatnam has a real and growing technology sector, with the Rushikonda IT park and a coworking market that has expanded alongside it, and desks are inexpensive by any international measure. Fibre from the main providers reaches the developed neighbourhoods at low prices and mobile data in India remains among the cheapest in the world with good coverage. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. English is widely used in professional settings, which distinguishes this from most cities of comparable cost, though Telugu is the language of daily life. The Eastern Naval Command is headquartered here, which shapes parts of the city and restricts photography in some areas near the port.
vizag.gettingAround: Visakhapatnam runs along the Bay of Bengal with hills behind it, and the beach road from RK Beach north is the walkable spine of the city. Autorickshaws and app-based taxis are cheap and the standard way to move, and the bus network is extensive if slow. Kailasagiri hill park sits above the city with a ropeway to the top. The airport has domestic connections and a small number of international routes. The narrow-gauge line up to Araku Valley through the Eastern Ghats is one of the more scenic rail journeys in the country.
vizag.visas: India has no digital nomad visa. Most visitors use the e-Visa, which is issued online and comes in thirty-day, one-year and five-year tourist variants depending on nationality, with each individual stay generally capped at ninety days and a shorter limit for some passports. The e-Visa does not permit employment in India, and remote work for a foreign employer is not addressed in the rules. Business visas exist for those with an Indian counterpart. Extensions inside the country are difficult, so plan the exit rather than assuming flexibility on arrival. Foreigners staying beyond a short visit are also required to register in some categories, so check whether the specific visa carries that obligation.
vizag.bestTime: November to February is the season, with daytime temperatures in the high twenties, low humidity by coastal Indian standards and clear skies. March to May is hot and increasingly humid, pushing into the mid thirties with little relief. The southwest monsoon reaches the coast in June and runs to September, bringing heavy rain and grey weeks. The other consideration is cyclones, which form in the Bay of Bengal and have hit this coast hard within living memory, with the highest risk in October and November at the end of the monsoon.
vizag.prosCons: Visakhapatnam is a rare combination: a genuine beach city with a growing technology sector, a working port, hills behind it and the Araku Valley coffee country a scenic train ride inland. Costs are extraordinarily low, English works professionally, and the food is exceptional. Against that, the summer heat is severe, the monsoon is long, cyclones are a real risk on this coast, and there is no foreign nomad community at all. Air quality around the industrial belt is poor, and the city is growing faster than its infrastructure in places.
vizag.whoFor: Visakhapatnam suits someone who wants an Indian base with a beach, a technology sector and English in professional use, at a cost that leaves almost any income comfortable. It works well for anyone already connected to India's IT economy, since the local network is real rather than nominal. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a foreign community, anyone sensitive to heat, and anyone planning a stay longer than the e-Visa allows, since extending inside the country is genuinely difficult. Time the arrival for the winter months. It also suits anyone who wants to see a mid-sized Indian city being rebuilt in real time, since the state is investing heavily here.

shymkent.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Shymkent, which is cheaper than Almaty and Astana and among the lowest figures for any city of a million people on this site. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $200 to $350, with the newer developments and the centre at the top of that range. Food is very cheap, with the bazaars supplying produce from the surrounding Turkestan region and the Uzbek border trade keeping prices down. Utilities are inexpensive but winter heating is a real cost. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
shymkent.whereToWork: Shymkent has a small coworking market, considerably behind Almaty's but real, serving a local economy of trade, agriculture and light industry. Kazakh internet is fast and remarkably cheap, with fibre widely available in the city and strong mobile coverage, and it is one of the country's genuine practical advantages. Power is reliable. Russian is the working language of business and daily life alongside Kazakh, with Uzbek widely spoken given the border and the population, and English is rare outside a few younger professionals. Some Russian makes an enormous difference here.
shymkent.gettingAround: Shymkent is a flat, spread-out city of over a million and the central districts around the Independence Park and the bazaars are walkable, while the rest needs transport. Buses are cheap and cover the city, and ride-hailing through the regional apps is inexpensive and the usual default. Shymkent airport has domestic flights and connections to Turkey, the Gulf and Central Asian capitals. Turkistan, with the Yasawi mausoleum that is the country's most important Islamic monument, is around two hours north, and the Uzbek border and Tashkent lie a similar distance southwest.
shymkent.visas: Kazakhstan gives citizens of around eighty countries thirty days visa-free on arrival, which is simple but short. The country launched a Neo Nomad Visa for remote workers in 2024, offering up to a year to people employed or contracted outside Kazakhstan who can demonstrate a monthly income around the low thousands of dollars, and the scheme is new enough that implementation details have shifted since the announcement. Confirm current requirements with a Kazakh mission rather than relying on secondary reporting. Longer stays otherwise run through work permits or the country's investor categories.
shymkent.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the comfortable windows, with warm dry days and the steppe green in spring. Shymkent is the warmest large city in Kazakhstan and its summers are hot and dry, regularly above thirty-five degrees through July and August, though the low humidity makes that more bearable than the number suggests. Winter is mild by Kazakh standards, which is a low bar but a real distinction, with daytime temperatures around freezing rather than the deep cold of the north. Snow falls but rarely settles for long.
shymkent.prosCons: Shymkent is an old Silk Road city and the warmest in Kazakhstan, with bazaars that still function as trade hubs rather than attractions, the Yasawi mausoleum at Turkistan two hours north, and the Aksu-Zhabagly reserve, the oldest protected area in Central Asia, within reach. Costs are very low and the internet is genuinely fast and cheap. Against that, there is no international community, English is rare, the summer is severe, and the city is functional rather than beautiful. Air quality in winter suffers from heating across the whole region. The city was also promoted to republic status in 2018, alongside Almaty and the capital, which brought a wave of public investment that is visible in the newer districts.
shymkent.whoFor: Shymkent suits someone with Russian, or the willingness to acquire some, who wants a very cheap Central Asian base with fast internet and easy access to Uzbekistan and the Silk Road sites. It works well for anyone travelling the region slowly rather than treating one city as a home. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs English, a foreign community or a professional network. Anyone considering the Neo Nomad Visa should check its current status directly, since the scheme is recent and the published requirements have not been stable.

bridgetown.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Bridgetown, which is expensive for the Caribbean and reflects an island that imports nearly everything it eats. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $900 to $1,500, with the west coast between Holetown and Speightstown at the top of that and the areas inland from the capital well below it. Groceries are the line that surprises people: imported goods carry a heavy markup and the supermarket bill can exceed the rent. Eating at a rum shop or the Friday fish fry at Oistins costs a fraction of a restaurant. The Barbados dollar is pegged at two to the United States dollar, so the maths never moves. This figure is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
bridgetown.whereToWork: Barbados built a remote work economy deliberately and the infrastructure followed. There are several coworking spaces around Bridgetown and along the west coast, some of them explicitly aimed at Welcome Stamp holders, and desks run from roughly $200 a month. Fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches most of the developed parts of the island at speeds that hold up for video calls, and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Power is reliable by regional standards, though outages happen in storm season. The island sits four hours behind central European time and one hour ahead of New York for half the year, which makes it one of the few places that can work a European morning and an American afternoon in the same day.
bridgetown.gettingAround: Bridgetown itself is walkable, with the Careenage, Parliament and the Garrison all within twenty minutes on foot, but the island is thirty-four kilometres end to end and most of what you would want is not in the capital. The government blue buses, yellow reggae buses and ZR vans cover the whole island cheaply and frequently, which makes Barbados unusually workable without a car. Driving is on the left and the roads are narrow, with the ring road around the coast being the pleasant one. Grantley Adams airport has direct flights to London, New York, Toronto and Miami, which is far better connectivity than most Caribbean islands manage.
bridgetown.visas: Barbados invented the category. The Welcome Stamp, launched in July 2020, is a twelve-month remote work visa for people employed or self-employed outside the country, requiring an expected annual income of around $50,000 and carrying a fee of roughly $2,000 for an individual or $3,000 for a family. Income earned under it is not taxed locally, which is the substantive part rather than the marketing. It is renewable. Short visits run visa-free for most Western nationalities, typically up to six months for British and Commonwealth citizens and three for others. The application is online and processing has generally been measured in days rather than months.
bridgetown.bestTime: December to May is the dry season and the reason the island is busy then, with daytime temperatures around thirty, low humidity by Caribbean standards and constant trade winds. June to November is the wet season and also the hurricane season, though Barbados sits on the eastern edge of the belt and is struck far less often than the islands to its west; Hurricane Elsa in 2021 was the first direct hit in decades. September and October are the wettest and quietest months and the cheapest to rent in. Crop Over, the sugar harvest festival that ends in a costumed parade, runs from June to early August and is the island at its loudest.
bridgetown.prosCons: Barbados has the most developed remote work infrastructure in the Caribbean, a visa built for the purpose, direct flights to three continents, an island bus network that genuinely works, and a calm west coast facing a wild Atlantic east coast twenty minutes away. English is the only language you need. Against that, it is expensive, the grocery bill is the part nobody budgets for, the nomad community is small and turns over quickly, and everything on an island of 280,000 people is eventually a short drive from everything else, which some find restful and others find small.
bridgetown.whoFor: Bridgetown suits someone who wants a Caribbean base with the paperwork already solved and can absorb the cost of living on an island that imports its food. The time zone makes it unusually good for anyone working across both American and European hours. It works for a full year rather than a season, which is what the visa is designed for. It is a poor fit for anyone on a tight budget, and anyone who needs a large professional network will find the island's economy narrow outside tourism, offshore finance and the university.

hamiltonbermuda.costOfLiving: Budget around $4,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Hamilton, which makes Bermuda one of the most expensive places on this site and, by several international measures, one of the most expensive places anywhere. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $2,200 to $3,200 and that is the ordinary market rather than the top of it. Everything on the shelf arrived by ship and the customs duty on it is substantial, so groceries cost roughly twice what they do in the eastern United States. There is no income tax, which offsets some of it for anyone earning locally and none of it for a visitor. This figure is our own estimate rather than measured data.
hamiltonbermuda.whereToWork: Bermuda's economy runs on insurance and reinsurance, which means the connectivity is genuinely business grade rather than adequate: fibre reaches most of the island, speeds are high and the professional services around it are what a global industry requires. There is a small coworking market in Hamilton aimed partly at the Work From Bermuda scheme. Mobile coverage is complete across twenty-one square miles. Power is reliable and expensive. Hamilton sits one hour ahead of New York, which puts a Bermuda afternoon squarely inside an American working day and a Bermuda evening at the end of a European one.
hamiltonbermuda.gettingAround: Bermuda does not let visitors rent cars, which is the single most important practical fact about the island and catches almost everyone out. Residents are limited to one car per household and tourists to none. What exists instead is a good public bus network, ferries across the Great Sound that are faster than the roads, scooters, pedal bikes and, since 2017, tiny two-seat electric minicars available for rent. Hamilton itself is small enough to cross on foot in fifteen minutes. The Railway Trail runs most of the length of the island on the old rail bed and is the best walking and cycling here.
hamiltonbermuda.visas: The Work From Bermuda Certificate is a one-year permit for people employed or studying remotely for an organisation outside Bermuda, with an application fee of around $263 and no stated minimum income, which makes it one of the cheapest and least demanding schemes anywhere. It is renewable. Applicants need health insurance and a clean record. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to ninety days. The generosity of the visa is not the constraint here; the cost of the accommodation you need to hold once you have it is.
hamiltonbermuda.bestTime: May to October is the warm half, with daytime temperatures in the high twenties, water warm enough to swim from June, and the pink sand beaches at Horseshoe Bay and Warwick Long Bay at their best. Bermuda is subtropical rather than tropical: winters are mild but breezy and grey, sitting around eighteen degrees, and the sea is too cold for most people from January to April. Hurricane season runs June to November and Bermuda is genuinely exposed, sitting alone in the Atlantic; the building code is strict for that reason and the island absorbs storms better than most.
hamiltonbermuda.prosCons: Bermuda gives you pink sand, the clearest water in the Atlantic, a wreck-diving coast, a mild subtropical climate and a one-hour flight to New York, with a remote work visa that costs almost nothing to obtain. It is safe, orderly and genuinely beautiful. Against that, the cost of living is close to prohibitive, the island is twenty-one square miles and you will know all of it within a month, visitors cannot drive, and the social scene is small and heavily weighted towards the insurance industry. It is not the Caribbean and does not have Caribbean prices or Caribbean weather.
hamiltonbermuda.whoFor: Hamilton suits a well-paid remote worker who wants proximity to New York, exceptional water and a very safe, very orderly island, and who can absorb rents that would be high in Manhattan. Anyone in insurance, reinsurance or financial services will find a real professional network here, which is rare on an island this size. It is a poor fit for anyone on a normal budget, anyone who needs space or variety, and anyone who assumed a car would be available. Check what accommodation actually costs before applying for the visa, not after.

georgetowncayman.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,800 a month as a solo remote worker in George Town, which is among the highest figures on this site and reflects an offshore financial centre where almost everything is imported. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $2,000 to $2,800, with anything on or near Seven Mile Beach at the top of that. Groceries are expensive enough that residents talk about it constantly, and eating out is priced for the finance industry. There is no income tax, no capital gains tax and no property tax, which is the whole reason the cost structure looks like this. The Cayman dollar is pegged above the United States dollar, at roughly 1.20, which catches people out. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
georgetowncayman.whereToWork: Connectivity here is excellent and not by accident: the islands host a large offshore banking, funds and insurance industry that could not operate otherwise. Fibre reaches essentially all of Grand Cayman, speeds are high and there are several coworking spaces around George Town and Camana Bay serving both the financial sector and the Global Citizen programme. Power is reliable and the grid was rebuilt to a higher standard after Hurricane Ivan in 2004. George Town runs on Eastern time without daylight saving, which keeps it aligned with New York in winter and an hour behind in summer.
