georgetowncayman.gettingAround: Grand Cayman is flat and long, and George Town, Seven Mile Beach and Camana Bay form a strip along the western side that most people move between daily. There is a minibus network that covers the main routes cheaply, and it works better than visitors expect, but most residents drive and driving is on the left. Cycling along the West Bay Road is feasible but the traffic is heavy at rush hour. Owen Roberts airport is minutes from town with direct flights to Miami, New York, Toronto and London. Little Cayman and Cayman Brac are short hops by light aircraft.
georgetowncayman.visas: The Global Citizen Concierge Programme is a two-year remote work certificate for people employed outside the Cayman Islands, and its income requirement is the highest of any scheme in the region: roughly $100,000 a year for an individual, $150,000 for a couple and $180,000 for a family with children, plus an application fee of around $1,469. That threshold is the point, not an accident, and it excludes most of the people who look at it. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to six months, granted at the discretion of the immigration officer on arrival.
georgetowncayman.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the calmest water for diving, and it is also the busiest and most expensive time. May to November is hotter and wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Grand Cayman was devastated by Hurricane Ivan in 2004 and the memory shapes how the island builds and prepares. September and October are the quietest months, the cheapest, and the ones with the highest storm risk. Water temperature barely moves all year, which is the diving argument for coming outside the season.
georgetowncayman.prosCons: Grand Cayman has Seven Mile Beach, wall diving off a drop-off that starts a few hundred metres offshore, the stingrays at the sandbar, and infrastructure to a standard almost nothing else in the Caribbean matches. There is no income tax and the professional network in finance is deep and international. Against that, the cost of living is extreme, the island is expensive in a way that is structural rather than seasonal, the Global Citizen income threshold rules out most applicants, and the character is closer to a well-run business district with beaches than to the Caribbean people imagine.
georgetowncayman.whoFor: George Town suits a high-earning remote worker, particularly anyone in funds, insurance or financial services, who wants excellent diving and infrastructure and can clear a six-figure income requirement. It works well for a two-year stay, which is what the certificate offers. It is a poor fit for anyone on an ordinary budget, anyone looking for a lively or local Caribbean culture, and anyone who wants somewhere cheap to sit with a laptop. The diving is genuinely world class and is the reason many people who came for the tax stay for longer.

willemstad.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Willemstad, which makes Curacao considerably cheaper than the Caribbean islands with the best-known nomad visas. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with Pietermaai and Punda at the top of that range and the residential districts inland well below it. Groceries are imported and priced accordingly, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the range wider and the markup lower than on smaller islands. Eating at a local snack or truk'i pan costs very little. The guilder is pegged to the United States dollar at around 1.79, and dollars are accepted almost everywhere. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
willemstad.whereToWork: Curacao has a real coworking scene for an island of 150,000, concentrated in Pietermaai and around the Punda side of the harbour, and much of it grew directly out of the @HOME remote work programme. Fibre from Flow reaches the developed parts of the island at reliable speeds and mobile data is inexpensive. Power is stable. Dutch is the language of administration and Papiamentu of daily life, but English is widely and comfortably spoken, which makes Curacao unusually easy to operate in. The island runs four hours behind central European time, so a Dutch afternoon is a Curacao morning.
willemstad.gettingAround: Willemstad is split by the St Anna Bay channel into Punda and Otrobanda, joined by the Queen Emma pontoon bridge, which swings open for shipping several times a day and is free to walk across. Both sides are walkable and the historic centre is compact. Beyond that the island needs a car: the best diving and the quiet beaches are spread along the western coast towards Westpunt, forty minutes away. Konvoi minibuses cover the main routes cheaply. Curacao's airport has direct flights to Amsterdam, Miami and across the region, which is a real advantage of the Dutch connection.
willemstad.visas: The @HOME in Curacao programme grants a six-month remote work permit to people employed or self-employed outside the island, with a straightforward online application and a modest fee, extendable for a further six months. Dutch nationals have residence rights and do not need it. Everyone else on a short visit gets up to ninety days visa-free for most Western nationalities. Curacao is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands rather than part of the European Union, so a Schengen visa does not apply here and time spent here does not count against a Schengen allowance.
willemstad.bestTime: Curacao sits below the hurricane belt, which is the single most useful thing to know about its calendar: the island is warm, dry and windy essentially all year, with daytime temperatures around thirty-one and rainfall low even in the wetter months from October to February. That makes it one of the few Caribbean destinations with no season to avoid. The trade winds blow constantly and take the edge off the heat. The busiest and priciest window is December to April, when the northern hemisphere arrives. Carnival runs for weeks before Lent and is the island at its most alive.
willemstad.prosCons: Willemstad is a UNESCO World Heritage site and looks like nowhere else in the Caribbean, a row of Dutch merchant houses painted in ice-cream colours along a working harbour channel. It sits outside the hurricane belt, has shore diving from dozens of points along the coast, real coworking, direct flights to Amsterdam, and costs meaningfully less than Barbados or the Cayman Islands. Against that, the island is dry and scrubby rather than lush, the nomad community is small, the six-month visa is shorter than the regional standard, and Willemstad outside the restored centre is an ordinary working city.
willemstad.whoFor: Willemstad suits someone who wants the Caribbean without the hurricane season, a genuinely distinctive city to live in, and diving straight off the shore rather than from a boat. Its Dutch links make it unusually practical for Europeans, both for flights and for the language. It works well for a six-month stretch. It is a poor fit for anyone expecting rainforest and waterfalls, since Curacao is a desert island, and for anyone who needs a large nomad scene. Divers will get more out of this island per dollar than almost anywhere in the region.

oranjestad.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker in Oranjestad, which sits between Curacao and Barbados on price and reflects an island whose economy is tourism from end to end. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $800 to $1,300, with anything near Palm Beach or Eagle Beach at the top of that and the inland neighbourhoods considerably cheaper. Groceries are imported and the markup is real, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the choice wide. Eating where Arubans eat, at a local snack or the fish shacks, costs a fraction of the resort strip. The florin is pegged at around 1.79 to the dollar and dollars circulate freely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
oranjestad.whereToWork: Aruba's connectivity is good and its power supply reliable, both underwritten by a tourism industry that cannot afford otherwise. Fibre reaches the developed western side of the island and mobile data is inexpensive with complete coverage. Coworking exists in a modest way around Oranjestad, though most remote workers here use apartments and hotel business centres. English is spoken universally alongside Papiamento, Dutch and Spanish, and Arubans switching between four languages in one conversation is entirely normal. The island runs four hours behind central European time, which puts a European afternoon at the start of the Aruban day.
oranjestad.gettingAround: Aruba is small, flat and easy. Oranjestad's centre is walkable and a free streetcar loops through it, and the Arubus network runs frequently up the western coast past the hotel strips to Palm Beach and down towards San Nicolas. That corridor is where almost everything is. A car is needed only for Arikok National Park, which covers nearly a fifth of the island on the wild windward side, and for the Natural Pool and the north coast, where the tracks demand four-wheel drive. Queen Beatrix airport is minutes from town with direct flights to Amsterdam, Miami and much of the eastern United States.
oranjestad.visas: Aruba's One Happy Workation programme is a ninety-day remote work arrangement, originally opened to United States nationals and since broadened, with a light application process and a modest fee. It is short by regional standards and closer to a formalised long visit than a residence permit. Dutch nationals have residence rights. Everyone else gets up to ninety days on arrival for most Western nationalities, with extensions possible through the immigration authority. Like Curacao, Aruba is part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands but not of the European Union, so Schengen rules do not apply.
oranjestad.bestTime: Aruba has the most consistent weather in the Caribbean and it is genuinely a selling point rather than a slogan: the island lies below the hurricane belt, averages under 450 millimetres of rain a year, and sits around thirty-one degrees every month with trade winds that never stop. There is no bad season. The busy and expensive window runs from mid-December to April, when North America arrives, and the quieter, cheaper months are May, June, September and October, with weather that is essentially identical. Carnival, which runs through January and February, is the island's largest event.
oranjestad.prosCons: Aruba offers the most reliable weather of anywhere in the Caribbean, wide white beaches, constant wind that makes it one of the world's best windsurfing and kitesurfing spots, a desert interior protected as a national park, safety that is genuinely high, and direct flights to Amsterdam and the eastern United States. Against that, it is heavily and visibly built for package tourism, the ninety-day permit is short, the island is small and largely developed along one coast, and there is very little nature outside the park. It is polished rather than characterful.
oranjestad.whoFor: Oranjestad suits someone who wants guaranteed weather, real safety and easy logistics, and who is happy on a small, developed island for a season rather than a year. Windsurfers and kitesurfers get more from Aruba than from almost anywhere, since the wind is dependable in a way it is nowhere else in the region. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting a long stay, given the ninety-day permit, or anyone hoping for jungle, rivers or mountains, none of which exist here. The eastern coastline is where the island stops looking like a resort.

nassau.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Nassau, which is expensive for what it is and reflects an economy built entirely on tourism and offshore finance. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,200 to $1,800, with Cable Beach and the areas near Paradise Island at the top of that. Groceries are the standing complaint: the Bahamas imports around ninety per cent of its food and the customs duty is heavy, so a supermarket shop costs roughly double the American equivalent. There is no income tax. The Bahamian dollar is pegged one to one with the United States dollar and both circulate. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
nassau.whereToWork: Nassau's connectivity is good in the developed areas, with fibre from Cable Bahamas and Aliv reaching most of New Providence at workable speeds and comprehensive mobile coverage. There is a small coworking presence, some of it created around the BEATS remote work permit. Power outages happen and anyone whose work cannot pause should ask what backup a building has before signing. The Bahamas runs on Eastern time with daylight saving, which keeps Nassau aligned with New York year-round and makes it the most convenient Caribbean base for anyone working American hours.
nassau.gettingAround: New Providence is a small island and Nassau covers most of it. Downtown around Bay Street is walkable, though it is built for cruise passengers and empties when the ships leave. Jitney minibuses cover the island cheaply and are the way most residents move; they stop running in the early evening. Taxis are expensive and metered fares are frequently a negotiation. Driving is on the left in cars mostly imported with left-hand drive, which is as strange as it sounds. Lynden Pindling airport has more direct connections to the United States than any other Caribbean airport, and the Family Islands are short hops by light aircraft.
nassau.visas: The Bahamas Extended Access Travel Stay, known as BEATS, is a one-year renewable permit for remote workers and students employed or enrolled outside the country, with an application fee of around $1,000 plus a smaller processing charge. It is handled online and is one of the more straightforward schemes in the region. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to ninety days, and British citizens receive longer. There is no income tax on money earned under the permit, which is the substantive benefit alongside the length. Anyone applying should note that the permit covers the whole country, so it can be used from a Family Island rather than from New Providence.
nassau.bestTime: December to April is the dry, cooler season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-six, low humidity and the calmest seas, and it is when prices and crowds peak. May to November is hotter and considerably wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; the Bahamas sits directly in the track and Hurricane Dorian in 2019 was catastrophic for Abaco and Grand Bahama, though Nassau was largely spared. September and October carry the highest risk and the lowest prices. Junkanoo, the street parade with its costumes and goatskin drums, runs on Boxing Day and New Year's Day.
nassau.prosCons: Nassau has the best flight connections to the United States of any Caribbean capital, a one-year remote work permit, no income tax, and seven hundred islands behind it that almost no visitor reaches. The water in the Exumas is as good as anywhere on earth. Against that, Nassau itself is expensive, dominated by cruise tourism along Bay Street, and carries a crime problem that residents and foreign governments both take seriously, with specific areas that visitors are consistently advised to avoid. The island is developed rather than beautiful, and the beauty is elsewhere in the chain.
nassau.whoFor: Nassau suits someone working American hours who wants a Caribbean base a short flight from the east coast, with the paperwork solved for a year and no income tax on it. It works best for people who treat Nassau as the airport and the Family Islands as the point, since the Exumas, Eleuthera and Long Island are what the country actually offers. It is a poor fit for anyone on a budget, and anyone moving here should read current safety guidance for New Providence properly rather than assuming a tourist destination is uniformly safe.

roseau.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Roseau, which makes Dominica one of the cheaper Eastern Caribbean islands and considerably cheaper than its better-known neighbours. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $500 to $900, and houses outside the capital are within reach at figures that would be impossible on Barbados. Dominica grows a great deal of its own food, which is unusual in the region and keeps the market cheap; imported goods carry the usual island markup. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar, so budgeting is simple. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
roseau.whereToWork: Dominica's connectivity is the honest weakness and the reason the score here is low rather than average. Fibre has reached parts of Roseau and Portsmouth and works well where it exists, but coverage is patchy outside the towns and speeds vary. Mobile data from Flow and Digicel is the practical fallback. Power cuts are not rare and the grid is still being rebuilt in places after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which destroyed much of the island's infrastructure. Anyone whose work cannot pause should ask about backup power before committing, and should treat a video-call-heavy schedule as a real constraint here.
roseau.gettingAround: Roseau is small and walkable, a grid of narrow streets between the river and the sea that can be crossed in fifteen minutes. Beyond it the island is mountainous and the roads are steep, winding and slow: Dominica is only 47 kilometres long but crossing it takes far longer than the distance suggests. Minibuses cover the main routes cheaply and stop early. A four-wheel drive helps for the trailheads. There is no international airport for large jets, so almost everyone arrives via a connection through Antigua, Barbados or Saint Martin into Douglas-Charles, an hour and a half from Roseau.
roseau.visas: Dominica's Work In Nature visa is an eighteen-month remote work permit, the longest single term offered anywhere in the Eastern Caribbean, open to people employed or self-employed outside the country who can show an annual income of around $50,000 and hold health insurance. The fee is roughly $800 for an individual. Applications are handled online. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities, typically for up to six months, granted at the border. Dominica also runs a citizenship by investment programme, which is a separate matter and should be researched independently rather than through the agents who market it.
roseau.bestTime: February to May is the driest and most comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and the trails at their most passable. Dominica is one of the wettest places in the Caribbean by design of its geography: mountains over 1,400 metres wring rain out of the trade winds, which is why there are 365 rivers and why the island is green in a way its neighbours are not. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season, and Dominica is exposed; Hurricane Maria in 2017 damaged or destroyed the majority of buildings on the island. Plan around September and October.
roseau.prosCons: Dominica is the Nature Island and the name is earned: rainforest running to the waterline, the second-largest boiling lake in the world at the end of a hard six-hour walk, hot springs, whale watching that runs almost year-round because sperm whales live offshore, and the Waitukubuli Trail down the length of the island. It is cheap and the eighteen-month visa is the region's longest. Against that, the internet is genuinely unreliable, there is no nomad community, getting here requires a connection, and the island is exposed to hurricanes in a way that shapes everything.
roseau.whoFor: Roseau suits someone who wants rainforest, rivers and hiking above all else, whose work tolerates an unreliable connection, and who is content with very little in the way of nightlife or company. Divers and hikers get more from Dominica than from anywhere else in the Eastern Caribbean. It is a poor fit for anyone with a demanding call schedule, anyone who wants beaches of white sand, since Dominica's are mostly volcanic and dark, and anyone who needs to be somewhere easy to fly in and out of at short notice.

stgeorges.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in St George's, which is mid-range for the Eastern Caribbean. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with anything near Grand Anse beach at the top of that range and the hillside neighbourhoods above the harbour cheaper. Grenada grows a serious amount of its own produce and the Saturday market is genuinely cheap; imported goods carry the standard island markup. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar. St George's University brings a large international student population that shapes the rental market. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
stgeorges.whereToWork: Grenada's connectivity is reasonable and improving, with fibre from Flow and Digicel reaching St George's, Grand Anse and the south of the island at workable speeds, and mobile data covering everywhere anyone lives. There is limited formal coworking, though the presence of St George's University, a large American medical school, means cafes and study spaces used to people working are easy to find. Power cuts happen but are not routine. The island runs four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in the northern winter, so a European afternoon lands at the start of the Grenadian working day and an American morning at the end of it.
stgeorges.gettingAround: St George's is built around a horseshoe harbour with steep streets rising from it, which makes it beautiful and hard work on foot. The Carenage around the water is walkable; the rest is a climb. Minibuses run constantly along the main routes to Grand Anse and around the island for very little, and they are how most people move. Driving is on the left and the roads through the interior are narrow and mountainous. Maurice Bishop airport is fifteen minutes from town with direct flights to London, New York, Miami and Toronto, which is good connectivity for an island of 110,000.
stgeorges.visas: Grenada has no dedicated remote work visa, which is the main practical gap against its neighbours. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to three months, with extensions available through the immigration department in St George's, and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer. Anyone wanting to stay past that applies for an extension of stay locally or a residence permit, which requires more documentation and patience. Grenada also operates a citizenship by investment programme that includes an E-2 treaty route to the United States, which is a substantial and separate decision rather than a nomad option.
stgeorges.bestTime: January to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, lower humidity and the calmest sea. June to December is wetter, and the hurricane season runs June to November; Grenada sits at the southern edge of the belt and is hit far less often than the islands north of it, though Hurricane Ivan in 2004 devastated the island and Beryl in 2024 struck Carriacou hard. August brings Spicemas, the carnival, with the pre-dawn Jouvert that covers everyone in oil and paint. September and October are the quietest and cheapest.
stgeorges.prosCons: Grenada is the spice island and it smells like it: nutmeg, mace and cinnamon growing on the hillsides, and a working nutmeg processing station you can walk through. St George's harbour is among the most beautiful in the Caribbean, Grand Anse is a three-kilometre white beach ten minutes from town, and the underwater sculpture park off Molinere is the first of its kind in the world. Against that, there is no remote work visa, no nomad community, connectivity is adequate rather than good, and the steep streets make the capital tiring to live in.
stgeorges.whoFor: St George's suits someone who wants a genuinely beautiful Caribbean town, hiking in the interior, and diving that includes both reefs and the Bianca C, the largest wreck in the Caribbean. The medical school gives the island an international layer most of its neighbours lack. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a long-stay visa, since three months is the practical limit without paperwork, and for anyone unwilling to climb hills daily. Time a visit around Spicemas in August if the carnival is the point, or avoid it entirely if it is not.

castries.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Castries, which reflects an island where tourism sets prices along the west coast. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with Rodney Bay and Gros Islet in the north at the top of that and the areas around Castries itself cheaper. Saint Lucia grows bananas, cocoa and a good deal of its own produce, and the Castries market is where the price difference shows. Imported goods carry the usual markup. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
castries.whereToWork: Connectivity in Saint Lucia is workable rather than strong: fibre reaches Castries, Rodney Bay and the developed western coast at reasonable speeds, and mobile data from Flow and Digicel covers the populated areas. Coworking exists in a small way around Rodney Bay, which is where most of the island's remote workers and long-stay visitors end up rather than in Castries itself. Power cuts happen. The island runs four hours behind central European time, which makes a European afternoon a Saint Lucian morning and gives a reasonable overlap in both directions.
castries.gettingAround: Castries sits around a deep harbour that takes cruise ships, and the central grid is walkable though busy and hot. Minibuses cover the island cheaply and frequently, running north to Rodney Bay and south along the coast to Soufriere, and they are the practical way to move. Driving is on the left and the west coast road to Soufriere is spectacular and slow, with hairpins the whole way. Hewanorra, the international airport, is at the far southern end of the island, an hour and a half from Castries, which is a longer transfer than most visitors expect.
castries.visas: Saint Lucia has no dedicated remote work visa, though it ran a Live It scheme during the pandemic that has not been maintained as a formal category. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to six weeks, with extensions available through the immigration department, and British and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer on arrival. Anyone planning a longer stay should ask for the maximum at the border and then extend locally, which is routine. Saint Lucia also operates a citizenship by investment programme, which is a separate decision and unrelated to remote work.
castries.bestTime: December to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, lower humidity and calm seas, and it is when prices are highest. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season; Saint Lucia sits within the belt and has taken direct hits, most recently Tropical Storm Bret and its neighbours in recent years. Saint Lucia Jazz in May and Carnival in July are the two events worth planning around. September and October are the wettest, quietest and cheapest, and also the months when many hotels close for maintenance.
castries.prosCons: Saint Lucia has the Pitons, two volcanic plugs rising straight out of the sea at Soufriere that are a UNESCO World Heritage site and genuinely unlike anything else in the Caribbean, a drive-in volcano with sulphur springs, rainforest walks and a serious sailing culture around Rodney Bay. Against that, there is no remote work visa, the airport is a long way from the capital, Castries itself is a working port town rather than a place people choose to live, and the crime rate is higher than several of its neighbours, with the usual advice about specific areas.
castries.whoFor: Castries suits someone who wants dramatic landscape within a short drive and is content to base themselves in Rodney Bay or Soufriere rather than the capital. Sailors get a great deal from Saint Lucia, which sits on the main Windward Islands route and hosts the finish of the Atlantic Rally for Cruisers each December. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a long-stay visa, and anyone arriving should plan the transfer from Hewanorra rather than discovering it. The Pitons are the reason to come and they are ninety minutes from the capital.

portofspain.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Port of Spain, which is cheap for the Caribbean and reflects an economy built on oil and gas rather than tourism. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $500 to $900, with Woodbrook, St Clair and Newtown at the top of that and the areas east of the city considerably cheaper. Food is inexpensive and Trinidad's is the best in the Caribbean by a distance, with doubles from a street cart costing almost nothing. Fuel is subsidised. The Trinidad and Tobago dollar floats within a managed band and foreign exchange can be hard to obtain locally. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
portofspain.whereToWork: Trinidad's connectivity is good by regional standards, underwritten by an energy sector that needs it: fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches most of the developed western corridor at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive. There is a small coworking scene around Port of Spain, serving local startups rather than visitors. Power is reliable. The island runs four hours behind central European time. English is the only language required. The professional network here is real but concentrated in energy, finance and government, and it is not one a visiting remote worker plugs into easily.
portofspain.gettingAround: Port of Spain is compact around Independence Square and the Queen's Park Savannah, the largest roundabout in the world and the city's green centre, and that core is walkable by day. Maxi taxis, the colour-coded minibuses, and route taxis cover the city and the corridor east towards Arima cheaply. Traffic on the Churchill Roosevelt and Beetham highways is severe at peak. Most residents drive, on the left. Piarco airport is forty minutes east. The ferry to Tobago takes around three hours and is how most people reach the quieter island, which is where the beaches are.
portofspain.visas: Trinidad and Tobago has no remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days, and Commonwealth citizens generally receive the same, with extensions applied for at the immigration division in Port of Spain. The process is bureaucratic rather than difficult. Anyone planning to stay longer needs a work permit tied to an employer, or a residence permit through marriage or descent. The country is not organised around long-stay visitors and the immigration system reflects that; plan around ninety days rather than assuming an extension. Anyone coming for Carnival should apply well ahead if a visa is needed at all, since the weeks around it are the busiest the immigration system sees.
portofspain.bestTime: January to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around thirty-one and the lowest rainfall, and it contains the event that defines the calendar. Trinidad Carnival, on the Monday and Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, is the largest in the Caribbean and the reason a great many people come at all; the season of fetes and panyard rehearsals runs for weeks before it and the city is fully booked. June to December is the wet season, with heavy afternoon rain. Trinidad sits south of the hurricane belt and is rarely struck, which is a genuine advantage over the rest of the region.
portofspain.prosCons: Trinidad invented the steelpan, calypso, soca and limbo, and its Carnival is the one every other Caribbean carnival is modelled on. The food is the best in the region, mixing African, Indian, Chinese, Creole and Syrian traditions on the same street. The Northern Range has rainforest and the Caroni swamp fills with scarlet ibis at dusk. It is cheap and outside the hurricane belt. Against that, the crime rate is the serious qualification: Trinidad has one of the higher murder rates in the Americas, and both residents and foreign governments treat parts of Port of Spain as no-go areas.
portofspain.whoFor: Port of Spain suits someone drawn to music, food and Carnival who is prepared to take the security situation seriously and organise their movements around it rather than ignore it. It is culturally the richest place in the Caribbean and almost no remote workers go there. It is a poor fit for anyone who wants a beach city, since Trinidad's coast is not its strength and Tobago is a separate trip, and for anyone who needs a long-stay visa. Read current government travel advice for Trinidad specifically, and take local advice on neighbourhoods seriously.

georgetownguyana.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Georgetown, and note that this figure has been moving upward fast. Guyana began producing offshore oil in 2019 and has since been among the fastest-growing economies in the world, which has pushed rents in the capital up sharply as international companies arrive. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $500 to $1,000 depending on how close it sits to the areas the oil sector has taken. Food from the markets is cheap and the produce is excellent. Imported goods carry a heavy markup. This is our own estimate rather than measured data, and it dates faster here than elsewhere.
georgetownguyana.whereToWork: Georgetown's connectivity has improved with the oil money but remains the weak point: fibre reaches parts of the city at workable speeds, mobile data from GTT and Digicel is the fallback, and neither is dependable enough to plan a day around without a backup. Power cuts are frequent enough that generators are standard in any serious building. There is a small coworking presence serving the energy sector and local startups. English is the official language, which is unusual in South America and is Guyana's single biggest practical advantage for an English-speaking visitor.
georgetownguyana.gettingAround: Georgetown is flat, laid out on a Dutch grid with drainage canals down the middle of several avenues, and much of it sits below sea level behind a seawall. The centre around Stabroek Market and the wooden St George's Cathedral is walkable by day. Minibuses cover the city and the coast road cheaply and drive alarmingly. Taxis are inexpensive and are the standard advice after dark. The interior is another matter entirely: Kaieteur Falls and the Rupununi savannah are reached by light aircraft, and there is no road network to most of the country.
georgetownguyana.visas: Guyana gives most Western nationalities and all Commonwealth citizens visa-free entry for up to ninety days, granted on arrival, with extensions available from the immigration department. There is no remote work visa and no particular framework for long-stay visitors. Anyone wanting to stay beyond ninety days applies locally, and the process is manageable but slow. Yellow fever vaccination is required if arriving from an endemic country and is sensible regardless given the interior. Guyana is a member of CARICOM, so regional nationals move more freely. Anyone heading into the interior should also note that visits to Amerindian villages require a permit arranged through the tour operator rather than on arrival.
georgetownguyana.bestTime: Guyana sits close to the equator and is hot and humid year-round, around thirty degrees every month. The calendar is set by rain rather than temperature, and there are two wet seasons: a long one from May to August and a shorter one from November to January. The drier windows, February to April and September to October, are the practical time to visit, and September is also when Kaieteur Falls is at its most dramatic against low water. Georgetown floods in heavy rain because the drainage system is old and the city is below sea level.
georgetownguyana.prosCons: Guyana is South America's only English-speaking country, with a wooden colonial capital unlike anything else on the continent, Kaieteur Falls, the highest single-drop waterfall in the world at nearly five times the height of Niagara, and rainforest covering four-fifths of the country. Costs are low and the culture, mixing Indian, African, Amerindian, Chinese and Portuguese, is genuinely distinctive. Against that, Georgetown has a serious crime problem that visitors must take seriously, the infrastructure is weak, and the oil boom is changing prices and the city faster than any guide can keep up with.
georgetownguyana.whoFor: Georgetown suits an experienced traveller who wants somewhere genuinely off the remote work map, is interested in the interior rather than the capital, and will organise their days around the security situation rather than hoping. Anyone working in energy, conservation or development will find real professional depth here right now. It is a poor fit for a first trip to South America, for anyone who needs reliable internet, and for anyone unwilling to read current travel advice properly. The interior is the reason to come; Georgetown is the way in.

paramaribo.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Paramaribo, which is cheap by any measure and reflects a small economy that has been through serious currency instability. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $350 to $700. Food is the standout: Suriname's markets are cheap and its cooking, drawing on Javanese, Hindustani, Chinese, Creole and Dutch traditions, is among the most varied anywhere per head of population. The Surinamese dollar has devalued sharply in recent years, so any figure quoted in it dates quickly and locals often price in United States dollars. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
paramaribo.whereToWork: Paramaribo's connectivity is modest: fibre from Telesur reaches parts of the city at workable speeds, mobile data is the fallback, and neither is fast by international standards. Power cuts happen. There is essentially no coworking aimed at foreigners. Dutch is the official language and the language of all administration, with Sranan Tongo as the common tongue between communities; English is spoken by younger people and in business but is not something to rely on. Anyone with Dutch will find Suriname dramatically easier than anyone without, which is the main practical filter here.
paramaribo.gettingAround: Paramaribo's historic centre is compact, flat and walkable, and the UNESCO-listed core of white wooden Dutch colonial buildings is genuinely the reason to be here. Minibuses and shared taxis cover the city cheaply. Most residents drive, on the left, in cars imported from Japan. Beyond the coastal strip the country is rainforest with almost no roads: the interior is reached by riverboat or light aircraft, and trips to the Upper Suriname River or Brownsberg are organised rather than improvised. Zanderij airport is an hour south with flights to Amsterdam, Miami and the region.
paramaribo.visas: Suriname introduced an e-visa and a tourist card system that most Western nationalities can use, typically granting ninety days, and the process is done online before travel rather than at the border. There is no remote work visa. Dutch nationals have easier access given the historic relationship. Extensions are handled locally through the immigration service. Yellow fever vaccination is required for arrivals from endemic countries and strongly advised regardless. Check the current requirement directly, since Suriname has changed its entry rules more than once in recent years. Anyone crossing overland to French Guiana or Guyana should check both sides separately, since the river crossings have their own rules and hours.
paramaribo.bestTime: Suriname has two dry seasons and two wet ones, which is unusual and worth planning around. The long dry season from August to November and the short one from February to April are the practical windows, with less rain and better river conditions for reaching the interior. Temperatures sit around thirty-one all year with humidity that never drops. The long rains from April to August make interior travel harder and the coast greyer. There are no hurricanes here: Suriname sits well south of the belt, which is a real advantage over the Caribbean islands.
paramaribo.prosCons: Paramaribo has a UNESCO World Heritage centre of white wooden Dutch buildings that looks like nowhere else in South America, a cathedral that is among the largest wooden structures in the western hemisphere, and a street where a mosque and a synagogue stand side by side and share a car park. The food and the ethnic mix are extraordinary for a country of 600,000 people, and rainforest covers most of it. Against that, Dutch is close to necessary, the internet is slow, the currency has been unstable, and there is no nomad presence whatsoever.
paramaribo.whoFor: Paramaribo suits a Dutch speaker, or someone willing to work in Dutch, who wants a genuinely unusual South American base at a very low cost and is interested in the interior. Anyone drawn to the mix of cultures will find more of it here per square kilometre than almost anywhere. It is a poor fit for anyone without Dutch, anyone whose work needs a fast connection, and anyone expecting the infrastructure of neighbouring Brazil. Getting to the rainforest requires organising a trip rather than a day out. It also suits anyone researching the Guianas, since Paramaribo is the most comfortable base of the three capitals and the easiest to reach from Europe.

roatan.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker on Roatan, which makes it one of the cheapest Caribbean islands anywhere and by a distance the cheapest with diving of this quality. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700, with West End and West Bay at the top of that and the eastern half of the island considerably below. Food from the mainland keeps grocery costs reasonable, though imported goods carry a markup. Honduras uses the lempira, but Roatan runs substantially on United States dollars and most prices are quoted in them. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
roatan.whereToWork: Roatan's connectivity is the weak point and it is the reason people either love the island or leave it. Fibre has reached West End and parts of the developed western half at speeds that work, but coverage is uneven, and power cuts are frequent enough that most established places run on an inverter or a generator. Mobile data from Tigo and Claro is the fallback. There is a small coworking presence in West End that grew out of the diving community. Anyone with a call-heavy schedule should test a specific property for a week before committing to a month.
roatan.gettingAround: Roatan is a long thin island, about fifty kilometres end to end, with one main road running its length. West End is walkable and is where most visitors base themselves, a single street of dive shops and restaurants along the water. Collectivo taxis run the main road cheaply and are the standard way to move; private taxis cost several times more and the difference is worth understanding before getting in. Scooters and rented cars work for the eastern half. The airport is near Coxen Hole with direct flights to Houston, Miami and mainland Honduras, plus a ferry to La Ceiba.
roatan.visas: Honduras has no remote work visa. It belongs to the CA-4 agreement with Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua, which grants most Western nationalities ninety days across all four countries combined rather than ninety days in each, a detail that catches out anyone planning a regional loop. Extensions of up to ninety further days can be applied for in Roatan or on the mainland. Leaving to Belize or Costa Rica resets the clock; leaving to Guatemala does not. Anyone planning a long stay should understand the CA-4 rule properly before arriving.
roatan.bestTime: March to September is the drier half and the best for diving, with calm water, visibility often over thirty metres and daytime temperatures around thirty-one. October to February is the wet season, with heavier rain and occasional cold fronts from the north that stir up the sea. The Atlantic hurricane season runs June to November and Roatan is exposed; Hurricane Mitch in 1998 and the 2020 storms Eta and Iota all affected the island. Whale sharks pass Utila, the next island west, between roughly February and April, which is the trip most divers here add.
roatan.prosCons: Roatan sits on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest in the world, and is the cheapest place on earth to get a diving certification, which is why a diving community has grown here rather than a nomad one. Costs are very low, English is widely spoken because of the island's Bay Islands history, and the water is exceptional. Against that, the internet is genuinely unreliable, Honduras has one of the higher homicide rates in the Americas even though Roatan itself is far calmer than the mainland, and the island's development has been fast and largely unplanned.
roatan.whoFor: Roatan suits a diver on a budget whose work survives a patchy connection, and it suits anyone who wants to spend three months getting qualified rather than three days. The community around the dive shops in West End is real and easy to join, which is unusual in the Caribbean. It is a poor fit for anyone with a demanding call schedule, anyone who wants a city, and anyone planning a long Central American loop without understanding the CA-4 rule. The reef is the reason to be here and it is worth the compromises.

sanpedrobelize.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in San Pedro, which is expensive for Central America and reflects an island where everything arrives by boat or plane. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300, with anything on the beach or north of the bridge at the top of that. Groceries cost considerably more than on the Belizean mainland, which is a short flight away and where many residents shop deliberately. The Belize dollar is pegged at two to the United States dollar and both circulate interchangeably. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
sanpedrobelize.whereToWork: San Pedro's connectivity is adequate rather than good: fibre from Belize Telemedia reaches much of the town at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the island, but both are expensive relative to what they deliver and outages happen. Power cuts are not rare. There is a small coworking presence and a scattering of cafes used to remote workers, growing out of the Work Where You Vacation programme. English is the official language of Belize, the only country in Central America where that is true, which removes the friction that Spanish-speaking neighbours carry.
sanpedrobelize.gettingAround: There are almost no cars on Ambergris Caye. Golf carts are the transport, and renting one is the first thing most arrivals do; the town itself is small enough to walk. Three sand and concrete streets run parallel to the beach, and the island stretches north over a bridge into quieter, more expensive territory. Water taxis run to Caye Caulker and to Belize City, and light aircraft fly to the mainland in fifteen minutes. Everything on the reef, from Hol Chan to the Blue Hole, is reached by boat, and the Blue Hole is a long day trip rather than a morning.
sanpedrobelize.visas: Belize's Work Where You Vacation programme grants a six-month remote work stay to people employed outside the country who can show an annual income of around $75,000 and hold health insurance, with a fee of roughly $500 for an individual. It is not renewable in place. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for thirty days on arrival, extendable monthly at an immigration office for a fee, which many long-stay visitors use instead of the formal programme. Belize is not part of the CA-4 agreement, so time here does not count against a Guatemalan or Honduran allowance.
sanpedrobelize.bestTime: Late November to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, low humidity, and the calmest water for diving and snorkelling. It is also the busy and expensive half. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season, and Belize is exposed; the island has been evacuated more than once. September and October are the wettest, quietest and cheapest. Sargassum seaweed has become a recurring problem on this coast between roughly April and August, and how much of it lands varies enormously year to year. The whale sharks that draw divers to Gladden Spit further south run from roughly March to June, which is a separate trip from the island.
sanpedrobelize.prosCons: San Pedro puts you on the Belize Barrier Reef with Hol Chan Marine Reserve and Shark Ray Alley twenty minutes offshore and the Great Blue Hole reachable in a day, in the only English-speaking country in Central America, with a six-month remote work visa and golf carts instead of traffic. The Maya sites of the mainland are a short flight away. Against that, it is expensive for the region, the internet is mediocre, the island is small and heavily touristed, and the sargassum seasons of recent years have been genuinely bad.
sanpedrobelize.whoFor: San Pedro suits a diver or snorkeller who wants the reef and English in the same place, and who can absorb prices closer to the Caribbean than to Central America. It works well for the six months the visa offers. It is a poor fit for anyone on a Central American budget, for whom the mainland or Caye Caulker will go much further, and for anyone whose work needs a reliable connection. Anyone weighing it against Caye Caulker should know that Caulker is cheaper, smaller and slower, which is the whole difference.

chisinau.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Chisinau, which makes it the cheapest capital in Europe by most measures. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $250 to $450, with the centre and Botanica at the upper end and the Soviet-era districts well below. Food is inexpensive and Moldova grows most of it: the markets are genuinely cheap and the wine is absurdly so, since this is a country with more vineyard per head than almost anywhere. Utilities in winter are the one line that rises sharply. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
chisinau.whereToWork: Moldova's internet is its standout practical advantage: the country has consistently ranked among the fastest and cheapest in the world for fixed broadband, and gigabit fibre in Chisinau costs a fraction of what it does in western Europe. Mobile data is similarly cheap and fast. There is a real coworking scene, driven by an IT sector that the Moldova IT Park tax regime has deliberately grown, and desks are inexpensive. Power is reliable, though the country's energy dependence has been a live political issue since 2022. Russian and Romanian are both widely spoken; English is limited outside the technology sector.
chisinau.gettingAround: Chisinau is flat, laid out on a Russian imperial grid, and the centre around Stefan cel Mare boulevard is easily walkable. Trolleybuses and minibuses cover the city for a few cents and run frequently. Taxis and ride-hailing are cheap. The city is compact enough that most people do not need a car. Chisinau airport has connections across Europe, though the choice narrowed after Ukrainian airspace closed and routes rerouted. Cricova and Milestii Mici, the underground wine cities, are half an hour out, and Transnistria, the unrecognised breakaway region, is an hour east and requires its own consideration.
chisinau.visas: Moldova gives most Western nationalities ninety days visa-free within any hundred and eighty, which is the standard European arrangement. There is no digital nomad visa, though the Moldova IT Park regime offers a flat seven per cent tax on turnover to registered technology companies, which some remote workers use by incorporating locally. Longer stays run through a residence permit, applied for at the Bureau for Migration, which requires a local basis such as employment, study or property. Moldova is an EU candidate country and its rules are moving, so confirm the current position directly.
chisinau.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable half, with warm dry summers reaching the high twenties and long evenings. Late September and early October are the best of the year, when the wine harvest brings the National Wine Day festival to the main square and the countryside is at its most attractive. Winter runs from December to February and is properly cold, sitting around freezing with snow, and the shoulder months of March and November are grey and wet. Moldova has a genuine continental climate rather than a Mediterranean one, which surprises people who place it further south than it is.
chisinau.prosCons: Chisinau is the cheapest capital in Europe with some of the fastest and cheapest internet anywhere, a real IT sector, and a wine country on its doorstep that includes the largest underground cellar on earth at Milestii Mici. It is safe, walkable and almost entirely undiscovered by remote workers. Against that, English is limited, the city is architecturally plain outside a few streets, there is no nomad community to speak of, and Moldova's position next to Ukraine is a live geopolitical consideration that anyone planning a long stay should think about rather than ignore.
chisinau.whoFor: Chisinau suits someone who wants European time zones, gigabit fibre and very low costs, and who does not need a scene or English to get by. Anyone with Russian or Romanian will find it dramatically easier. It works well for a ninety-day stretch, which is what the visa-free allowance gives. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a nomad community or a beautiful city, and anyone considering it should read current guidance given the war in Ukraine next door. The wine alone justifies a visit in September. It also suits anyone curious about a country almost nobody visits, since Moldova receives fewer tourists than any other country in Europe.

dushanbe.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Dushanbe, which is among the lowest figures on this site. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $200 to $400, with the centre near Rudaki Avenue at the top of that. Food from the bazaars is very cheap and the produce, particularly the fruit, is famously good; Tajikistan grows apricots, melons and pomegranates that the whole region buys. Imported goods and anything electronic are expensive and hard to find. The somoni is stable but not freely convertible outside the country. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
dushanbe.whereToWork: Dushanbe's connectivity is the real constraint: Tajikistan has among the slowest and most expensive internet in the region, the state controls the backbone, and access has been restricted during politically sensitive periods. Fibre reaches parts of the capital at modest speeds and mobile data is the common fallback. Power supply in the capital is reliable, though the rest of the country still sees winter rationing. There is essentially no coworking. Russian is the working language of business and Tajik of daily life; English is rare. Anyone planning to work here should treat the connection as the thing to verify first.
dushanbe.gettingAround: Dushanbe is a low-rise city laid out along Rudaki Avenue, a long tree-lined boulevard that most of the centre hangs off, and the walkable core is genuinely pleasant with fountains and parks along its length. Marshrutka minibuses and buses cover the city for very little, and taxis are cheap and usually unmetered, so agree the fare first. Dushanbe airport has connections to Istanbul, Dubai, Moscow and the region. The Pamir Highway, the second-highest road in the world, starts here and runs east towards the Wakhan Corridor and Kyrgyzstan, which is why most foreign visitors come at all.
dushanbe.visas: Tajikistan operates an e-visa that most nationalities can obtain online in a few days, typically valid for forty-five to sixty days, and it is one of the more straightforward systems in Central Asia. There is no remote work visa. Anyone intending to travel the Pamir Highway needs an additional GBAO permit for the Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region, which can be requested with the e-visa application and is checked at road posts. Registration with the authorities is required for stays beyond a set period, usually handled by the hotel. Rules here change, so confirm directly before booking.
dushanbe.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the comfortable windows, with warm dry days and the mountains accessible. Dushanbe sits low at around 800 metres and its summers are hot, regularly above thirty-five degrees in July and August, though the dry air makes that more bearable than the number suggests. Winter is cold and grey with snow, and the air quality in the capital drops sharply as coal heating comes on. The Pamir Highway season is short, roughly June to September, and the passes are closed by snow outside it.
dushanbe.prosCons: Dushanbe is the gateway to the Pamirs, which is one of the great mountain regions on earth and almost entirely unvisited, and the city itself is greener and more pleasant than its reputation, with a genuinely walkable central boulevard. Costs are among the lowest anywhere and the fruit is remarkable. Against that, the internet is slow and politically controlled, English is rare, there is no nomad presence at all, air quality in winter is poor, and Tajikistan is an authoritarian state where political topics are best left alone. The city was also rebuilt on a Soviet plan with the widest boulevards in Central Asia, which makes it feel larger and emptier than its population.
dushanbe.whoFor: Dushanbe suits a traveller heading into the Pamirs who needs a base to arrange permits, buy supplies and rest, rather than a place to sit and work for months. Anyone with Russian will find it far easier. It is a poor fit for anyone whose work depends on a fast or uncensored connection, which is the honest disqualifier for most remote workers. Come for the mountains, plan the connection around what the country actually offers, and time it for the short Pamir season. Anyone attempting the Pamir Highway should also plan the GBAO permit and the vehicle before arriving, since neither is quick to arrange once here.

bandarseribegawan.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Bandar Seri Begawan, which is moderate for Southeast Asia and reflects an oil state with subsidised fuel and no income tax. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Food is inexpensive, particularly at the night markets and the Gadong food court, and Brunei's cooking sits between Malay and Bornean traditions. Petrol costs a fraction of the regional price. There is no alcohol spend because there is no legal alcohol sale, which removes a line most budgets carry. The Brunei dollar is pegged one to one with the Singapore dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
bandarseribegawan.whereToWork: Brunei's connectivity is good: fibre reaches most of the developed area at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, underwritten by a state that can afford the infrastructure. Power is entirely reliable. There is very little coworking, since the country has almost no visiting professional population, so remote work happens from apartments and the cafes around Gadong. English is widely spoken and is a language of instruction and business, which makes Brunei one of the easier places in the region to operate in. The country runs on the same time as Singapore and Kuala Lumpur.
bandarseribegawan.gettingAround: Bandar Seri Begawan is small and the centre around the Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque is walkable, but the country assumes a car and public transport is thin: buses exist and are infrequent, and there is no rail. Petrol is so cheap that everyone drives. Water taxis cross to Kampong Ayer, the water village of stilted houses that has stood on the river for centuries and still holds thousands of people, and they cost almost nothing. Brunei airport has connections across the region. Ulu Temburong National Park, primary rainforest reached by longboat, is the country's main draw and takes a full day.
bandarseribegawan.visas: Brunei gives visa-free entry to most Western nationalities, typically thirty days for British citizens and ninety for some others, granted on arrival, and the rules vary more by nationality than in most countries so check yours specifically. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require an employment pass tied to a local sponsor. Visitors should understand that Brunei applies Sharia law, that alcohol cannot be sold although non-Muslims may import a small personal allowance, and that public behaviour standards are stricter than elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Anyone travelling on to Sabah or Sarawak should note that Brunei splits Malaysian Borneo in two, so the overland route crosses several borders in a day.
bandarseribegawan.bestTime: Brunei is equatorial and hot all year, around thirty-two degrees every month with high humidity, so the calendar turns on rain rather than temperature. January to May is the drier half and the better window, particularly for the rainforest at Ulu Temburong, where the canopy walkway and river journeys depend on water levels and weather. The wetter months from September to January bring heavy afternoon downpours. Ramadan changes daily life substantially, with restaurants closed during daylight and a quieter public rhythm, and it is worth knowing which weeks it falls in.
bandarseribegawan.prosCons: Brunei is one of the safest countries in the world, has some of the best-preserved primary rainforest in Borneo an hour from its capital, a water village that is a living settlement rather than an exhibit, and infrastructure paid for by oil. English works everywhere and there is no income tax. Against that, there is no nightlife of any kind, no alcohol, no nomad community, very little to do after dark, and a legal and social framework considerably stricter than its neighbours. It is quiet in a way that suits few people for long.
bandarseribegawan.whoFor: Bandar Seri Begawan suits someone who wants a very safe, very quiet, English-speaking base in Borneo with rainforest close by, and who does not drink or mind that nobody else can. It works well for a few weeks built around Ulu Temburong and the water village rather than as a long stay. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting nightlife, company or a scene, and anyone travelling with a partner should understand the country's laws on personal conduct before arriving rather than after. It also suits anyone with business in Borneo, since Brunei is the most comfortable and best-connected base on the island's northern coast.

dili.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Dili, which is moderate for Southeast Asia and higher than a country this poor suggests, because Dili's rental market was shaped by the international missions that followed independence. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Timor-Leste uses the United States dollar as its currency, so nothing needs converting, though the coins are local. Food from the markets is cheap and the coffee, which is the country's main export outside oil, is excellent and absurdly inexpensive. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
dili.whereToWork: Dili's connectivity is poor and it is the main practical obstacle: the country relies on a limited submarine connection, prices are high relative to speed, and outages are common. Mobile data from Telkomcel and Telemor is the usual fallback. Power cuts happen regularly and anyone whose work cannot pause needs a building with backup. There is essentially no coworking. Tetum and Portuguese are the official languages, Indonesian and English are widely understood, and English is more common than in most of the region because of the long international presence. Anyone working with Australia will find the time zone useful, since Dili sits within an hour of the eastern Australian working day.
dili.gettingAround: Dili is a small coastal capital laid out along the waterfront, and the central strip from the Government Palace east towards the Cristo Rei statue is walkable. Microlet minibuses cover the city for a few cents and taxis are cheap. Most expatriates drive, and a four-wheel drive is needed for anywhere outside the capital, because Timor-Leste's roads are mountainous and in poor condition; the drive to Baucau or the south coast takes far longer than the distance suggests. The ferry to Atauro Island takes a couple of hours and is the trip most visitors come for.
dili.visas: Timor-Leste grants a thirty-day visa on arrival at Dili airport to most nationalities for a fee of around $30, and it is straightforward. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are available from the immigration service in Dili, and a longer stay can be arranged through a business or work visa with local sponsorship. Portuguese citizens and some others have separate arrangements. The land border with Indonesian West Timor has its own requirements and is not the same process as arriving by air, so check that route separately if planning it.
dili.bestTime: May to November is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty-one, clear water for diving and the roads passable. December to April is the wet season, when heavy rain makes the mountain roads difficult and the sea murkier. Diving is the reason many people come and the visibility is best between roughly June and September. The waters around Atauro Island were found in a 2016 survey to have the highest average reef fish diversity recorded anywhere in the world, which is not a claim the country makes loudly enough.
dili.prosCons: Timor-Leste has the most biodiverse reef waters ever surveyed half an hour off its capital, mountains rising to nearly three thousand metres, coffee that is among the best in Asia, and almost no tourists at all. It is the youngest country in Asia and its independence history is recent and openly told, at the Chega and Resistance museums. Against that, the internet is genuinely bad, the roads are worse, medical facilities are limited, prices are higher than the region for what you get, and there is no nomad infrastructure whatsoever.
dili.whoFor: Dili suits a diver, or someone working in development or conservation, who wants somewhere genuinely unvisited and whose work tolerates a poor connection. Atauro is the reason to come and it is extraordinary. It is a poor fit for anyone with a call-heavy schedule, anyone on a tight budget expecting Southeast Asian prices, and anyone who wants infrastructure. The country is easier for an English speaker than most of its neighbours, which is the one thing that consistently surprises people who go. It also suits anyone interested in how a country builds itself from nothing, since the institutions here are younger than most of the people using them.

thimphu.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,500 a month as a solo remote worker in Thimphu, and understand that the figure is dominated by one line rather than by rent. Bhutan charges most foreign visitors a Sustainable Development Fee of $100 per person per night, reduced from $200 in September 2023, which is roughly $3,000 over a thirty-day month before accommodation, food or anything else. Discount structures for longer stays have been introduced and changed more than once. Rent and food are cheap by comparison: a flat runs a few hundred dollars and eating locally costs very little. Indian, Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals pay a far lower fee. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
thimphu.whereToWork: Thimphu's connectivity is adequate rather than good: fibre reaches parts of the city at modest speeds, mobile data from Bhutan Telecom and TashiCell covers the valley, and the whole country runs on a limited international link routed through India. Outages happen. There is no coworking. English is a language of instruction in Bhutanese schools and is widely spoken in the capital, which makes Bhutan far easier to operate in than its isolation suggests. The country runs six hours ahead of London and thirty minutes ahead of India, which is one of the world's few half-hour offsets.
thimphu.gettingAround: Thimphu is the only national capital in the world with no traffic lights: an intersection in the centre is directed by a policeman in a decorated booth, and an attempt to install lights was abandoned because people disliked them. The city sits in a north-south valley and the central grid is walkable. City buses and shared taxis are cheap. Paro, with the country's only international airport, is an hour away on a mountain road, and the approach into it is among the most demanding commercial landings anywhere, flown only by a small number of certified pilots. Roads elsewhere are slow and winding.
thimphu.visas: Bhutan does not operate an ordinary tourist visa in the way other countries do. Almost every foreign visitor needs a visa applied for online through the Department of Immigration, costing around $40, and must pay the Sustainable Development Fee for every night of the stay. Independent travel has been permitted since 2022, so a guide is no longer mandatory outside protected areas, which was a substantial change. Indian nationals enter under a separate arrangement with a much lower fee. There is no remote work visa and no framework for long stays outside employment or study.
thimphu.bestTime: March to May and September to November are the two good windows. Spring brings rhododendron across the hills and clear mountain views; autumn is drier still and holds the tsechu festival season, when masked dances are performed in the dzongs and the Thimphu tsechu fills the capital for three days. Thimphu sits at around 2,300 metres, so summers are mild rather than hot, reaching the mid twenties, and the monsoon from June to August brings cloud that hides the mountains. Winter is cold, dropping below freezing at night, with occasional snow and the clearest air of the year.
thimphu.prosCons: Bhutan is the only country that measures itself on Gross National Happiness rather than output, the only one that is carbon negative, and the only one whose constitution requires that sixty per cent of its land stay forested. The dzongs, the Tiger's Nest monastery above Paro and the Buddha Dordenma above Thimphu are genuinely extraordinary, and the country is safe and orderly. Against that, the Sustainable Development Fee makes a long stay expensive in a way no other country matches, the internet is mediocre, there is no nomad presence, and nightlife is essentially nonexistent.
thimphu.whoFor: Thimphu suits someone taking a deliberate, budgeted few weeks in a country that has decided not to compete on price, and who wants Himalayan trekking and living Buddhist practice rather than a cheap base. Anyone interested in how a small state manages tourism deliberately will find Bhutan the case study. It is a poor fit for anyone counting costs, since the nightly fee dwarfs everything else, and for anyone wanting a long stay, which the system is designed to prevent. Do the arithmetic on the fee before anything else. Anyone hoping to trek the Snowman Trek or the Trans Bhutan Trail should build the fee into the trip length from the start, since both take weeks.

nosybe.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker on Nosy Be, which is cheap by international standards though noticeably more expensive than mainland Madagascar, because the island runs on tourism. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $500, with Ambatoloaka and the west coast beaches at the top of that and Hell-Ville, the main town, below it. Food from the market is very cheap and the seafood is excellent. Imported goods carry a heavy markup on an island this remote. The ariary has been weak for years, which helps a visitor and hurts everyone living here. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
nosybe.whereToWork: Nosy Be's connectivity is poor and it is the main constraint on working here. Mobile data from Telma, Orange and Airtel is the primary connection for most people and speeds vary by hour and location; fixed lines exist in a few hotels and better guesthouses. Power cuts are routine across Madagascar and the island is no exception, so an inverter or a generator is standard in anything aimed at visitors. There is no coworking. French is the language of business and administration, Malagasy of daily life, and English is limited to the tourism trade.
nosybe.gettingAround: Nosy Be is about twenty-five kilometres across and Hell-Ville, properly Andoany, is the administrative town at its southeast corner. Taxis, mostly ageing Renaults, and taxi-brousse minibuses cover the island cheaply, and scooters are the common rental. The roads are variable and get worse in the wet season. Fascene airport has seasonal direct flights from Milan and Paris and connections through Antananarivo, Nairobi and Reunion, which makes the island considerably easier to reach than most of Madagascar. Boats run constantly to Nosy Komba, Nosy Tanikely and the smaller islands, which is what most visitors come for.
nosybe.visas: Madagascar grants a visa on arrival to most nationalities at the main airports, and since 2023 stays of up to fifteen days have been free of the visa fee, with thirty, sixty and ninety-day options available for a charge. The process is done at the airport and is straightforward, though queues can be long. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays run through a residence permit applied for locally, which takes time and local support. Check the current fee structure directly, since Madagascar has revised it more than once in recent years.
nosybe.bestTime: April to November is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty and calm seas. The wet season from December to March brings heavy rain and the cyclone risk, and Madagascar is one of the most cyclone-exposed countries in the world; the northwest coast is hit less often than the east but is not immune. The wildlife calendar is the other consideration: humpback whales pass between roughly July and September and whale sharks arrive from September to December, which is the reason many divers time a trip for the end of the dry season.
nosybe.prosCons: Nosy Be is the easiest way into Madagascar's wildlife, with lemurs in the Lokobe reserve on the island itself, whale sharks and humpbacks offshore in season, and Nosy Tanikely's marine reserve half an hour away by boat. The island grows ylang-ylang and smells of it. It is warm, cheap and reachable directly from Europe in season. Against that, the internet is bad, power cuts are routine, French is close to necessary, Madagascar's poverty is severe and visible, and petty crime around the tourist areas requires ordinary caution. The island is also considerably easier to reach than the rest of Madagascar, which is either its main convenience or the reason it feels less like the country.
nosybe.whoFor: Nosy Be suits a diver or naturalist with some French whose work tolerates a weak connection, and who wants Madagascar's wildlife without the long overland journeys the mainland demands. It works well for a few weeks in the dry season. It is a poor fit for anyone with a call-heavy schedule, anyone without French, and anyone expecting the infrastructure that the direct European flights might imply. The rest of Madagascar is a different and much harder trip, which is worth understanding before treating this island as representative. Anyone planning to continue to Antananarivo or the southern reserves should treat that as a separate expedition rather than a side trip from here.

blantyre.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Blantyre, which is low even by regional standards. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450, with Nyambadwe and Sunnyside at the top of that and the areas towards Limbe cheaper. Food from the markets costs very little and Malawi grows most of what it eats. Imported goods are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable, since the country has repeatedly run short of foreign exchange. The kwacha was devalued by around forty-four per cent in late 2023, so any figure in it dates fast. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
blantyre.whereToWork: Blantyre's connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of the city and works reasonably where it exists, and mobile data from TNM and Airtel is the common fallback, though Malawian data prices are high relative to income. Power cuts are frequent and scheduled load shedding is a fact of life, so anything serious runs on an inverter or a generator. There is a small coworking presence serving local business rather than visitors. English is an official language and the medium of education and business, which removes the language friction entirely and is Malawi's clearest practical advantage.
blantyre.gettingAround: Blantyre spreads across hills, with the older commercial centre and the separate town of Limbe forming a twin core about eight kilometres apart. Minibuses cover both cheaply and are how most people move; they fill before they leave. Taxis and a growing number of ride-hailing options work in the centre. Most expatriates drive, on the left. Chileka airport is twenty minutes out with regional connections through Addis Ababa, Nairobi and Johannesburg. Mount Mulanje is an hour and a half east and Lake Malawi's southern shore about three hours north, which is what most weekends here are for.
blantyre.visas: Malawi requires a visa of most nationalities, obtained through an e-visa system before travel or on arrival at the main entry points, typically costing around $50 for a thirty-day single entry with longer options available. The process is straightforward by regional standards. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at an immigration office in Blantyre or Lilongwe. Business and employment permits require local sponsorship and take considerably longer. Malawi has changed its visa fees more than once, so confirm the current schedule before travelling. Anyone travelling on to Zambia or Tanzania overland should check those requirements separately, since neither shares an arrangement with Malawi.
blantyre.bestTime: May to August is the cool dry season and the most comfortable window, with daytime temperatures in the low twenties at Blantyre's altitude and cold nights. September to November is hot and dry, building towards the rains, and can be genuinely uncomfortable in the lowlands. The wet season from December to April brings heavy rain that makes some roads difficult and the mountain hard going, though it is also when the country is greenest. Mount Mulanje, whose Sapitwa peak at just over 3,000 metres is the highest in central Africa, is best climbed between May and October.
blantyre.prosCons: Malawi is called the warm heart of Africa and the reputation for friendliness is genuinely earned.
