Blantyre has Mount Mulanje on its doorstep, Lake Malawi within a morning's drive with freshwater snorkelling among hundreds of endemic cichlid species, and living costs among the lowest anywhere. English works everywhere. Against that, the power supply is unreliable, the economy has been under severe strain with recurrent fuel and foreign exchange shortages, medical facilities are limited, and there is no nomad community and very little visitor infrastructure in the city itself. Blantyre is also the older of Malawi's two main cities and carries the colonial architecture that Lilongwe, built as a capital in the 1970s, does not.
blantyre.whoFor: Blantyre suits someone who wants an English-speaking African base at a very low cost, with real mountains and a remarkable lake within reach, and whose work can survive load shedding. Anyone in development, conservation or health will find a substantial professional network here, since Malawi hosts a great deal of that work. It is a poor fit for anyone needing reliable power or a foreign community. Anyone staying should sort out a power backup and a plan for the fuel shortages before they become urgent rather than after. It also suits anyone who intends to climb Mulanje properly, since the massif rewards a week of hut-to-hut walking far more than a day trip.

victoriafalls.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Victoria Falls, which is high for Zimbabwe and reflects a town whose entire economy is tourism. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Food and goods are priced for visitors in the centre and considerably less in the residential areas of Chinotimba. Zimbabwe's currency history is its own subject: the country uses United States dollars for most transactions alongside the ZiG, introduced in April 2024 after a series of failed currencies, and prices in dollars are the reliable ones. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
victoriafalls.whereToWork: Victoria Falls has better connectivity than most of Zimbabwe because tourism demands it: fibre reaches the town centre and the lodges at workable speeds, and mobile data from Econet and NetOne covers the area, though Zimbabwean data prices are high. Power cuts are a national problem driven partly by low water at Kariba, and load shedding is routine, so lodges and serious businesses run on generators or solar. There is no coworking. English is an official language and universally used, which makes Zimbabwe one of the easier African countries to work from.
victoriafalls.gettingAround: Victoria Falls is a small town and its centre is walkable, with the falls themselves a fifteen-minute walk from the main street, though warthogs and the occasional elephant on the roads are a genuine consideration rather than a joke. Taxis and shuttles cover the lodges. The Victoria Falls Bridge crosses to Zambia and Livingstone, and walking across it is straightforward with the right visa. Victoria Falls airport has direct flights from Johannesburg, Nairobi, Addis Ababa and Cape Town. Hwange National Park, one of Africa's great elephant reserves, is two hours south.
victoriafalls.visas: Zimbabwe issues visas on arrival to most nationalities at the airport and land borders, typically around $30 for a single entry and $45 for a double. The more useful option here is the KAZA UniVisa, roughly $50, which covers both Zimbabwe and Zambia for thirty days and allows unlimited crossings between them plus a day trip into Botswana at Kazungula, which matters a great deal in a town where the falls are split across a border. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require an extension applied for locally.
victoriafalls.bestTime: The falls are a different sight in every season and there is no single best time, only a choice. February to May is peak flow, when the Zambezi is at its highest and the spray is so heavy that the falls are often invisible from close range and the viewing paths are drenched. June to August is the balanced window, with strong water and clear views, and it is the busiest. September to December is low water, when the eastern cataracts can dry to bare rock but the Devil's Pool on the Zambian side opens and the rafting below the gorge is at its best.
victoriafalls.prosCons: Victoria Falls is a kilometre and a half of river dropping a hundred metres into a gorge, twice the height of Niagara, and living beside it does not stop being remarkable. Hwange and Chobe are both within reach, the rafting below the falls is world class, and English is universal. Against that, the town is entirely a tourism economy with the prices that implies, Zimbabwe's power and currency problems are constant background noise, there is no nomad community, and everything beyond the falls and the parks requires organising a trip.
victoriafalls.whoFor: Victoria Falls suits someone who wants to be beside one of the natural wonders of the world with a national park two hours away, and whose work tolerates load shedding. It works well for a month or two rather than a year, since the town is small and the novelty of the falls is not infinite. It is a poor fit for anyone on a tight budget, since tourism pricing applies to residents too, and anyone needing reliable power. The UniVisa makes treating Livingstone as the same town entirely practical.

lusaka.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Lusaka, which is moderate for southern Africa. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $600, with Kabulonga, Rhodes Park and the areas around the embassies at the top of that and the townships far below. Food from the markets is inexpensive and Zambia grows its own maize, vegetables and beef. Imported goods carry a markup and fuel prices have been volatile. The kwacha has weakened substantially over the last decade, which is worth knowing when reading older figures. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
lusaka.whereToWork: Lusaka's connectivity is reasonable: fibre reaches the better residential and commercial areas at workable speeds and mobile data from MTN, Airtel and Zamtel is widely used. The serious problem is electricity. Zambia depends on hydropower from Kariba, and the drought of 2024 pushed the country into load shedding measured in many hours a day, which is the single most important practical fact about working here right now. Anything serious runs on solar and batteries. There is a small coworking scene serving local startups. English is the official language and used throughout.
lusaka.gettingAround: Lusaka spreads out along a few main arteries, with Cairo Road as the old commercial spine and the newer malls and offices scattered east and south. It is not a walkable city and the distances are real. Blue minibuses cover the routes cheaply and are how most people move, and ride-hailing works in the central areas. Most expatriates drive, on the left. Kenneth Kaunda airport is half an hour out with connections through Johannesburg, Nairobi, Addis Ababa and Dubai. South Luangwa, which invented the walking safari, is a long drive or a short flight east.
lusaka.visas: Zambia removed visa requirements for citizens of a substantial list of countries in 2022, including the United Kingdom, most of the European Union and the United States, so many visitors now enter free for up to ninety days. Everyone else uses the e-visa system or obtains one on arrival. The KAZA UniVisa, covering Zambia and Zimbabwe for thirty days, is the practical option for anyone based around Livingstone. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a permit through employment or investment, applied for locally. Confirm the current list, since it has changed.
lusaka.bestTime: May to August is the cool dry season and the most comfortable, with daytime temperatures in the mid twenties at Lusaka's 1,280 metres and cold nights. September and October are hot and dry, reaching the mid thirties, and are also the best months for wildlife viewing as animals concentrate around the remaining water in South Luangwa. The wet season from November to April brings heavy afternoon storms and turns the country green, and many safari camps close entirely between January and March because the roads become impassable. Anyone planning a safari should note that the walking-safari season in South Luangwa runs roughly June to October and the camps simply close outside it.
lusaka.prosCons: Lusaka is a functional, safe-enough African capital with English throughout, a mild highland climate, and access to South Luangwa and the Lower Zambezi, two of the best and least crowded safari destinations on the continent. Costs are moderate and the country is politically stable by regional standards. Against that, the load shedding driven by the Kariba drought is severe and has been for over a year, the city itself is sprawling and short on character, there is no nomad community, and petty crime requires ordinary urban caution. The city is also the natural hub for the region, with better flight connections than Lilongwe, Harare or Gaborone and a more stable currency than Zimbabwe's.
lusaka.whoFor: Lusaka suits someone using Zambia as a base for the parks rather than for the capital, who needs English and a stable country, and who will invest in solar and batteries before anything else. Anyone in conservation, mining or development will find real professional depth. It is a poor fit for anyone whose work cannot survive scheduled outages, and for anyone wanting a walkable or characterful city. Treat Livingstone and the falls, six hours south, as the other half of what the country offers. Anyone weighing Lusaka against Livingstone should know that Livingstone is smaller and prettier and Lusaka is where the work and the flights actually are.

douala.costOfLiving: Budget around $950 a month as a solo remote worker in Douala, which is moderate for central Africa though the city is more expensive than its neighbours because it is the region's main port. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $600, with Bonapriso and Bonanjo at the top of that and the outer quarters well below. Food from the markets is cheap and Cameroonian cooking is among the best in the region. Imported goods carry a heavy markup. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes currency volatility entirely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
douala.whereToWork: Douala's connectivity is workable rather than good: fibre reaches parts of the commercial districts, mobile data from MTN and Orange is the usual answer, and speeds are modest for the price. Power cuts are frequent and any serious office runs a generator. There is a small startup and coworking scene, more developed than the country's profile suggests, concentrated around Bonanjo and Akwa. French is the language of everything in Douala, which sits in the francophone Littoral region; English is Cameroon's other official language but you will not get far on it here.
douala.gettingAround: Douala is a large, hot, congested port city and it is not walkable in any meaningful sense. Yellow shared taxis are the standard way to move and cost very little, hailed by calling out your destination and a price. Motorcycle taxis, the bendskin, are faster and considerably more dangerous. Traffic is heavy and the rain floods the streets regularly. Douala airport has connections across Africa and to Paris and Brussels. Kribi, with beaches and the Lobe Falls that drop straight into the sea, is around three hours south and is the escape most residents take.
douala.visas: Cameroon requires a visa of almost all visitors, and since 2023 an e-visa system has replaced most consular applications, issued for thirty or ninety days with an approval usually returned within days. A yellow fever certificate is required on entry. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a residence permit arranged through an employer or a local sponsor. Anyone planning travel beyond Douala should read current government advice carefully: the Far North faces a Boko Haram insurgency and the Northwest and Southwest regions have been in armed conflict since 2017.
douala.bestTime: Douala sits just north of the equator on a wet coast and it is hot and humid all year, around thirty-one degrees with humidity that never drops. The calendar turns entirely on rain. December to February is the short dry season and by far the most comfortable window. The long rains from June to October are extraordinary: Douala is one of the wettest large cities in the world, and nearby Debundscha at the foot of Mount Cameroon is among the wettest places on earth. August is the peak and the city floods regularly.
douala.prosCons: Douala is the economic engine of central Africa, with a port that serves several landlocked countries, a food culture that is among the continent's best, real business energy, and the euro-pegged CFA franc removing currency risk. Kribi's beaches and Mount Cameroon are within a few hours. Against that, the climate is genuinely punishing, the city is congested and short on charm, French is essential, crime requires real caution, and the Anglophone conflict in the neighbouring Southwest region means the obvious excursions towards Buea and Limbe carry a security warning that should be read rather than assumed away.
douala.whoFor: Douala suits a French speaker with business in central Africa who needs the region's best flight connections and its main port, and who can handle the heat and the congestion. It is a working city rather than a destination. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, anyone sensitive to humidity, and anyone looking for a pleasant place to sit with a laptop, which Douala is not. Anyone planning to travel around Cameroon should read the current regional advisories properly before deciding where they can go. Anyone whose interest is Cameroon's landscape rather than its commerce should look at Yaounde or the west, since Douala is the port and behaves like one.

cotonou.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Cotonou, which is low even for West Africa. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with Haie Vive and Cadjehoun, the districts around the embassies and the airport, at the top of that and the inland quarters well below. Food from the markets is very cheap and Beninese cooking is good, built on maize, cassava, peanut sauces and grilled fish from the lagoon. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, so there is no currency risk and no black market rate to navigate. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
cotonou.whereToWork: Cotonou's connectivity is modest: fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data from MTN and Moov is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed as across West Africa. Power cuts are frequent and any serious business runs a generator. There is a small startup and coworking presence, helped by government efforts to position Benin as a digital services centre, though it serves locals rather than visitors. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, and English is genuinely rare, which is the main practical filter for working here.
cotonou.gettingAround: Cotonou is flat, spread between the Atlantic and Lake Nokoue, and it is not a walkable city. Zemidjan motorcycle taxis, recognisable by their yellow shirts, are the dominant transport and cost very little, though they demand a helmet and some nerve. Shared taxis cover longer routes. Traffic on the main axes is heavy. Cotonou airport has connections across West Africa and to Paris and Brussels. Ganvie, the stilt village of some twenty thousand people built out on the lake, is half an hour away by boat, and Ouidah, the historic centre of the slave trade and of Vodun, is an hour west.
cotonou.visas: Benin has one of the most open visa policies in Africa: since 2019 it has been visa-free for all African nationals, and everyone else uses a straightforward e-visa applied for online, typically thirty or ninety days, approved within a few days. There is no remote work visa. A yellow fever certificate is required on entry. Longer stays run through a residence permit applied for locally. Benin is a member of ECOWAS, so travel to Togo, Nigeria and Ghana is straightforward for regional nationals and needs separate arrangements for everyone else.
cotonou.bestTime: November to February is the main dry season and by far the best window, with less humidity and daytime temperatures around thirty-one. The harmattan blows Saharan dust south in December and January, which drops visibility and irritates anyone with a respiratory sensitivity. The long rains run from April to July and a shorter wet spell returns in September and October. Coastal humidity is constant regardless of season. The Vodun festival on the tenth of January at Ouidah is the country's largest event and draws practitioners from across the diaspora. Pendjari National Park in the far north is only reliably reachable in the dry months, which is another reason the calendar matters here.
cotonou.prosCons: Benin is where Vodun comes from, and it is a state religion here rather than a curiosity: the annual festival at Ouidah, the sacred forest at Kpasse and the Temple of Pythons are living practice. Ganvie on the lagoon is one of the most extraordinary settlements in Africa. Pendjari National Park in the north holds West Africa's best remaining wildlife. Costs are very low and the visa policy is open. Against that, French is essential, the internet is weak, power cuts are routine, and Cotonou itself is a hot, congested working city rather than an attractive one.
cotonou.whoFor: Cotonou suits a French speaker with an interest in West African history and religion, who wants a very cheap base with an open visa policy and can work through unreliable power. Anyone researching the slave trade, Vodun or the region's art will find Benin unusually rich. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, anyone needing reliable infrastructure, and anyone hoping for a beach city, since swimming off this coast is dangerous. Ouidah and Ganvie are the reasons to be here rather than Cotonou itself. It also suits anyone moving overland between Lagos and Accra, since Benin sits on that road and is the calmest stop along it.

mahe.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month as a solo remote worker on Mahe, which makes Seychelles one of the more expensive places in this batch and reflects an island nation that imports almost everything. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,400, with Beau Vallon and the northwest coast at the top of that and the areas around Victoria and the south considerably cheaper. Self-catering is what keeps a budget here in one piece: restaurant prices are set for resort guests, while the market in Victoria and the local takeaways are a different economy entirely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
mahe.whereToWork: Seychelles has better connectivity than its remoteness suggests: the country is served by submarine cable and fibre reaches most of Mahe at workable speeds, with mobile data from Cable and Wireless and Airtel covering the island. Prices are high. Power is reliable. There is very little coworking, so remote work happens from guesthouses and self-catering apartments. English is one of three official languages alongside French and Seychellois Creole, and it is used throughout government and business, which makes the country straightforward to operate in. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset convenient, since Seychelles sits two hours ahead of central European time for most of the year.
mahe.gettingAround: Mahe is about twenty-seven kilometres long with a mountainous spine, and Victoria, the smallest capital in Africa, sits on its northeast coast. Buses cover the island cheaply and frequently, and the network genuinely works, which is unusual for a small island and means a car is optional rather than essential. The coastal roads are narrow and the cross-island routes steep. The airport is ten minutes from Victoria with direct flights to Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa, Paris and Nairobi. Ferries run to Praslin and La Digue, the other main islands, in about an hour.
mahe.visas: Seychelles has the most open border policy in the world: it requires no visa of any nationality. Every visitor receives a visitor's permit on arrival, initially for up to three months, extendable up to a total of twelve months in any year on payment of a fee, provided you can show accommodation, means and a return ticket. There is no separate remote work visa because the ordinary permit already does the job. It is not a residence permit and does not allow working for a Seychellois employer, which is the one limit worth understanding.
mahe.bestTime: Seychelles is warm all year, around twenty-nine degrees every month, and the calendar is set by two trade winds. The southeast trades from May to September bring cooler, windier, drier weather, better hiking and good conditions for sailing, though seaweed collects on some southeastern beaches. The northwest trades from November to March bring warmer, calmer, wetter weather with the best diving visibility and the flattest sea. April and October are the transition months and the most settled of all. The islands sit outside the cyclone belt, which is a real advantage in this ocean.
mahe.prosCons: Seychelles has the granite boulder beaches that appear on every list of the world's best, an interior of mountain rainforest with the Vallee de Mai on Praslin holding the coco de mer palm found nowhere else, giant tortoises, and no visa requirement for anyone on earth. English works everywhere and the country is safe. Against that, it is expensive, the islands are small and quickly exhausted, there is no nomad community, and the economy is so dominated by high-end tourism that the middle of the market barely exists. Prices also vary far more by island than visitors expect, with La Digue and Praslin costing noticeably more than the south of Mahe.
mahe.whoFor: Mahe suits someone who wants extraordinary beaches and hiking with no visa paperwork at all, and who will self-cater rather than eat out. The twelve-month extendable permit is quietly one of the most generous arrangements anywhere for a long stay. It is a poor fit for anyone on a tight budget or anyone needing a professional community. Anyone staying a while should use the bus network and rent in the south rather than the northwest, which is where the price difference on this island actually lies. It also suits anyone who has been refused a visa elsewhere, since Seychelles is the one country on earth that asks for none from anybody.

apia.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Apia, which is moderate for the Pacific and lower than most of the region's capitals. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $400 to $700. Food from the market at Maketi Fou is cheap and Samoa grows taro, breadfruit and bananas in quantity; imported goods carry the heavy markup that every Pacific island pays for freight. The tala is stable. Fales, the open-sided beach huts let by families along the south coast, are a genuinely cheap way to stay outside the capital. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
apia.whereToWork: Samoa's connectivity improved substantially with the Tui-Samoa submarine cable in 2018, and fibre now reaches Apia at speeds that work, though prices are high and coverage thins outside the capital. Mobile data from Digicel and Vodafone covers the populated coast. Power cuts happen. There is essentially no coworking. English is an official language alongside Samoan and is used throughout government and business. Samoa moved across the international date line in 2011 to align with Australia and New Zealand, so it now sits a day ahead of American Samoa two hours away.
apia.gettingAround: Apia runs along a harbour on the north coast of Upolu and its centre is walkable, with the market, the flag-tiled Immaculate Conception cathedral and the waterfront all within twenty minutes. Brightly painted wooden buses cover the island cheaply on no fixed timetable and are an experience in themselves. Most residents drive, and Samoa switched from driving on the right to the left in 2009, which makes it one of very few countries ever to have done so. Faleolo airport is forty minutes west with flights to Auckland, Fiji and Sydney. The ferry to Savaii takes ninety minutes.
apia.visas: Samoa grants a free entry permit on arrival to citizens of most countries for up to ninety days, which is generous and requires only a passport, onward ticket and proof of accommodation. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for locally through the immigration office. Longer stays require a work or residence permit with local sponsorship. The simplicity of entry is one of Samoa's practical advantages over several of its Pacific neighbours, where the paperwork is heavier and the fees higher. Anyone island-hopping should note that American Samoa, two hours away by air, is United States territory and needs its own separate permission.
apia.bestTime: May to October is the dry season and the comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine, lower humidity and the calmest seas. November to April is the wet season and also the cyclone season, and Samoa sits in the belt; the islands have taken serious hits, most memorably Cyclone Evan in 2012. The 2009 tsunami, caused by an offshore earthquake, killed nearly two hundred people on the south coast, and evacuation routes are marked there for good reason. Independence celebrations at the start of June are the biggest event of the year.
apia.prosCons: Samoa is where fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, still orders daily life more visibly than tradition does almost anywhere: village councils, Sunday observance that closes the country, and a formality of manner that visitors notice within a day. The To Sua ocean trench, the Piula cave pool and the waterfalls of the south coast are remarkable, and Robert Louis Stevenson's house above Apia is a genuinely good museum. Against that, it is remote, expensive to reach, the internet is adequate rather than good, and Sunday closure catches out anyone who has not planned for it.
apia.whoFor: Apia suits someone who wants a Pacific base with real cultural depth rather than a resort, who is comfortable with a slow pace and with a country that stops entirely on Sundays. The ninety-day free entry makes a long stay unusually simple. It is a poor fit for anyone needing fast internet, nightlife or a professional network. Anyone coming should read a little about fa'a Samoa first, since the social rules here are more visible and more consequential than in most places visitors go. It also suits anyone drawn to Savaii, the larger and quieter island, which has the lava fields and blowholes and a fraction of the visitors.

nukualofa.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Nuku'alofa, which is moderate for the Pacific. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $350 to $650. Food from the Talamahu market is cheap and Tonga grows root crops, coconut and fruit in quantity, but almost everything else is imported and the freight cost shows on every shelf. The pa'anga is stable and remittances from Tongans abroad are a substantial part of the economy. Prices rose after the 2022 eruption and have not fully settled. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
nukualofa.whereToWork: Tonga's connectivity is the honest weak point and the reason the score here is low. The country depends on a single submarine cable, and when the Hunga Tonga eruption severed it in January 2022 the entire nation was cut off from the internet for weeks. The cable has been repaired and a backup arrangement exists, but the vulnerability is structural. Fibre reaches parts of Nuku'alofa and mobile data from Digicel and TCC is the fallback. Power cuts happen. There is no coworking. English is an official language alongside Tongan and is widely used.
nukualofa.gettingAround: Nuku'alofa sits on the north coast of Tongatapu, a flat coral island, and the centre around the market and the waterfront is walkable. Minibuses cover the island cheaply on loose schedules and taxis are inexpensive. Most residents drive, on the left. Fua'amotu airport is thirty minutes south with flights to Auckland, Sydney and Fiji. Ferries and small aircraft reach Vava'u and Ha'apai, the northern island groups, and Vava'u is where the sailing and most of the whale swimming happens, which is what brings most visitors to the country at all.
nukualofa.visas: Tonga grants a visitor's visa on arrival to citizens of most countries for thirty-one days, free of charge, extendable in-country up to six months for a fee. It is simple and requires a passport, onward ticket and proof of accommodation. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a business or residence visa with local sponsorship. Anyone planning to swim with humpbacks should know that the activity is licensed and regulated, and that operating outside a licensed tour is not permitted. Anyone arriving by yacht should clear in at Nuku'alofa, Vava'u or Ha'apai, since those are the designated ports of entry for the kingdom.
nukualofa.bestTime: May to October is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-six and lower humidity. It also contains the reason most people come: humpback whales migrate to Tongan waters to calve between roughly July and October, and Tonga is one of a very small number of places in the world where swimming with them is legal and regulated. November to April is the wet season and the cyclone season, and Tonga is exposed. The Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption and tsunami of January 2022 was among the most violent volcanic events ever recorded.
nukualofa.prosCons: Tonga is the only Pacific nation never colonised, still a kingdom, and the sense of a country running on its own terms is immediate. Swimming with humpback whales in Vava'u between July and October is something almost nowhere else permits. The Ha'apai group has genuinely empty islands. Against that, the internet is fragile in a way that has already cut the country off once, the infrastructure is limited, there is very little to do in Nuku'alofa itself, Sunday closes everything by law, and the cyclone and volcanic exposure are real.
nukualofa.whoFor: Nuku'alofa suits someone whose reason for coming is the whales, the sailing in Vava'u or the empty islands of Ha'apai, and who treats the capital as the way in rather than the destination. Work that tolerates an unreliable connection is close to a requirement. It is a poor fit for anyone with a call-heavy schedule, anyone wanting nightlife, and anyone who has not accounted for a country that legally closes on Sundays. Time the trip for the whale season or the case for coming weakens considerably. It also suits sailors, since Vava'u is one of the great cruising grounds of the Pacific and has a charter fleet to match.

rarotonga.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker on Rarotonga, which is expensive for the Pacific and reflects an island that uses the New Zealand dollar and imports from New Zealand. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries carry the freight cost that every remote island pays, and the difference between shopping at the Punanga Nui market on a Saturday and shopping at a supermarket is substantial. There is no local income tax on foreign earnings. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
rarotonga.whereToWork: The Cook Islands are served by the Manatua submarine cable, completed in 2020, which transformed connectivity from satellite-dependent to genuinely workable, and fibre now reaches most of Rarotonga at reasonable speeds. Prices are high. Mobile data from Vodafone Cook Islands covers the island. Power is reliable and increasingly solar. There is a small amount of coworking. English is an official language alongside Cook Islands Maori and is used everywhere. Rarotonga sits ten hours behind London and is a day behind New Zealand despite being two hours ahead of it in clock terms, which confuses everybody.
rarotonga.gettingAround: Rarotonga is thirty-two kilometres around and has exactly one ring road, which two buses circle all day: one clockwise, one anticlockwise, and that is the entire public transport system. It works. Scooters are the common rental and a local licence is issued at the police station, which used to involve a practical test and has become a formality. Cycling the ring road is easy and flat. The interior is mountainous and crossed by the Cross-Island Track past the Needle. The airport is on the ring road with flights to Auckland, Sydney and, seasonally, Los Angeles and Tahiti.
rarotonga.visas: The Cook Islands grant thirty-one days on arrival to citizens of most countries with no visa and no fee, extendable in-country month by month up to six months for a modest charge. New Zealand citizens have open access. Cook Islanders hold New Zealand passports, since the country is in free association with New Zealand. There is no remote work visa, but the extendable thirty-one day permit does the same job with less paperwork than most schemes. Longer stays require a permit through employment or business. Anyone extending should do it before the permit lapses rather than after, since the immigration office treats an overstay far less lightly than the easy entry suggests.
rarotonga.bestTime: April to November is the dry season and the comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-six, low humidity and the calmest lagoon. December to March is the wet season and the cyclone season, and while the Cook Islands are hit less often than Vanuatu or Fiji, the exposure is real. The shoulder months of April, May, October and November are the best combination of weather and price. The Te Maeva Nui festival at the start of August, marking self-government, is the largest cultural event of the year and worth timing around.
rarotonga.prosCons: Rarotonga has one of the most beautiful lagoons in the Pacific at Muri, a mountainous green interior you can walk across in a morning, no building taller than a coconut palm by law, and a genuinely safe, easy, English-speaking society running on New Zealand dollars. The submarine cable made working here possible. Against that, it is expensive, very small, there is no nomad community, the choice of anything is limited by the size of the island, and getting here means Auckland for almost everyone. The law capping building height at a coconut palm is also the reason the island looks the way it does, and it is enforced.
rarotonga.whoFor: Rarotonga suits someone who wants an easy, safe, English-speaking Pacific island where the paperwork is trivial and the lagoon is the reason to be there. Anyone working New Zealand or Australian hours will find the time zone awkward but the flights simple. It works well for a month or two, and the permit extends to six. It is a poor fit for anyone needing variety, a professional network or low costs. Aitutaki, an hour north by air, has the lagoon that Rarotonga is often mistaken for. It also suits anyone travelling with children, since the island is small, safe and shallow-watered in a way few Pacific destinations manage.

papeete.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Papeete, which makes French Polynesia one of the most expensive places in this batch and among the most expensive in the Pacific. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,200 to $1,900. The cost of imported food is the standing local grievance and has driven protests more than once; a supermarket shop costs far more than in mainland France, which is where much of it comes from. The CFP franc is pegged to the euro. Eating from the roulottes, the food trucks that fill the waterfront at dusk, is the way locals manage it. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
papeete.whereToWork: French Polynesia is served by the Honotua and Natitua submarine cables, which give Tahiti connectivity well above the Pacific norm, and fibre reaches Papeete at good speeds. Prices are high. Mobile data from Vini and Vodafone covers the populated coast. Power is reliable. There is a small amount of coworking in Papeete. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Tahitian widely spoken; English is limited outside the tourism industry, which is the main practical filter here. Tahiti sits ten hours behind Paris, which is an awkward overlap with France.
papeete.gettingAround: Papeete sits on the northwest coast of Tahiti and its centre, around the market and the waterfront, is walkable. Le Truck buses and their modern replacements cover the island's coastal road cheaply. Most residents drive and traffic into Papeete at peak is genuinely bad for a city this size. The ferry to Moorea takes thirty minutes and runs constantly, which is why many people who work in Papeete live there instead. Faa'a airport is on the edge of the city with flights to Paris, Los Angeles, Auckland, Tokyo and the outer archipelagos.
papeete.visas: French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France but is not in the Schengen area, so Schengen rules and Schengen day counts do not apply here. European Union citizens have freedom of movement and can live and work without a permit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. There is no dedicated remote work visa. Longer stays for non-EU citizens run through a French long-stay visa applied for before travel, and the process is the French one, which is thorough. The separation from Schengen is the detail that catches people out in both directions.
papeete.bestTime: May to October is the dry season and the comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, lower humidity and the calmest water. November to April is the wet season, hotter and more humid, with the cyclone risk concentrated in January and February, though French Polynesia is hit less often than the western Pacific. July is the Heiva festival, a month of dance and sport competitions that is the cultural event of the year and fills accommodation across the islands. Humpback whales pass between roughly August and October. Anyone planning the Tuamotus should also know that the diving there peaks with the grouper aggregation at Fakarava in June and July.
papeete.prosCons: Tahiti is the gateway to 118 islands across five archipelagos, with Moorea thirty minutes away by ferry, Bora Bora and the Tuamotu atolls beyond, and some of the best diving in the world at Fakarava and Rangiroa. The connectivity is unusually good for the Pacific and the French administration means the infrastructure works. Against that, the cost of living is severe, French is close to necessary, Papeete itself is a busy port city that most visitors pass through rather than stay in, and everything beyond Tahiti costs another flight. The cost of living has also been a live political issue for years, and the protests over food prices are a recurring feature rather than a one-off.
papeete.whoFor: Papeete suits a French speaker, ideally an EU citizen who can stay without a permit, who wants the Pacific with functioning infrastructure and can absorb the prices. Divers get more from the Tuamotus than from almost anywhere on earth. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, anyone on a budget, and anyone who imagined Bora Bora from the capital, which is a working city of traffic and container ships. Most people who stay a while end up living on Moorea and commuting by ferry. It also suits anyone with a European passport looking for a Pacific base without a visa problem, which is a rarer combination than it sounds.

basseterre.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Basseterre, which is mid-range for the Eastern Caribbean. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with Frigate Bay and the areas near the beaches at the top of that and the streets behind the capital well below. The islands import most of their food and the markup shows, though the Saturday market and the local fish are cheap. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar, so budgeting needs no conversion. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
basseterre.whereToWork: Saint Kitts has reasonable connectivity for its size: fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches Basseterre, Frigate Bay and the developed south at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the island. There is very little formal coworking, so remote work happens from apartments and a handful of cafes. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. English is the only language required. The federation sits four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in the northern winter, which gives a usable overlap in both directions. The cruise terminal at Port Zante brings several thousand people ashore on ship days, which changes how busy the centre feels from one morning to the next.
basseterre.gettingAround: Basseterre is small and its centre around the Circus and Independence Square is walkable in twenty minutes. Minibuses cover the island cheaply and frequently along the coastal road, and they are the practical way to move. Driving is on the left and a local permit is required. The Saint Kitts Scenic Railway, built to carry sugar cane and now running a tourist circuit, is the last operating railway in the West Indies. A ferry crosses to Nevis in around forty-five minutes, several times a day. Nevis is a separate island with its own administration and its own rhythm, and the crossing is cheap enough to make a day there routine.
basseterre.visas: Saint Kitts and Nevis has no dedicated remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days, with British and Commonwealth citizens often receiving longer, and extensions applied for locally at the immigration department. The federation runs the oldest citizenship by investment programme in the world, launched in 1984, which is a substantial and separate decision rather than a nomad route and should be researched independently of the agents who market it. Anyone planning a long stay should ask for the maximum on arrival. Anyone moving between the two islands should note that Nevis has its own immigration desk at the ferry terminal, though it is a formality for a visitor.
basseterre.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, lower humidity and the calmest sea, and it is when prices peak. May to November is hotter and wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Saint Kitts sits within the belt though it has been struck less often than several of its neighbours. Sugar Mas, the national carnival, runs from mid-December into early January rather than before Lent, which is unusual in the region and worth knowing. The rainforest interior is walkable year-round, and the crater at the top of Mount Liamuiga is a hard day out in any season.
basseterre.prosCons: Saint Kitts has Brimstone Hill Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage site and the most complete surviving fortification of its kind in the Americas, a working scenic railway, a rainforest interior below a dormant volcano, and Nevis forty-five minutes across the channel with its own peak and its own pace. It is quiet and safe by regional standards. Against that, there is no remote work visa, no nomad community, the island is small enough to exhaust in a month, and the economy leans heavily on cruise arrivals and citizenship sales. The closure of the sugar industry in 2005 also ended two centuries of the island's economy in a single year, which is visible in the abandoned estates.
basseterre.whoFor: Basseterre suits someone who wants a genuinely quiet Eastern Caribbean base with real history and easy English, and who is content with ninety days rather than a year. The Nevis ferry makes a two-island stay practical, which is unusual. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a long-stay visa or a professional network, neither of which exists here. Anyone weighing it against Antigua or Barbados should know that Saint Kitts is smaller, calmer and less organised for visitors than either. It also suits anyone interested in Caribbean industrial history, since the railway, the estates and the fortress together tell that story unusually completely.

kingstown.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Kingstown, which makes Saint Vincent one of the cheaper Eastern Caribbean islands. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $450 to $800, and the Grenadines are a different economy entirely, with Mustique and Canouan priced for people who arrive by private aircraft. Saint Vincent grows a great deal of its own produce and the Kingstown market is genuinely cheap. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
kingstown.whereToWork: Connectivity in Saint Vincent is adequate rather than good: fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches Kingstown and the developed south at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the main island and the larger Grenadines. There is essentially no coworking. Power cuts happen and the 2021 volcanic eruption disrupted supply across the north of the island for months. English is the only language required. Anyone planning to work from Bequia or further down the chain should treat connectivity as considerably weaker than on the main island. Anyone working with Europe should note the four-hour offset behind central European time, which puts a European afternoon at the start of the Vincentian day.
kingstown.gettingAround: Kingstown is compact, built along a harbour with the market and the cathedral within a few streets of each other, and it is walkable though hot and steep in places. Minibuses cover Saint Vincent cheaply and are how everyone moves. The Grenadines are reached by ferry from Kingstown, with Bequia an hour away and the smaller islands beyond, and the ferry timetable governs everything. Argyle International Airport opened in 2017 and finally gave the country direct flights from North America, which changed how easy it is to reach. Bequia is the practical Grenadine base for a longer stay, being large enough to have shops and a hospital while still an hour from the capital.
kingstown.visas: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines has no remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to a month, extendable at the immigration department in Kingstown, and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer on arrival. The extension process is routine but must be started before the initial stay expires. Anyone planning several months should ask for the maximum at the border and then extend. The country also runs no citizenship by investment programme, which distinguishes it from most of its neighbours. Anyone arriving by yacht clears in at Kingstown, Bequia, Union Island or Chateaubelair, and the paperwork is separate from an arrival by air.
kingstown.bestTime: January to May is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-nine and the calmest sailing conditions in the Grenadines, which is what most visitors come for. June to November is wetter and the hurricane season runs through it. The other consideration here is volcanic: La Soufriere at the northern end of Saint Vincent erupted explosively in April 2021, covering the island in ash and displacing tens of thousands, and it remains an active volcano that is monitored continuously. The Vincy Mas carnival falls in late June and early July, unusually late in the regional calendar, and is the island's largest event.
kingstown.prosCons: Saint Vincent is the gateway to the Grenadines, a chain of thirty-two islands including Bequia, Mustique and the Tobago Cays, which together make one of the finest sailing grounds in the world. The main island has rainforest, waterfalls and the Botanical Gardens, founded in 1765 and the oldest in the western hemisphere. Costs are low. Against that, there is no remote work visa, the internet is mediocre, the volcano is genuinely active, and Kingstown itself is a working port town rather than a place people choose to live. Saint Vincent is also one of very few Caribbean islands with black volcanic sand on much of its coast, which surprises people expecting the Grenadines.
kingstown.whoFor: Kingstown suits a sailor above all: the Grenadines are the reason to be here and the country's whole geography points at them. It works for anyone who wants a cheap, green, English-speaking island with almost no other foreigners on it. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a long-stay visa or reliable connectivity, and anyone whose interest is the smaller islands should budget for the ferries and accept that internet gets worse the further down the chain you go. It also suits anyone drawn to hiking, since the walk up La Soufriere and the Vermont nature trail are among the best in the Eastern Caribbean.

englishharbour.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker at English Harbour, which is expensive for the region and reflects a yachting economy. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300, with anything on the water at the top of that and the villages inland considerably cheaper. Antigua imports nearly all of its food and the supermarket bill is the line most people underestimate. Eating at a local place in Falmouth or Liberta costs a fraction of the dockyard restaurants. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
englishharbour.whereToWork: Antigua's connectivity is reasonable and better around English Harbour than the island average, because the yachting industry needs it: fibre reaches the dockyard area and Falmouth at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island. There is a small amount of coworking in St John's and around the harbour, some of it created for holders of the Nomad Digital Residence visa. Power cuts happen. English is the only language required, and the international sailing crowd means the working population here is unusually cosmopolitan for an island of ninety thousand. Anyone whose work involves the marine industry will find a genuine professional network here, in a way that is true of very few small islands.
englishharbour.gettingAround: English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour sit next to each other at the southern end of Antigua and both are walkable, with Nelson's Dockyard, the restaurants and the marinas within twenty minutes of each other. Minibuses run to St John's, the capital, in about forty minutes for very little. Driving is on the left and a local permit is required. V. C. Bird International is the best-connected airport in the Eastern Caribbean, with direct flights to London, New York, Miami and Toronto, which is a genuine advantage of basing here. The walk up to Shirley Heights from the dockyard takes about forty minutes and is the standard way to reach the Sunday evening party.
englishharbour.visas: Antigua and Barbuda's Nomad Digital Residence is a two-year remote work visa for people employed or self-employed outside the country who can show an annual income of around $50,000, with a fee of roughly $1,500 for an individual and more for a family. Two years is among the longest terms offered anywhere and the application is handled online. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to three months. The country also runs a citizenship by investment programme, which is a separate matter. Anyone applying should know that the two years run from approval rather than arrival, so it is worth timing the application to the intended stay.
englishharbour.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the sailing season, with steady trade winds, daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and the harbour full. Antigua Sailing Week at the end of April is the largest regatta in the Caribbean and fills every bed in the south of the island. May to November is hotter and wetter and the hurricane season runs through it; Antigua was spared in 2017 while Barbuda, its sister island, was rendered uninhabitable by Hurricane Irma and evacuated entirely. Barbuda is reachable by ferry or a short flight and is slowly being rebuilt, with its frigate bird colony among the largest in the world.
englishharbour.prosCons: Nelson's Dockyard is the only continuously working Georgian naval dockyard in the world, a UNESCO World Heritage site that is still a marina rather than a museum, and the Sunday sunset party at Shirley Heights above it has run for decades. Antigua has a two-year nomad visa, the region's best flight connections and a claimed beach for every day of the year. Against that, it is expensive, the nomad community is small and heavily overlapping with the sailing one, and the island empties considerably outside the season. The dockyard's Georgian buildings are also still in commercial use as hotels, offices and marina facilities, which is why it feels like a place rather than an exhibit.
englishharbour.whoFor: English Harbour suits a sailor, or someone who wants to be around sailing, with a two-year visa and the budget for a yachting town. The international crowd here is real and easy to join, which is rare on a small island. It works for a full year rather than a season. It is a poor fit for anyone on a tight budget or anyone wanting a city, since St John's is forty minutes away and modest. Anyone arriving in Sailing Week should book months ahead. It also suits anyone with a family, since Antigua's schools and medical facilities are better than most islands of comparable size can offer.

roadtown.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Road Town, which is expensive and reflects an offshore financial centre and the world's busiest charter yacht base. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,200 to $1,800. Everything arrives by ship and the grocery bill is high even by Caribbean standards. The territory uses the United States dollar, which removes any conversion. Rents rose sharply after Hurricane Irma in 2017 destroyed much of the housing stock and have not fully settled. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
roadtown.whereToWork: The British Virgin Islands host tens of thousands of registered companies and the connectivity reflects that: fibre reaches Road Town and the developed parts of Tortola at solid speeds, and the professional services around the financial sector are substantial. Mobile coverage is good on Tortola and thinner on the outer islands. Power was rebuilt after Irma and is more reliable than before. There is a small amount of coworking. The territory runs on Atlantic time, an hour ahead of New York in the northern winter. Anyone working with London will find the four-hour offset workable, since a British afternoon lands at the start of the Virgin Islands day.
roadtown.gettingAround: Road Town is small and its waterfront is walkable, but Tortola is mountainous and everything else needs a vehicle; driving is on the left in cars mostly imported with the wheel on the left, which takes adjustment. Open-air safari taxis run the main routes. The real transport here is the ferry: boats leave Road Town and West End constantly for Virgin Gorda, Jost Van Dyke and the United States Virgin Islands, and the whole territory is organised around them. Terrance B. Lettsome airport handles regional connections only. The ferry to St Thomas takes about forty-five minutes and crosses an international border, so a passport and the American entry rules both apply.
roadtown.visas: The British Virgin Islands have no dedicated remote work visa, though the territory ran a one-year Work in Nature programme after the pandemic that has not been maintained as a standing category. Most Western nationalities enter for up to thirty days on arrival, extendable at the immigration department, and British citizens receive longer. Anyone planning several months should ask for the maximum at the border and extend locally. Working for a British Virgin Islands employer requires a work permit, which is a separate and considerably harder process. Anyone arriving by yacht clears customs and immigration separately at Road Town, West End or Jost Van Dyke, and the fees differ by vessel and season.
roadtown.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the charter season, with steady trade winds, flat anchorages and daytime temperatures around twenty-eight. It is also when every mooring ball is taken and prices peak. May to November is hotter and wetter and the hurricane season runs through it; Hurricane Irma in September 2017 passed directly over the territory as a category five and destroyed most of the buildings on Tortola, which is still visible and still shapes what things cost. Anyone chartering should book the winter season many months ahead, since the fleet is finite and the good weeks go first.
roadtown.prosCons: The British Virgin Islands are the charter yacht capital of the world for a reason: sixty islands within sight of each other, consistent trade winds, short line-of-sight passages and anchorages like the Baths on Virgin Gorda and the beach bars of Jost Van Dyke. It is safe, English-speaking and uses the dollar. Against that, it is expensive, there is no remote work visa, Road Town itself is a functional port and financial district rather than an attractive town, and the hurricane exposure is not theoretical. Recovery from Irma also reshaped the territory's building code, and much of what has been rebuilt since is considerably more storm-resistant than what stood before.
roadtown.whoFor: Road Town suits a sailor or someone in offshore finance, and it is genuinely hard to justify for anyone who is neither. If the plan is to charter or crew, this is the best base in the Caribbean and the case makes itself. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a long-stay visa, anyone on a budget, and anyone expecting a town rather than a harbour with offices around it. The ferries are the point; anyone who will not use them should look elsewhere. It also suits anyone in the offshore corporate sector, where the professional depth here is genuinely international rather than local.

charlotteamalie.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,700 a month as a solo remote worker in Charlotte Amalie, which is expensive even by American standards and reflects a territory that imports everything. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,300 to $1,900. Groceries cost substantially more than the American mainland and electricity is among the most expensive under the United States flag, which residents discuss constantly. There is no need to convert anything, since the territory uses the dollar and is part of the United States customs zone. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
charlotteamalie.whereToWork: Connectivity is good: the territory is served by submarine cable, fibre reaches most of St Thomas at solid speeds, and American carriers operate here with domestic roaming, so a United States mobile plan works without international charges. That last point is a genuine practical advantage over every other Caribbean island. There is a small coworking presence. Power outages are more frequent than on the mainland and the grid was heavily damaged in 2017. The territory runs on Atlantic time year-round. Anyone with an American employer will also find payroll, banking and tax entirely domestic here, which removes a set of problems every other Caribbean base creates.
charlotteamalie.gettingAround: Charlotte Amalie is built around a harbour on steep ground and the waterfront and Main Street are walkable, though the residential streets above involve the ninety-nine steps and several other staircases cut into the hillside. Safari taxis, open-sided trucks with bench seats, run the main routes cheaply. Driving is on the left, in cars almost all imported from the American mainland with the wheel on the left, which is genuinely disorienting. Ferries run to St John, St Croix and the British Virgin Islands. Cruise ships berth at Havensight and Crown Bay, and on a four-ship day the town centre is genuinely difficult to move through.
charlotteamalie.visas: This is United States territory, so for American citizens there is no visa question at all: no passport is required to travel from the mainland and there is no limit on how long you may stay or work. That makes the United States Virgin Islands the simplest Caribbean option available to Americans by a wide margin. Everyone else needs a United States visa or an ESTA under the Visa Waiver Programme, with the same ninety-day limit and the same prohibition on productive work that applies on the mainland. Anyone travelling on to the British Virgin Islands should note that is a separate country with its own entry rules, despite the forty-five minute ferry.
charlotteamalie.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the highest prices, since this is when the cruise ships and the mainland arrive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; St Thomas was hit by both Irma and Maria within two weeks in September 2017 and the recovery took years. Carnival on St Thomas runs through April and is the largest event of the year. St John's Virgin Islands National Park covers roughly two-thirds of that island and is reachable by a twenty-minute ferry in any season.
charlotteamalie.prosCons: For an American, the Virgin Islands are the Caribbean without any paperwork at all: no passport, no visa, no time limit, a domestic mobile plan and the dollar. Charlotte Amalie has a genuine Danish colonial core with Fort Christian dating from 1672, and St John, twenty minutes by ferry, is two-thirds national park. Against that, it is expensive, the crime rate is high enough that both residents and the State Department name specific areas to avoid, and the town is heavily shaped by cruise retail. Electricity costs here are also among the highest anywhere under the American flag, which is a real and recurring line in any household budget.
charlotteamalie.whoFor: Charlotte Amalie suits an American remote worker who wants the Caribbean with no immigration friction whatsoever, and for that specific person nothing else on this site competes. It works indefinitely rather than for a season. It is a poor fit for anyone outside the United States, for whom the ordinary American visa rules apply with none of the compensating benefits, and for anyone on a budget. Read current safety guidance for St Thomas rather than assuming a United States flag means low crime. It also suits anyone who sails, since the territory sits at one end of the same island chain the British Virgin Islands charter fleet works.

providenciales.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,200 a month as a solo remote worker on Providenciales, which makes Turks and Caicos one of the most expensive places on this site. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,600 to $2,400, with anything near Grace Bay at the top of that. Groceries are the standing complaint: everything is imported, there is no local agriculture to speak of, and a supermarket shop costs well over double the American equivalent. There is no income tax and the territory uses the dollar. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
providenciales.whereToWork: Connectivity is good for a small territory: fibre reaches the developed parts of Providenciales at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the island. Prices are high. There is a small amount of coworking. Power is reasonably reliable and expensive. English is the only language required. The islands run on Eastern time with daylight saving, which keeps Providenciales aligned with New York year-round and makes it a straightforward base for anyone working American hours. There is no formal remote work programme to build a community around, so the foreign population here is resort staff and second-home owners rather than nomads. Anyone hoping to find other remote workers will have to look harder than the marketing suggests.
providenciales.gettingAround: Providenciales is flat and spread out along a few main roads, and it is not walkable in any useful sense: the island assumes a car and most visitors rent one. Taxis exist and are expensive, with fares set by a published tariff rather than a meter. Driving is on the left. Grace Bay's hotel strip is the one stretch where walking works. Ferries run to North and Middle Caicos, and light aircraft reach South Caicos, Salt Cay and Grand Turk, the actual capital, which almost no visitor sees. Grand Turk, the actual seat of government, sits an hour away by air and receives a fraction of the visitors that Providenciales does.
providenciales.visas: Turks and Caicos has no dedicated remote work visa. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days on arrival, and British citizens receive the same, with extensions available from the immigration department for a fee. The territory has discussed a formal digital nomad scheme more than once without introducing one. Anyone wanting to work for a local employer needs a work permit, which is expensive and tied to a sponsor. For a stay of up to three months the ordinary arrival stamp is all that is required. Anyone considering a longer stay should also know that property purchase does not confer residence here, despite how often the two are marketed together.
providenciales.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the calmest water, and it is when the islands are busiest and most expensive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Hurricanes Irma and Maria both affected the territory in 2017. September and October are the quietest and cheapest months and carry the highest risk. Water temperature stays swimmable all year, which is the argument for coming outside the season. Humpback whales pass through the Turks Island Passage between January and April, which is the one seasonal wildlife event worth timing a visit around.
providenciales.prosCons: Grace Bay is repeatedly named the best beach in the world and the claim is defensible: twelve kilometres of white sand over a reef-protected shelf with water that stays turquoise to the horizon. The barrier reef system here is the third largest on earth, the diving off West Caicos and French Cay is exceptional, and there is no income tax. Against that, the cost of living is severe, there is no remote work visa, the island is flat and undramatic away from the water, and almost everything is built for resort tourism.
providenciales.whoFor: Providenciales suits a well-paid remote worker who wants the best beach in the Caribbean, is working American hours, and can absorb prices closer to Bermuda than to the rest of the region. Divers get a great deal here. It is a poor fit for anyone on an ordinary budget and anyone wanting a stay longer than ninety days, since there is no mechanism for it. Anyone weighing it against the Bahamas should note the Bahamas has a one-year permit and Turks and Caicos does not. It also suits anyone whose work is genuinely location-independent and whose employer pays a salary that treats accommodation as an afterthought.

philipsburg.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Philipsburg, which is expensive and reflects an island of forty thousand people that receives well over a million visitors a year. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $900 to $1,500. Groceries are imported and the markup is heavy, though the French side of the island has cheaper supermarkets and many residents shop there deliberately, which is a genuinely useful trick. The Netherlands Antillean guilder is pegged to the dollar and dollars circulate everywhere. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
philipsburg.whereToWork: Sint Maarten's connectivity is reasonable: fibre reaches the developed parts of the Dutch side at workable speeds and mobile data covers the whole island, though a French SIM and a Dutch SIM behave differently on the two halves and roaming charges can appear without warning. There is a small amount of coworking. Power cuts happen. Dutch is official on the southern half and French on the northern, but English is the working language of almost everything commercial on both sides, which is what makes this island unusually easy to operate in.
philipsburg.gettingAround: Philipsburg is a narrow strip between Great Bay and the Great Salt Pond, and Front Street runs its length in twenty minutes on foot. Beyond that a car is needed, and the island is small enough to drive across in forty minutes. Minibuses cover the main routes cheaply. The border between the Dutch and French sides is marked by a monument and nothing else: there are no checks, no barrier and no formality, and most people cross several times a week without noticing. Princess Juliana airport sits at the western end of the island and its approach over Maho Beach, where aircraft pass a few metres above sunbathers, is the island's best-known image.
philipsburg.visas: This is where the island gets complicated. Sint Maarten, the Dutch side, is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and grants most Western nationalities up to ninety days on arrival. Saint-Martin, the French side, is a French overseas collectivity outside the Schengen area, and European Union citizens have freedom of movement there. Because the border is unmarked, which side you are legally staying on is a question of where you sleep rather than where you walk, and the two sets of rules run in parallel. Anyone staying long term should establish clearly which side their lease is on, since that determines which set of immigration rules they are actually living under.
philipsburg.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the highest prices, since this is when North America and the cruise ships arrive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it. Sint Maarten's exposure is not theoretical: Hurricane Irma passed directly over the island in September 2017 as a category five, destroying most of the buildings and the airport terminal, and the recovery took years. Anyone visiting in the low season should check what is open before booking, since a substantial share of the restaurants close in September and October.
philipsburg.prosCons: Sint Maarten is the smallest landmass in the world divided between two sovereign states, and the difference between the Dutch and French halves is real: different food, different prices, different administration, and no border to speak of between them. The airport is one of the best-connected in the Eastern Caribbean and the eating, particularly on the French side at Grand Case, is the best in the region. Against that, it is expensive, heavily built for cruise tourism, and the hurricane exposure is severe. The two sides also have different price levels on almost everything, so a household that shops deliberately across the border spends noticeably less than one that does not.
philipsburg.whoFor: Philipsburg suits someone who wants two countries on one island, exceptional food and the region's best flight connections, and who can absorb the prices. Anyone who cooks will find the French supermarkets genuinely change the budget. It works for ninety days rather than a year, since neither side offers a remote work visa. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting quiet, since this is a busy commercial island, or anyone who dislikes cruise crowds, which arrive by the thousand on most winter mornings. It also suits anyone who sails, since Simpson Bay Lagoon is one of the largest enclosed anchorages in the Caribbean and the bridge opens twice a day.

kralendijk.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Kralendijk, which is expensive for a small island and reflects an economy built almost entirely on diving. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300. Everything is imported and groceries carry a markup, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the choice wide. Bonaire uses the United States dollar rather than a guilder, which is unusual in the Dutch Caribbean and removes any conversion. Diving is the line that dominates any real budget here. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
kralendijk.whereToWork: Bonaire's connectivity is good for its size: fibre reaches Kralendijk and the developed west coast at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island. Prices are high. Power is reliable and increasingly wind-generated, since the island runs a substantial wind farm. There is a small amount of coworking aimed at the long-stay diving population. Dutch is official and Papiamentu is the language of daily life, but English is widely spoken and Spanish is common given Venezuela is eighty kilometres away. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset behind central European time makes a European afternoon into a Bonairean morning, which is a workable overlap.
kralendijk.gettingAround: Kralendijk is small and walkable along its waterfront, but Bonaire's whole proposition requires a vehicle: the diving is from the shore, at some ninety marked entry points along the western coast identified by painted yellow stones at the roadside, and reaching them means a pickup truck with tanks in the back. That is what almost every visitor rents. The island is flat and cyclable in the south. Flamingo International airport is minutes from town with connections through Curacao, Amsterdam and Miami. The southern half of the island is salt pans and flamingo colonies, and the road around them makes a flat circuit that most residents cycle at least once.
kralendijk.visas: Bonaire is a special municipality of the Netherlands rather than a constituent country, which makes its status different from Curacao or Aruba, though it sits outside the European Union and outside Schengen. Dutch and European Union citizens can live and work here with minimal formality. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days on arrival. There is no dedicated remote work visa, but the ninety days plus the ease of a short exit to Curacao makes a longer stay practical for anyone willing to manage it. Anyone diving here must complete a short orientation and buy an annual marine park tag before entering the water, which is enforced rather than nominal.
kralendijk.bestTime: Bonaire sits below the hurricane belt and is dry, warm and windy essentially all year, around thirty degrees every month with very little rain, so there is no season to avoid. That consistency is the island's quiet advantage over most of the Caribbean. The busiest and most expensive window is December to April. October to December brings what rain there is. Diving conditions barely change through the year, which is why the island's visitor numbers are far steadier than its neighbours'. Sea turtles nest on the beaches between May and December, and the marine park restricts access to some stretches of shore during the season.
kralendijk.prosCons: Bonaire made its entire surrounding sea a national park in 1979, one of the first marine reserves anywhere, and the result is shore diving of a quality that nowhere else offers from a roadside: ninety marked entry points, healthy reef within swimming distance of the shore, and no boat required for most of it. The island is safe, outside the hurricane belt and uses the dollar. Against that, it is expensive, very quiet, small enough to exhaust quickly, and there is essentially nothing to do that is not underwater. The island also runs a substantial share of its electricity from wind, which is unusual in the Caribbean and shows in a grid that is more reliable than most.
kralendijk.whoFor: Kralendijk suits a diver, and the honest answer is that it suits almost nobody else. For someone who wants to dive most days for months at a low marginal cost, Bonaire is arguably the best place on earth and the island is organised entirely around making that easy. It is a poor fit for anyone who does not dive, anyone wanting nightlife or a city, and anyone on a budget. Non-divers will find the island beautiful and be finished with it in a week. It also suits anyone learning to dive, since shore entries at your own pace are a far better way to build hours than a boat schedule allows.

pointeapitre.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Pointe-a-Pitre, which is expensive for the Caribbean and reflects the cost structure of a French department where much of the food is shipped from Europe. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries cost noticeably more than in mainland France, which has driven serious protests here more than once. The local markets and the lolos, the small Creole grills, are considerably cheaper. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Anyone comparing with the independent islands nearby should note that European healthcare and schooling are included in what the higher cost of living buys.
pointeapitre.whereToWork: Guadeloupe has European infrastructure and it shows: fibre reaches the developed parts of the archipelago at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive, and French mobile plans work here without roaming charges, which is a substantial advantage for anyone based in Europe. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene around Pointe-a-Pitre and Le Gosier. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Guadeloupean Creole spoken among locals; English is limited outside tourism. Anyone working with mainland France should note the five-hour offset, which puts a French afternoon at the start of the Guadeloupean working day and makes mornings the overlap.
pointeapitre.gettingAround: Guadeloupe is shaped like a butterfly, with Grande-Terre's limestone plain on one wing and Basse-Terre's rainforest volcano on the other, joined by a bridge over a narrow channel. Pointe-a-Pitre sits at the join and is the commercial centre. Buses cover the main routes and most residents drive; the roads are European-standard and the traffic into Pointe-a-Pitre at peak is heavy. Ferries run to Marie-Galante, Les Saintes and La Desirade, and the airport has direct flights to Paris. Basse-Terre, confusingly, is both the name of the western wing and of the actual administrative capital, which sits at its southern end rather than in Pointe-a-Pitre.
pointeapitre.visas: Guadeloupe is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union, though it lies outside the Schengen area, which is a distinction that catches people out in both directions. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here without any permit at all, which makes Guadeloupe one of the simplest Caribbean options available to any European. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Longer stays for non-EU citizens require a French long-stay visa applied for before travel. Anyone travelling on to Dominica or the independent islands nearby should note those are separate countries with their own entry rules, despite the short ferry.
