pointeapitre.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, known locally as careme, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, lower humidity and the calmest sea. June to November is the wet season, called hivernage, and the hurricane season runs through it; Guadeloupe sits within the belt. Carnival here runs from January through to Ash Wednesday and is a serious, weeks-long affair rather than a single parade. The Route du Rhum, the transatlantic solo yacht race from Saint-Malo, finishes here every four years. La Soufriere, the volcano on Basse-Terre, is walkable year-round but is in cloud most days, so an early start is the only reliable way to see anything from the top.
pointeapitre.prosCons: Guadeloupe gives you the Caribbean with European infrastructure, French healthcare, the euro and no visa question at all for Europeans, plus La Soufriere's rainforest volcano, the Cousteau reserve at Pigeon Island and the Carbet falls. The food is genuinely excellent, mixing French technique with Creole ingredients. Against that, French is close to necessary, the cost of living is high and politically contentious, Pointe-a-Pitre itself is a working port rather than an attractive town, and unemployment on the islands is severe. The archipelago also includes Marie-Galante, Les Saintes and La Desirade, which are quieter and cheaper than the two main wings and reachable by ferry.
pointeapitre.whoFor: Pointe-a-Pitre suits a French speaker, and especially a European Union citizen, who wants the Caribbean without any immigration process and with infrastructure that works. Divers get the Cousteau reserve and hikers get a volcano. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, since English will not carry you far here, and for anyone on a budget. Anyone weighing Guadeloupe against Martinique should know they are similar in status and different in character, Guadeloupe being wilder and Martinique more polished. It also suits anyone with children, since the schools here are French state schools and the healthcare is the French system rather than a Caribbean approximation.

fortdefrance.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Fort-de-France, which sits at much the same level as Guadeloupe and reflects the same French department cost structure. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with Schoelcher and the Pointe du Bout side at the top of that. Imported food is expensive and the price of it has driven repeated protest movements across the French Caribbean. The market and the local snack bars are far cheaper. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
fortdefrance.whereToWork: Martinique's infrastructure is European: fibre reaches most of the developed west coast at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and French plans roam here without charge. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene in Fort-de-France and around Le Lamentin. French is the language of everything, with Martinican Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited outside the tourism industry. Anyone working with Europe will find the five-hour offset behind Paris workable in one direction and awkward in the other. Anyone in the rum trade will find genuine professional depth here, since Martinique produces the only appellation-controlled rum in the world.
fortdefrance.gettingAround: Fort-de-France is built around a bay with the Savane park and the extraordinary Schoelcher Library at its centre, and the core is walkable. A ferry crosses the bay to Trois-Ilets and Pointe du Bout in twenty minutes, which is faster and pleasanter than driving around. Buses cover the island and most residents drive; the road north to Saint-Pierre and the Route de la Trace through the rainforest are both excellent drives. The airport has direct flights to Paris and across the region. The ferry across the bay is also the cheapest way to reach the beaches of the south, which are considerably better than anything in the city itself.
fortdefrance.visas: Martinique is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while sitting outside the Schengen area. European Union citizens can live and work here with no permit and no time limit, which is the single most useful fact about the island for any European reading this site. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Non-EU citizens wanting longer need a French long-stay visa applied for before travel, and the process is the French one rather than a Caribbean one. Anyone travelling on to Saint Lucia or Dominica, both visible from the island on a clear day, should note those are separate countries with their own rules.
fortdefrance.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and lower humidity, and it is the busiest window. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season runs through it. Carnival, running for the five days before Ash Wednesday and ending with the burning of Vaval, is the island's largest event and quite unlike the Trinidadian version. The rainforest north of the island is wet in any season, which is why Mount Pelee is so often in cloud. The Tour des Yoles, a race of traditional sailing boats around the island each summer, is the sporting event Martinicans care about most.
fortdefrance.prosCons: Martinique has Mount Pelee, whose 1902 eruption destroyed Saint-Pierre and killed thirty thousand people in minutes, leaving ruins you can walk through, along with rainforest, rum distilleries producing the only appellation-controlled rum in the world, and the Caribbean's most developed restaurant culture outside Trinidad. European infrastructure and no visa question for Europeans. Against that, French is essential, costs are high and contentious, and Fort-de-France has real urban problems that the tourist brochures do not mention. The island also produced Aime Cesaire and Frantz Fanon, whose work shaped how the whole francophone world thinks about colonialism, and both are taken seriously here.
fortdefrance.whoFor: Fort-de-France suits a French speaker, ideally a European Union citizen, who wants the Caribbean with functioning institutions and a serious food and rum culture. Anyone interested in volcanology will find Pelee and the ruins of Saint-Pierre remarkable. It is a poor fit for anyone without French and anyone on a budget. Most long-stay visitors base themselves in Trois-Ilets or the south rather than in the capital, which is worth knowing before booking a flat in the city. It also suits anyone drawn to rum as a subject rather than a drink, since the distilleries here are working agricultural businesses open to visitors.

cayenne.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker in Cayenne, which is expensive for South America and reflects a French department where almost everything is imported from Europe. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries cost substantially more than in mainland France, and the cost of living has driven serious social movements here. The markets, particularly the Hmong market at Cacao and the Saturday market in Cayenne, are the exception and are genuinely good. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
cayenne.whereToWork: French Guiana has European infrastructure in a South American setting: fibre reaches Cayenne and Kourou at workable speeds, mobile coverage is good along the coastal strip and effectively absent inland, and French plans roam here without charge. Power is reliable in the towns. There is a small amount of coworking, much of it connected to the space industry at Kourou. French is the language of everything, with Guianese Creole widely spoken; English is rare. The territory sits four hours behind Paris. Anyone working with mainland France should note the four-hour offset, which is the smallest of any French overseas territory and makes a full working overlap possible.
cayenne.gettingAround: Cayenne is compact around the Place des Palmistes with its royal palms, and the centre is walkable. Buses are limited and most residents drive. The single coastal road runs west to Kourou and Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni and east towards the Brazilian border at Saint-Georges, and that road is essentially the whole road network: the interior is rainforest reached by river, and there is no road to Brazil's interior or to Suriname except a ferry across the Maroni. Kourou, with the European spaceport, is about an hour west along that road, and launches are visible from Cayenne on a clear night.
cayenne.visas: French Guiana is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union, outside the Schengen area. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here without a permit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Non-EU citizens wanting longer need a French long-stay visa obtained before travel. Yellow fever vaccination is mandatory for entry, which is unusual for European Union territory and is enforced. The land borders with Brazil and Suriname have their own procedures. Anyone crossing to Suriname takes a pirogue across the Maroni at Saint-Laurent, and anyone crossing to Brazil uses the bridge at Saint-Georges, each with its own hours.
cayenne.bestTime: French Guiana is equatorial and hot all year at around thirty-one degrees with high humidity. The calendar turns on rain: the long dry season from July to November is the practical window, with a short drier spell in March. The heavy rains from December to June make interior travel difficult. Leatherback turtles nest on the beaches near Cayenne and at Awala-Yalimapo between March and July, which is one of the great wildlife spectacles in the Americas and the reason to time a visit. Anyone hoping to watch a rocket launch should check the schedule well in advance, since dates move and the viewing sites are allocated rather than open.
cayenne.prosCons: French Guiana is the European Union on the edge of the Amazon: rainforest covering ninety-eight per cent of the territory, Europe's spaceport at Kourou launching Ariane rockets over the Atlantic, the penal colony ruins on the Iles du Salut where Papillon was set, and leatherback turtles nesting on the beaches. The infrastructure is French and the euro is the currency. Against that, it is expensive, French is essential, the crime rate in Cayenne is high by European standards, and the interior is genuinely hard to reach. Illegal gold mining in the interior is also a serious environmental and security problem that shapes what is possible outside the coastal strip.
cayenne.whoFor: Cayenne suits a French speaker with a serious interest in the Amazon or in space, who wants European institutions on a South American frontier. Anyone able to watch an Ariane launch from Kourou will remember it. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, anyone expecting South American prices, and anyone whose plan involves overland travel, since the road network essentially ends at the coast. Read current safety guidance for Cayenne rather than assuming European territory means European crime rates. It also suits anyone researching the Amazon, since the territory's forest is among the least disturbed anywhere and the research infrastructure is French.

thevalley.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in The Valley, which is expensive and reflects an island of fifteen thousand people that imports everything and has positioned itself at the top of the Caribbean market. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $1,100 to $1,700. Groceries are heavily marked up and many residents shop in Sint Maarten, twenty minutes away by ferry, where prices are lower. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar and both circulate. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
thevalley.whereToWork: Anguilla's connectivity is good for its size: fibre reaches most of the island at workable speeds and mobile data is comprehensive, both of which the government invested in specifically to support its remote work programme. There is a small amount of coworking. Power is reasonably reliable and expensive. English is the only language required. The island runs four hours behind central European time and one ahead of New York in winter, giving a workable overlap in both directions for anyone splitting time between the two. Anyone needing anything the island does not have will find Sint Maarten twenty minutes away by ferry, with a far larger airport and considerably more choice.
thevalley.gettingAround: Anguilla is flat, sixteen kilometres long and has no traffic to speak of, which makes it one of the easiest islands anywhere to move around. A car is still needed since the settlements are spread out and there is no public transport worth the name; driving is on the left and a temporary local licence is required. The Valley is the administrative centre rather than a town in any real sense. Ferries and light aircraft run to Sint Maarten in twenty minutes, which is the practical connection to the wider world.
thevalley.visas: Anguilla introduced a remote work programme in 2020 that grants stays of up to twelve months to people working for employers outside the island, with a fee of around $2,000 for an individual and more for a family, plus proof of health insurance and a clean record. It was one of the earliest such schemes anywhere and remains straightforward. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to three months. British citizens receive the same, since Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory. Anyone applying should note that the fee is not refundable if the application is declined, and that proof of income and insurance are both checked properly.
thevalley.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight, low humidity and the calmest sea, and it is when the island is busiest and most expensive. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Anguilla is exposed and Hurricane Irma in 2017 caused severe damage across the island. Many restaurants and hotels close entirely between September and October, which is worth checking before booking a long stay in those months. Anguilla's boat racing season, with traditional wooden sloops raced by whole villages, runs through the summer and is the island's genuine national sport.
thevalley.prosCons: Anguilla has thirty-three beaches on a flat coral island with no rivers to muddy the water, which is why the sand at Shoal Bay and Rendezvous Bay is as white as it is. It has one of the earliest and most generous remote work visas anywhere, very low crime, and a restaurant scene disproportionate to its size, built on the same French Caribbean supply chain that feeds Saint-Martin. Against that, it is expensive, extremely quiet, and there is genuinely very little to do beyond the beaches. The absence of rivers is also why Anguilla has no rainforest and almost no elevation, which is the trade-off that produces the water clarity.
thevalley.whoFor: The Valley suits someone who wants twelve months on an exceptionally beautiful, safe and quiet island, and who has the income to absorb the cost and the temperament for the silence. The visa is one of the best available anywhere. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting nightlife, a community or a city, and anyone whose work needs stimulation from its surroundings. Anguilla is deliberately calm and it does not pretend otherwise, which is either exactly right or exactly wrong. It also suits anyone with a family who wants somewhere genuinely safe, since Anguilla's crime rate is among the lowest in the Caribbean.

andorralavella.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in Andorra la Vella, which is cheaper than the Alpine countries around it and expensive by Spanish standards. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $700 to $1,200, and the rental market is genuinely tight because the country is small and much of the housing stock is holiday property. The tax position is the real financial story: Andorra charges a maximum of ten per cent income tax and four and a half per cent value added tax, the lowest in Europe, which is why duty-free shopping fills the main street. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
andorralavella.whereToWork: Andorra has invested seriously in connectivity: the state telecoms company has rolled fibre to essentially every household in the country, which makes it one of the best-connected places in Europe per head, and speeds are high. Mobile coverage is complete in the valleys and patchy on the high passes. Power is entirely reliable. There is a small coworking scene, and the government has actively courted digital businesses with a residence category aimed at them. Catalan is the official language, with Spanish and French widely spoken; English is limited outside tourism and the newer arrivals.
andorralavella.gettingAround: Andorra la Vella and the neighbouring town of Escaldes-Engordany run together along a narrow valley floor and the whole strip is walkable, which is fortunate because the traffic through it is heavy. Buses cover the parishes and the ski areas cheaply. The country has no airport and no railway, so everyone arrives by road: Barcelona is around three hours by bus, Toulouse two and a half, and the nearest stations are at L'Hospitalet and Lleida. That isolation is the single most important practical fact about living here. The road tunnels under the high passes mean the country stays open through winter, which was not true within living memory.
andorralavella.visas: Andorra is not in the European Union and not in Schengen, though it has no border controls with France or Spain in practice and uses the euro. Visitors need whatever permission the Schengen states require to reach it, since there is no other way in. There is no remote work visa. Residence comes in two forms: active residence requires running a company here, and passive residence requires a substantial investment in Andorran assets plus an interest-free deposit with the state, currently in the region of several hundred thousand euros. Anyone counting Schengen days should note that Andorra is not in the area, though reaching it requires crossing France or Spain, which are.
andorralavella.bestTime: December to April is the ski season and the busiest half, with Grandvalira and Ordino-Arcalis together forming the largest ski area in the Pyrenees and the reason most visitors come at all. June to September is the walking season, with the high valleys open, wildflowers and daytime temperatures in the low twenties at this altitude. May and November are the shoulder months when much of the country simply closes. Andorra la Vella sits above a thousand metres, so winters are properly cold and snow in the town itself is normal.
andorralavella.prosCons: Andorra offers the lowest tax rates in Europe, fibre to nearly every home, the largest ski area in the Pyrenees, and a genuinely safe and orderly country of eighty thousand people in a mountain valley. It uses the euro without being in the European Union. Against that, there is no airport and no train, the residence routes require serious money rather than a job, the capital is a traffic-heavy shopping strip rather than an attractive town, and Catalan or Spanish is close to necessary for daily life. The country also has no army, no airport and no railway, and manages the highest life expectancy in the world, which is an odd combination of facts.
andorralavella.whoFor: Andorra la Vella suits someone who skis or walks seriously, who is either passing through on a Schengen allowance or is prepared to engage with the residence rules and their cost, and who does not mind a three-hour bus to the nearest airport. The tax position matters only if you actually establish residence. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting a city, anyone without Spanish or Catalan, and anyone who assumed the low tax rates apply to a visitor, which they do not. It also suits anyone who cycles, since the climbs out of the valley are among the hardest and best known in professional road racing.

monaco.costOfLiving: Budget around $5,200 a month as a solo remote worker in Monaco, which makes it by a distance the most expensive place on this site. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $3,500 to $5,000 and that is the ordinary market rather than the top of it: Monaco has the highest property prices per square metre in the world. Groceries and restaurants are priced for the residents, though the market at La Condamine and a short trip into France are both considerably cheaper. There is no income tax for residents other than French nationals. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
monaco.whereToWork: Monaco's infrastructure is as good as anywhere in Europe: fibre throughout, comprehensive 5G, and a state that has invested in being an early adopter of network technology. Power is entirely reliable. There is coworking, aimed largely at the financial and yachting sectors. French is the official language and the language of administration, with Italian and English both widely spoken given the international population; a majority of residents are not Monegasque. The principality sits in central European time and functions as part of the French Riviera economy. Anyone working with London should note the one-hour offset, which makes a British afternoon and a Monegasque one almost entirely overlapping.
monaco.gettingAround: Monaco is two square kilometres and can be crossed on foot in half an hour, though it is built up a steep hillside and the walk involves a network of public lifts and escalators that residents use constantly and visitors rarely find. Buses cover the principality. There is a railway station, entirely underground, with frequent trains along the coast to Nice in twenty minutes and Ventimiglia in Italy. Nice airport is thirty minutes by road or seven minutes by the helicopter shuttle, which is a genuinely normal way to arrive here.
monaco.visas: Monaco is not in the European Union but is in the Schengen area in practice, with its border controls handled by France under a long-standing arrangement, so Schengen rules and Schengen day counts apply exactly as they would in France. There is no remote work visa. Residence requires proving accommodation in the principality, which given the property market is the real barrier, along with a substantial deposit with a Monaco bank, generally several hundred thousand euros. The tax advantage applies to residents and to nobody else. Anyone considering residence should also budget for the annual renewal process, which requires demonstrating continued means and occupancy of the property.
monaco.bestTime: May to September is the warm half, with daytime temperatures in the high twenties and the Mediterranean swimmable from June. Two events dominate the calendar and both fill every room in the principality and along the coast: the Rolex Masters tennis in April and the Formula One Grand Prix over a weekend in late May, when the streets become the circuit and the whole place is closed to ordinary traffic. Winter is mild, around thirteen degrees, and the principality is noticeably quieter and cheaper. The Monaco Yacht Show in late September is the third of the events that fills the principality and is the largest of its kind anywhere.
monaco.prosCons: Monaco has the lowest crime rate in the world, no income tax for residents, a Mediterranean climate, the Oceanographic Museum that Jacques Cousteau ran for thirty years, and the Alps an hour inland. Nice airport is half an hour away with connections everywhere. Against that, the cost of accommodation is the entire story: the residence requirement is proving you have somewhere to live in the most expensive property market on earth, the principality is very small, and the social scene is narrow and heavily weighted towards wealth. The principality has also reclaimed a substantial part of its territory from the sea, and continues to, which is the only way it can grow at all.
monaco.whoFor: Monaco suits almost nobody reading this site as a place to move to, and it is included because it is one of the few places whose figures are worth seeing plainly. As a base for ninety days on a Schengen allowance it is possible and expensive. As a residence it requires capital rather than income. It is a poor fit for anyone whose interest is cost of living, community or space. Anyone drawn to the Riviera should look at Nice or Menton, both of which are ten minutes away and a different economy.

vaduz.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Vaduz, which reflects Swiss prices without Swiss scale. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,600 to $2,400, and the rental market is very tight because the country has forty thousand people and strict planning rules. Groceries are Swiss-priced, which is to say among the highest in Europe, though many residents shop over the border in Austria where the same basket costs considerably less. The Swiss franc is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
vaduz.whereToWork: Liechtenstein has the infrastructure of a wealthy Alpine state: fibre throughout, comprehensive mobile coverage, entirely reliable power, and a financial sector that requires all of it. There is very little coworking, because the country has almost no visiting professional population. German is the official language and Alemannic dialect is what people actually speak, which is difficult even for German speakers; English works in business and banking. The country sits in central European time and functions economically as part of the Swiss and Austrian Rhine valley. Anyone working with London should note the one-hour offset, which leaves a British and a Liechtenstein working day almost entirely aligned.
vaduz.gettingAround: Vaduz has around five thousand inhabitants and can be walked end to end in twenty minutes. Liechtenstein has no airport and no railway station of any consequence, though the Austrian line clips the northern corner. Buses run frequently within the country and across the border to Buchs and Sargans in Switzerland and Feldkirch in Austria, and they are how almost everyone travels. Zurich airport is around ninety minutes by train and bus. Malbun, the small ski area, is half an hour up the valley. The Rhine footbridge to Sevelen in Switzerland is a covered wooden crossing and one of the pleasanter ways to leave the country on foot.
vaduz.visas: Liechtenstein is not in the European Union but is in the European Economic Area and in the Schengen area, so Schengen rules and day counts apply. It is also in a customs and currency union with Switzerland. There is no remote work visa. Residence is genuinely difficult: the country operates a strict annual quota on residence permits for European Economic Area nationals, allocated partly by lottery, and permits for everyone else are rarer still. This is the hardest country in Europe to move to legally. Anyone counting Schengen days should note that Liechtenstein is inside the area, so time here counts exactly as time in Switzerland or Austria would.
vaduz.bestTime: June to September is the walking season, with the high paths above Malbun and Steg open, alpine flowers and daytime temperatures in the low twenties. December to March brings snow and a small but genuine ski area at Malbun, which is uncrowded because almost nobody outside the region knows it exists. The Rhine valley floor where Vaduz sits gets fog and inversions through the winter, so the mountain villages are often above the cloud when the capital is under it. National Day on the fifteenth of August is the one big public event.
vaduz.prosCons: Liechtenstein is safe, orderly, wealthy and spectacularly located, with the Alps rising directly behind the Rhine valley and walking paths from the capital into the mountains. The infrastructure is Swiss-standard and the country is small enough to know completely. Against that, it is very expensive, there is essentially nothing to do after dark, the residence quota makes moving here close to impossible, and Vaduz is a town of five thousand people rather than a city, with all that implies for company and choice. The prince's castle above the town is also a private residence rather than a museum, so it can be walked to and not entered.
vaduz.whoFor: Vaduz suits someone in private banking or the trust sector with a reason to be here, or a walker spending a Schengen allowance in a beautiful and largely unvisited corner of the Alps. It works for weeks rather than years, because the residence system is built to keep the population where it is. It is a poor fit for anyone hoping to settle, anyone on a budget, and anyone who needs a social life. Sargans and Feldkirch, both twenty minutes away, are where most people actually go out. It also suits anyone walking the Rhine or the Alpine passes, since the country's marked paths connect directly into the Swiss and Austrian networks.

torshavn.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Torshavn, which is expensive and reflects a North Atlantic archipelago that imports nearly everything except fish and lamb. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $900 to $1,400 and the rental market is tight, since the islands have fifty-four thousand people and a housing shortage. Groceries are Nordic-priced and eating out is expensive. Heating is a substantial year-round line rather than a winter one. The Danish krone is the currency, issued locally as Faroese notes. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
torshavn.whereToWork: The Faroes are among the best-connected small territories anywhere: submarine cables to Denmark and Iceland, fibre to essentially every household, and mobile coverage through a network of sub-sea tunnels that link the main islands. Speeds are high and reliable. Power is reliable and increasingly wind and hydro. There is a small coworking presence in Torshavn. Faroese is the language of daily life and Danish is taught throughout; English is widely and comfortably spoken, particularly by anyone under fifty. Anyone working with the United Kingdom will find the islands on the same clock through the year, which is a smaller adjustment than the geography suggests. The tunnels also carry mobile signal, so a drive between islands does not drop a call.
torshavn.gettingAround: Torshavn is small and its centre, including the turf-roofed peninsula of Tinganes where the government has sat since the Viking age, is walkable in half an hour. The islands are connected by a remarkable network of sub-sea tunnels, one of which contains the world's first undersea roundabout, along with ferries and helicopters run as public transport at subsidised fares. Buses within Torshavn are free. Vagar airport is around forty-five minutes away by road and tunnel, with flights to Copenhagen, Reykjavik and a handful of European cities. The helicopter service to the outlying islands is subsidised as public transport and is one of the cheapest scheduled helicopter flights anywhere.
torshavn.visas: The Faroe Islands are an autonomous territory of Denmark but are not in the European Union and not in the Schengen area, which is the detail that catches almost everyone out: a Schengen visa does not admit you here, and time spent here does not count against a Schengen allowance. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a Faroese residence permit, which is administered separately from the Danish system. Anyone flying via Copenhagen should note that the Faroe leg is treated as an external border crossing despite both being Danish territory.
torshavn.bestTime: May to September is the practical window, with long days, temperatures in the low teens and the puffin colonies at Mykines occupied between roughly May and August. The Faroes have some of the most changeable weather anywhere: locals say you can experience all four seasons in an afternoon and they are not exaggerating, with fog, sun and horizontal rain in the same hour. Winter is dark, wet and windy rather than cold, rarely below freezing, with storms that close the tunnels and cancel flights. The Olavsoka festival at the end of July, marking the opening of parliament, is the largest gathering of the year and fills Torshavn entirely.
torshavn.prosCons: The Faroe Islands are eighteen basalt islands rising vertically out of the North Atlantic, with sea cliffs, grass-roofed houses, a waterfall that falls off a cliff into the ocean at Gasadalur and some of the emptiest landscape in Europe. The connectivity is excellent, the country is exceptionally safe, and English works everywhere. Against that, the weather is genuinely difficult, it is expensive, there are almost no trees and very little daylight in winter, and the grindadrap whale hunt is a real thing that visitors should read about rather than discover.
torshavn.whoFor: Torshavn suits a photographer, a walker, or anyone who genuinely likes weather rather than merely tolerating it, and whose work benefits from excellent connectivity in an extremely quiet place. The islands are outside Schengen, which makes them useful for anyone managing a European day count. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs sun, company or a scene. Anyone considering a winter stay should understand that the darkness and the wind are the defining experience rather than a footnote. It also suits anyone who fishes or sails, since the waters here are among the most productive in the North Atlantic and the harbours are working ones.

nuuk.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Nuuk, which is expensive and reflects a town of nineteen thousand people that everything must be shipped or flown to. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,100 to $1,700 and housing is genuinely scarce, with waiting lists that are a standing feature of Greenlandic life. Groceries are Nordic-priced with an Arctic freight premium on top, and fresh produce is limited and expensive. Heating runs all year. The Danish krone is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
nuuk.whereToWork: Greenland's connectivity has improved substantially with submarine cable to Iceland and Canada, and fibre reaches Nuuk at workable speeds, though prices are high and capacity outside the main towns is limited. Mobile coverage exists in the settlements and nowhere between them. Power is reliable and largely hydroelectric. There is a small amount of coworking. Greenlandic is the official language and Danish is universally taught; English is widely spoken among younger people and in business, which makes Nuuk considerably easier than its remoteness suggests. Anyone working with Europe should note that Greenland sits several hours behind, which makes a European afternoon into a Greenlandic morning.
nuuk.gettingAround: Nuuk is compact enough to walk across in forty minutes and has a small bus network. The important fact about Greenland is that there are no roads between towns, anywhere in the country: every journey beyond the immediate area is by aircraft, helicopter or boat, and weather cancels all three regularly. Nuuk's new international airport opened in late 2024, giving the capital direct flights from Copenhagen for the first time and ending decades of routing everyone through Kangerlussuaq. Ilulissat, with its UNESCO-listed icefjord, is a further flight north and is the trip most visitors add to a Nuuk stay.
nuuk.visas: Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark but is not in the European Union, having left in 1985, and is not in the Schengen area. A Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, which is the detail that matters most for planning. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a Greenlandic residence permit, administered separately from Denmark's. Anyone flying via Copenhagen should note that the Greenland leg is an external border crossing, with passport control in both directions.
nuuk.bestTime: June to August is the summer, with temperatures around ten degrees, very long days and the fjords ice-free and navigable, and it is when almost all visitors come. September to April brings the northern lights, which are visible from Nuuk on clear nights through the whole dark half of the year. Winter is cold but moderated by the sea, sitting around minus eight in Nuuk rather than the extremes further north. Ice conditions rather than temperature govern what is possible in any given month. Nuuk sits just below the Arctic Circle, so there is no true midnight sun here, though June nights never get properly dark.
nuuk.prosCons: Nuuk sits at the mouth of one of the largest fjord systems on earth, with icebergs drifting past the town, whales in the fjord in summer and the northern lights overhead for half the year. It is the world's northernmost capital and, since 2024, directly reachable from Europe. Greenlandic culture is living rather than preserved. Against that, it is expensive, housing is genuinely hard to find, the winter darkness is severe, and there is no road to anywhere, which shapes every plan you might make. Greenland is also the largest island in the world with one of the smallest populations, at around fifty-six thousand people across two million square kilometres.
nuuk.whoFor: Nuuk suits someone with a real reason to be in the Arctic, whether research, photography or a long-held pull towards it, whose work tolerates weather-dependent travel and who has arranged accommodation before arriving rather than after. The new airport has made a short stay far more practical than it was. It is a poor fit for anyone on a budget, anyone who needs daylight, and anyone who assumed they could drive to the next town, which is not possible anywhere in the country. It also suits anyone interested in how a small nation handles self-government, since Greenland has been steadily taking powers back from Denmark since 1979.

gibraltar.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Gibraltar, which is expensive and reflects six and a half square kilometres with thirty-four thousand people on it. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,400 to $2,000 and the housing market is one of the tightest in Europe, because there is no land. Groceries are cheaper than the United Kingdom on some things and dearer on others, and a great many residents shop in Spain, where the same basket costs substantially less. The Gibraltar pound trades at par with sterling. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
gibraltar.whereToWork: Gibraltar's economy runs on online gaming, financial services and shipping, all of which require serious connectivity, and it has it: fibre throughout, comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power. There is a small coworking market. English is the official language and universally used, with Spanish widely spoken and llanito, the local mix of Andalusian Spanish and English, heard constantly. The territory sits in central European time, an hour ahead of the United Kingdom, which is a small but real consideration for anyone working British hours. Anyone considering the gaming sector should know it is the territory's largest private employer and the reason much of the infrastructure exists at all.
gibraltar.gettingAround: Gibraltar is walkable end to end, though the Rock rises 426 metres above the town and getting up it means the cable car, a taxi tour or a serious walk. There is a small bus network. The airport runway crosses Winston Churchill Avenue, the main road to Spain, so the road closes whenever an aircraft moves, which is exactly as strange as it sounds. The land border with Spain at La Linea is a few minutes' walk from the centre, and the queue to cross it can be anything from nothing to two hours.
gibraltar.visas: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory outside both the European Union and the Schengen area, and its status since Brexit has been under negotiation for years without a concluded treaty, which means the arrangements at the Spanish border can change. British citizens have the right of abode. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for short visits. There is no remote work visa. Anyone planning to live here and cross into Spain regularly should follow the current position, since a Schengen day count may or may not apply depending on how the border is being run.
gibraltar.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the best months, with warm dry weather in the mid twenties and the migration seasons, when Gibraltar sits directly under one of the busiest bird flyways in the world and raptors cross the strait in thousands. July and August are hot and crowded with day visitors from the Costa del Sol. Winter is mild at around sixteen degrees and wetter, with the levanter, an easterly wind that pins a cloud over the top of the Rock for days at a time. The Barbary macaques on the upper Rock are present year-round and will take anything carried in a bag, which is a warning rather than a charm.
gibraltar.prosCons: Gibraltar is British, English-speaking and sits at the mouth of the Mediterranean with Africa visible across the strait, dolphins in the bay and the only wild monkeys in Europe on the upper Rock. The tax regime is favourable and the professional sector in gaming and finance is real. Against that, it is very small, the housing market is severe, the border queue into Spain is a recurring daily frustration, and the unresolved post-Brexit status is a genuine uncertainty rather than a technicality. The Rock is also honeycombed with more than fifty kilometres of military tunnels, considerably more tunnel than road, most of it dug during the Second World War.
gibraltar.whoFor: Gibraltar suits someone working in online gaming, shipping or financial services, or a British citizen who wants Mediterranean weather with British institutions and English throughout. Birdwatchers get one of the great migration crossings in the world. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting space, since six square kilometres is genuinely small, and anyone unwilling to deal with a land border that can take two hours on a bad morning. Most people who work here live in Spain and cross daily, which is worth understanding before committing. It also suits anyone who dives, since the bay holds a substantial number of wrecks and the water is warmer than the Atlantic side of the strait.

douglasiom.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,300 a month as a solo remote worker in Douglas, which is broadly comparable to a prosperous British provincial town with a tighter housing market. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $900 to $1,400. Groceries are close to United Kingdom prices, since the supply chain is the same, though everything crosses the Irish Sea and the freight shows in some categories. The island has its own income tax with a cap on total liability, which is why a number of high earners live here. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
douglasiom.whereToWork: The Isle of Man has invested heavily in connectivity because its economy depends on it: the island hosts substantial e-gaming, financial services and insurance sectors, fibre reaches most of Douglas and the main towns at solid speeds, and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking market. English is the only language required, though Manx Gaelic is taught in schools and appears on signage. The island keeps the same time as the United Kingdom, which removes any offset for anyone working British hours. The island also runs its own top-level internet domain and its own postal service, which is the kind of independence that surprises people who assume it is part of Britain.
douglasiom.gettingAround: Douglas is built along a two-mile sweep of bay with a promenade the length of it, and the centre is walkable. The island has a genuinely unusual transport heritage still in daily use: a horse-drawn tram along the Douglas promenade, the Manx Electric Railway north to Ramsey, the Snaefell Mountain Railway to the island's only peak, and a steam railway south to Port Erin, all of them Victorian and all still running. Buses cover the rest. The ferry to Liverpool and Heysham takes a few hours and the airport has connections across Britain and Ireland.
douglasiom.visas: The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom and never part of the European Union, though it sits within the Common Travel Area with Britain and Ireland. British and Irish citizens can live and work here freely. Everyone else needs the island's own immigration permission, which is administered separately from the United Kingdom's and includes a work permit system. There is no remote work visa. Arrivals from Britain and Ireland face no routine border control, which is the practical consequence of the Common Travel Area.
douglasiom.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable half, with daytime temperatures in the high teens, long days and the coastal paths at their best. The calendar is dominated by one event: the Isle of Man TT, a motorcycle road race held on closed public roads over a fortnight in late May and early June, which fills every bed on the island and is the reason many people have heard of the place at all. Winter is mild but wet and windy, sitting around seven degrees, with ferry cancellations in a serious blow.
douglasiom.prosCons: The Isle of Man has the oldest continuous parliament in the world, Tynwald, which has met since around 979, a coastal path running the whole way round the island, Victorian railways still in service, and a genuine financial and e-gaming sector for an island of eighty-four thousand people. It is safe, English-speaking and an hour from Britain. Against that, the weather is grey and wet, the island is small, immigration for non-British arrivals is not straightforward, and the TT fortnight makes normal life on the island impossible. The island is also a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in its entirety, the only whole nation to hold that designation, which shapes how the countryside is managed.
douglasiom.whoFor: Douglas suits someone working in e-gaming, insurance or fund administration, or a British or Irish citizen who wants a quiet, safe island with real institutions and no immigration friction. The tax cap matters only to genuinely high earners. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs sunshine, anyone outside the Common Travel Area without a work permit, and anyone hoping to visit during the TT without having booked a year in advance. It also suits anyone who walks, since the Raad ny Foillan coastal path runs around the whole island in about a week, and anyone who rides, for obvious reasons. The Calf of Man at the southern tip is a bird observatory reachable by boat in summer.

sanmarino.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month as a solo remote worker in San Marino, which is broadly similar to the surrounding Italian region and slightly cheaper on some things because the republic sets its own indirect taxes. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $600 to $1,000, and much of the affordable housing is in the lower towns of Borgo Maggiore and Dogana rather than on the mountain itself. Groceries are Italian-priced, which is to say reasonable. The euro is the currency although San Marino is not in the European Union. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
sanmarino.whereToWork: San Marino's connectivity is good: fibre reaches the populated areas at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with the surrounding Italian networks also reaching most of the republic. Power is reliable. There is very little coworking, since the republic has almost no visiting professional population. Italian is the only language of daily life and administration; English is limited outside the tourism economy on the mountain. The republic sits in central European time and functions economically as part of Emilia-Romagna. Anyone working with the rest of Europe will find no offset at all, since the republic keeps central European time like the country entirely surrounding it.
sanmarino.gettingAround: San Marino is built on and around Monte Titano, and the historic city on top is entirely pedestrian, reached by road, by a cable car from Borgo Maggiore below, or on foot up a serious climb. The republic has no airport and no railway; the old electric line from Rimini closed in 1944 and its tunnels are still visible. Buses run to Rimini in about fifty minutes, which is where the nearest station and the coast are. Bologna airport is around two hours away. Rimini's beaches are close enough that a great many Sammarinese treat the Adriatic coast as their summer, and the bus runs frequently in season.
sanmarino.visas: San Marino is not in the European Union and not formally in Schengen, but it has open borders with Italy on every side and no border controls at all, so in practice reaching it means entering Schengen through Italy and the day count applies there. There is no remote work visa. Residence in San Marino is tightly controlled and generally requires either substantial investment or a genuine employment relationship with a Sammarinese company, and the process is slow. Anyone counting Schengen days should treat time in San Marino as time in Italy, since there is no border and no separate record of entry.
sanmarino.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, with warm dry weather, clear views across to the Adriatic and fewer of the day-trippers who come up from the Rimini beaches in summer. July and August are hot and the mountain is busy. Winter is cold and often in cloud at this altitude, with the city on the ridge frequently sitting above or inside a bank of fog while the plain below is clear, which is either atmospheric or oppressive depending on the day. The Medieval Days festival at the end of July fills the old city with re-enactment and crossbow competitions, which is the republic's largest event.
sanmarino.prosCons: San Marino claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and the oldest constitutional republic in the world, founded by a stonemason in the fourth century, and its three towers on the ridge of Monte Titano are visible for fifty kilometres. It is safe, cheap by Western European standards, and the views across to the Adriatic are exceptional. Against that, it is tiny, Italian is essential, the historic centre is largely given over to duty-free shops and tourist retail, and there is no airport or railway. The republic also issues its own stamps and coins, minted in euro but with Sammarinese designs, which are collected far beyond the country itself.
sanmarino.whoFor: San Marino suits an Italian speaker who wants a very quiet hilltop base within an hour of the Adriatic coast and two of Bologna, and who is spending a Schengen allowance rather than trying to settle. The republic is more pleasant out of season than its reputation suggests, once the day-trippers have gone. It is a poor fit for anyone without Italian, anyone needing a community, and anyone hoping the sovereignty translates into an easier residence route than Italy's, which it does not. It also suits anyone cycling in Emilia-Romagna, since the climb up Monte Titano is a serious one and the descent to the coast is thirty kilometres.

libreville.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Libreville, which is expensive for Africa and reflects an oil economy with a small population and heavy import dependence. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with Quartier Louis and the areas near the embassies at the top of that. Groceries are expensive and much of what is on the shelves is French. Gabon has consistently ranked among the costlier African capitals for expatriates. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes currency risk entirely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
libreville.whereToWork: Libreville's connectivity is modest: fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data from Airtel and Moov is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed. Power cuts happen and any serious office runs a generator. There is very little coworking. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, and English is genuinely rare, which is the main practical filter for working here. The country sits in central European time in the northern winter, which makes it one of the easiest African bases for anyone working European hours.
libreville.gettingAround: Libreville stretches along the Atlantic coast with the Boulevard du Bord de Mer running its length, and that seafront is the most pleasant part of the city to be in. Shared taxis, hailed by calling out a destination and a price, are the standard way to move and cost very little. Traffic is heavy on the main axes. Leon Mba airport is close to the centre with flights to Paris, Istanbul and across West and Central Africa. The national parks, which are Gabon's real case, are reached by internal flight or a long drive.
libreville.visas: Gabon operates an e-visa system that most nationalities can apply for online before travel, with approval usually returned within a few days and the visa issued on arrival, typically for stays of up to ninety days. A yellow fever certificate is required for entry. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a residence permit arranged through an employer or local sponsor, which is slow. Gabon has changed its entry procedures more than once in recent years, so confirm the current position directly rather than relying on older guidance.
libreville.bestTime: Gabon sits on the equator and is hot and humid all year at around thirty degrees. The calendar turns entirely on rain, and there are two dry seasons: a long one from June to September and a short one in December and January, which are the practical windows. The long rains from February to May and the shorter ones in October and November are heavy. The long dry season is also when the beaches at Loango are best for seeing forest elephants and buffalo come out onto the sand, which is Gabon's signature image.
libreville.prosCons: Gabon protects around eleven per cent of its territory in national parks, created in a single decision in 2002, and the country is nearly ninety per cent forest with a population of two and a half million. Loango National Park has elephants and hippos on Atlantic beaches, which exists nowhere else. Against that, Libreville is expensive, French is essential, the internet is weak, the country has had political instability including a coup in 2023, and reaching the parks requires organisation and money rather than a bus ticket. The country is also one of the few in Africa where forest cover has increased rather than fallen, largely because the oil economy never required logging revenue.
libreville.whoFor: Libreville suits a French speaker with a serious interest in Central African wildlife and the budget to reach it, or someone working in the oil, timber or conservation sectors where the professional network here is real. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, anyone on a budget, and anyone expecting the parks to be accessible from the capital, which they are not. Read current guidance on Gabon's political situation before planning a long stay rather than after arriving. It also suits anyone interested in gorilla and forest elephant research, since Gabon holds the largest remaining populations of both in Central Africa.

freetown.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Freetown, which is genuinely cheap and reflects one of the lower-income countries anywhere. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $500, with Aberdeen and the peninsula near the beaches at the top of that and the central and eastern districts well below. Market food costs very little and Sierra Leonean cooking is good. Imported goods are expensive. The leone was redenominated in 2022, dropping three zeros, so older prices quoted anywhere need checking. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
freetown.whereToWork: Freetown's connectivity is weak: fibre has reached parts of the city and works where it exists, mobile data from Orange and Africell is the common fallback, and neither is fast. Power cuts are frequent and generators are standard in anything serious. There is a small startup and coworking presence, more developed than the country's profile suggests. English is the official language and the medium of education and government, with Krio, an English-based creole, as the lingua franca across the country. That combination makes Sierra Leone far easier for an English speaker than its neighbours.
freetown.gettingAround: Freetown sits on a mountainous peninsula and the city climbs steeply from the harbour, which makes it hard going on foot and heavily congested by vehicle. Poda-poda minibuses and okada motorcycle taxis are how most people move and both cost very little. The airport is at Lungi, across the estuary from the city, and reaching it means a ferry, a water taxi or a long drive around, which is the single most awkward piece of logistics in the country and should be planned rather than improvised. The peninsula road south from the city to Tokeh and River Number Two passes a string of beaches and is the best drive in the country.
freetown.visas: Sierra Leone requires a visa of most nationalities, available through an e-visa system before travel or on arrival at Lungi airport, typically for thirty days with longer options. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department in Freetown. The country is a member of ECOWAS, so regional nationals move freely. Entry procedures have changed several times in recent years, so confirm the current requirement rather than relying on an older account. Anyone travelling on to Guinea or Liberia overland should check those requirements separately, since neither shares an arrangement with Sierra Leone.
freetown.bestTime: November to April is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty and the beaches at their best. The harmattan blows Saharan dust down in December and January. The rains from May to October are among the heaviest in West Africa: Freetown receives well over three metres a year, the mountain slopes above the city are prone to landslides, and the 2017 Regent landslide killed more than a thousand people. Plan around August, which is the wettest month by a distance. Turtles nest on the peninsula beaches between September and March, and Tiwai Island's primate reserve is most accessible in the dry months.
freetown.prosCons: Freetown was founded in 1792 by freed slaves from Nova Scotia and the history is present in the architecture, the Krio language and the Cotton Tree that stood at the centre of the city until it fell in 2023. The peninsula beaches south of the city are as good as anything in West Africa and almost nobody visits them. English works everywhere and costs are very low. Against that, the internet is poor, the airport transfer is genuinely awkward, infrastructure is limited, and the country is still recovering from a civil war and an Ebola epidemic.
freetown.whoFor: Freetown suits an experienced traveller who wants an English-speaking West African base at very low cost, whose work tolerates an unreliable connection, and who will treat the peninsula beaches as the reason to be there. Anyone in development or public health will find a substantial professional network. It is a poor fit for a first trip to West Africa, anyone needing reliable power, and anyone who has not planned the Lungi airport crossing before arriving with luggage and a flight time. It also suits anyone drawn to the country's music, since Sierra Leonean palm-wine guitar and its descendants are a genuine and living tradition.

serrekunda.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month as a solo remote worker in Serrekunda, which is among the cheapest figures on this site. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $200 to $400, with the coastal strip at Kololi and Bijilo at the top of that and the inland streets well below. Market food is very cheap and the Gambia grows a good deal of its own produce, with the fish from Tanji among the best value anywhere. Imported goods carry a markup. The dalasi has weakened steadily, which helps a visitor. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
serrekunda.whereToWork: Connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of the coastal strip and mobile data from Africell, QCell and Gamcel is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed and evening congestion common. Power cuts are frequent and any serious business runs a generator. There is a small coworking presence around the tourist coast. English is the official language and the medium of education and government, with Mandinka, Wolof and Fula the languages of daily life, which makes the Gambia unusually straightforward for an English speaker in a francophone region.
serrekunda.gettingAround: Serrekunda is the country's largest town and runs into Bakau, Kololi and the coastal resort strip without much of a break, and the whole area is flat and walkable in parts. Shared taxis and gelly-gelly minibuses cover it cheaply. The Gambia is essentially a strip of land either side of one river, three hundred kilometres long and rarely fifty wide, so most travel is either along the coast or up the river by boat or road. Banjul International airport is twenty minutes away with charter flights from northern Europe. The river trip upcountry to Janjanbureh and the Wassu stone circles takes several days and is the part of the country almost no visitor sees.
serrekunda.visas: The Gambia grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries and a number of European states for up to ninety days, with everyone else obtaining a visa on arrival or in advance. The rules vary more by nationality than in most countries, so check yours specifically. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department. The country is a member of ECOWAS, so regional nationals move freely, and a yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries. Anyone travelling on to Senegal, which surrounds the Gambia entirely, should note the border crossings have their own hours and their own paperwork.
serrekunda.bestTime: November to May is the dry season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around thirty-two, low humidity and the charter flights running from Europe. This is also the birdwatching season, and the Gambia's bird list is enormous for a country this size, which is why a substantial share of its visitors carry binoculars. June to October is the wet season, hot and humid with heavy rain, and much of the tourist infrastructure closes entirely. The harmattan brings dust in December and January. Kartong and the southern beaches are quieter than the main strip in any season, and the fish landing at Tanji is worth an early morning.
serrekunda.prosCons: The Gambia is the smallest country in mainland Africa, a strip along one river, and it is genuinely easy: English throughout, a short flight from Europe, very low costs, long Atlantic beaches and some of the best birdwatching on the continent. Against that, the internet is weak, the tourist strip has a well-documented problem with hustling and with sex tourism that visitors should be aware of, the economy is fragile, and there is very little to the country beyond the coast and the river. The Gambia also has one of the highest densities of bird species per square kilometre anywhere, which is why the country's guides are among the best in Africa.
serrekunda.whoFor: Serrekunda suits a birdwatcher, or anyone who wants a very cheap English-speaking West African base within six hours of Europe and whose work survives a patchy connection. The river trips upcountry are the part most visitors miss and the part worth doing. It is a poor fit for anyone needing reliable internet or a professional community, and anyone staying on the tourist strip should expect persistent approaches, which is the single most common complaint visitors make about the country. It also suits anyone tracing West African history, since Juffureh and Kunta Kinteh Island on the river are central to that story and reachable in a day.

djibouti.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month as a solo remote worker in Djibouti, which is expensive for the region and reflects a small country that imports almost everything and hosts several foreign military bases whose personnel set the rental market. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $600 to $1,000, with the European Quarter and Heron at the top of that and the Balbala districts far below. Imported food is costly and local produce is limited by the climate. The franc is pegged to the United States dollar. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
djibouti.whereToWork: Djibouti sits at the landing point of several of the submarine cables that carry traffic between Europe and Asia, which is a genuinely unusual asset, though the domestic market is a state monopoly and retail prices are high relative to speed. Fibre reaches the city at workable speeds and mobile data covers the populated areas. Power is reliable and expensive. There is very little coworking. French and Arabic are the official languages, Somali and Afar are the languages of daily life, and English is limited outside the military and shipping sectors.
djibouti.gettingAround: Djibouti City is compact and the European Quarter around Place Menelik is walkable, though the heat makes that a morning and evening activity for much of the year. Shared taxis and minibuses cover the city cheaply. The country is small enough to cross in a day: Lac Assal, the lowest point in Africa at 155 metres below sea level, is two hours west, and Lac Abbe's limestone chimneys are a longer drive. The railway to Addis Ababa, rebuilt in 2017, takes around twelve hours. The ferry across the Gulf of Tadjoura to Obock and Tadjoura itself is the pleasanter way to reach the northern coast and the diving.
djibouti.visas: Djibouti operates an e-visa system that most nationalities can apply for online before travel, typically for stays of up to ninety days, with approval returned in a few days. Visas on arrival have been available at times and the policy has shifted, so the e-visa is the reliable route. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a residence permit through an employer, and the military and shipping sectors account for most of them. Anyone travelling on to Ethiopia by the railway should arrange that visa separately and well ahead, since it is not issued at the border.
djibouti.bestTime: November to February is the only comfortable window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and manageable humidity. The rest of the year is severe: Djibouti is one of the hottest inhabited places on earth, and from June to August temperatures regularly exceed forty-five degrees with the khamsin wind off the desert making it worse. The whale shark season in the Gulf of Tadjoura runs from roughly October to February, which is both the coolest period and the reason most independent visitors come. Anyone hoping to see the whale sharks should book ahead for December and January, since the licensed operator capacity is genuinely limited.
djibouti.prosCons: Djibouti has Lac Assal, the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water in the world, the otherworldly limestone chimneys of Lac Abbe, and whale sharks gathering in the Gulf of Tadjoura every winter in numbers that are internationally significant. It sits at one of the world's great strategic chokepoints, which is why so many countries have bases here. Against that, it is very expensive for what it is, brutally hot for most of the year, French is close to necessary, and there is little to do in the city.
djibouti.whoFor: Djibouti suits a French speaker with a specific reason to be there, whether shipping, the military, development work or the whale sharks, rather than anyone looking for a general base. The landscape is genuinely extraordinary and almost entirely unvisited. It is a poor fit for anyone without French, anyone sensitive to heat, and anyone on a budget, since the presence of several foreign militaries has pushed prices well above what the local economy would otherwise support. It also suits anyone drawn to geology, since the Afar triple junction here is one of the few places on earth where continental rifting is visible at the surface.

saotome.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Sao Tome, which is moderate for the region and higher than a country this small might suggest, because almost everything is imported and the islands sit a long way off the West African coast. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $350 to $650. Market food is cheap and the fish is exceptional. The dobra was redenominated in 2018 and is pegged to the euro through an arrangement with Portugal, which removes currency volatility. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
saotome.whereToWork: Sao Tome's connectivity is weak and it is the main practical constraint. The islands are served by a single submarine cable and domestic prices are high relative to speed, with mobile data from CST and Unitel the usual fallback. Power cuts are frequent and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking. Portuguese is the official language and the language of everything; Forro and the other creoles are spoken at home, and English is genuinely rare. Portuguese is close to necessary here. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset trivial, since the islands keep the same time as London through most of the year.
saotome.gettingAround: The city of Sao Tome is small and its centre around the cathedral, the fort and the market is walkable in half an hour. Shared taxis and motorcycle taxis cover the island cheaply. The main island is only fifty kilometres long and a road runs most of the way round it, though the southern section is rough. Principe, the smaller island, is reached by a short flight or a long boat crossing, and it is quieter and considerably more expensive to stay on. Obo National Park covers roughly a third of the country and its trails start close to the road, which makes the forest unusually accessible.
saotome.visas: Sao Tome and Principe abolished visa requirements for citizens of the European Union, the United States and several other countries in 2017, granting stays of up to fifteen days visa-free, with a straightforward e-visa available for longer. That makes entry unusually easy for a country this obscure. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays run through a residence permit applied for locally. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries. Confirm the current position directly, since the policy has been adjusted more than once. Anyone flying in should note that connections run mainly through Lisbon, Accra and Libreville, and that the schedules are thin enough to shape a trip.
saotome.bestTime: June to September is the gravana, the main dry season and the practical window, with less rain and daytime temperatures around twenty-eight. A shorter dry spell runs through January and February. The islands sit on the equator and are hot and humid throughout, with the southern half of Sao Tome among the wettest places in Africa. Sea turtles nest on the beaches between October and March and whales pass between July and October, both of which are reasons to time a visit. The southern beaches around Praia Jale and Praia Piscina are the ones worth the drive, and the road to them is rough in any season.
saotome.prosCons: Sao Tome and Principe are two volcanic islands on the equator, once the largest cocoa producer in the world, whose abandoned plantation houses stand in the forest with trees growing through them. Principe is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with a fraction of a thousand visitors a year. It is safe, the fish and cocoa are exceptional, and almost nobody goes. Against that, the internet is poor, Portuguese is essential, flights are limited and expensive, and there is very little infrastructure of any kind aimed at visitors. The country also produces some of the finest cocoa in the world from the old plantation estates, several of which now run their own small chocolate operations.
saotome.whoFor: Sao Tome suits a Portuguese speaker who wants somewhere genuinely unvisited and beautiful, whose work tolerates a weak connection, and who is interested in the plantation history or the birdlife, which includes a remarkable number of endemic species for so small a country. It is a poor fit for anyone without Portuguese, anyone needing reliable internet, and anyone on a schedule, since the flights are few and cancellations are not unusual. It also suits birdwatchers, since the islands hold around thirty endemic species in an area smaller than most national parks, which is a density found almost nowhere else. Divers get uncrowded reef with no operators competing for it.

maseru.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month as a solo remote worker in Maseru, which is low and reflects a small economy closely tied to South Africa's. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $250 to $450. Food is cheap and much of it comes across the border from South Africa, which is where a great many residents shop deliberately, since Bloemfontein is around two hours away. The loti is pegged one to one with the South African rand and rand circulate freely alongside it. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
maseru.whereToWork: Maseru's connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of the city and mobile data from Vodacom Lesotho and Econet is the common fallback, with prices high relative to income. Power comes largely from the Muela hydropower station and is more reliable than in several neighbouring countries, though cuts happen. There is very little coworking. English is an official language alongside Sesotho and is the medium of education, government and business, which removes the language barrier entirely and is Lesotho's clearest practical advantage. Anyone working with Europe will find the offset small, at one or two hours ahead of London depending on the season, which is a workable overlap.
maseru.gettingAround: Maseru sits on the border, with the Maseru Bridge crossing into South Africa at the edge of the city centre, and the town itself is compact enough to walk in parts. Minibus taxis cover the city and the country cheaply. Beyond the lowland strip Lesotho is mountainous and the roads are serious: the Sani Pass, one of the highest road passes in Africa, requires a four-wheel drive and is one of the great drives on the continent. Moshoeshoe I airport has limited connections, and most people fly into Johannesburg. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project dams in the interior are worth the drive in their own right, and the road to Katse is tarred the whole way.
maseru.visas: Lesotho grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for up to fourteen or ninety days depending on nationality, with an e-visa available for everyone else. The rules vary by passport more than in most countries, so check yours. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for locally. Because Lesotho is entirely surrounded by South Africa, anyone arriving overland needs South African entry first, and the two sets of rules both apply to any land journey. Anyone crossing at Maseru Bridge should allow time at month end and on holidays, when the queues of people working in South Africa are longest.
maseru.bestTime: March to May and September to November are the best months, with mild dry weather and the mountain passes open. Lesotho is the only country in the world entirely above a thousand metres and the altitude governs everything: summers from December to February are warm in the lowlands and stormy in the mountains, and winters from June to August bring real snow to the highlands, with skiing at Afriski, one of only a handful of ski resorts in Africa. Maseru itself sits at 1,600 metres and gets frost. Afriski above Butha-Buthe runs from roughly June to August and is one of only two ski areas in southern Africa, which surprises most visitors.
maseru.prosCons: Lesotho is the Mountain Kingdom and the name is literal: the entire country sits above a thousand metres, the Maloti range runs through it, Sehlabathebe National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Maletsunyane Falls drops two hundred metres in a single sheet. English works everywhere and costs are very low. Against that, Maseru itself is a functional border town rather than an attractive city, the internet is weak, the country has one of the highest HIV rates in the world, and everything beyond the lowlands requires a serious vehicle.
maseru.whoFor: Maseru suits someone who wants an English-speaking base for the Maloti mountains at very low cost, particularly a walker, a rider or anyone drawn to Basotho pony trekking, which is the traditional way to travel here. It works as a gateway rather than a destination. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting a city, anyone needing reliable connectivity, and anyone without a vehicle capable of the mountain roads, which is what the country is actually for. It also suits anyone interested in dinosaur trackways, since Lesotho's sandstone holds some of the best-preserved footprints anywhere and several sites are open.

mbabane.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month as a solo remote worker in Mbabane, which is low and reflects a small economy inside South Africa's customs union. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $300 to $550. Food is cheap and largely South African, and many residents shop across the border or in Manzini, the larger commercial city half an hour away. The lilangeni is pegged one to one with the South African rand and rand circulate freely. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data. Anyone comparing with South Africa should note that the customs union keeps most goods at similar prices, so the saving is in rent rather than in shopping.
mbabane.whereToWork: Eswatini's connectivity is modest: fibre has reached parts of Mbabane and Manzini and mobile data from Eswatini Mobile and MTN is the common fallback. Power comes largely from South Africa and is affected when that grid is under strain. There is very little coworking. English is an official language alongside siSwati and is the medium of education, government and business, which removes the language barrier. The country sits two hours ahead of London in the northern winter, which is a workable offset for European hours. Anyone needing anything the capital lacks will find Manzini half an hour east, which is larger and holds most of the country's commerce.
mbabane.gettingAround: Mbabane is a small highland capital and its centre is walkable, though the town is built across steep ground. Minibus taxis and kombis cover the country cheaply.
