Eswatini is small enough to cross in a few hours: Manzini is thirty minutes east, Hlane and Mkhaya game reserves an hour or so beyond that, and Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary sits in the Ezulwini valley between Mbabane and Manzini, close enough to visit on an afternoon. King Mswati III airport has limited connections and most people fly into Johannesburg, four hours away by road.
mbabane.visas: Eswatini grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for up to thirty or ninety days depending on nationality, with an e-visa available for everyone else. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department. The country belongs to the Southern African Customs Union with South Africa, Botswana, Lesotho and Namibia, which governs trade rather than movement, so each border still has its own immigration process. Anyone entering overland from South Africa or Mozambique should check the border post hours, since several of the smaller crossings close in the early evening.
mbabane.bestTime: April to September is the dry season and the comfortable window, with warm days in the low twenties at Mbabane's altitude and cold nights. October to March is the wet season, hotter and with heavy afternoon storms, and it is when the lowveld game reserves are greenest. The Umhlanga reed dance in late August and the Incwala kingship ceremony around December and January are the two great national events, both of them living ceremonies rather than performances for visitors. The Ezulwini valley between Mbabane and Manzini holds most of the country's craft markets and the Mantenga cultural village, and is pleasant year-round.
mbabane.prosCons: Eswatini packs a great deal into a small area: Mlilwane and Hlane hold rhino, elephant and big cats within an hour of the capital, Malolotja is serious mountain walking country, and the Ezulwini valley is genuinely beautiful. English works everywhere, it is cheap, and the country is calmer and safer than most of its neighbours. Against that, it is one of the last absolute monarchies in the world and pro-democracy protests in 2021 were met with force, the HIV prevalence is the highest anywhere, and Mbabane itself is very quiet.
mbabane.whoFor: Mbabane suits someone who wants an English-speaking southern African base with game reserves and mountains within an hour, at a fraction of South African prices, and who is content with a very small capital. It works well as part of a longer regional trip rather than alone. It is a poor fit for anyone needing a city or a professional network. Anyone staying should read about the country's political situation rather than treating it as a purely scenic destination. It also suits anyone drawn to Swazi craft, since the candle, glass and weaving workshops in the Malkerns valley are genuine businesses rather than displays.

saintdenis.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month as a solo remote worker in Saint-Denis, which is expensive for the Indian Ocean and reflects a French department where much of the food arrives from Europe. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $700 to $1,100. Groceries cost noticeably more than mainland France and the price of living here has driven serious protest movements, including the gilets jaunes actions that were more sustained on Reunion than almost anywhere. The euro is the currency. This is our own estimate rather than measured data. Anyone comparing with Mauritius nearby should note that Reunion costs considerably more and offers European healthcare and schooling in exchange.
saintdenis.whereToWork: Reunion has European infrastructure: fibre reaches most of the coastal ring at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and French plans roam here without charge, which matters for anyone based in Europe. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene in Saint-Denis and Saint-Pierre. French is the language of everything, with Reunion Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited. The island sits three hours ahead of Paris in the northern winter, which makes a French morning into a Reunionese afternoon. Anyone working with mainland France should note that the offset flips with European daylight saving, which changes the overlap by an hour twice a year.
saintdenis.gettingAround: Saint-Denis sits on the north coast and its centre, with the Creole townhouses along the Rue de Paris and the Barachois seafront, is walkable. A coastal road rings the island and the new coastal highway west of the capital is one of the most expensive roads ever built in France, running partly on a viaduct over the sea because of rockfalls. Buses cover the ring. The interior, with its three cirques and the volcano, is reached by mountain roads and on foot. Roland Garros airport has direct flights to Paris.
saintdenis.visas: Reunion is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while sitting outside the Schengen area, which is the detail that matters: a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here with no permit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Longer stays for non-EU citizens require a French long-stay visa applied for before travel. Anyone travelling on to Mauritius, forty minutes away by air, should note that is a separate country with its own entry requirements.
saintdenis.bestTime: May to November is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, with daytime temperatures around twenty-five on the coast and the hiking trails in the cirques at their best. December to April is the wet season and the cyclone season, and Reunion sits directly in the Indian Ocean cyclone belt; the island holds several world records for rainfall in a single day. Piton de la Fournaise, one of the most active volcanoes on earth, erupts most years, and eruptions are announced and viewable from designated points. Mafate, the cirque reachable only on foot or by helicopter, is walkable year-round but the trails are genuinely hard after heavy rain.
saintdenis.prosCons: Reunion is one of the best hiking destinations anywhere: three collapsed volcanic cirques with villages reachable only on foot, over a thousand kilometres of marked trail, and an active volcano that erupts most years. It has European infrastructure, French healthcare and no visa question for Europeans. Against that, it is expensive, French is essential, the cost of living is politically contentious, and shark attacks have led to a swimming ban on much of the west coast that has been in place for over a decade. The island's Creole culture, mixing African, Indian, Chinese and European elements, is also more visible in daily life here than in most French departments.
saintdenis.whoFor: Saint-Denis suits a French speaker, ideally a European Union citizen, whose main interest is hiking or volcanology, since Reunion is genuinely world class at both. Anyone who runs will know it as the home of the Grand Raid, one of the hardest ultramarathons anywhere. It is a poor fit for anyone without French and anyone expecting a beach holiday, since the swimming restrictions on the west coast are real and the island's case is the interior rather than the shore. It also suits anyone drawn to the Indian Ocean's volcanic geology, since Piton de la Fournaise is among the most studied and most accessible active volcanoes anywhere.

macau.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,400 a month as a solo remote worker in Macau, which is expensive and reflects one of the most densely populated places on earth with a gaming economy behind its property prices. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $1,100 to $1,700. Food is the compensation: Macau eats extraordinarily well at every price point, and a bowl of noodles or a Portuguese-influenced set lunch costs very little. The pataca is pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, which is itself pegged to the United States dollar, and Hong Kong dollars circulate freely. This is our own estimate rather than measured data.
macau.whereToWork: Macau's connectivity is excellent: fibre throughout, comprehensive 5G and entirely reliable power, all underwritten by an economy that turns over more gaming revenue than anywhere else in the world. There is a small coworking market. Cantonese is the language of daily life, Portuguese remains co-official and appears on every street sign though few people speak it, and Mandarin and English are both widely used in business and tourism. The territory sits eight hours ahead of London, on the same clock as Hong Kong and mainland China. Anyone working with Europe will find the eight-hour offset means a European morning lands at the end of the Macau working day, which is a narrow overlap.
macau.gettingAround: Macau is small and much of the peninsula is walkable, though it is dense and hilly. Buses are cheap and comprehensive, and the casinos run free shuttle buses between the ferry terminals, the airport and their properties, which locals use as a de facto transport network. A light rail line serves Taipa and Cotai. Ferries run to Hong Kong in an hour, and the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, the longest sea crossing in the world, opened in 2018 and carries buses across in about forty minutes. The Cotai strip, built on reclaimed land between the islands of Taipa and Coloane, holds most of the newer casinos and did not exist thirty years ago.
macau.visas: Macau is a Special Administrative Region of China with its own immigration system entirely separate from the mainland's, and it is generous: most Western nationalities receive between thirty and ninety days visa-free on arrival, with British citizens getting six months. A Chinese visa does not admit you here and is not needed. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a work permit tied to an employer or an investment residency route. Crossing to mainland China from Macau is a full international border with a Chinese visa required. Anyone using Macau as a way to reset a Hong Kong stay should note both territories keep their own records and the practice is well understood by both.
macau.bestTime: October to December is the best window, with warm dry days in the low twenties, low humidity and clear air. March to May is humid and often foggy. Summer from June to September is hot, humid and the typhoon season, and Macau is exposed; Typhoon Hato in 2017 flooded the city and killed ten people. Winter is mild at around fifteen degrees. The Macau Grand Prix, run on public streets in November, is the only race in the world where both cars and motorcycles compete on the same circuit. Coloane, the southern island, keeps a village and a stretch of black sand beach that most visitors never reach and is the quietest part of the territory.
macau.prosCons: Macau is four hundred years of Portuguese administration on the edge of China and the result is genuinely unlike anywhere else: baroque churches and Chinese temples on the same street, a UNESCO World Heritage historic centre, and a food culture that invented its own cuisine from the collision. It has the world's largest gaming industry, excellent infrastructure and a generous visa policy. Against that, it is expensive, extremely dense, dominated by the casino economy, and the air quality reflects its position in the Pearl River Delta. Macanese cuisine is also recognised as the world's first fusion food, developed over four centuries from Portuguese, Chinese, Malay and Indian ingredients.
macau.whoFor: Macau suits someone who wants a compact, extremely safe, well-connected Asian base with remarkable food and a visa policy that asks almost nothing, and who is not bothered by casinos. It is a genuinely underrated place to spend a month. It is a poor fit for anyone wanting space or nature, since the territory is thirty square kilometres and mostly built, and anyone hoping to use it as a base for mainland China, which requires a separate visa and a full border crossing. It also suits anyone interested in colonial architecture, since the historic centre survives more completely here than anywhere else in East Asia.

koror.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month as a solo remote worker in Koror, which is expensive and reflects a Pacific island nation of eighteen thousand people that imports almost everything. A one-bedroom place runs roughly $800 to $1,300. Groceries carry the full Pacific freight markup and fresh produce is limited. Palau uses the United States dollar, which removes any conversion. Diving is the line that dominates a real budget here, along with the environmental fees the country charges visitors. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured data.
koror.whereToWork: Palau's connectivity improved substantially with the Belau submarine cable and a second connection added since, and fibre reaches Koror at workable speeds, though prices are high and outages happen. Mobile data covers the populated islands. Power is reliable in Koror and expensive. There is essentially no coworking. Palauan and English are both official and English is used throughout government, business and education, which makes Palau one of the easiest Pacific nations to operate in. The country sits nine hours ahead of London. Anyone working with Australia will find the offset small, at an hour behind eastern Australian time, which makes that the practical business overlap.
koror.gettingAround: Koror is the country's main town and is compact enough to move around by taxi or the occasional bus, though most visitors rent a car. A causeway connects Koror to Babeldaob, the much larger and almost empty main island, where a single ring road passes the new capital at Ngerulmud, a purpose-built complex serving a country of eighteen thousand. Everything that matters, though, is by boat: the Rock Islands, the dive sites and Jellyfish Lake are all reached from the Koror harbours. Babeldaob also holds the Ngardmau waterfall and the stone monoliths at Badrulchau, both of which almost no visitor reaches.
koror.visas: Palau grants visa-free entry to citizens of most countries for thirty days, extendable in-country, and to United States citizens indefinitely under the Compact of Free Association. On arrival every visitor must sign the Palau Pledge, stamped into the passport, a commitment to act responsibly toward the environment addressed to the children of Palau, which is the only such requirement anywhere. There is no remote work visa. An environmental impact fee is charged on departure and a separate permit is needed for the Rock Islands. Anyone diving should budget for the Rock Islands permit and the Jellyfish Lake surcharge separately, since both are charged in addition to the dive itself.
koror.bestTime: Palau is warm and humid all year at around thirty degrees, and the calendar turns on rain and wind. November to April is the drier half with the calmest seas and the best diving visibility, and it is the busy season. May to October is wetter, and while Palau sits at the edge of the western Pacific typhoon belt it is struck far less often than the Philippines or Guam. Diving is possible year-round and the manta and shark aggregations at German Channel and Blue Corner are not seasonal. Anyone hoping to dive Blue Corner should be aware it is a current dive requiring a reef hook, and operators will ask about logged experience.
koror.prosCons: Palau made its entire exclusive economic zone a marine sanctuary in 2015, closing eighty per cent of it to commercial fishing, and the diving that results is regularly called the best in the world: Blue Corner, German Channel, the Ulong Channel and dozens of Second World War wrecks. The Rock Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage site and Jellyfish Lake holds millions of stingless jellyfish. Against that, it is expensive, very small, English-speaking but extremely remote, and there is essentially nothing to do that is not on or under the water.
koror.whoFor: Koror suits a diver, and like Bonaire the honest answer is that it suits almost nobody else. For someone who wants world-class diving with English throughout and the dollar as currency, Palau is exceptional and the country has organised its entire environmental policy around keeping it that way. It is a poor fit for anyone who does not dive, anyone on a budget, and anyone who needs variety, since the islands are small and the flights in and out are few and long. It also suits anyone interested in Pacific war history, since the Peleliu battlefield south of Koror is largely as it was left in 1944.

hagatna.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month in Guam, which is expensive for the region and unsurprising once you know that almost everything arrives by ship from the United States or Asia. A one-bedroom runs roughly $900 to $1,500, with Tumon and Tamuning at the top and the villages inland cheaper. Groceries carry a visible freight markup and imported produce is the worst of it. Utilities are high because air conditioning runs constantly and power costs more than on the mainland. Eating out is the one area of relief: Chamorro barbecue, Filipino canteens and Korean restaurants are all inexpensive. The territory uses the United States dollar, so there is no conversion to think about.
hagatna.whereToWork: Connectivity is genuinely good. Guam is a landing point for several trans-Pacific submarine cables and the island's position in the network is one of its strategic assets, so fibre reaches most developed areas and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the populated west coast. Power is reliable by Pacific standards, though typhoons interrupt it. Coworking is limited to a handful of small operators, and most remote workers use hotel business centres in Tumon or work from home. The time zone is the real consideration: Guam sits ten hours ahead of GMT and fifteen hours ahead of United States Eastern time, which puts an American working day squarely in the middle of your night.
hagatna.gettingAround: A car is close to essential. Guam is about fifty kilometres long and built around Marine Corps Drive, the highway that runs the length of the developed west coast, with no rail and a bus network that is thin and slow. Rental cars are widely available and cheap by island standards. Tumon and Hagatna are walkable within themselves but not to each other. A B Won Pat International Airport sits between the two and connects to Tokyo, Seoul, Manila and Honolulu with a frequency no other Micronesian island comes close to, which is what makes Guam the practical hub for the whole region.
hagatna.visas: Guam is a United States territory with its own immigration arrangement, and it is more open than the mainland. The Guam and Northern Mariana Islands visa waiver programme admits citizens of a set of Asian countries, including South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong, for forty five days without a visa. Everyone else needs the same United States visa or ESTA they would need for the mainland, and an ESTA is valid here. There is no remote work visa and working on a visitor status is not permitted. United States citizens need only proof of identity and can live and work here indefinitely.
hagatna.bestTime: December to June is the dry season and the practical window, with temperatures around thirty degrees, lower humidity and calmer seas for diving. July to November is the wet season and the typhoon season, and Guam sits in the most active typhoon basin on earth. The island is built for it, with concrete construction and serious building codes, but a direct hit closes everything for days. Water temperature barely moves all year, so diving is a question of visibility rather than warmth. The shoulder months of November and June often give the best combination of price, weather and space.
hagatna.prosCons: The case for Guam is infrastructure without leaving the tropics: American medical care, reliable power, good connectivity, a proper airport and everything in English, on an island with reef diving and a genuinely distinct Chamorro culture. The case against is cost, distance and scale. It is expensive, it is a very long way from anywhere except East Asia, and fifty kilometres of island runs out of new things faster than most people expect. The military presence is large and shapes the island's economy and land use. There is essentially no remote worker community, so the social side is what you build yourself.
hagatna.whoFor: Guam suits anyone who wants tropical Pacific living with American systems underneath it: divers, people working on Asian time zones, and anyone with a family who wants schools and hospitals that work. It also suits people already connected to the region through work or military service. It does not suit anyone on a budget, anyone who needs a nomad scene to plug into, or anyone whose clients are in Europe or the Americas, because the time difference is brutal in both directions. Anyone considering a longer stay should also weigh the typhoon season honestly, since a serious storm can close the airport and the ports for the better part of a week.

saipan.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month, which makes Saipan noticeably cheaper than Guam a short flight south. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,200, and the collapse of the Chinese tourism market left a good deal of accommodation looking for tenants. Groceries carry the same Pacific freight markup as everywhere out here, and imported produce is expensive. Eating out is cheap, with Filipino, Korean, Chinese and Chamorro food all widely available and priced for local wages rather than visitors. Utilities are the sting: power on Saipan is expensive and air conditioning runs most of the year. The United States dollar is the currency.
saipan.whereToWork: Connectivity is adequate rather than good. Saipan was on a single ageing submarine cable for years and outages were a recurring problem; a second connection has improved matters but speeds and prices still lag Guam. Mobile data covers the populated west coast. Power is less reliable than on Guam and generators are common in businesses. There is essentially no coworking, so most people work from accommodation. Like Guam, Saipan runs ten hours ahead of GMT, which suits work with East Asia and is punishing for anything on American or European hours.
saipan.gettingAround: You need a car. Saipan is about twenty kilometres long with a single main road down the west coast through Garapan and Susupe, no useful public transport, and attractions scattered from Banzai Cliff in the north to the airport in the south. Rentals are cheap and plentiful. Garapan, the main town, is walkable within itself. Saipan International Airport connects to Guam several times a day and directly to Seoul, Tokyo and a shifting set of Chinese cities, with Guam the reliable route to anywhere else. The road to the Forbidden Island lookout and the northern cliffs is worth the drive.
saipan.visas: The Northern Mariana Islands are a United States commonwealth and share Guam's visa arrangement. The Guam and Northern Mariana Islands visa waiver programme admits citizens of several Asian countries, including South Korea, Japan and Taiwan, for forty five days, and there is a separate discretionary parole arrangement for Chinese and Russian visitors that has been suspended and restored more than once. Everyone else needs a United States visa or ESTA. There is no remote work visa and visitor status does not permit work. United States citizens can live and work here without any permission at all.
saipan.bestTime: December to June is the dry season and the best window, warm at around thirty degrees with lower humidity and the clearest water for diving the Grotto. July to November brings the rains and the typhoons, and Saipan has taken direct hits, including Typhoon Yutu in 2018 which was among the strongest storms ever to strike United States soil. Recovery from that took years and is still visible in places. Sea temperature is warm year round. The dry season is also when the island is busiest with Korean and Japanese visitors, which is a small effect these days.
saipan.prosCons: The case for Saipan is world-class diving at a price no comparable destination matches, American legal and medical systems, everything in English, and an island that is genuinely quiet. The Grotto is one of the best-known cavern dives anywhere and it is fifteen minutes from town. The case against is thinner infrastructure than Guam, an economy that has been in difficulty since the tourism collapse, some visible dereliction, and very limited flight options. Connectivity is workable but not something to stake a business on. There is no remote worker community whatsoever.
saipan.whoFor: Saipan suits divers above all, and anyone who wants a quiet tropical base with United States systems at a lower cost than Guam or Hawaii. It suits people working East Asian hours. It also suits anyone drawn to Pacific war history, since the 1944 battlefield sites are unfenced and largely as they were left. It does not suit anyone who needs reliable high-speed connectivity, anyone wanting a social scene, or anyone working with Europe or the Americas. It also suits anyone who wants a genuinely quiet island with American paperwork, since the population is under fifty thousand and the northern half is close to empty.

pagopago.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,800 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $1,000, and the rental market is small enough that what is available at any moment matters more than the average. Groceries are expensive because almost everything is shipped in, and the local supermarkets carry American brands at a markup. Fish and taro from the market are cheap. Utilities are high, with power costing well above mainland United States rates. Eating out is limited and the options are mostly Samoan, Korean and Chinese at modest prices. American Samoa uses the United States dollar and the postal system is domestic United States mail, which is a genuine practical advantage.
pagopago.whereToWork: Connectivity has improved substantially. American Samoa was dependent on a single cable for years and the Hawaiki cable now provides a second route, so fibre in Pago Pago is workable and mobile data covers the main island. It is not fast by mainland standards and it is expensive. Power is reasonably reliable. There is no coworking of any kind and remote workers use their accommodation. The time zone is unusual and worth understanding: American Samoa is eleven hours behind GMT and does not observe daylight saving, which puts it a full day behind Samoa, forty kilometres away, across the international date line.
pagopago.gettingAround: The aiga buses, privately owned and brightly painted, run along the main road around Tutuila and are cheap, frequent enough and part of the experience. A car makes life easier and rentals are available. Tutuila is small, about thirty kilometres long, and the road follows the coast with the ridge in the middle. Pago Pago International Airport connects to Honolulu twice a week and to Apia in Samoa several times a week on a short hop, and that is essentially the whole schedule. Getting here is the single hardest part of being here.
pagopago.visas: American Samoa is a United States territory but it is outside the federal immigration system, which surprises people. A United States visa or ESTA does not admit you, and United States citizens are not automatically entitled to enter either. Most visitors need an entry permit, which for many nationalities is issued on arrival for thirty days provided you have onward travel. Longer stays require an application to the territory's immigration office in advance. It is also the only United States territory where people are born United States nationals rather than citizens.
pagopago.bestTime: May to September is the dry season and the practical window, cooler at around twenty nine degrees with lower humidity. October to April is the wet season and the cyclone season, and Tutuila is genuinely wet: the mountains catch enormous rainfall and Pago Pago harbour is one of the rainiest inhabited spots in the world. The National Park of American Samoa is walkable year round but the trails are slippery in the wet months. Sea temperature is warm throughout. Sunday is worth planning around, since the territory observes it seriously and most things close.
pagopago.prosCons: The case for American Samoa is a spectacular natural setting almost nobody visits: Pago Pago harbour is a drowned volcanic crater with ridges rising straight out of it, and the only United States national park south of the equator sits on the same island. Samoan culture here is intact and central to daily life. The case against is isolation, cost, very limited flights and almost nothing in the way of services. Rain is constant for half the year. There is no remote worker presence at all and the visa arrangement is more restrictive than people assume.
pagopago.whoFor: American Samoa suits anyone drawn to Polynesian culture in a place that has not been rebuilt around visitors, hikers who want a national park to themselves, and people with a genuine connection to the territory. It suits divers and snorkellers willing to work without an operator. It does not suit anyone who needs reliable services, anyone on a schedule that cannot absorb a cancelled weekly flight, or anyone who wants a social scene, because there is not one. It also suits anyone researching Pacific fisheries or climate, since the tuna cannery in the harbour is the territory's economic centre and its politics run through everything here.

majuro.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,900 a month, which is high for what you get and reflects an atoll importing essentially everything. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,200 and decent housing is genuinely scarce. Groceries are expensive and fresh produce is limited and irregular, with tinned and frozen food doing much of the work. Fish is cheap and excellent. Utilities cost a great deal because power is diesel-generated and water is collected rainfall or desalinated. Eating out is limited to a handful of restaurants at modest prices. The Marshall Islands use the United States dollar, and United States postal rates apply, which helps with shipping.
majuro.whereToWork: Connectivity is the main constraint. Majuro is served by a submarine cable and speeds are workable for email and light video, but capacity is limited, prices are high and outages happen. Mobile data covers the atoll. Power is diesel-generated and cuts occur. There is no coworking. Anyone whose work depends on constant high-bandwidth calls should treat Majuro as a difficult place to operate. The time zone is twelve hours ahead of GMT, which puts you a day ahead of most clients and makes the overlap with Asia and Australia the practical one.
majuro.gettingAround: Majuro is a coral ribbon about fifty kilometres long and rarely more than a few hundred metres wide, so there is one road and everything is on it. Shared taxis run the length of it for a fixed low fare and are the normal way to move, flagged down anywhere. Bicycles work well on the flat. Amata Kabua International Airport sits on the atoll and connects to Honolulu and Guam on the United Airlines island hopper, a legendary route that stops at several Micronesian atolls on the way, plus flights to Fiji and Kiribati.
majuro.visas: The Marshall Islands are generous. Most Western nationalities receive thirty days visa-free on arrival, extendable in-country, and United States citizens may live and work here indefinitely under the Compact of Free Association, the arrangement that also allows Marshallese citizens to live and work in the United States. There is no remote work visa. Anyone planning a long stay should confirm the current position with the immigration office directly, since the rules for extensions have shifted. Proof of onward travel is normally required at check-in rather than on arrival. Anyone arriving on the island hopper should note that the flight crosses several atolls and that a missed connection can mean waiting several days for the next one.
majuro.bestTime: December to April is the drier season and the best window, with steadier trade winds and less rain. May to November is wetter. Temperatures barely move from around twenty nine degrees all year and the humidity is constant. The Marshall Islands sit outside the main typhoon belt, which is a real advantage, but king tides now regularly wash across the road, and that is the more relevant hazard here. Sea temperature is warm year round and the lagoon is calm on the leeward side whatever the season. Anyone planning around the king tides should know they follow the lunar calendar rather than the seasons, and the highest of them are published locally in advance.
majuro.prosCons: The case for Majuro is that it is one of the few places where the consequences of sea level rise are visible from a normal street, in a country arguing its own case at every climate conference, and a lagoon that is genuinely beautiful. Diving and fishing are exceptional and uncrowded. The case against is almost everything practical: expensive, limited food, thin connectivity, very few flights, minimal medical care and no professional community. The nuclear testing legacy at Bikini and Enewetak still shapes the country's politics and health. The country also runs the second largest ship registry in the world, which is why so many vessels anywhere carry a Marshall Islands flag on the stern.
majuro.whoFor: Majuro suits people with a working reason to be here: climate researchers, development and health staff, fisheries people, and anyone connected to the Compact relationship with the United States. It suits divers who want wrecks and reef with nobody on them. It does not suit anyone treating this as a lifestyle destination, anyone needing reliable connectivity, or anyone who would find a very small, very flat, very isolated place difficult. It also suits anyone interested in maritime law or shipping registration, since the registry is administered from here and is central to how the country funds itself.

kolonia.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,500 a month, which makes Pohnpei one of the more affordable places in the north Pacific. A one-bedroom runs roughly $400 to $800. Local produce is genuinely cheap and Pohnpei grows a great deal of its own food, which is unusual out here: bananas, breadfruit, taro and yam are everywhere, and the fish is excellent and inexpensive. Imported goods carry the usual freight markup. Utilities are moderate. Eating out is limited to a handful of restaurants and small canteens at low prices. The Federated States of Micronesia use the United States dollar and United States postal rates apply.
kolonia.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Pohnpei is served by a submarine cable and speeds in Kolonia are usable for email and light work, but bandwidth is limited, prices are high and reliability is patchy. Mobile data covers the populated coast. Power cuts happen. There is no coworking. This is not a place to run a call-heavy business from. The time zone is eleven hours ahead of GMT, which works for Asia and Australia and is difficult for anything else. Rain is heavy enough that it affects the connection on bad days. Anyone working with Australia will find the offset workable, at an hour ahead of eastern Australian time, which makes that the most practical business overlap available.
kolonia.gettingAround: Kolonia is small and walkable, and the rest of Pohnpei is reached by the circumferential road that runs most of the way around the island, though not quite the whole way. Shared taxis are cheap and the usual way to move. A rental car helps if you want to reach the waterfalls and the inland trails. Pohnpei International Airport is on a causeway just outside town and is a stop on the United Airlines island hopper between Guam and Honolulu, which is the route in and out for most people, plus connections to Chuuk and Kosrae.
kolonia.visas: The Federated States of Micronesia grant thirty days visa-free on arrival to most nationalities, extendable in-country, and United States citizens may live and work here indefinitely under the Compact of Free Association. There is no remote work visa. A visit to Nan Madol requires a separate permit and a local guide, arranged through the Madolenihmw chiefs, and this is genuinely enforced rather than a formality. Proof of onward travel is normally requested. Confirm the current position with immigration before a long stay. Anyone continuing to Chuuk or Kosrae should note those are separate states of the federation with their own arrangements for permits and local guides, though the entry rules are national.
kolonia.bestTime: There is no dry season worth the name. Pohnpei is one of the wettest places on earth, receiving several metres of rain a year and considerably more in the interior, and rain falls in every month. January to March is marginally drier and is the usual window. Temperatures sit around thirty degrees all year with very high humidity. The islands lie at the southern edge of the typhoon belt and are hit less often than Guam or the Philippines. Diving visibility is best in the drier months, and the wrecks and reef walls are worth the trip.
kolonia.prosCons: The case for Pohnpei is Nan Madol, a city of basalt logs built on artificial islets in a lagoon between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries and abandoned before any European saw it, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site and unlike anything else in the Pacific. Add rainforest, waterfalls and diving with nobody on it, at a genuinely low cost. The case against is the rain, the isolation, thin connectivity and very limited services. Medical care is basic and evacuation is a long way. Pohnpei also produces sakau, the local kava, which is drunk in nakas across the island and is central to social and ceremonial life rather than a novelty.
kolonia.whoFor: Pohnpei suits archaeologists and anyone drawn to Nan Madol, divers, and people with a working connection to Micronesia. It suits anyone who genuinely does not mind rain, because the rain here is not a season but a condition. It does not suit anyone with bandwidth-dependent work, anyone who wants nightlife or a social scene, or anyone uncomfortable being a long way from a hospital. It also suits anyone drawn to remote fieldwork, since the interior rainforest is barely surveyed and the island holds a number of species found nowhere else on earth.

honiara.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $400 to $800, with the areas near the ridge and the diplomatic quarter at the top. Market produce is cheap and the Honiara Central Market is the best value in the country, with fish, root vegetables and fruit at genuinely low prices. Imported goods carry a heavy markup and the supermarkets are expensive. Utilities cost a lot because power is diesel-generated and among the most expensive in the Pacific. Eating out is limited, with a handful of Chinese and Asian restaurants and the hotel dining rooms. The Solomon Islands dollar is the currency.
honiara.whereToWork: Connectivity has improved with the Coral Sea cable, which landed in 2019 and gave Honiara a real internet connection for the first time, so fibre in the centre and the better hotels is workable. Mobile data from Our Telekom and Bmobile covers the town and the main road. Power is unreliable and generators are standard in any serious business. There is no coworking. The time zone is eleven hours ahead of GMT, which puts Honiara an hour ahead of eastern Australia and makes that the practical business overlap. Anyone travelling to the outer provinces should assume no connectivity at all beyond patchy mobile coverage near the larger settlements, and plan the work accordingly.
honiara.gettingAround: Minibuses run along the single coastal road through Honiara for a very low flat fare and are the normal way to move, though they are crowded and stop constantly. Taxis are available and cheap by the hour. Walking in town is possible by day and generally avoided after dark. Honiara International Airport, formerly Henderson Field and the object of the 1942 campaign, is about eleven kilometres east and connects to Brisbane, Port Moresby, Nadi and Port Vila. Domestic flights and ships reach the outer provinces, and the ship schedules are approximate.
honiara.visas: The Solomon Islands grant visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for up to ninety days, issued as a visitor's permit on arrival. Everyone else applies in advance. There is no remote work visa and working on a visitor's permit is not permitted. Extensions are applied for at the immigration office in Honiara. Proof of onward travel and accommodation is normally requested at the airport, and it is worth having both printed. Anyone continuing to the Western Province for diving should note that domestic flights are frequently rescheduled and that building slack into a trip is the norm rather than caution.
honiara.bestTime: May to October is the drier, cooler season and the practical window, with south-easterly trade winds and better diving visibility. November to April is the wet season and the cyclone season, with heavy rain and the risk of flooding in Honiara, which has flooded severely more than once. Temperatures sit around thirty degrees all year with high humidity throughout. The diving is world class in either season, with the wrecks of Iron Bottom Sound offshore, but visibility and sea state are better in the dry months. The Solomon Islands sit within the cyclone belt but are struck less often than Vanuatu or Fiji, and the storms that do arrive usually track south of the main group.
honiara.prosCons: The case for the Solomon Islands is diving and history that exist nowhere else in this combination: Iron Bottom Sound holds dozens of ships and aircraft lost in the 1942 campaign, and the reefs beyond are among the most biodiverse on earth. Costs are low and the country is genuinely uncrowded. The case against is Honiara itself, which has a real problem with street crime and has seen serious rioting, most recently in 2021, along with poor infrastructure, unreliable power and limited medical care. This needs current advice rather than assumption.
honiara.whoFor: The Solomon Islands suit divers above all, and anyone drawn to the Pacific war, since Guadalcanal is where the ground campaign turned. They suit development and conservation workers, of whom there are a good number. They do not suit anyone wanting a comfortable or safe-feeling capital, anyone needing reliable infrastructure, or anyone without a specific reason to be here, because Honiara is a working town rather than a destination in itself. It also suits anyone drawn to the outer islands, since Marovo Lagoon in the Western Province is the largest saltwater lagoon in the world and is reachable in a day from Honiara.

funafuti.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month, which is high for a country with almost nothing to buy, and that is precisely why: every tin, every litre of fuel and every sheet of roofing arrives by ship, and the ships are infrequent. A one-bedroom runs roughly $400 to $800 and the rental market is tiny and mostly informal. Fish is cheap and abundant. Fresh produce is limited, irregular and expensive, with pulaka, breadfruit and coconut doing much of the work. Utilities cost a great deal because power is diesel-generated. Tuvalu uses the Australian dollar alongside its own coins, which circulate only here.
funafuti.whereToWork: Connectivity is the hardest constraint on this list. Tuvalu had no submarine cable for most of its history and relied on satellite, which meant slow, expensive and weather-dependent internet; a cable connection has been in progress and coverage remains limited and unreliable. Mobile data exists on Funafuti and thins to nothing on the outer atolls. Power cuts happen. There is no coworking, no business centre and no fallback. Anyone whose work requires a stable connection should treat Tuvalu as unworkable rather than difficult. The time zone is twelve hours ahead of GMT.
funafuti.gettingAround: You walk, or you borrow a scooter. Funafuti's main islet, Fongafale, is about twelve kilometres long and a few hundred metres wide at most, and in places narrow enough to see both the lagoon and the ocean from the middle of the road. There are no formal taxis. The airstrip runs down the centre of the settlement and doubles as the town's open space, used for football and socialising between the few flights. Funafuti International Airport is served by Fiji Airways from Suva a handful of times a week, and that is the only scheduled connection to the country.
funafuti.visas: Tuvalu grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for one month, issued on arrival, with extensions available in-country up to three months. Everyone else applies in advance, and because Tuvalu has almost no diplomatic missions, that usually means through the High Commission in Suva. There is no remote work visa. Proof of onward travel is required and is genuinely checked, since leaving depends on a flight that runs a few times a week and is often full. Anyone hoping to visit the outer atolls should plan around the government ship, which runs on an approximate schedule and is the only way to reach most of them.
funafuti.bestTime: May to October is the drier, cooler season and the practical window, with steadier trade winds. November to April is the wet season and the cyclone season, and Tuvalu is dangerously exposed: the highest natural point in the country is about four and a half metres and most of it is barely two. Temperatures sit around thirty degrees year round. King tides now flood parts of Fongafale several times a year regardless of the weather, pushing seawater up through the porous coral from below, which is the image the country has taken to every climate conference.
funafuti.prosCons: The case for Tuvalu is that almost nobody goes, which for a certain kind of traveller is the entire point, and that the country is at the front of the argument about sea level rise in a way no report conveys. The government has begun creating a digital replica of the nation and has leased its .tv domain for a substantial share of national revenue. The case against is everything practical: no reliable internet, a few flights a week, minimal medical care, very little to eat and nowhere to go once you have walked the atoll.
funafuti.whoFor: Tuvalu suits journalists, climate researchers, development staff and anyone with a specific working reason to be here, plus the small number of travellers collecting countries. It suits anyone who genuinely wants to be somewhere with no distractions. It does not suit a remote worker in any ordinary sense, because the connectivity cannot support one, and it does not suit anyone who would find a very small, very flat, very quiet place hard, which most people do after a week. It also suits anyone studying atoll hydrology, since the freshwater lens under Fongafale is thin, contested and central to whether the country remains habitable.

alofi.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $900, though the rental market on an island of about seventeen hundred people is mostly word of mouth and self-catering units aimed at visitors. Groceries are expensive: Niue imports almost everything from New Zealand and the ship arrives roughly monthly, so what is on the shelf depends on when it last came. Local produce, taro, coconut crab and fish, is cheap when available. Utilities are high because power is diesel-generated. The New Zealand dollar is the currency and New Zealand banking largely applies.
alofi.whereToWork: Connectivity is better than the population would suggest. Niue has invested in island-wide wifi and the connection, while not fast, is usable for normal remote work, and the government has actively courted people who want to work from here. Power is reasonably reliable. There is no coworking, but several accommodation providers cater to longer stays. The time zone is eleven hours behind GMT, the same as American Samoa, which puts Niue a day behind New Zealand two hours away by plane and makes overlap with almost anywhere a puzzle worth solving before you arrive.
alofi.gettingAround: You need a vehicle. Niue is a single raised coral island about sixty kilometres around, with one road circling it and tracks running down to the sea caves and chasms, and there is no public transport of any kind. Rental cars and scooters are available and a Niue driving licence, issued at the police station for a small fee, is a required souvenir. Hanan International Airport is served by Air New Zealand from Auckland twice a week, and that is the only scheduled flight to the country in either direction.
alofi.visas: Niue is self-governing in free association with New Zealand, and Niueans are New Zealand citizens. Visitors of most nationalities receive thirty days visa-free on arrival, and New Zealand citizens may stay indefinitely. Extensions are available. There is no formal remote work visa, but Niue has been unusually welcoming to long-stay visitors and the small population makes arrangements more personal than procedural. Proof of onward travel and pre-booked accommodation is required, and the accommodation requirement is enforced because there are only so many beds on the island. Anyone hoping to swim with the humpbacks should also note that the activity is licensed, that operator numbers are deliberately capped, and that bookings go early in the season.
alofi.bestTime: April to November is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, with temperatures around twenty six degrees and the clearest water. December to March is the wet season and the cyclone season, and Cyclone Heta devastated Alofi in 2004, destroying much of the settlement and pushing the hospital inland. Whale season runs roughly July to October, and Niue is one of the few places on earth where swimming with humpbacks is permitted and genuinely happens. Visibility in the water is extraordinary year round because there are no rivers on the island to carry silt.
alofi.prosCons: The case for Niue is water clarity that is difficult to overstate, often visible to eighty metres, sea caves and chasms you walk into from the road, humpback whales in season and a population small enough that people know you within a week. It is also one of the safest places anywhere. The case against is that it is very small, very quiet, expensive to supply, served by two flights a week, and short on medical care. Anything you cannot buy on the island waits for the ship. The island also has no rivers and no natural harbour, so boats are lifted in and out of the water by crane at Alofi, which is worth watching once.
alofi.whoFor: Niue suits divers, snorkellers and anyone drawn to whales, along with people who want somewhere genuinely quiet with a usable internet connection, which is a rarer combination than it sounds. It suits New Zealanders, who face no immigration friction at all. It does not suit anyone who needs choice, nightlife or a professional community, and it does not suit anyone uncomfortable with two flights a week being the whole schedule. It also suits writers and anyone else whose work benefits from having nothing else to do, which is a genuine and much-cited reason people come here for a month.

longyearbyen.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,400 a month. A room or a small flat runs roughly $900 to $1,600, and housing is the binding constraint here rather than the price: almost all of it is tied to an employer, and finding somewhere to live without a job on the island is genuinely difficult. Groceries arrive by ship and plane and cost noticeably more than mainland Norway, though Svalbard is outside the Norwegian tax area so alcohol and tobacco are cheaper and rationed by quota. Eating out is expensive. Heating and clothing are real budget lines in a place that is below freezing most of the year.
longyearbyen.whereToWork: Connectivity is excellent and surprises people. Longyearbyen sits at the end of a dedicated fibre link to the mainland, laid to serve the satellite ground station on the plateau above town, which downloads data from polar-orbiting satellites on every pass. That gives a settlement of about two and a half thousand people better internet than most European towns. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking presence and several cafes people work from. The time zone is central European, the same as Oslo, so working with Europe is straightforward and the darkness is the only complication.
longyearbyen.gettingAround: Longyearbyen is walkable end to end in twenty minutes and that is essentially the whole road network: about fifty kilometres of road exist in all of Svalbard and none of it leaves the settlements. Beyond the town you travel by snowmobile in winter, by boat in summer, or on foot with a rifle, because polar bears are present across the archipelago and carrying protection outside the settlement is a legal requirement. Svalbard Airport is three kilometres out and connects to Oslo and Tromso daily in season, which is a genuinely good link for somewhere this far north.
longyearbyen.visas: Svalbard is unlike anywhere else. The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 gives citizens of every signatory country the right to live and work here without a visa, a residence permit or a work permit, regardless of nationality, and that has never been repealed. Svalbard is not part of the Schengen area, so time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, but you will pass through Schengen to reach it. The catch is practical: there is no welfare system, and anyone unable to support themselves can be required to leave. Anyone planning to stay should arrange work and housing before arriving, because the treaty gives the right to be here and no right at all to be supported here.
longyearbyen.bestTime: March to May is the best combination, with snow still on the ground for snowmobiling and dog sledding, returning daylight and temperatures around minus ten. June to August is the midnight sun, with continuous daylight, boat access to the fjords and temperatures a few degrees above freezing. Late October to mid-February is the polar night, when the sun does not rise at all and the town runs on street lighting and northern lights, which is either the reason to come or the reason not to. There is no month here that is warm.
longyearbyen.prosCons: The case for Longyearbyen is that nowhere else combines genuine Arctic wilderness, excellent internet, Norwegian standards of safety and services, and the right to simply turn up and stay. Glaciers, polar bears and the Global Seed Vault are all within sight of the town. The case against is the darkness, which is four months long and affects people more than they expect, the cost, the difficulty of finding housing, and the fact that leaving town at all requires equipment, a rifle and usually a guide. Svalbard also has no burial ground in use, because bodies do not decompose in permafrost, and seriously ill residents are flown to the mainland rather than treated locally.
longyearbyen.whoFor: Longyearbyen suits researchers, guides, photographers and anyone whose work is genuinely location-independent and who wants somewhere extreme with functioning infrastructure. It suits people who like winter rather than tolerate it. The visa freedom makes it unusually accessible to nationalities that struggle everywhere else. It does not suit anyone who needs sunlight, anyone who wants to hike freely without a rifle, or anyone hoping to arrive without accommodation arranged. It also suits anyone whose nationality makes ordinary travel difficult, since the treaty right to live and work here applies regardless of passport and is unique in the world.

mariehamn.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month, which is Nordic pricing without a Nordic city's choice. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, cheaper than Helsinki or Stockholm and not by as much as the size difference suggests. Groceries are Finnish prices, which are high, and the archipelago's ferry logistics do not help. Eating out is expensive and the choice is limited outside the summer season. The compensations are real: heating is included in most rentals, public services are excellent and the tax-free status of the islands within the European Union means alcohol and some goods are cheaper on the ferries. The euro is the currency.
mariehamn.whereToWork: Connectivity is excellent. Aland has Finnish infrastructure, which means fibre through the town, comprehensive mobile coverage and entirely reliable power. There is a small coworking scene and the islands have actively marketed themselves to remote workers, with the local government running programmes to attract residents to a place with a shrinking population. Everything administrative is digital and works. The time zone is eastern European, two hours ahead of GMT in winter, which gives a workable overlap with the rest of Europe and an early finish against anything in the Americas.
mariehamn.gettingAround: Mariehamn is small and flat and the bicycle is the default: Aland has an extensive network of cycle paths and the islands are laid out for them. Buses connect the main island's villages. Beyond that, the archipelago runs on ferries, most of them free or nearly so between the inhabited islands, and working out the timetables is part of living here. Mariehamn Airport has limited connections to Helsinki and Stockholm, but the practical route is the ferry: large ships run to both Stockholm and Turku daily and take five to six hours.
mariehamn.visas: Aland is part of Finland and part of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens can live and work here with no permit and everyone else needs the same Schengen visa or residence permit they would need for mainland Finland. The islands do sit outside the European Union value added tax area, which is why the ferries sell duty free, but that is a tax arrangement rather than a border. One genuine local rule: acquiring land and full residency rights requires hembygdsratt, a regional citizenship with a five year qualifying period.
mariehamn.bestTime: June to August is the season, with long days, temperatures around twenty degrees, the archipelago open by boat and the islands at their busiest. May and September are quieter and still pleasant. Winter from December to March is cold, dark and very quiet, with the sea sometimes freezing enough to close the smaller ferry routes, though the main Stockholm and Turku ships run all year. The islands empty out of visitors entirely between October and April, which is either a drawback or the reason to come. Anyone planning around the ferries should note that the Stockholm and Turku routes are also the islands' duty free lifeline and are busiest on Friday and Sunday evenings.
mariehamn.prosCons: The case for Aland is a demilitarised, Swedish-speaking, self-governing archipelago inside the European Union with Nordic infrastructure, almost no crime, an enormous amount of water and space, and a government that actively wants more residents. The case against is the winter, which is long and dark, the small population, which means a limited social and professional scene, and the language: Aland is monolingually Swedish by law, and Finnish will not help you here. Prices are high and the choice of everything is narrow. Aland also fought a quiet diplomatic battle in the 1920s to join Sweden and lost it at the League of Nations, which is why the autonomy and the demilitarisation exist at all.
mariehamn.whoFor: Aland suits Swedish speakers, sailors, cyclists and anyone who wants Nordic quality of life in a place with genuine space around it. It suits European Union citizens especially, since the paperwork disappears entirely. It suits families, given the schools and the safety. It does not suit anyone who needs a city, anyone who struggles with dark winters, or anyone who cannot get by in Swedish, because Swedish here is not optional in the way it is in Helsinki. It also suits anyone drawn to maritime history, since the Pommern, a four-masted barque moored in Mariehamn, is the last of the grain-trade windjammers preserved unaltered.

sthelier.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,600 a month, and Jersey is genuinely expensive. A one-bedroom runs roughly $1,400 to $2,000, and housing is tightly controlled: the island operates a residential qualification system that restricts what most newcomers may rent or buy, which pushes new arrivals into a smaller and pricier part of the market. Groceries cost more than mainland Britain because everything ships in, though the island's own dairy, potatoes and seafood are excellent. Eating out is expensive. Income tax is a flat twenty per cent with no capital gains or inheritance tax, which is the reason a great deal of money is here.
sthelier.whereToWork: Connectivity is outstanding. Jersey rolled out fibre to every property on the island years ahead of most of Europe, and gigabit connections are standard rather than premium. Mobile coverage is complete and power is entirely reliable. There is a real coworking scene serving the finance and digital sectors, and Digital Jersey runs a hub in St Helier. The time zone is the same as London, including daylight saving, so working with the United Kingdom is seamless and Europe is an hour away. This is one of the best-connected small islands anywhere.
sthelier.gettingAround: St Helier is walkable and the island is only about fifteen kilometres across, so a bicycle covers most of it, helped by the green lanes where vehicles are limited to twenty five kilometres an hour and give way to walkers and cyclists. LibertyBus runs a decent network. Driving is easy but parking in St Helier is a permanent irritation and uses a paycard system. Jersey Airport connects to London, Southampton, Manchester and several European cities, and ferries run to Saint-Malo, Guernsey and Poole. Anyone driving should know that the island's speed limits are low even by British standards, topping out at about sixty four kilometres an hour, and are enforced.
sthelier.visas: Jersey is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom and not part of the European Union, with its own immigration rules that broadly mirror British ones. Most visitors who can enter the United Kingdom can enter Jersey, and the Common Travel Area means no routine passport check arriving from Britain. Working is a different matter: Jersey controls employment tightly through a registration card system tied to residential status, and taking a job without the right permission is not possible. There is no remote work visa. Anyone planning to stay longer than a visit should resolve the housing qualification first, since it determines what may be rented and is not something an employer can waive.
sthelier.bestTime: May to September is the season, with temperatures around twenty degrees, long evenings and the beaches at their best. Jersey has the mildest climate in the British Isles and the second largest tidal range in the world, around twelve metres, which means the island grows by roughly a third at low tide and the seabed at Seymour Tower is walkable with a guide. Winter is mild but wet and windy, and the tourist infrastructure thins considerably. Late spring is when the island looks best, before the summer crowds arrive. Anyone visiting in summer should book the Ecrehous or Minquiers boat trips early, since the offshore reefs are only reachable on certain tides and the operators are few.
sthelier.prosCons: The case for Jersey is exceptional infrastructure on a small, safe, mild island: gigabit internet everywhere, low tax, excellent seafood, beaches and cliff paths, and an hour to London. The case against is cost and control. Housing is expensive and rationed by a qualification system that treats most newcomers as temporary, the island is small enough to feel closed after a while, and the finance industry dominates the economy and much of the conversation. The German occupation of 1940 to 1945 is still a live part of the island's memory.
sthelier.whoFor: Jersey suits people working in finance, law or digital services who want a low-tax base with British systems, and anyone with a family who values safety and schools. It suits sea swimmers, cyclists and walkers. It does not suit anyone arriving without a job or a housing route, because the residential qualification system will block most of what they want to rent, and it does not suit anyone looking for a cheap island. It also suits anyone drawn to occupation history, since the Jersey War Tunnels and the coastal fortifications are among the most complete Atlantic Wall remains anywhere.

stpeterport.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,500 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $1,300 to $1,900, and like Jersey the island restricts its housing market, dividing it into Local and Open markets with the Open market considerably more expensive and the route most newcomers take. Groceries cost more than mainland Britain. Eating out is expensive but the seafood is exceptional and the island's own dairy is famous. Income tax is a flat twenty per cent with a cap on very high incomes, and there is no capital gains, inheritance or value added tax, which is the reason the finance sector is here.
stpeterport.whereToWork: Connectivity is very good. Guernsey has invested heavily in fibre and most of the island now has it, with reliable power and complete mobile coverage. There is a small but real coworking and digital sector alongside the finance industry, and Digital Greenhouse in St Peter Port is the hub. The time zone matches London, including daylight saving, so United Kingdom work is seamless. Guernsey is slightly less far along on fibre than Jersey and slightly cheaper, which is a fair summary of the difference between the two islands generally. Anyone comparing the two islands should also weigh the sector: Guernsey's finance industry leans towards insurance and funds where Jersey's leans towards banking and trusts.
stpeterport.gettingAround: St Peter Port is compact and steep, built up the hill from the harbour in narrow lanes and steps, and walkable if you accept the gradient. The island is about ten kilometres across with a decent bus network at a flat low fare. Cycling works well. Guernsey Airport connects to London, Southampton and Jersey, and ferries run to Jersey, Saint-Malo and Poole. The smaller islands of Herm and Sark are reachable by boat in twenty and fifty minutes, and Sark famously has no cars at all. Anyone driving should be ready for the filter in turn system at unmarked junctions, which is a local convention rather than a rule and works better than it sounds.
stpeterport.visas: Guernsey is a Crown Dependency with its own immigration rules that broadly mirror British ones, and the Common Travel Area means no routine passport check arriving from Britain. Most people who can enter the United Kingdom can enter Guernsey as a visitor. Working and living here is controlled through the population management regime, which ties employment and housing together and issues permits by category. There is no remote work visa, though the island has an Open market housing route that gives more flexibility than Jersey's system does. Anyone planning to stay should resolve the housing category first, since Local and Open market properties carry different rights and the distinction governs everything else.
stpeterport.bestTime: May to September is the season, mild at around twenty degrees, with the cliff paths on the south coast at their best and the sea warm enough to swim. Guernsey shares Jersey's enormous tidal range and mild maritime climate. Winter is mild but wet and windy, and the island is very quiet. Victor Hugo wrote through fifteen winters here in exile and found them productive, which is one way to read the season. Late spring, when the cliff paths are in flower, is when the island looks best. Anyone visiting should try to reach Sark on a clear day, since it has no cars, no street lighting and was designated the world's first Dark Sky Island in 2011.
stpeterport.prosCons: The case for Guernsey is a smaller, quieter and slightly cheaper version of Jersey with the same tax treatment, better preserved lanes and a genuinely lovely capital of narrow streets above a working harbour. Hauteville House, where Hugo wrote Les Miserables, is open and extraordinary. The case against is the same as Jersey's: an expensive and rationed housing market, a finance-dominated economy, and an island small enough that the social scene is limited. Flights are fewer than Jersey's and the weather closes the airport more often than people expect. The occupation of 1940 to 1945 also runs deeper here than on Jersey, since Alderney held the only Nazi concentration camps on British soil and the sites are still visible.
stpeterport.whoFor: Guernsey suits finance and legal professionals wanting a low-tax base, and anyone who prefers a quieter island to Jersey's slightly busier one. It suits walkers, sea swimmers and anyone drawn to the smaller islands nearby. It does not suit anyone arriving without a housing route through the Open market or an employment permit, and it does not suit anyone who needs frequent, reliable flights, because fog grounds them regularly. It also suits anyone who wants a genuinely walkable harbour town, since St Peter Port's stepped lanes and Regency terraces are among the best preserved in the Channel Islands.

vaticancity.costOfLiving: Nobody rents in Vatican City, so the figure here is really Rome around it: budget about $2,500 a month to live within walking distance of St Peter's. A one-bedroom in Prati or Borgo runs roughly $1,200 to $1,800, and those two districts carry a premium for the address and the calm. Groceries at the Trionfale market a few streets north are among the best value in Rome. Eating out ranges from tourist prices on the Via della Conciliazione to genuinely cheap in Prati's back streets, and the difference is a two minute walk. The euro is the currency and Italian banking applies.
vaticancity.whereToWork: Practically speaking you work in Rome. Fibre reaches most of Prati and Borgo at good speeds, mobile coverage is complete and Italian plans work throughout. Power is reliable. There is a reasonable coworking market in Prati and across the river in the centre, and the cafes around the Vatican walls are quieter than anywhere near the Pantheon. Vatican City itself has its own telephone country code, its own postal service, its own radio station and its own internet domain, none of which a visitor uses. The time zone is central European, so European work is straightforward.
vaticancity.gettingAround: Everything here is walking. Vatican City is under half a square kilometre and you cross it on foot in minutes, with the museums entrance on the north wall and St Peter's Square on the east. Rome's metro line A stops at Ottaviano and Cipro, both a few minutes from the walls, and buses and trams run along the river. Roma San Pietro station is a short walk south. Fiumicino airport is about forty minutes by taxi or a train from Termini, and Ciampino is further out and mostly serves budget carriers.
vaticancity.visas: Vatican City has no border control and no visa of its own: you enter from Italy and the entry rules that matter are Italy's, which means the Schengen ninety day rule for most non-European visitors and free movement for European Union citizens. Time spent here counts against a Schengen allowance in practice because you are in Italy to get here. Residence in the Vatican itself is granted only to those working for the Holy See, and its citizenship is functional and temporary rather than something anyone acquires by living here.
vaticancity.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the best months, warm at around twenty three degrees and without the July and August heat that regularly pushes past thirty five. Winter is mild at around twelve degrees and much quieter, which makes it the best time to see the museums without queuing for an hour. Easter and Christmas bring enormous crowds to St Peter's Square. The Sistine Chapel and the museums are open most weekdays and closed on Sundays except the last Sunday of the month, when entry is free and the queues are correspondingly long.
vaticancity.prosCons: The case is simple and hard to argue with: the Sistine Chapel, the Raphael Rooms, the Laocoon and St Peter's Basilica are within a few hundred metres of each other, and living beside them means seeing them on a Tuesday morning rather than in a two hour queue. Prati is a genuinely pleasant Roman neighbourhood. The case against is that the immediate surroundings are the most tourist-saturated square kilometre in Europe, prices reflect it, and the Vatican itself closes at night, so the area empties in a way central Rome does not.
vaticancity.whoFor: This suits art historians, students of the Renaissance, and anyone whose interest in Rome is specifically the Vatican collections, which reward repeated visits far more than a single one. It suits people who want a quieter, more residential Rome than the centro storico while staying walkable to everything. It does not suit anyone looking for a nomad community, anyone on a budget, or anyone who would find the constant flow of pilgrims and tour groups wearing, because it does not stop. It also suits anyone attending a papal audience, since the general audience on Wednesday mornings is free and tickets are obtained from the Prefecture of the Papal Household in advance.

minsk.costOfLiving: Budget around $750 a month, which makes Minsk one of the cheapest capitals in Europe. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the centre and the areas near the metro at the top and the Soviet-era microdistricts considerably cheaper. Groceries are inexpensive and Belarusian dairy and produce are good. Eating out is genuinely cheap: a full meal in an ordinary cafe costs a few dollars and even the better restaurants are modest by European standards. Utilities are low and heating is centralised. The Belarusian ruble was redenominated in 2016, so older prices need a factor of ten thousand applied.
minsk.whereToWork: Connectivity is good and this is not an accident. Belarus built a serious software industry through its High Technology Park, which produced World of Tanks and Viber among others, so fibre is widespread, speeds are decent and prices are low. Mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. Coworking exists in the centre and the standard is reasonable. The complication is not technical: international payment cards issued abroad often do not work, several Western services are unavailable, and sanctions make banking and receiving money genuinely awkward. Plan the money side before arriving.
minsk.gettingAround: Minsk has a clean, cheap and fast metro with three lines, and the fare is a few cents. Buses, trolleybuses and trams cover the rest, and the city was rebuilt after 1944 on a scale that makes it easy to navigate and long to walk: Independence Avenue runs fifteen kilometres in a straight line. Taxis and Yandex Go are cheap. Minsk National Airport connects to Moscow, Istanbul, Dubai and a shrinking set of other destinations, since European Union carriers no longer fly here and European airspace is closed to Belarusian ones.
minsk.visas: Belarus operates a visa-free scheme that has expanded considerably: citizens of most European countries, including the whole European Union, may enter for up to thirty days without a visa. The conditions matter. The visa-free entry generally applies when arriving at Minsk National Airport or by certain land crossings, requires medical insurance, and specifically excludes arrival from or departure to Russia, because that border is not an international one and has no controls. There is no remote work visa. Check the current rules directly, since this policy has changed repeatedly. Anyone entering overland should also note that Belarus requires compulsory medical insurance bought locally at the border, and that the paperwork is checked rather than assumed.
minsk.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable window, with temperatures around twenty two degrees in July and long evenings. Winter from December to February is properly cold, often around minus five to minus ten, with snow on the ground for months, though the city clears it efficiently and the metro makes it manageable. April and October are grey and wet. Minsk is greener than its reputation suggests, with large parks along the Svislach river, and summer is when that shows. Independence Day on the third of July is the biggest event in the calendar.
minsk.prosCons: The case for Minsk is cost, order and a coherent architectural idea: the city was almost entirely destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt in Stalinist neoclassicism on a monumental scale, which produces something genuinely unlike anywhere else. It is clean, very safe from street crime, the metro works and living costs are a fraction of the rest of Europe. The case against is political: Belarus is an authoritarian state, the 2020 protests were suppressed severely, sanctions complicate money and travel, and the war next door shapes everything. The city's Great Patriotic War museum and the memorial at Khatyn also make plain how completely Belarus was destroyed between 1941 and 1944, which explains a great deal about the country.
minsk.whoFor: Minsk suits people with a specific reason to be here: family connections, business ties, Russian-language study, or an interest in Soviet urbanism, which the city offers in an unusually complete form. It suits developers, given the local industry. It does not suit anyone who needs Western banking to work smoothly, anyone uncomfortable in a country where political expression carries real consequences, or anyone hoping for an easy visa run to elsewhere in Europe, because the flight options are now narrow. It also suits anyone drawn to the Belovezhskaya Pushcha forest on the Polish border, the last stretch of the primeval woodland that once covered the European plain and home to wild bison.

bujumbura.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500, with the Rohero and Kiriri areas near the embassies at the top. Market produce is very cheap and Burundi grows good coffee, bananas and vegetables. Imported goods carry a heavy markup and the supermarkets serving the expatriate community are expensive. Fish from Lake Tanganyika, particularly mukeke and the small ndagala, is cheap and excellent. Utilities are modest but power cuts are frequent. Burundi is one of the poorest countries in the world by income per head, which is visible everywhere and shapes what the low prices mean.
bujumbura.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Burundi is landlocked and its bandwidth arrives overland through Tanzania and Kenya, which makes it expensive and slow, and fibre reaches only parts of Bujumbura. Mobile data from Lumitel and Econet is the usual fallback. Power cuts are frequent enough that any serious office runs a generator. There is almost no coworking. Anyone with call-heavy work should treat this as a real constraint rather than a nuisance. The time zone is two hours ahead of GMT, which gives a workable European overlap and an early start against the Americas.
