bujumbura.gettingAround: Shared minibuses and motorbike taxis cover Bujumbura cheaply and are how most people move. Taxis are available and inexpensive by the hour. The city is spread along the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika and is flat near the water, rising steeply into the hills behind, which is where the better housing sits. Bujumbura International Airport is about eleven kilometres north and connections are limited: Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Kigali and Dar es Salaam, mostly on regional carriers. The road to Kigali takes about six hours and is the common overland route.
bujumbura.visas: Burundi requires a visa of most nationalities. An e-visa system operates and is the usual route, with visas issued for thirty days and extendable in Bujumbura, and visa on arrival has been available at times but is not something to rely on. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. The rules have changed more than once in recent years and the fees are payable in United States dollars, so confirm the current position directly with the immigration department before travelling. Anyone crossing overland to Rwanda should note that the border has closed and reopened several times in recent years and the current status is worth confirming the week before travelling.
bujumbura.bestTime: June to August is the long dry season and the practical window, warm at around twenty eight degrees on the lake shore with clear skies. There is a shorter dry spell in December and January. The rains from February to May and again from September to November are heavy, and Bujumbura floods, with the roads out of the city sometimes cut. Temperatures on the lake shore are consistently warm while the hills behind are noticeably cooler, and the difference of a few hundred metres is worth several degrees. Anyone visiting Kibira National Park in the north should note that its trails are close to impassable in the rains and that the chimpanzee tracking is a dry season activity.
bujumbura.prosCons: The case for Bujumbura is Lake Tanganyika, which is the second deepest and second oldest lake in the world and has sand beaches at Saga and Karera that would be famous anywhere else, along with genuinely low costs and a compact, walkable centre. Burundian drumming is UNESCO-listed and unlike anything else. The case against is serious: Burundi has severe poverty, a fragile political situation after the 2015 crisis, real street crime, weak medical care and limited infrastructure. This needs current government advice, not assumptions. The country's political capital also moved to Gitega in 2019, so Bujumbura remains the economic centre while the government has largely relocated inland.
bujumbura.whoFor: Bujumbura suits development, health and humanitarian workers, of whom there are a good number, and researchers working on the Great Lakes. It suits anyone with a regional connection through Rwanda or Tanzania. It does not suit anyone treating this as a destination, anyone who needs reliable connectivity or power, or anyone without a support network here, because the practical difficulty of daily life is considerably higher than the price level would suggest. It also suits anyone studying the Great Lakes ecosystem, since Lake Tanganyika holds hundreds of endemic cichlid species and is one of the most studied freshwater bodies in the world.

gustavia.costOfLiving: Budget around $3,600 a month, which makes Saint Barthelemy among the most expensive places on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $2,000 to $3,000 and villa rates in high season run into thousands per night, which is the market this island serves. Groceries are imported through Saint Martin and priced accordingly, with a French supermarket selling French products at a substantial markup. Restaurants are excellent and expensive throughout. There is no meaningful budget tier: the island decided decades ago what it was going to be. The euro is the currency and French banking applies.
gustavia.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Saint Barthelemy has fibre in Gustavia and the main settlements, French mobile networks with roaming that costs European visitors nothing, and reliable power. The infrastructure was rebuilt substantially after Hurricane Irma in 2017. There is no coworking in any formal sense, but the villas and hotels are equipped for people who work. The time zone is four hours behind GMT, which gives a comfortable overlap with both the eastern United States and, in the morning, with Europe, and that combination is one of the genuine practical arguments for the eastern Caribbean.
gustavia.gettingAround: You need a small car, and small is the operative word: the roads are steep, narrow and full of hairpins, and the island's rental fleet is mostly Mini Mokes and compact hatchbacks for that reason. Gustavia itself is walkable. Saint Barthelemy is only about twenty five square kilometres, so nothing is more than fifteen minutes away. Gustaf III Airport has one of the shortest and most demanding commercial runways in the world, approached over a hill and landing towards a beach, served by small aircraft from Saint Martin and San Juan.
gustavia.visas: Saint Barthelemy is a French overseas collectivity, part of the French Republic but outside the European Union customs and Schengen areas, so a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. French and European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and may live and work here without a permit. Most other Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. There is no remote work visa. Arriving through Sint Maarten means clearing that territory's entry rules first. Anyone arriving by the small aircraft from Saint Martin should also note that the two territories keep separate records, and that the flight is treated as an international one.
gustavia.bestTime: December to April is the dry season, the high season and the reason the island exists economically, with temperatures around twenty seven degrees, low humidity and the harbour full. Prices in that window are extraordinary and everything books months ahead. May, June and November are the shoulder months and the best value. Hurricane season runs June to November and Irma in 2017 caused severe damage across the island. August and September are the quietest months, when many restaurants close entirely and the island belongs to residents. The Saint Barth Bucket Regatta in March and Les Voiles de Saint-Barth in April are the two events that fill the harbour, and accommodation around them is booked a year ahead.
gustavia.prosCons: The case for Saint Barthelemy is that it is genuinely beautiful, genuinely safe, has fourteen beaches for a population of about ten thousand, French food and wine at the standard you would expect, and infrastructure that works. Gustavia's Swedish street grid and warehouse buildings, left from the century when Sweden owned the island, give it a character no other Caribbean harbour has. The case against is the price, which filters everything, and the scale: this is a small island with one town and a season. Gustavia is also the only Caribbean harbour named after a Swedish king, and the street names, the belfry and the three forts are what remains of that period.
gustavia.whoFor: Saint Barthelemy suits people with the budget to be here and a reason to want the eastern Caribbean specifically: the time zone works for American and European clients on the same day, the island is safe, and the food is excellent. It suits sailors. It does not suit anyone on an ordinary budget, anyone looking for a community of remote workers, or anyone who wants variety, because the island is small and the season shapes everything about it. It also suits anyone drawn to the approach into Gustaf III Airport, which requires a specific pilot certification and is regularly listed among the most demanding commercial landings anywhere.

marigot.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,200 a month on the French side, which is expensive by Caribbean standards and considerably cheaper than Saint Barthelemy next door. A one-bedroom runs roughly $900 to $1,400, with Terres Basses and the Baie Nettle strip at the top. Groceries in the French supermarkets are imported and pricey, though crossing to the Dutch side for some shopping is normal and legal, since there is no border post. Restaurants in Grand Case, which markets itself as the gourmet capital of the Caribbean, are excellent and expensive. The euro is the currency on this side and dollars are widely accepted.
marigot.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Fibre reaches parts of Marigot and the main settlements, French mobile networks operate with free roaming for European visitors, and power is generally reliable, though the recovery from Hurricane Irma in 2017 took years and some infrastructure still shows it. There is limited coworking. The time zone is four hours behind GMT, which gives a good working overlap with the eastern United States all afternoon and with Europe in the morning, one of the more genuinely useful positions on this site for anyone with clients on both sides.
marigot.gettingAround: A car is the practical answer. The island is about eighty seven square kilometres shared between France and the Netherlands, with a single ring road and no border checks between the two halves, though the road narrows and the traffic backs up badly around Marigot and Simpson Bay. Shared minibuses run the main routes cheaply. Marigot itself is walkable. Princess Juliana International Airport on the Dutch side is the island's air link and one of the busiest in the eastern Caribbean, with direct flights to Europe and North America. Anyone crossing to the Dutch side regularly should also know that the two halves use different currencies and different plug standards, which catches people out more often than the border does.
marigot.visas: Saint Martin is a French overseas collectivity, part of France and the European Union but outside the Schengen area, so a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. European Union citizens may live and work here without a permit. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. The Dutch side, Sint Maarten, is a separate country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands with its own rules, and although nobody checks the internal border, the two sides do keep separate records. Anyone planning a long stay should also weigh which side to base on, since the French side offers European Union rights and the Dutch side offers a lower cost of living.
marigot.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the high season, warm at around twenty seven degrees with low humidity and the whole island busy. May, June and November are quieter and better value. Hurricane season runs June to November, and this island took the full force of Irma in 2017, which was the strongest Atlantic hurricane on record at landfall and destroyed a large part of the built environment. Recovery has been substantial but uneven. September is the quietest month and much of the tourist economy shuts. Carnival on the French side runs in February and March before Lent, while the Dutch side holds its own in April, so the island effectively gets two.
marigot.prosCons: The case for the French side is the food, which is genuinely a cut above anything else in the region at Grand Case, the beaches, the ability to live in France while working American hours, and the freedom of movement for European Union citizens. Two legal systems on one small island produce useful arbitrage in several directions. The case against is that Saint Martin has real crime problems by regional standards, the recovery from Irma is incomplete, traffic is bad, and the island is heavily dependent on a cruise and charter economy.
marigot.whoFor: Saint Martin suits European Union citizens who want a Caribbean base with no immigration friction and a time zone that works for both sides of the Atlantic. It suits sailors, since the lagoon is one of the largest in the Caribbean and a major charter hub. It suits anyone who takes food seriously. It does not suit anyone wanting quiet, anyone uncomfortable with the security situation, or anyone hoping for a cheap island, because this is not one. It also suits anyone who enjoys the oddity of the arrangement itself, since the 1648 Treaty of Concordia dividing the island is among the oldest border agreements still in force anywhere.

brades.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $1,000, and the housing stock is limited because the population fell from about twelve thousand to under five thousand after the volcanic crisis and much of what was built is in the exclusion zone. Groceries are imported and expensive, with the supply chain running through Antigua. Local produce and fish are cheaper. Utilities are moderate. Eating out is limited to a handful of places at modest prices. Montserrat uses the East Caribbean dollar, which is pegged to the United States dollar at a fixed rate.
brades.whereToWork: Connectivity is adequate. Montserrat has a submarine cable connection and fibre reaches the inhabited north, with speeds workable for normal remote work, and mobile coverage across the safe zone. Power is reasonably reliable. There is no coworking. The island has actively marketed a remote work visa and has infrastructure adequate to support one, which is unusual for somewhere this small. The time zone is four hours behind GMT, giving a good overlap with the eastern United States and a workable morning with Europe. Anyone considering the remote work stamp should confirm the current income threshold and insurance requirement directly, since the scheme has been adjusted since it was introduced.
brades.gettingAround: You need a car. The habitable northern third of the island is about ten kilometres across, with steep, winding roads and no public transport beyond a few minibuses. Brades, Salem and Little Bay are the main settlements and none of them is walkable to the others. John A Osborne Airport in the north is served by small aircraft from Antigua several times a day, a fifteen minute flight, and a ferry also runs from Antigua. The exclusion zone in the south is entered only with permission and a guide. Anyone taking the ferry from Antigua should allow for it being weather-dependent, and for the schedule changing seasonally in a way the airline connection does not.
brades.visas: Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and grants visa-free entry to citizens of the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Canada and most Commonwealth countries for up to six months. It also operates a Remote Work Stamp, a formal one year visa for remote workers with proof of employment outside Montserrat, minimum income and health insurance, which is one of the more straightforward such schemes in the Caribbean. Arriving requires transiting Antigua, so that country's entry rules apply first. Anyone applying for the remote work stamp should budget for the application fee and for proof of income, both of which are checked rather than taken on trust.
brades.bestTime: December to April is the dry season and the practical window, with temperatures around twenty seven degrees and low humidity. The rains from June to November are heavier and this is also the hurricane season. The volcano is the other calendar: Soufriere Hills has been intermittently active since 1995 and its state determines what is accessible, with the Montserrat Volcano Observatory publishing the current hazard level. Ash falls happen. The observatory itself is open to visitors and is the best introduction to what happened here. The Saint Patrick's Day festival in March is the island's biggest event and marks a 1768 slave rebellion, which is why Montserrat's Irish heritage is commemorated the way it is.
brades.prosCons: The case for Montserrat is a formal remote work visa, an English-speaking British territory, genuine safety, and a landscape unlike anywhere else in the Caribbean: the buried town of Plymouth is visible from the viewing points and is the only abandoned capital city in the Americas. The island is green, quiet and largely undeveloped. The case against is that it is very small and very quiet, with a population under five thousand, minimal shopping, one flight route in, and a volcano that remains active. Montserrat is also where George Martin built AIR Studios in 1979, and the Rolling Stones, Dire Straits and Paul McCartney all recorded here before Hurricane Hugo destroyed it in 1989.
brades.whoFor: Montserrat suits remote workers who want a formal visa, a quiet English-speaking base and low prices, and who genuinely mean it about quiet. It suits geologists and anyone drawn to the volcano, which is among the most studied in the world. It suits birdwatchers, since the Montserrat oriole exists nowhere else. It does not suit anyone who needs choice, nightlife or company, and it does not suit anyone who would find living beside an active volcano unsettling. It also suits divers, since the reefs off the north coast are almost entirely unvisited and the volcanic activity has created new underwater terrain since the 1990s.

stpierre.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, and the housing stock is small, wooden and brightly painted, which is the town's defining look. Groceries arrive by ship from Halifax and by air, and prices reflect that: this is French retail with North Atlantic freight on top. The local fish is excellent and cheap. Heating is a serious budget line, since the winters are long and the buildings are old. Eating out is limited to a handful of restaurants but the bread, cheese and wine are genuinely French, shipped from France. The euro is the currency.
stpierre.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Saint Pierre and Miquelon has a fibre connection through Canada and French telecoms infrastructure on the islands, so speeds in the town are workable and reliable, with mobile coverage across the inhabited areas. Power is reliable. There is no coworking. The time zone is unusual and worth noting: the archipelago runs three hours behind GMT, which is thirty minutes ahead of Newfoundland next door and an hour ahead of the Canadian mainland, and it observes European daylight saving dates rather than North American ones. Anyone working with mainland France should also note that the daylight saving dates differ from North America's, so the offset shifts twice a year on European rather than Canadian schedules.
stpierre.gettingAround: Saint-Pierre is walkable end to end in twenty minutes and the island is only about twenty six square kilometres, with a road network you exhaust in an afternoon. Cars exist and are barely needed. Miquelon, the larger island, is reached by a ferry that takes about an hour and has its own small settlement and a long sand isthmus with wild horses on it. Saint-Pierre Airport connects to Montreal, Halifax and St John's, and a ferry runs to Fortune in Newfoundland in about ninety minutes. Anyone crossing to Newfoundland should book the ferry ahead in summer and expect it to be cancelled in rough weather, which happens often enough to build slack into any plan.
stpierre.visas: Saint Pierre and Miquelon is a French overseas collectivity, part of France but outside the European Union and outside Schengen, so a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. French and European Union citizens have freedom of movement and may live and work here. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days. Arriving overland means transiting Canada, so Canadian entry rules apply first, and that catches out people who assumed a French territory would be simple. Anyone flying in from Canada should also carry proof of onward travel, since the airline checks it and the archipelago's schedules leave little room to improvise a departure.
stpierre.bestTime: July to September is the season, and it is a short one: temperatures reach around eighteen degrees, the fog lifts more often and the ferry and flight schedules are at their fullest. Winter from December to March is cold, windy and snowy, with the sea often too rough for the ferry. Fog is the defining weather here and can sit over the islands for days in any season, which is why the approach to the airport is so often diverted. Spring is late and cold. The Basque and Breton festivals in August are the liveliest weeks of the year, and they are when the archipelago's fishing heritage is most visible in the town.
stpierre.prosCons: The case for Saint Pierre and Miquelon is that it is genuinely France, with French administration, French food, French schools and the euro, twenty kilometres off Newfoundland, and that combination exists nowhere else. The town is small, safe and remarkably pretty in its painted timber. The case against is the weather, which is cold, wet and foggy for most of the year, the isolation, the tiny population of about six thousand, and the fact that almost everything of interest is exhausted within a week. The islands also hold the only guillotine ever used in North America, which was shipped from Martinique in 1889, used once, and is now in the museum.
stpierre.whoFor: This suits French speakers who want North America without leaving France, anyone drawn to the North Atlantic, and people with a working reason to be here in fisheries or administration. It suits anyone interested in the Prohibition era, since the islands ran an enormous smuggling trade into the United States in the 1920s and the warehouses are still standing. It does not suit anyone who needs sunshine, choice or company, and it does not suit anyone without French, since English is thin here. It also suits anyone drawn to the cod fishery that shaped the North Atlantic for four centuries, since these islands are what remains of the French stake in it.

stanley.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100 and the rental market is very small, with most housing tied to employment or government. Groceries arrive by ship from Britain roughly monthly and by air, so the shelves depend on when the last delivery came and prices are high. Local lamb and fish are cheap and excellent. Heating is a substantial cost given the wind and the cold. Eating out is limited to a few pubs and restaurants. The Falkland Islands pound is pegged to sterling at par and British notes circulate alongside it.
stanley.whereToWork: Connectivity is the weakest thing about the islands. There is no submarine cable, so all bandwidth arrives by satellite, which makes it slow, expensive and metered in a way that shapes daily life. Data allowances are a normal topic of conversation here. Mobile coverage exists in Stanley and thins to nothing in Camp, the term for everywhere outside the town. Power is reliable and increasingly wind-generated. Anyone with bandwidth-dependent work should treat the Falklands as genuinely difficult rather than merely slow. Anyone planning an extended stay should price the data allowance carefully, since exceeding it is expensive and video calls consume it far faster than most people expect.
stanley.gettingAround: Stanley is small and walkable along its waterfront. Beyond the town, Camp is reached by unsealed roads and four-wheel drive, or by the Falkland Islands Government Air Service, which flies small aircraft to the settlements and outer islands on a schedule published the evening before. Mount Pleasant airport, about fifty kilometres west, handles the military airbridge from Britain and the weekly LATAM flight from Santiago via Punta Arenas, which is the only commercial connection to South America. Anyone flying to the outer islands should expect the schedule to be confirmed by radio the night before, and to be reshuffled by weather without much notice.
stanley.visas: The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own immigration rules. Citizens of the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States and most Commonwealth countries receive up to twenty four months as visitors, subject to proof of onward travel, accommodation and sufficient funds, all of which are genuinely checked on arrival. Working requires a work permit arranged by an employer in advance. There is no remote work visa. Anyone arriving on the South America route needs to satisfy Chilean transit requirements as well. Anyone arriving on the military airbridge from Brize Norton should note that seats are limited, that priority goes to service personnel, and that civilian bookings are made well in advance.
stanley.bestTime: October to March is the southern summer and the only realistic window, with temperatures around thirteen degrees, long daylight and the wildlife at its most active. Penguin colonies are busiest from October to February, black-browed albatross nest through the summer, and elephant seals haul out in spring. Winter from May to August is cold, dark and windy with limited flights. The wind is the constant here rather than the temperature: it blows hard in every season and is what makes thirteen degrees feel considerably colder. Anyone hoping to see king penguins at Volunteer Point should allow a full day, since the drive across Camp takes several hours each way in a four-wheel drive.
stanley.prosCons: The case for the Falklands is wildlife on a scale that is hard to convey: five penguin species, enormous albatross colonies, elephant seals and sea lions, all approachable and almost entirely unvisited outside the short cruise season. The islands are safe, English-speaking and orderly. The case against is the satellite internet, the cost, the wind, the isolation, and the fact that the 1982 war and the ongoing sovereignty dispute with Argentina shape the place in ways a visitor notices quickly. Landmines were only fully cleared in 2020. The islands also run one of the most valuable fisheries in the South Atlantic, and the squid licences it sells fund most of the government's budget.
stanley.whoFor: The Falklands suit wildlife photographers, biologists and anyone whose priority is birds and marine mammals rather than comfort. They suit people with a working reason to be here in fisheries, government or the military. They do not suit anyone with bandwidth-dependent work, because satellite internet cannot support it, and they do not suit anyone who wants warmth, shelter from the wind, or the option of leaving on short notice. It also suits anyone drawn to the 1982 conflict, since the battlefields at Goose Green, Tumbledown and Mount Longdon are all reachable and are marked and explained.

malabo.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,000 a month, which is expensive for central Africa and reflects an oil economy with a small population importing almost everything. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,200, with the areas near the embassies and the newer developments at the top. Groceries in the supermarkets serving the oil sector are very expensive; the local markets are far cheaper and the produce is good, since Bioko island is volcanic and fertile. Eating out ranges from cheap local canteens to expensive hotel restaurants with little in between. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro.
malabo.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Equatorial Guinea has a submarine cable connection and fibre reaches parts of Malabo, but the market is effectively a state monopoly, prices are high and reliability is poor. Mobile data is the usual fallback. Power cuts happen and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking. Access to information is also restricted in ways that matter: internet shutdowns have occurred around elections. The time zone is one hour ahead of GMT, which makes European working hours straightforward. Anyone planning a stay should also arrange a local contact in advance, since almost everything here works through introduction rather than through published information.
malabo.gettingAround: Shared taxis are the normal way to move around Malabo and are cheap, flagged down on the street and shared with whoever is going the same way. The city is small and the colonial centre is walkable. A car helps for reaching Pico Basile or the south of Bioko island, and the road up the volcano is spectacular. Malabo International Airport is about seven kilometres from the centre with connections to Madrid, Addis Ababa, Casablanca and regional West African cities, plus the domestic hop to Bata on the mainland. Anyone travelling to the mainland region of Rio Muni should note that Bata is a separate flight and that the new planned capital, Ciudad de la Paz, is being built inland from it.
malabo.visas: Equatorial Guinea has one of the most difficult visa regimes in Africa. Most nationalities need a visa applied for in advance at an embassy, with an invitation letter, proof of accommodation and often a yellow fever certificate, and the process is slow and inconsistent. United States citizens are a notable exception and may enter without a visa. There is no remote work visa. Photography is restricted around government and military installations and this is enforced seriously. Register your plans and confirm requirements well ahead. Anyone photographing anything at all should ask first, since cameras attract official attention here in a way that visitors from most countries find surprising and occasionally expensive.
malabo.bestTime: December to February is the driest window on Bioko and the most comfortable, warm at around thirty degrees. The rest of the year is wet, and the south of the island is extraordinarily so: Ureca receives among the highest rainfall in Africa. Temperatures barely move all year. Turtle nesting on the southern beaches runs roughly November to February and is the island's great natural event, though reaching those beaches requires a serious expedition in any season. Anyone climbing Pico Basile should arrange a permit and a guide in advance, since the road passes military installations and the summit is a restricted area.
malabo.prosCons: The case for Bioko is genuine: an active volcano rising three thousand metres out of the Gulf of Guinea, primary rainforest with several endemic primates, nesting turtles, and Spanish colonial architecture in Malabo that survives better than most of the region's. Spanish is the working language, which is unusual in Africa. The case against is serious: Equatorial Guinea is among the most closed and most authoritarian states in the world, the visa process is genuinely obstructive, and the oil wealth has not reached most of the population. The country is also the only Spanish-speaking state in Africa, a legacy of Spanish rule that ended in 1968 and is still visible in the architecture and the schooling.
malabo.whoFor: Malabo suits people with a working reason to be here in oil, gas, diplomacy or conservation, and Spanish speakers specifically, since Spanish opens everything and English opens very little. It suits biologists working on Bioko's primates or turtles, which is real and ongoing research. It does not suit independent travellers, given the visa regime, and it does not suit anyone uncomfortable in a country where photography and movement are restricted and questions are unwelcome. It also suits anyone drawn to Bioko's drill monkeys, which are among the most endangered primates in Africa and are the focus of a long-running conservation programme on the island.

luanda.costOfLiving: Budget around $2,100 a month. Luanda was repeatedly ranked the most expensive city in the world for expatriates through the 2010s, and while the kwanza's fall has changed that, costs for anyone living an imported lifestyle remain high. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,300, with the Ilha and the Marginal at the top. Imported groceries are very expensive; the local markets are cheap and the fish is excellent. Eating out splits sharply between local canteens at a few dollars and expatriate restaurants at European prices. The kwanza has devalued substantially and cash still matters.
luanda.whereToWork: Connectivity is moderate. Angola has submarine cable capacity and Luanda has fibre in the better districts, with speeds workable for normal remote work, though prices are high relative to income. Mobile data from Unitel and Africell is widespread and Africell's entry improved both price and coverage. Power cuts happen and generators are standard. There is a small but growing coworking scene aimed at the local startup community. The time zone is one hour ahead of GMT, which makes European hours straightforward. Anyone planning to work here should also budget for a generator or a building that has one, since the outages are frequent enough to interrupt a working day regularly.
luanda.gettingAround: Luanda's traffic is the defining daily experience: the city has grown far faster than its roads and journeys that look short take an hour. The blue and white candongueiro minibuses cover the city cheaply and chaotically. Taxis and Yango are available and reasonable. A new light rail and the expanded Marginal have helped a little. Dr Antonio Agostinho Neto International Airport opened in 2023 about forty kilometres south, replacing the old Quatro de Fevereiro, with connections to Lisbon, Sao Paulo, Dubai and across Africa. Anyone travelling to the new airport should allow considerably more time than the distance suggests, since the road south leaves the city through some of its worst traffic.
luanda.visas: Angola transformed its visa regime in 2018 and again since, and it is now far more open than its reputation. Citizens of a long list of countries, including much of Europe, the United States and Brazil, receive up to thirty days visa-free on arrival, and an e-visa covers most of the rest. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Longer stays require a work or residence visa applied for in advance, and the process remains slow. Anyone extending a stay should start the process early, since Angolan administrative procedures are slow and overstaying carries fines that are enforced at the airport.
luanda.bestTime: May to September is the cacimbo, the cool dry season, and the practical window: temperatures around twenty four degrees with overcast skies and almost no rain. October to April is the hot rainy season, humid and up to thirty degrees, with heavy downpours that flood parts of the city. The Benguela current keeps the coast cooler than its latitude suggests, which is why Luanda is drier and milder than Kinshasa on the same parallel. The beaches south at Cabo Ledo are best in the dry season. Anyone heading south should note that Kissama National Park is about seventy kilometres away and that the Benguela railway inland reaches the highlands in a day.
luanda.prosCons: The case for Luanda is a genuinely dramatic setting on a curved bay, a Portuguese colonial core, one of the most energetic music scenes in Africa in kuduro and semba, and an economy that is opening after decades of closure. Angolan cooking is excellent. The case against is cost, traffic, and a serious gap between the wealth on the Marginal and the musseque settlements behind it. Street crime is a real concern, infrastructure is uneven, and the civil war that ended in 2002 still shapes the country. Luanda's Ilha, the sand spit closing the bay, also holds most of the city's beach bars and restaurants and is where the city goes at weekends.
luanda.whoFor: Luanda suits people working in oil, gas, construction, diplomacy or development, and Portuguese speakers especially, since Portuguese is essential and English is thin. It suits anyone drawn to Angolan music, which is exported across the continent. It does not suit budget travellers, anyone who needs to move around a city quickly, or anyone without a local network, because Luanda is difficult to navigate without one and expensive to navigate badly. It also suits anyone interested in the Atlantic slave trade, since Luanda was its largest single port and the Museu Nacional da Escravatura sits on the site of the old chapel.

moroni.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500. Market produce is cheap and the islands grow their own cassava, banana and coconut, along with the vanilla, ylang-ylang and cloves that are the country's main exports. Imported goods carry a heavy markup because the shipping is infrequent. Fish is cheap and good. Utilities are unreliable rather than expensive, with power cuts a daily fact. Eating out is limited and inexpensive. The Comorian franc is pegged to the euro through an arrangement with France, which removes currency risk.
moroni.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. The Comoros are served by a submarine cable and fibre reaches parts of Moroni, but capacity is limited, prices are high and outages are common. Mobile data from Comores Telecom and Telma covers the populated areas. Power cuts are frequent and prolonged, and generators are essential for any serious work. There is no coworking. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a workable European overlap in the afternoon and an early start with Asia. Anyone planning to work here should assume the power will fail at some point in every working day, and should treat a charged laptop battery as the actual infrastructure.
moroni.gettingAround: Shared taxis run the roads on Grande Comore for a low fixed fare and are the normal way to move. Moroni's medina is walkable and genuinely medieval in layout, with narrow lanes and carved doors. A car is useful for the road around the island and the climb towards Mount Karthala. Prince Said Ibrahim International Airport is about twenty kilometres north with connections to Dar es Salaam, Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Paris and Mayotte, and inter-island flights and boats reach Anjouan and Moheli. Anyone travelling between the islands should allow generous margins, since the inter-island flights and boats are both unreliable and the sea crossing can be rough.
moroni.visas: The Comoros are straightforward. Almost every nationality receives a visa on arrival at Moroni airport, valid for forty five days and issued for a modest fee payable in euros, with extensions available in-country. There is no remote work visa. A yellow fever certificate is required from travellers arriving from endemic countries. Anyone travelling on to Mayotte should understand that it is French territory with entirely different requirements, and the Comoros dispute its status, which makes that route politically loaded. Anyone arriving should carry euros in cash for the visa fee, since card payment is not available at the airport and the amount is fixed rather than negotiable.
moroni.bestTime: May to October is the cool dry season and the practical window, warm at around twenty six degrees with lower humidity and calmer seas. November to April is the hot wet season and the cyclone season, and Cyclone Kenneth caused severe damage in 2019. Whale season runs roughly July to October, when humpbacks pass through the Mozambique Channel, and turtle nesting on Moheli runs through much of the year. Climbing Mount Karthala, one of the largest active craters in the world, is a dry season undertaking. Anyone climbing Karthala should also budget two days and a guide, since the ascent starts near sea level and the crater rim is above two thousand metres.
moroni.prosCons: The case for the Comoros is that they are among the least visited countries on earth with genuinely good reasons to go: Mount Karthala's crater, the Swahili stone town of Moroni with its old Friday mosque on the water, whale watching, and Moheli's marine park. Costs are low. The case against is infrastructure that barely functions, frequent power cuts, weak connectivity, limited medical care, and a political history of roughly twenty coups and attempted coups since independence in 1975. The Comoros also produce most of the world's ylang-ylang, the flower distilled for perfume, and the small distilleries on Grande Comore can be visited.
moroni.whoFor: The Comoros suit divers, anyone drawn to Swahili coast culture, and travellers who genuinely want somewhere unvisited. They suit French speakers, since French is the working language alongside Comorian and Arabic. They do not suit anyone needing reliable power or internet, anyone on a schedule, or anyone expecting tourist infrastructure, because outside a handful of hotels there is essentially none. It also suits anyone drawn to the coelacanth, the fish thought extinct for sixty million years until one was landed off these islands in the twentieth century, and preserved specimens are held in Moroni. The country is also among the least visited on earth, which for some travellers is the entire argument.

mamoudzou.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,700 a month, and Mayotte is expensive in a way that causes genuine political tension: it is the poorest department of France while carrying French import costs, and the gap between the two is the source of recurring protest. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $1,000. Supermarket groceries are French products at a heavy freight markup. The local markets are far cheaper. Utilities are moderate but water shortages are a serious recurring problem. Eating out is limited and mostly Comorian and Malagasy at modest prices. The euro is the currency.
mamoudzou.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable by regional standards. Mayotte has French telecoms infrastructure and submarine cable capacity, so fibre reaches Mamoudzou and mobile coverage is good, with French plans roaming without charge. Power is mostly reliable. There is very little coworking. The bigger practical constraint is water: Mayotte has suffered severe droughts with rationing that cut supply to households for days at a time, which affects everything about daily life. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, giving a workable European afternoon overlap. Anyone planning a long stay should also check the current water situation directly, since the rationing schedules change and they determine a great deal about daily life.
mamoudzou.gettingAround: Mamoudzou is on Grande-Terre and the airport is on Petite-Terre, so the barge across the lagoon is part of daily life and runs frequently and cheaply. Shared taxis cover Grande-Terre. Traffic into Mamoudzou in the morning is heavy for a place this size. A car is useful but the roads are limited and congested. Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi International Airport connects to Paris, Reunion, Madagascar and the Comoros, with the Paris route long and expensive but direct. Anyone landing at night should note that the barge runs on a reduced schedule after dark, and that the crossing is the only practical link between the two islands.
mamoudzou.visas: Mayotte is a French overseas department and part of the European Union, but it is outside the Schengen area and operates its own entry rules, which are stricter than mainland France's. A Schengen visa does not admit you and a Mayotte visa does not admit you to Schengen. European Union citizens have freedom of movement and may live and work here. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. Immigration enforcement here is intense, given the scale of irregular arrivals from the Comoros. Anyone travelling on to the Comoros should understand the sovereignty dispute, since the Comoros claim Mayotte and the route is treated as sensitive on both sides.
mamoudzou.bestTime: May to October is the dry, cooler season and the practical window, at around twenty six degrees with better visibility in the lagoon. November to April is hot, humid and wet, and Mayotte lies in the cyclone belt: Cyclone Chido caused catastrophic damage in December 2024 and recovery is ongoing. Whale season runs roughly July to October when humpbacks calve in the lagoon, which is one of the largest and best enclosed in the world, and that is the island's outstanding natural asset. Anyone diving the lagoon should aim for the passe en S on the western barrier, which is the best known site and is a dry season dive for visibility.
mamoudzou.prosCons: The case for Mayotte is the lagoon, which is enormous, double-barriered and holds dugongs, turtles and calving humpbacks, all inside French territory with European healthcare and schooling. The case against is substantial and worth stating plainly: Mayotte has the highest poverty rate in France, serious problems with crime and gang violence, chronic water shortages, and severe social tension around immigration from the Comoros. Cyclone Chido destroyed a large share of the informal housing in 2024. The island also voted overwhelmingly to become a French department in 2009, which is why its status differs so sharply from the rest of the archipelago.
mamoudzou.whoFor: Mayotte suits French public servants, teachers and medical staff on posting, of whom there are many, and divers and marine biologists drawn to the lagoon. It suits French speakers, since French is essential. It does not suit independent travellers looking for an easy island, anyone uncomfortable with the security situation, or anyone who would find the water rationing and the visible poverty hard to live alongside. It also suits anyone drawn to Mayotte's dugongs, a small and threatened population that is among the few remaining anywhere in the western Indian Ocean.

nouakchott.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500, with Tevragh Zeina, the diplomatic and business quarter, at the top and the older districts considerably cheaper. Market produce is inexpensive and the fish landed at the Port de Peche is among the best value anywhere on the Atlantic coast, sold straight off the boats in the afternoon. Imported goods carry a heavy markup. Utilities are modest and power is generally available. Eating out is limited and cheap, mostly Mauritanian and Senegalese. The ouguiya was redenominated in 2018, so older prices need a factor of ten applied.
nouakchott.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak but improving. Mauritania has submarine cable capacity landing at Nouakchott and fibre reaches parts of the city, with speeds workable for ordinary remote work in the better districts. Mobile data from Mauritel, Mattel and Chinguitel covers the populated areas and is the usual fallback. Power is reasonably reliable in the centre. There is almost no coworking. Sand is a genuine equipment hazard here and gets into everything. The time zone is GMT with no daylight saving, which makes European and West African work straightforward. Anyone staying through the harmattan should also plan for dust, since it works into laptop fans and connectors and is a genuine cause of hardware failure here.
nouakchott.gettingAround: Shared taxis and minibuses cover Nouakchott cheaply and are the normal way to move, though the city is spread out and largely low-rise across a flat sandy plain, which makes walking unrewarding. A car helps considerably. Nouakchott-Oumtounsy International Airport opened in 2016 about twenty five kilometres north with connections to Paris, Casablanca, Istanbul, Dakar and Nouadhibou. The other route out is the iron ore train from Nouadhibou, which is among the longest trains in the world and carries passengers free on top of the ore. Anyone taking the ore train should know it runs about seven hundred kilometres, takes the better part of a day, and offers no shelter at all on the open wagons.
nouakchott.visas: Mauritania issues visas on arrival at Nouakchott airport and at the main land borders for most nationalities, valid for thirty days and payable in euros in cash, which is the part people are unprepared for. Applying in advance at an embassy is also possible. A yellow fever certificate is required from travellers arriving from endemic countries. There is no remote work visa. Travel to the north and east of the country carries security advisories and the border regions with Mali should be checked carefully before any overland plan. Anyone arriving overland from Morocco should also allow several hours at the Guerguerat crossing, which involves a stretch of unmarked no man's land between the two posts.
nouakchott.bestTime: November to March is the only comfortable window, warm at around twenty eight degrees with cooler nights and the Atlantic breeze taking the edge off. April to October is very hot, regularly above forty degrees inland, and the harmattan carries Saharan dust across the city for weeks at a time. Rain is negligible in any month. The Banc d'Arguin National Park north of the city, a UNESCO site where the Sahara meets the Atlantic, is best in winter when the migratory birds are present in enormous numbers. Anyone visiting Chinguetti should aim for the cooler months as well, since the town sits deep in the Adrar and the manuscript libraries are family-run and open on request.
nouakchott.prosCons: The case for Mauritania is a landscape and a set of experiences that exist nowhere else: the iron ore train, the Adrar's desert oases at Chinguetti and Ouadane with their medieval libraries, and the Banc d'Arguin where millions of migratory birds meet the desert. Costs are low and the Atlantic fish is exceptional. The case against is that Nouakchott itself is a functional rather than an attractive city, connectivity is limited, the heat is severe for most of the year, and security advisories apply to much of the country. Mauritania also only abolished slavery in law in 1981 and criminalised it in 2007, and the practice persists in forms that human rights organisations continue to document.
nouakchott.whoFor: Nouakchott suits people with a working reason to be here in mining, fisheries, development or diplomacy, and travellers using it as the base for the Adrar and the ore train. It suits French and Arabic speakers, since English is genuinely rare. It does not suit anyone looking for a comfortable city, anyone needing strong connectivity, or anyone travelling in summer, because the heat here is not something to work around. It also suits birdwatchers, since the Banc d'Arguin is one of the most important wintering sites on the East Atlantic flyway and holds millions of shorebirds each season.

bissau.costOfLiving: Budget around $850 a month, which makes Bissau one of the cheapest capitals in West Africa. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400. Market produce is very cheap and the country grows good cashew, rice and fruit, with cashew nuts making up most of its exports. Fish and seafood from the estuary and the Bijagos are inexpensive and excellent. Imported goods carry a markup and the supermarkets are limited. Eating out is cheap, with Portuguese-influenced Guinean cooking and grilled fish the mainstays. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro, which removes currency risk.
bissau.whereToWork: Connectivity is weak. Guinea-Bissau has limited submarine cable capacity and fibre reaches only parts of Bissau, with mobile data from MTN and Orange the usual answer at prices that are high relative to income. Power cuts are frequent and prolonged, and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking. Anyone with call-heavy work should treat this as a genuine constraint. The time zone is GMT with no daylight saving, which makes European work straightforward and is one of the few unambiguous practical advantages here. Anyone working here should budget for a generator or an inverter, since the public supply is intermittent enough that a working day cannot be planned around it.
bissau.gettingAround: Shared taxis, painted blue and white and shared with whoever is going the same way, cover Bissau for a low fixed fare and are the normal way to move. The old colonial centre around the Praca dos Herois Nacionais is walkable. Roads outside the capital vary sharply and several are impassable in the rains. Osvaldo Vieira International Airport is about eight kilometres from the centre with connections to Lisbon, Dakar and Casablanca. Boats to the Bijagos archipelago leave from the port and the schedules are approximate. Anyone heading to the Bijagos should allow days rather than hours, since the pirogues and the ferry both depend on tides and on having enough passengers to sail.
bissau.visas: Guinea-Bissau requires a visa of most nationalities. An e-visa system operates and is the usual route, with visas issued for thirty to ninety days, and visa on arrival has been available at the airport for those who apply online first. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for in Bissau. The country has had repeated coups and attempted coups since independence, so the current political situation is worth checking before any plan. Anyone applying for the e-visa should print the approval and carry it, since the airport process still runs on paper and the online record is not always accessible there.
bissau.bestTime: November to May is the dry season and the practical window, warm at around thirty degrees with lower humidity, and it is also the best time for the Bijagos. June to October is the wet season and Guinea-Bissau is genuinely wet, with roads outside the capital deteriorating badly and some becoming impassable. Carnival in February is the biggest event in the calendar and is a serious one, with masks and drumming from across the country converging on Bissau for several days. Anyone visiting the Bijagos should aim for the dry months, since the islands' accommodation is limited and several of the lodges close entirely during the rains.
bissau.prosCons: The case for Guinea-Bissau is the Bijagos, an archipelago of eighty eight islands that is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, matrilineal in its social organisation, home to saltwater hippos and nesting turtles, and visited by almost nobody. Bissau itself has a decayed Portuguese colonial core that is genuinely atmospheric. Costs are very low. The case against is instability, weak infrastructure, unreliable power, limited medical care, and the country's long-standing role as a transit point in the cocaine trade, which shapes its politics. The country also has one of the highest cashew dependencies in the world, so the annual price of a single crop moves the whole economy and the mood with it.
bissau.whoFor: Guinea-Bissau suits travellers heading for the Bijagos, conservation and development workers, and Portuguese speakers, since Portuguese and Crioulo are the working languages and English is very rare. It suits birdwatchers and anyone drawn to matrilineal societies, which the Bijagos genuinely are. It does not suit anyone needing reliable infrastructure, anyone on a fixed schedule, or anyone uncomfortable in a country where the political situation can change quickly. It also suits anyone drawn to turtle nesting, since Poilao in the Bijagos hosts one of the largest green turtle rookeries in the Atlantic and is a sacred island.

mindelo.costOfLiving: Budget around $950 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the streets near the Praca Nova and the seafront at the top. Market produce is reasonable and the fish is excellent and cheap, though Sao Vicente is dry and grows little of its own food, so much arrives from Santo Antao across the channel or from the mainland. Imported goods carry a markup. Utilities are moderate and water is desalinated. Eating out is inexpensive and good, with grogue, the local cane spirit, cheap everywhere. The escudo is pegged to the euro.
mindelo.whereToWork: Connectivity is reasonable. Cape Verde has submarine cable capacity and fibre reaches Mindelo at workable speeds, with mobile data from CVMovel and Unitel covering the island. Power is generally reliable. There is a small coworking presence and the country has actively courted remote workers with a formal visa, which has brought a modest but real community, mostly to Sal and Santa Maria rather than here. The time zone is one hour behind GMT, which gives an excellent European overlap and a workable American afternoon. Anyone comparing the islands should note that Sal and Boa Vista have the larger remote worker presence and the direct European charter flights, while Sao Vicente has the culture.
mindelo.gettingAround: Mindelo is compact and walkable, laid out around Porto Grande bay with the main streets running back from the water. Shared minibuses, called hiaces, cover the rest of Sao Vicente cheaply. Taxis are inexpensive. The ferry to Santo Antao takes about an hour and is the reason most visitors come, since that island holds the best hiking in the archipelago. Cesaria Evora Airport is about seven kilometres out with connections to Lisbon, Praia and the other islands. Anyone hiking Santo Antao should take the morning ferry and stay over, since the Ribeira Grande valleys and the Cova crater need a full day and the last boat back is early.
mindelo.visas: Cape Verde abolished visa requirements for citizens of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and several other countries, who now register online through the EASE system before travel and pay an airport security fee on arrival, for stays up to thirty days. Everyone else applies for a visa. The country also operates a formal Remote Working Programme, a six month renewable visa for remote workers with proof of income and insurance, which is among the more straightforward such schemes anywhere. Anyone using the remote working visa should apply before travelling, since it is issued in advance rather than converted from a tourist entry after arrival.
mindelo.bestTime: November to June is the best window, warm at around twenty five degrees with steady trade winds and low humidity. The winds are strongest from December to March, which is why Sao Vicente and neighbouring Sal are serious kitesurfing and windsurfing destinations. August to October is warmer and marginally wetter, though Cape Verde is dry in every month and drought is a recurring national problem. The Baia das Gatas music festival in August and Mindelo's carnival in February are the two events that fill the town. Anyone coming for the wind should note that the strongest and steadiest months are December to March, which is also when the international kitesurfing events are held.
mindelo.prosCons: The case for Mindelo is that it is the cultural capital of Cape Verde and it feels like it: Cesaria Evora sang the morna here, live music runs most nights, the carnival is the biggest in the country, and the setting on Porto Grande bay under Monte Cara is genuinely striking. Add a formal remote work visa, a European time zone and low costs. The case against is that Sao Vicente is dry and largely barren, water is scarce, and the island is small enough to exhaust quickly without the ferry to Santo Antao.
mindelo.whoFor: Mindelo suits musicians and anyone drawn to Cape Verdean music, which is the island's genuine claim, along with kitesurfers and hikers using it as the gateway to Santo Antao. It suits remote workers who want the formal visa and a European time zone at low cost. It does not suit anyone wanting lush landscapes, since this island has none, and it does not suit anyone needing a large city, because Mindelo is a town of about seventy thousand. It also suits anyone drawn to the morna, which UNESCO added to its intangible heritage list in 2019 and which is still played live in Mindelo most nights of the week.

ashgabat.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,000 a month, though costs here are difficult to state plainly because Turkmenistan operates parallel exchange rates and the gap between the official and unofficial manat has been very wide. A one-bedroom runs roughly $300 to $600 at official rates. Subsidised utilities were a national policy for decades and have been progressively withdrawn. Local bazaar produce is cheap; imported goods are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Eating out is inexpensive by international standards. Bring cash: international cards frequently do not work and withdrawing money can be genuinely difficult.
ashgabat.whereToWork: Connectivity is the worst on this site. Turkmenistan has among the most restricted and slowest internet in the world, with a state monopoly, extensive filtering that blocks most social media and messaging services, and speeds that make video calls impractical. VPNs are blocked and their use is discouraged in ways that carry risk. There is no coworking. Anyone whose work requires open internet access should treat Turkmenistan as unworkable rather than difficult. The time zone is five hours ahead of GMT. Anyone with work that depends on cloud services, messaging or video should assume none of it will function reliably, and should not plan to be productive here.
ashgabat.gettingAround: Ashgabat is laid out on a monumental scale with wide boulevards and enormous distances between buildings, so walking is possible but slow and the summer heat makes it unpleasant. Taxis are cheap and plentiful, including informal ones, and buses cover the city. The city holds a Guinness record for the highest density of white marble buildings, and the effect is striking and strange. Ashgabat International Airport connects to Istanbul, Dubai, Moscow and a small number of other cities, with Turkmenistan Airlines operating most of them. Anyone photographing the city should also be careful, since government buildings, the presidential palace and many public monuments cannot be photographed and this is enforced.
ashgabat.visas: Turkmenistan has one of the most restrictive visa regimes in the world. Independent tourism is effectively not permitted: almost every visitor needs a letter of invitation obtained through a licensed local tour operator, an approved itinerary and a state-assigned guide, and the application is frequently refused without explanation. A five day transit visa exists for those crossing between two neighbouring countries and is also frequently refused. There is no remote work visa and no realistic route to a long independent stay. Anyone applying should also allow months rather than weeks, since the letter of invitation is processed by the state migration service and the timeline is entirely unpredictable.
ashgabat.bestTime: April to May and September to October are the only comfortable windows, warm at around twenty five degrees. Summer from June to August is severe, regularly above forty degrees in a city surrounded by the Karakum desert, and winter can drop below freezing. Rainfall is negligible year round. The Darvaza gas crater, the burning pit in the desert north of the city, is best visited in the cooler months and requires an overnight camp, which is one of the few things the tour operators reliably arrange. Anyone visiting Merv or Kunya-Urgench should note that both are a long way east and north of the capital and that internal travel is arranged through the same operator.
ashgabat.prosCons: The case for Ashgabat is that there is nothing else like it: a capital rebuilt almost entirely in white marble and gold since the 1990s, with monumental architecture, empty boulevards and a personality cult expressed in stone. Nearby Nisa is a UNESCO-listed Parthian city and Merv, further east, was once among the largest cities in the world. The case against is comprehensive: the visa regime, the surveillance, the internet restrictions, the heat, and a state that controls what visitors see and where they go. The Darvaza crater has also been burning since a Soviet drilling accident, and the government has repeatedly announced plans to extinguish it without doing so.
ashgabat.whoFor: Turkmenistan suits determined travellers collecting difficult countries, archaeologists working on Parthian and Silk Road sites, and people posted here by an employer. It does not suit remote workers in any sense, because the internet cannot support the work and the visa regime does not permit the stay. Anyone going should understand that they will be accompanied, that photography is restricted, and that the country is among the most closed in the world. It also suits anyone drawn to the Akhal-Teke horse, the national symbol and one of the oldest breeds in the world, which the state maintains with considerable ceremony.

erbil.costOfLiving: Budget around $900 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $500, with the areas near Empire World and the newer compounds considerably higher and aimed at the international sector. Market produce is cheap and Kurdish cooking makes good use of it. Imported goods are available and reasonably priced given the trade with Turkey. Eating out is inexpensive and the kebab and the breakfast culture are both excellent. Utilities cost more than the headline suggests because private generator subscriptions are normal alongside the grid. The Iraqi dinar is used and United States dollars circulate widely.
erbil.whereToWork: Connectivity is moderate. Erbil has fibre in the newer districts and the international compounds, with speeds workable for normal remote work, and mobile data covers the city. Power is the constraint rather than bandwidth: the grid does not supply full-time electricity and almost every building is also connected to a neighbourhood generator, which is billed separately and is simply how the city works. There is a small coworking scene. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, which gives a good European overlap. Anyone renting here should ask specifically about the generator subscription and its amperage, since that number determines what you can run during the daily grid outages.
erbil.gettingAround: Erbil is built in concentric rings around the citadel mound, which makes the layout unusually easy to understand and the traffic unusually circular. Taxis are cheap and plentiful and are the normal way to move, with ride-hailing apps available. The bazaar and Shar Park at the foot of the citadel are walkable. Erbil International Airport is about five kilometres west with connections to Istanbul, Dubai, Doha, Frankfurt and much of the region, and it has been the Kurdistan Region's link to the world for two decades. Anyone driving to Sulaymaniyah or Duhok should expect checkpoints along the way, which are routine, orderly and require a passport rather than causing any difficulty.
erbil.visas: The Kurdistan Region issues its own entry permits separately from the federal Iraqi government, and they are considerably easier to obtain. Citizens of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and a number of other countries receive a visa on arrival at Erbil or Sulaymaniyah, valid for thirty days and extendable. A Kurdistan Region permit does not automatically allow travel to federal Iraq, which requires a separate federal visa. There is no remote work visa. Confirm the current position, since both regimes have changed repeatedly. Anyone intending to continue to Baghdad or the south should arrange the federal visa separately and in advance, since the regional permit does not cover that travel.
erbil.bestTime: March to May and October to November are the best windows, warm at around twenty five degrees, with the spring bringing green hills across the region that surprise people who expect only desert. Summer from June to September is severe, regularly above forty five degrees, and the city largely moves indoors or to the mountains at Shaqlawa and Rawanduz. Winter is cool and wet at around ten degrees with snow in the mountains. Newroz, the Kurdish new year on the twenty first of March, is the biggest event of the year.
erbil.prosCons: The case for Erbil is a citadel mound that has been continuously occupied for perhaps six thousand years, making it one of the oldest inhabited sites on earth and a UNESCO World Heritage site, sitting above a working bazaar in a city that is genuinely calm and inexpensive. The mountains north are beautiful. The case against is that this is Iraq, and while the Kurdistan Region has been far more stable than the rest of the country, the security situation is regional, changeable and requires current government advice rather than assumption.
erbil.whoFor: Erbil suits people working in energy, reconstruction, diplomacy or humanitarian work, of whom there are a considerable number, and archaeologists, since the region holds an extraordinary density of sites. It suits travellers drawn to Kurdish culture and hospitality, which is genuine and much remarked on. It does not suit anyone uncomfortable with a changeable security picture, anyone who needs uninterrupted mains power, or anyone travelling in high summer. It also suits anyone drawn to Mesopotamian archaeology, since Nineveh, Nimrud and a dozen other sites are within a few hours and are slowly reopening to researchers.

asmara.costOfLiving: Budget around $800 a month, though as in Turkmenistan the figure needs a caveat: Eritrea has a closed economy, a fixed official exchange rate and strict currency controls, and what things cost depends heavily on which rate applies. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400 at official rates. Local produce and bread are cheap. Imported goods are expensive and often simply unavailable, which is the more relevant constraint. Eating out is inexpensive and the Italian legacy means genuinely good coffee and pasta alongside Eritrean food. Cash is essential and declaring foreign currency on arrival is compulsory.
asmara.whereToWork: Connectivity is the worst in Africa and among the worst anywhere. Eritrea has the lowest internet penetration in the world, no meaningful mobile data for most of its history, and dial-up-era speeds in the internet cafes that serve as most people's access. Fibre exists in a very limited form. Power cuts are frequent. There is no coworking and no realistic way to run a remote job from here. The time zone is three hours ahead of GMT, which is academic given the connection. Anyone needing to reach clients should plan on doing so before arriving and after leaving, because the connection here cannot be relied on for anything time-sensitive.
asmara.gettingAround: Asmara is walkable and genuinely pleasant to walk, which is unusual for an African capital: the centre is compact, the streets are ordered on the Italian plan, and the altitude keeps it cool. Buses and shared taxis are very cheap. The Eritrean Railway to Massawa, built by the Italians and rebuilt by hand with original locomotives, runs occasional excursions down the escarpment. Asmara International Airport has limited connections, mainly to Cairo, Dubai and Addis Ababa since the 2018 rapprochement with Ethiopia. Anyone travelling beyond the capital should apply for the internal permit several days ahead, since it names specific destinations and is checked at posts on every road.
asmara.visas: Eritrea requires a visa of every nationality, applied for in advance at an embassy, with an invitation or a booking and a process that is slow and frequently refused. There is no visa on arrival and no e-visa. Travel outside Asmara requires a separate internal travel permit, applied for in the capital and issued for specific destinations, and this is enforced at checkpoints. There is no remote work visa. Photography is restricted and military and government buildings must not be photographed at all. Anyone applying should also expect to be asked for a detailed itinerary, and should understand that refusal without reason is common and carries no route of appeal.
asmara.bestTime: September to March is the best window, dry and mild at around twenty two degrees thanks to the altitude of about 2,300 metres, which makes Asmara far more comfortable than its latitude suggests. The main rains fall from June to August and are heavy but short. Nights are cool year round and a jacket is needed. The coast at Massawa is a different climate entirely and is brutally hot for most of the year, so the descent from the highlands is best made in the cooler months. Anyone visiting the Dahlak archipelago off Massawa should aim for the cooler months, since the Red Sea coast is among the hottest inhabited places on earth in summer.
asmara.prosCons: The case for Asmara is unique and worth stating carefully: the city is an intact Italian modernist and Art Deco capital, built in the 1930s and barely altered since, and it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017 for exactly that. The Fiat Tagliero service station, shaped like an aeroplane, and the Cinema Impero are among the finest buildings of their period anywhere. The case against is the state: Eritrea has indefinite national service, extensive restrictions on movement and expression, and effectively no internet. The city's evening passeggiata along Harnet Avenue is also a genuine daily ritual, and it is the clearest surviving trace of the Italian period in ordinary life.
asmara.whoFor: Asmara suits architects and anyone drawn to twentieth century modernism, for whom the city is close to unmatched, along with travellers who want somewhere genuinely unvisited and are prepared for the constraints. It suits people with family connections. It does not suit remote workers in any sense, because the internet cannot support the work, and it does not suit anyone who would find internal travel permits, checkpoints and photography restrictions difficult to accept. It also suits cyclists, since Eritrea is the most cycling-obsessed country in Africa, the Tour of Eritrea is a national event, and the sport is another Italian inheritance.

pakse.costOfLiving: Budget around $620 a month, which puts Pakse among the cheapest places on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $150 to $350, with the riverfront and the newer blocks near the centre at the top. Market food costs very little and the Bolaven plateau above the town grows the country's best coffee, so a good cup is cheap here in a way it is not elsewhere in Laos. Imported goods carry a markup, and Thailand across the river is where people go for anything the town does not stock. Utilities are inexpensive. The kip has lost a great deal of value in recent years, which helps a visitor and hurts residents considerably.
pakse.whereToWork: Connectivity is workable rather than good. Fibre reaches the centre of Pakse at speeds adequate for video calls on a good day, and mobile data from Unitel and Lao Telecom covers the town and the main roads. Power is reasonably reliable, though cuts happen in the wet season. There is no coworking, so most people work from guesthouses or the riverfront cafes, several of which have understood what a laptop customer wants. The time zone is seven hours ahead of GMT, which gives a comfortable European afternoon overlap and works well with the rest of Southeast Asia. Anyone with call-heavy work should test the connection before committing to a month.
pakse.gettingAround: Pakse is small enough to walk across in half an hour and flat, so bicycles work well. Tuk-tuks and jumbos cover the rest cheaply, and rented motorbikes are the usual way people reach the Bolaven plateau, which is the point of being here: the loop takes two or three days past waterfalls and coffee farms. Pakse International Airport is a few kilometres northwest with flights to Vientiane, Bangkok, Siem Reap and Ho Chi Minh City. Buses run south to Si Phan Don, the four thousand islands where the Mekong splits, and east into Vietnam. The Thai border at Chong Mek is about forty kilometres west and is a straightforward crossing.
pakse.visas: Laos issues visas on arrival at Pakse airport and at the main land borders for most nationalities, valid for thirty days for a fee in United States dollars in cash, and an e-visa is also available in advance. Extensions of a further thirty days are applied for at the immigration office in town. There is no remote work visa and working on a tourist visa is not permitted. Overstaying carries a daily fine that is enforced on departure. Anyone crossing to Thailand and back should note that the Lao visa is not multiple entry by default, so a return means paying for a new one at the border.
pakse.bestTime: November to February is the cool dry season and the best window, with temperatures around thirty degrees, low humidity and clear skies. March to May is very hot, regularly above thirty five and uncomfortable on the plateau road. The rains from June to October are heavy and the waterfalls on the Bolaven are at their most spectacular then, which is the argument for coming in the wet season despite the mud. The Mekong is high and fast from August to October and low enough to expose sandbars by March. Boun Bang Fai, the rocket festival, falls in May and is worth arranging a trip around.
pakse.prosCons: The case for Pakse is that it is a genuinely relaxed river town at very low cost, with the Bolaven plateau's waterfalls and coffee farms immediately above it, the Khmer temple of Wat Phou an hour south, and Si Phan Don a few hours further. It is far less visited than Luang Prabang and considerably cheaper. The case against is that Pakse itself is a modest town rather than a destination, connectivity is adequate rather than good, medical care is limited with Ubon Ratchathani in Thailand the serious option, and there is no community of remote workers to speak of. Air quality in the March burning season is poor.
pakse.whoFor: Pakse suits motorcyclists and anyone drawn to the Bolaven loop, coffee people, and travellers moving slowly through southern Laos who want a base rather than a stop. It suits anyone whose budget is the binding constraint, since very few places offer this quality of life at this price. It does not suit anyone who needs a reliable connection for client calls, anyone wanting nightlife or a professional community, or anyone unwilling to ride a motorbike, because that is how the interesting part of this region is reached. Families will find the medical situation the main concern rather than anything else.

mawlamyine.costOfLiving: Budget around $550 a month, which is very low even by Myanmar's standards. A one-bedroom runs roughly $120 to $300. Market produce is cheap and Mon State grows a great deal of its own food, so fruit, fish and vegetables cost very little. Restaurant meals are inexpensive and Mon cooking is one of the best regional cuisines in the country. Imported goods are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Utilities are cheap but the supply is the problem rather than the price. The kyat has been extremely volatile since 2021 and the gap between official and market rates is wide, so any figure here needs checking against current conditions rather than trusted.
mawlamyine.whereToWork: Connectivity is poor and the reason is political rather than technical. Myanmar's military authorities have imposed sustained internet restrictions since 2021, including shutdowns, VPN blocking and throttling, and Mon State has been affected along with the rest of the country. Fibre exists in Mawlamyine and mobile data works, but neither can be relied on and the interruptions are deliberate rather than accidental. Power cuts are frequent and prolonged, with generators standard in any business. There is no coworking. The time zone is six and a half hours ahead of GMT. Anyone considering remote work here should treat the connection as unavailable rather than unreliable and plan accordingly.
mawlamyine.gettingAround: Mawlamyine is walkable along the riverfront and up to the pagoda ridge, and trishaws and motorbike taxis cover the rest very cheaply. The town sits on the east bank of the Thanlwin at one of the widest river mouths in Myanmar, with Bilu Kyun, the large island opposite, reached by ferry and worth a day for its craft villages.
