Winter from December to March is cold, often minus ten, with snow lying for months and the Narva river freezing, which is when the two castles facing each other across it look their best. The darkness is the harder part: this is the eastern edge of Estonia and December daylight runs from about nine to three. Anyone hoping to see the two fortresses framed together should walk the promenade south of the castle, which is where the view everyone photographs is taken from.
narva.prosCons: The case for Narva is unlike anywhere else in the European Union: a city that is over ninety per cent Russian-speaking, with Hermann Castle and Ivangorod fortress staring at each other across a river that is the external border of the European Union and NATO, and where the geopolitics of the last few years are visible from a park bench. Costs are the lowest in Estonia and the digital infrastructure is the best in Europe. The case against is a city with real economic difficulty, a shrinking population, very little English, and a border situation that is genuinely uncertain.
narva.whoFor: Narva suits Russian speakers, journalists, researchers and anyone whose interest is the eastern edge of Europe as a live subject rather than a historical one. It suits people using Estonia's digital nomad visa who want the lowest possible costs. It suits anyone drawn to Soviet-era urbanism, since Narva is among the most complete examples in the European Union. It does not suit anyone expecting Tallinn's old town charm, anyone without Russian who wants to integrate, or anyone uncomfortable living beside a border that is currently a matter of serious international concern.

bydgoszcz.costOfLiving: Budget around $820 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, well below Warsaw or Krakow, with the streets around the Old Market and the Mill Island at the top. Market produce is cheap and Poland's own food is good and inexpensive. Eating out costs little: a full meal in an ordinary restaurant runs under fifteen dollars. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a long winter. Poland uses the zloty rather than the euro, which has been a modest advantage for foreign earners over recent years. The city has an unusually large amount of housing for its population.
bydgoszcz.whereToWork: Connectivity is good and cheap. Poland has extensive fibre and among the best value mobile data in Europe, with comprehensive coverage and reliable power. There is a real coworking scene and a substantial business services sector: Bydgoszcz has become a location for shared service centres and software work, which means the professional infrastructure is better than the city's profile suggests. The time zone is central European. Administrative processes have improved but still involve queues and paper more often than the Baltic states, which is worth knowing before comparing the two.
bydgoszcz.gettingAround: Bydgoszcz is flat and has an extensive tram network, which makes getting around cheap and simple, with buses filling the gaps. The centre is walkable and the Brda river and the canal system run through it, with a genuine island in the middle of the city. Bicycles work well. Bydgoszcz Ignacy Jan Paderewski Airport has limited service, so Gdansk two hours north or Warsaw three hours southeast are the practical air connections. The railway station is well connected, and Torun, a UNESCO-listed medieval town, is forty five minutes away. Anyone using the airport should check the schedule carefully, since the routes served have changed repeatedly and Gdansk is often the more practical option despite the distance.
bydgoszcz.visas: Poland is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, registering for residence after three months. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a temporary residence and work permit for longer ones, and Poland's system is notoriously slow, with waits of many months in some voivodeships. There is no dedicated digital nomad visa. Poland does offer a Business Harbour programme for IT specialists from certain countries, which has been the practical route for many.
bydgoszcz.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable window, with July around twenty four degrees and the riverside and the island at their best. Spring and autumn are pleasant and short. Winter from December to February is cold, often around freezing or below, with grey skies for weeks and the air quality problem that affects much of Poland: coal heating in the surrounding region pushes winter particulates well above guidance. The Bydgoszcz Music Festival and the Camerimage cinematography festival, which is internationally significant, both fall outside the summer. Anyone here in November should look at the Camerimage schedule, since the festival brings cinematographers and directors from across the world and fills the city's hotels.
bydgoszcz.prosCons: The case for Bydgoszcz is a genuinely handsome and underrated Polish city at low cost: a granary-lined river, an island park in the middle of the centre, extensive Art Nouveau and eclectic architecture from its Prussian period, and the Man Crossing the River sculpture suspended above the water, which has become the city's emblem. Camerimage brings serious international attention each November. The case against is the winter air quality, limited flight connections, a slow immigration system for non-Europeans, and a city that few people outside Poland have heard of. The city was also part of Prussia until 1920, which is why its centre looks more German than most of Poland and why the granaries and the canal exist at all.
bydgoszcz.whoFor: Bydgoszcz suits people working in software or business services, since there is a real employer base here, and anyone who wants a Polish city without Krakow's tourism or Warsaw's prices. It suits cinematographers and film people during Camerimage, which is among the most respected festivals in its field. It suits European Union citizens, for whom the paperwork is light. It does not suit anyone sensitive to winter air pollution, anyone who needs frequent direct flights, or anyone from outside the European Union hoping for a quick residence process. It also suits anyone drawn to Torun forty five minutes away, a UNESCO-listed medieval town that survived the war intact and is where Copernicus was born.

aberdeen.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,600 a month, which makes Aberdeen noticeably cheaper than Edinburgh and considerably cheaper than London. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, and the market has softened as the oil industry contracted, so there is more choice than there was. Groceries are ordinary British prices. Eating out is moderate and the seafood is genuinely good. Utilities are a real cost, since the winters are long, though Scotland's housing is generally better insulated than England's. Council tax is a separate annual charge that catches people out when they compare with mainland Europe.
aberdeen.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Aberdeen at reasonable speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a real coworking scene and a substantial professional base, since the city has been the centre of the North Sea oil and gas industry for fifty years and is now trying to convert that expertise into offshore wind and hydrogen. The universities add a research layer. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which is the most convenient position on this site for anyone splitting work between Europe and North America.
aberdeen.gettingAround: Aberdeen is walkable in the centre along Union Street and compact enough to cover on foot or by bicycle, though the wind and the rain temper the enthusiasm. Buses cover the city and First Aberdeen runs a decent network. Aberdeen Airport has flights across the United Kingdom, to several European cities and, unusually, a great many helicopter movements to the offshore platforms. Trains run to Edinburgh in about two and a half hours and to London in seven. The ferry to Orkney and Shetland leaves from the harbour. Anyone driving north should know that the coast road towards Peterhead and Fraserburgh passes some of the best cliff scenery in Scotland and takes about an hour.
aberdeen.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, which has been phased in and now covers most visitors, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a United Kingdom employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within limits. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require a sponsored work visa, the Global Talent route, or one of the other categories, and the salary thresholds have risen substantially since 2024. Anyone working remotely for an overseas employer while visiting should read the current visitor rules carefully, since the permitted activities are defined narrowly and have changed recently.
aberdeen.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around eighteen degrees and long days: Aberdeen sits far enough north that midsummer light lasts past ten at night. April and October are cool and changeable. Winter from November to March is dark, wet and windy, with sunrise after eight and sunset before four in December, and the North Sea weather makes it feel rawer than the temperature suggests. Snow falls but rarely settles long in the city. The beach is beautiful and cold in every month. Anyone visiting in summer should also consider the dolphins at Torry Battery, where the Moray Firth population is regularly visible from the headland above the harbour mouth.
aberdeen.prosCons: The case for Aberdeen is a city built almost entirely from local granite, which gives it an architectural coherence found nowhere else in Britain and which genuinely sparkles in sunlight, along with a long beach, Royal Deeside and the Cairngorms an hour west, and a professional job market that is unusual for a city this size. Costs are well below the rest of urban Britain. The case against is the weather, which is grey and windy for much of the year, and an economy still working out what comes after oil.
aberdeen.whoFor: Aberdeen suits energy professionals, engineers and researchers, since the transition from oil to offshore wind is happening here and the expertise is concentrated. It suits hillwalkers and skiers, given the Cairngorms. It suits anyone working across Europe and North America, since the time zone serves both. It does not suit anyone who needs sunshine or mild winters, anyone wanting a large international community, or anyone from outside the United Kingdom without a sponsored job, since the visa routes are narrow and expensive. It also suits anyone drawn to castles, since Aberdeenshire holds more of them per square mile than anywhere else in Britain and several are open through the year.

inverness.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,550 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, and the market is tight because the Highlands have a genuine housing shortage made worse by short-term lets. Groceries cost a little more than the Scottish average, since everything comes up the A9. Eating out is moderate, with good local seafood, beef and game. Utilities are a serious cost given the winters, and rural Highland properties are often on oil or electric heating rather than gas, which is more expensive again. Council tax applies on top of rent.
inverness.whereToWork: Connectivity is better than the Highlands' reputation suggests. Fibre reaches most of Inverness at good speeds and the Scottish Government's rural broadband programmes have extended coverage, though it thins quickly once you leave the city. Mobile coverage in Inverness is comprehensive and becomes patchy in the glens. Power is reliable, with occasional weather-related outages. There is a small coworking scene and a growing remote worker presence, since the Highlands have actively marketed themselves to people leaving cities. The time zone is GMT with British summer time. Anyone planning to work from a rural cottage should test the connection before committing, since coverage in the glens varies enormously and satellite is sometimes the only answer.
inverness.gettingAround: Inverness is small and walkable, laid out along the River Ness with the castle above it, and covering the town on foot takes twenty minutes. Buses cover the city and the region, with Stagecoach running the Highland network. A car is close to essential for anything beyond the town, since the glens and the coast are where the interest is. Inverness Airport has flights to London, Amsterdam and several United Kingdom cities. The railway runs south to Edinburgh in three and a half hours and the Kyle line west to Skye is among the great scenic routes.
inverness.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a United Kingdom employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within limits. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays run through sponsored work visas, the Global Talent route or family categories. Scotland has argued for a distinct migration route to address rural depopulation, and it does not currently exist. Anyone working remotely for an overseas employer while visiting should read the current visitor rules carefully, since what is permitted is defined narrowly and has changed recently.
inverness.bestTime: May to September is the season, with July around seventeen degrees, long days and the Highlands at their most accessible. Late May and early June are ideal: the days are long, the hills are green and the midges have not yet reached full strength, which they do from late June through August and which is a genuine consideration rather than a joke. September and October give autumn colour and clear air. Winter from November to March is dark and wet, with the northern lights occasionally visible on clear nights. Anyone walking between June and August should carry midge repellent and consider a head net, which locals use without embarrassment and which visitors usually buy on day two.
inverness.prosCons: The case for Inverness is that it is the only real town in the Highlands and gives access to some of the best landscape in Europe: Loch Ness at the door, the Cairngorms an hour south, Skye and the west coast two hours away, and the North Coast 500 route starting here. It is safe, English-speaking and small enough to know quickly. The case against is the housing shortage, the weather, the midges, and a town that is genuinely quiet, with a limited job market outside tourism, healthcare and public services.
inverness.whoFor: Inverness suits hillwalkers, climbers, cyclists and anyone whose priority is being close to the Highlands rather than being in a city. It suits people who already work remotely and want a British base with landscape at the door, and the Highlands actively want incomers. It suits whisky people, since Speyside is an hour east. It does not suit anyone who needs a city's amenities, anyone hoping to find work locally without one already arranged, or anyone who would be badly affected by a wet, dark winter. It also suits anyone drawn to Culloden, four miles east, where the 1746 battle ended the Jacobite rising and where the visitor centre is one of the better ones in Britain.

dundee.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,400 a month, which makes Dundee one of the cheaper cities in the United Kingdom. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $950, kept moderate by a very large student population across two universities. Groceries are ordinary British prices. Eating out is inexpensive by British standards and the city has more good independent places than it once did. Utilities run through a cold winter. Council tax applies separately. Dundee has among the lowest average incomes of any Scottish city, which is reflected in the cost of living and in other things too.
dundee.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of the city at reasonable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with reliable power. There is a genuine coworking and creative scene, driven by the universities and by a video games industry that has been here since the 1980s: Grand Theft Auto and Lemmings both came out of Dundee, and the sector still employs a substantial number of people. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which serves both Europe and North America better than almost anywhere else on this site. Anyone in the games industry should know that Abertay University runs the oldest computer games degree in the world, which is why the sector settled here in the first place.
dundee.gettingAround: Dundee is compact and walkable, with the waterfront redevelopment putting the V&A, the station and the Discovery within a few minutes of each other. Buses cover the city cheaply and cycling works, though the Law and the hills behind the centre are steep. Dundee railway station is on the east coast line, with Edinburgh about seventy minutes away and London around six hours. Dundee Airport has a limited service to London. The Tay road and rail bridges cross to Fife, and St Andrews is half an hour away. Anyone heading for the hills should note that Glen Clova and the Angus glens are within an hour, and that they are far quieter than the Cairngorms proper.
dundee.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a United Kingdom employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within limits. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays run through sponsored work visas or the Graduate route, which is relevant here given the universities and lets international graduates stay and work for two years after finishing. Anyone working remotely for an overseas employer while visiting should read the current visitor rules carefully, since the permitted activities are narrow and were tightened recently.
dundee.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around eighteen degrees and Dundee benefiting from being on the drier east coast, which gets noticeably more sunshine than Glasgow. April and October are cool and changeable. Winter from November to March is dark and cold rather than snowy, with short days and a good deal of grey. The city's position on the Tay estuary means haar, the cold sea fog, rolls in on some summer days and drops the temperature abruptly, which is a local speciality. Anyone visiting in July should look at the Dundee Flower and Food Festival, and anyone here in September at Discovery Film Festival, both of which fill the waterfront.
dundee.prosCons: The case for Dundee is a city that has genuinely reinvented itself: the V&A Dundee, designed by Kengo Kuma and opened in 2018, anchored a waterfront rebuild, and the UNESCO City of Design designation reflects a real design and games sector rather than a marketing exercise. Costs are low, the universities keep it young, and the east coast light is good. The case against is that Dundee still has severe deprivation in parts, a drug death rate that has been among the worst in Europe, and a job market outside the universities and games that is thin.
dundee.whoFor: Dundee suits designers, game developers and academics, since those are the three sectors with real depth here. It suits students and graduates, given the universities and the Graduate route. It suits anyone who wants a low-cost British base with good rail connections and the east coast within reach. It does not suit anyone expecting a polished city, since the regeneration is genuine but partial, and it does not suit anyone hoping to find general professional work locally without a remote income or a specific sector fit. It also suits anyone drawn to polar history, since Captain Scott's ship the Discovery was built in Dundee and is moored at the waterfront beside the V&A.

derry.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,350 a month, which makes Derry among the cheapest cities in the United Kingdom and Ireland. A one-bedroom runs roughly $550 to $850, well below Belfast and a fraction of Dublin two hours south. Groceries are ordinary British prices, and the border means many people shop on whichever side the exchange rate favours that month. Eating out is inexpensive. Utilities run through a wet rather than a cold winter. Rates, Northern Ireland's version of council tax, apply separately. The cost gap with the Republic across the border is a genuine and much-discussed local feature.
derry.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Derry at reasonable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with reliable power. There is a small coworking scene and a growing technology and business services presence, helped by Ulster University's Magee campus and by the city's push to attract investment. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which serves Europe and North America equally well. One practical oddity: mobile phones near the border regularly roam onto Irish networks and back, which can produce unexpected charges if the plan does not cover it.
derry.gettingAround: Derry is compact and the walled city is best covered on foot, with the mile-long circuit of the seventeenth century walls itself the obvious walk. Buses cover the city and Translink runs the regional network. The Peace Bridge and the Craigavon Bridge cross the Foyle. The railway to Belfast takes about two hours and is among the most scenic lines in Ireland, running along the coast at Castlerock and Downhill. City of Derry Airport has limited service. Donegal, in the Republic, begins about ten minutes away by road. Anyone crossing into Donegal should note that the Republic uses the euro and kilometres while the North uses sterling and miles, and the change happens without any sign to mark it.
derry.visas: Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom, so United Kingdom rules apply: most non-visa nationals need an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. There is no digital nomad visa. The Common Travel Area means no routine passport control on the land border with the Republic of Ireland, but the immigration rules of each jurisdiction still apply, and crossing does not extend or reset either. Anyone planning to move between the two regularly should understand that distinction properly. Anyone driving across the border regularly should also check that their vehicle insurance covers both jurisdictions, since it does not always and the crossing is unmarked.
derry.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around eighteen degrees and long evenings. Derry is on the wet side of Ireland and rain is a constant possibility in every month, so the difference between the seasons is daylight rather than dryness. Winter from November to February is dark and damp rather than freezing. The Halloween festival at the end of October is the city's great event, among the largest in Europe, and fills every bed in the city and a good part of Donegal. Anyone coming for Halloween should book accommodation many months ahead, since the festival draws tens of thousands and the city has nowhere near enough beds for them.
derry.prosCons: The case for Derry is that it is the last completely walled city built in Europe, with the seventeenth century circuit intact and walkable, and that its recent history is presented with unusual honesty: the Bogside murals, the Museum of Free Derry and the Bloody Sunday memorial are a few minutes from the walls. Costs are low and Donegal's coast is on the doorstep. The case against is a city that still carries real division, visible in flags, murals and interfaces, along with high unemployment and limited flight connections. The name itself is contested, with Derry and Londonderry both in official use, and which one a person says is often read as a statement about something else entirely.
derry.whoFor: Derry suits anyone interested in the Troubles and their aftermath, which the city addresses more directly than anywhere else in Northern Ireland. It suits walkers and surfers, given Donegal and the Causeway coast. It suits people who want a very low-cost British base with a genuine sense of place. It does not suit anyone who would be uncomfortable in a city where political identity is visible on the streets, and it does not suit anyone needing frequent direct flights, since Belfast or Dublin is the practical airport. It also suits anyone drawn to Irish traditional music, since the pubs around Waterloo Street host sessions most nights and the standard is high rather than performative.

kilkenny.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,650 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $800 to $1,200, and Ireland's housing shortage is the defining economic fact here as everywhere in the country, with supply tight and rents having risen sharply over the past decade. Groceries are expensive by European standards. Eating out is expensive, though Kilkenny has an unusually good restaurant scene for a town of its size. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a mild damp winter. Local property charges apply to owners rather than renters, unlike the British system. Anyone comparing with Dublin should note that rents here run well under half the capital's, which is the main reason people have moved out along the railway line.
kilkenny.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Kilkenny at reasonable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with reliable power. Ireland's National Broadband Plan has extended fibre well into rural areas around the town. There is coworking, and the government has funded a network of remote working hubs across the country as a deliberate policy of moving jobs out of Dublin, several of which are within reach. The time zone is GMT with Irish standard time, which serves Europe in the afternoon and North America comfortably in the evening. Anyone considering one of the state-funded remote working hubs should look at the Connected Hubs network, which lists them nationally and is genuinely well organised.
kilkenny.gettingAround: Kilkenny is small and entirely walkable, with the castle at one end of the Medieval Mile and St Canice's Cathedral at the other, and the whole route takes twenty minutes. Buses cover the town and the region. The railway runs to Dublin in about ninety minutes and to Waterford in forty. Dublin Airport is roughly two hours by road or by direct bus. A car helps for reaching the countryside, and the Nore valley, Jerpoint Abbey and the Wicklow mountains are all within reach. Anyone walking the Medieval Mile should pick up the trail map, since the route links the castle, the cathedral and a dozen buildings that are easy to walk past unnoticed.
kilkenny.visas: Ireland is a member of the European Union but not of the Schengen area, so it operates its own visa system: European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, and most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. Ireland is not in Schengen, so time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, which is a genuinely useful feature for anyone managing that limit. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require an employment permit or one of the other immigration categories. Anyone using Ireland to pause a Schengen clock should keep the entry and exit evidence, since proving where you were is your responsibility rather than the border's.
kilkenny.bestTime: May to September is the season, with July around nineteen degrees and long evenings. Ireland's weather is unreliable in every month, so the difference is daylight and probability rather than certainty. The Cat Laughs comedy festival in June and the Kilkenny Arts Festival in August are the two events that fill the town and are both genuinely good. Winter from November to February is mild, wet and dark, rarely freezing but persistently grey. Spring comes early and the countryside is green in every month, which is the compensation. Anyone visiting during the arts festival in August should book early, since the town's accommodation fills and prices in that week bear no relation to the rest of the year.
kilkenny.prosCons: The case for Kilkenny is a medieval city that survived: black limestone buildings, a castle held by the Butler family for six centuries, a thirteenth century cathedral with a round tower you can still climb, and slipways and lanes that follow their original lines. It has a genuine arts and craft scene and better food and pubs than a town of twenty seven thousand should support. The case against is Irish costs, a housing market under real strain, and a town small enough that the choice in most things runs out quickly.
kilkenny.whoFor: Kilkenny suits anyone who wants an Irish base outside Dublin with real character and good rail links, particularly people working remotely for European or American employers. It suits craftspeople, since the Kilkenny design tradition is genuine and the workshops are working ones. It suits anyone who takes pubs seriously. It does not suit anyone on a tight budget, anyone who needs a city, or anyone arriving without accommodation arranged, because Ireland's rental market is difficult in a way that surprises people from elsewhere in Europe. It also suits hurling supporters, since Kilkenny is the most successful county in the sport's history and Nowlan Park on a championship day is a genuine spectacle.

ostend.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,550 a month, which is moderate for Belgium and cheaper than Brussels or Ghent. A one-bedroom runs roughly $700 to $1,100, with the seafront apartments at the top and the streets behind the station considerably cheaper. Groceries are ordinary Belgian prices. Eating out is where Ostend spends: the seafood, particularly the grey shrimp and the sole, is genuinely good and priced accordingly. Utilities are moderate. Belgium's tax and social contributions are among the highest in Europe, which matters for anyone employed here rather than remotely. Anyone comparing with the rest of the coast should note that Knokke to the northeast is considerably more expensive and De Panne to the southwest a little cheaper.
ostend.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Belgium has extensive fibre and cable, with comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power, and Ostend is well served. There is a small coworking presence. The time zone is central European. The genuine practical advantage here is position: Ostend is an hour from Bruges and Ghent, ninety minutes from Brussels, and within reach of Lille, and the train network makes all of it straightforward without a car. Anyone working across Europe will find the connections better than the town's size suggests. Anyone registering with the commune should allow several weeks and bring more documents than the list requires, since Belgian administration is thorough rather than quick.
ostend.gettingAround: The Kusttram, the coastal tram, runs the entire sixty seven kilometres of the Belgian coast from De Panne to Knokke and passes through Ostend, which makes it the longest tram line in the world and the practical way to move along the coast. The town itself is flat, compact and made for bicycles. Trains to Brussels take about ninety minutes and to Bruges fifteen. Ostend-Bruges Airport has limited service. The port handles ferries and freight, and the beach runs the length of the seafront. Anyone using the coastal tram should buy a day pass rather than single tickets, since the line runs the full sixty seven kilometres and the fares add up quickly.
ostend.visas: Belgium is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, registering with the commune within days of arriving, which is a genuine requirement rather than a formality. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. There is no digital nomad visa. Belgian administration is famously layered, with federal, regional and communal responsibilities, and the commune is where most practical business is done. Anyone staying beyond three months should start the commune registration immediately on arrival, since the residence process runs from that date rather than from any later application.
ostend.bestTime: June to September is the season, with July around twenty degrees and the beach and the tram both busy. Belgian coastal summers are unreliable and the sea is cold in every month, which locals accept and visitors find surprising. April, May and October are quiet and often pleasant. Winter from November to March is grey, wet and windy, with the seafront blasted by North Sea weather, though the town does not empty entirely the way smaller resorts do. The light in winter is what drew the painters here. The Theater Aan Zee festival at the end of July fills the town with performance for ten days and is the cultural high point of the year here.
ostend.prosCons: The case for Ostend is a seaside town with a real year-round population, excellent rail connections to the rest of Belgium and beyond, genuinely good food, and an artistic legacy that is more substantial than the beach suggests: James Ensor lived and worked here and his house is open, and the Mu.ZEE collection is good. The coastal tram is a genuine pleasure. The case against is the weather, the wind, a certain postwar architectural bleakness along the front, and prices that are Belgian rather than cheap. Ostend was also Leopold II's favourite resort and much of the grand seafront architecture dates from that period, which the town's museums address rather than avoid.
ostend.whoFor: Ostend suits anyone who wants a European Union base with a beach, fast trains and no need for a car, particularly people working across European time zones. It suits cyclists, since the coast and the Flemish interior are both flat and comprehensively provided for. It suits anyone who takes seafood or Belgian beer seriously. It does not suit anyone expecting Mediterranean weather, anyone wanting a picturesque old town, since Bruges is fifteen minutes away and Ostend is not that, or anyone on a tight budget. It also suits anyone drawn to James Ensor, whose house on the seafront is preserved and whose masks and skeletons remain among the strangest things in Belgian art.

vigo.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,150 a month, which makes Vigo cheaper than Madrid or Barcelona and comparable with the rest of Galicia. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $800, with the areas near the marina and Samil beach at the top. Market produce is very good and cheap, and the Mercado da Pedra sells the seafood that Vigo lands in enormous quantities. Eating out is inexpensive and the standard is high: this is one of the best places in Spain to eat, and the prices do not reflect that. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a wet mild winter.
vigo.whereToWork: Connectivity is very good. Spain has extensive fibre at high speeds and low prices, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a real coworking scene in Vigo, helped by the university and by an automotive and technology sector that is substantial: the Stellantis plant here is one of the largest car factories in Europe. The time zone is central European, which is an hour ahead of solar time in Galicia and shapes the very late Spanish day. Spain's digital nomad visa applies here as elsewhere. Anyone working from Galicia should also expect the local rhythm, since lunch runs from two until four and the working day finishes correspondingly late.
vigo.gettingAround: Vigo is built up a steep hillside above its ria, so walking is hard work in one direction and easy in the other, and the city has installed a series of public escalators and lifts to deal with it. Buses cover the city cheaply. The Ave high speed line reaches Madrid in about four hours and Porto is two hours south by road. Vigo Airport has domestic and limited European flights. The ferries to the Cies Islands, which are the reason many people come, leave from the port in summer.
vigo.visas: Spain is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering for an NIE number and on the padron once resident. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. Spain operates a digital nomad visa under its 2023 startups law, valid for up to a year initially and renewable to five, with an income threshold and a favourable tax regime for qualifying applicants, and it has become one of the most used schemes in Europe.
vigo.bestTime: June to September is the season, with July around twenty four degrees and the Cies Islands accessible, though the ferry requires a permit that is capped daily and books out. Galicia is the wet corner of Spain and rain is a genuine feature: Vigo gets more than most Spanish cities and the winter is grey and damp rather than cold. May and October are pleasant and quiet. The Festa da Reconquista in March, when the city dresses in period costume to commemorate expelling Napoleon's troops, is the local event. Anyone hoping to reach the Cies should apply for the permit online well in advance, since the daily visitor number is capped and the summer allocation goes quickly.
vigo.prosCons: The case for Vigo is seafood and setting: this is Europe's largest fishing port by value of catch, the ria is beautiful, and the Cies Islands half an hour offshore have a beach that British newspapers once called the best in the world and that is protected as a national park with capped daily visitor numbers. Costs are well below the Spanish cities people have heard of. The case against is the rain, which is persistent, a city that is industrial and steep rather than pretty, and Galician, which is spoken widely alongside Spanish.
vigo.whoFor: Vigo suits anyone who takes seafood seriously, which is the honest headline, along with sailors, walkers on the coastal Camino, and people using Spain's digital nomad visa who want the Atlantic rather than the Mediterranean. It suits anyone working European hours. It does not suit anyone who came to Spain for sunshine, since Galicia is the rainy part, and it does not suit anyone wanting a beautiful historic centre, because Vigo's is small and the city around it is working rather than charming. It also suits anyone walking the Portuguese Camino, since the coastal route to Santiago passes through Vigo and the city is a natural stage on it.

evora.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,050 a month, which is moderate for Portugal and considerably cheaper than Lisbon. A one-bedroom runs roughly $450 to $750, though the university and the tourist market together keep the centre tighter than the town's size suggests. Market produce is cheap and the Alentejo produces excellent bread, cheese, olive oil and wine, most of it locally. Eating out is inexpensive and the regional cooking, heavy on pork, bread and coriander, is distinctive. Utilities are moderate, with summer cooling the main cost rather than winter heating. Anyone comparing with Lisbon should note that rents here run well under half the capital's, which is why a good number of people have moved inland since the Lisbon market tightened.
evora.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Portugal has extensive fibre at reasonable speeds and prices, comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power. There is a small coworking presence, helped by the University of Evora, which was founded in 1559 and is among the oldest in Portugal. The time zone is GMT with Western European summer time, which gives a good overlap with the rest of Europe and a workable afternoon with the eastern United States. Portugal's digital nomad visa and the broader D7 route both apply here and have brought a substantial number of people to the country.
evora.gettingAround: Evora inside the walls is small and entirely walkable, which is the point: the historic centre is a compact grid of whitewashed houses that has changed little since the sixteenth century. Buses cover the modern town outside the walls. The train to Lisbon takes about ninety minutes and buses are frequent. A car is needed to see the Alentejo properly, since the megalithic sites, the cork oak plantations and the hill towns are spread across an emptier landscape than most of Europe still has. Lisbon Airport is the practical air connection.
evora.visas: Portugal is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering with the local council. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. Portugal operates a digital nomad visa introduced in 2022, with a temporary stay version for up to a year and a residence version renewable towards permanent residence, both requiring proof of remote income above a threshold. The D7 passive income route is the other common one.
evora.bestTime: March to May and September to October are the best windows, warm at around twenty two degrees with the Alentejo green in spring and golden in autumn. Summer from June to August is severe: the Alentejo is among the hottest parts of Portugal and forty degrees is normal in July, with the town emptying into the shade in the afternoons. Winter is mild at around twelve degrees and wet, and the plains can be foggy. The wildflowers across the Alentejo in April are one of the better sights in southern Europe.
evora.prosCons: The case for Evora is a walled town that UNESCO listed in 1986 and that genuinely earns it: a Roman temple standing in the middle of it, a cathedral, a Chapel of Bones lined with the remains of five thousand people, and an aqueduct that houses have been built into. The Alentejo around it holds more megaliths than anywhere in the Iberian peninsula. Costs are low and the food and wine are excellent. The case against is the summer heat, a very quiet winter, and a town small enough that most people exhaust it in a season.
evora.whoFor: Evora suits anyone drawn to Roman and medieval Portugal, to megalithic archaeology, or to wine, since the Alentejo produces a great deal of Portugal's best and the estates are visitable. It suits people using Portugal's residence routes who want somewhere quieter and cheaper than Lisbon or the Algarve. It suits walkers and cyclists in spring and autumn. It does not suit anyone who cannot tolerate a genuinely hot summer, and it does not suit anyone who needs a city, because Evora is a town of fifty thousand and behaves like one.

banjaluka.costOfLiving: Budget around $700 a month, which is very low for Europe. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400, with the streets near the centre and the Vrbas at the top. Market produce is cheap and the region grows a great deal of its own food, with the produce markets genuinely good. Eating out is inexpensive: a full meal with drinks runs under fifteen dollars almost anywhere, and the grilled meat is the regional speciality. Utilities are moderate and heating runs through a proper continental winter. The convertible mark is pegged to the euro, which removes currency risk.
banjaluka.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Bosnia has extensive fibre at low prices in the cities, with comprehensive mobile coverage and generally reliable power, and Banja Luka is well served. There is a small coworking scene and a growing software outsourcing sector, which is one of the country's few genuine growth industries. The time zone is central European, so European work is straightforward. The practical friction is banking and administration rather than technology: Bosnia's divided governmental structure means procedures vary by entity and can be slow and opaque. Anyone opening a bank account should allow time and paperwork, since Bosnia's two entities and the district each run their own administration and the rules differ between them.
banjaluka.gettingAround: Banja Luka is flat along the Vrbas and easy to walk, with the centre, the fortress and the riverside all within twenty minutes of each other. Buses cover the rest cheaply and taxis are inexpensive. Bicycles work well. Banja Luka International Airport has very limited service, so Zagreb, about three hours by road, is the practical air connection, with Belgrade about five. Buses run to Sarajevo in around five hours on a slow mountain road. The Vrbas canyon upstream is where the rafting happens and is half an hour away.
banjaluka.visas: Bosnia and Herzegovina grants visa-free entry of ninety days in any one hundred and eighty to citizens of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia and a long list of others, which is generous and straightforward. Bosnia is not in the European Union or Schengen, so time here does not count against a Schengen allowance, which makes it a genuinely useful base for people managing that limit. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require a temporary residence permit, applied for locally, and the process is slow.
banjaluka.bestTime: May to September is the comfortable window, with July around twenty seven degrees and the Vrbas at its best for rafting and swimming. Spring and autumn are pleasant and short. Winter from December to February is cold, often around freezing with snow, and brings the region's serious air quality problem: coal and wood heating across the valley pushes particulate readings among the worst in Europe during still winter weeks, which is the single biggest health consideration here. Summer air is clean by comparison. Anyone here in winter should watch the air quality readings rather than the temperature, since the still weeks in December and January are when the valley traps the smoke.
banjaluka.prosCons: The case for Banja Luka is a green, walkable riverside city at very low cost, with the Vrbas canyon and its rafting half an hour upstream, thermal springs nearby, and a ninety day visa-free allowance that does not touch a Schengen clock. The Kastel fortress and the rebuilt Ferhadija mosque are both central. The case against is the winter air quality, which is genuinely bad, very limited flight connections, and the political situation: Banja Luka is the seat of Republika Srpska and the entity's relationship with the Bosnian state has been a source of recurring instability.
banjaluka.whoFor: Banja Luka suits anyone who wants European costs at a fraction of European prices without spending Schengen days, particularly people working European hours who need somewhere to sit out the ninety day limit. It suits rafters, kayakers and anyone drawn to the Vrbas. It suits software people, given the local sector. It does not suit anyone sensitive to winter air pollution, anyone needing frequent flights, or anyone who would find the region's unresolved politics uncomfortable to live alongside. It also suits anyone drawn to the Vrbas canyon itself, since the rafting season runs from spring meltwater through the summer and the river is genuinely serious water in April.

namur.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,650 a month, which makes Namur cheaper than Brussels and considerably cheaper than Luxembourg an hour and a half east. A one-bedroom runs roughly $750 to $1,100, with the streets near the confluence and the old town at the top. Groceries are ordinary Belgian prices, which are moderate by western European standards. Eating out is reasonable and Wallonia's beer, cheese and charcuterie are all good and local. Utilities run through a damp rather than a cold winter. Belgium's tax and social contributions are among the highest in Europe, which matters if you are employed here rather than remotely.
namur.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Belgium has extensive fibre and cable coverage, with comprehensive mobile service and reliable power, and Namur is well provided as a regional capital. There is a small coworking presence, helped by the university and by the parliament of Wallonia being based here. The time zone is central European, so European work is straightforward and the American afternoon is reachable. The practical friction in Belgium is administrative rather than technical: registering with the commune is a genuine requirement within days of arrival and the process is thorough rather than quick.
namur.gettingAround: Namur is compact and walkable, laid out where the Sambre meets the Meuse with the citadel on the ridge above and a cable car up to it. Buses cover the rest and cycling along both rivers is good, with the RAVeL network of former railway and towpath routes running for hundreds of kilometres from here. Trains reach Brussels in about an hour, Luxembourg in ninety minutes and Liege in forty five, which makes this an unusually well connected small city. Brussels Airport is around ninety minutes by direct train. Anyone cycling the RAVeL should know that the network runs on disused railway lines and canal towpaths, which means it is almost entirely flat and separated from traffic.
namur.visas: Belgium is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, though registration with the commune within eight days of arrival is a legal requirement rather than a formality. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones, with the single permit combining work and residence for most employment routes. There is no digital nomad visa. Belgian administration is layered across federal, regional and communal levels, and the commune is where most practical business happens.
namur.bestTime: May to September is the season, with July around twenty three degrees and the rivers and the citadel at their best. Belgian summers are unreliable and rain is possible in every month, which locals accept. April and October are quiet and often pleasant. Winter from November to March is grey, damp and dark rather than cold, rarely freezing hard. The Fetes de Wallonie in September fill the city for several days and are the biggest event in the region, and Namur's Christmas market runs through December. The citadel's underground tunnels stay cool through the summer and are among the few genuinely comfortable places in the city during a heatwave.
namur.prosCons: The case for Namur is a genuinely handsome small city where two rivers meet under a citadel that has been fortified since Roman times, with a walkable centre, excellent rail connections to Brussels, Luxembourg and Germany, and Wallonia's hills and the Ardennes immediately to the south. Costs are well below Brussels. The case against is the weather, which is grey for half the year, a French-speaking administration that expects French, and a city small enough that the cultural offer is limited next to Brussels an hour away. Namur is also the seat of the Walloon Parliament and government, which gives a city of a hundred and ten thousand a political weight it would not otherwise carry.
namur.whoFor: Namur suits French speakers who want a Belgian base outside Brussels with the rail links to make that workable, and anyone whose work spans Europe. It suits cyclists particularly, since the RAVeL network and the Meuse valley are genuinely first rate. It suits people who want the Ardennes within reach. It does not suit anyone without French, since Wallonia operates in it and English will not carry you through the commune, and it does not suit anyone who needs a large city's choice in anything. It also suits anyone drawn to the Ardennes, since the Meuse valley south of the city and the caves at Han-sur-Lesse are both within an hour by road.

udine.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,350 a month, which makes Udine one of the better value cities in northern Italy. A one-bedroom runs roughly $550 to $850, well below Venice, Milan or Verona. Market produce is good and cheap, and Friuli produces excellent wine, prosciutto from San Daniele up the road, and Montasio cheese. Eating out is inexpensive by northern Italian standards and the frico, a fried cheese and potato dish, is the regional signature. Utilities are moderate. The region's proximity to Slovenia and Austria means cross-border shopping is a normal part of household economics here.
udine.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Italy has extended fibre substantially in recent years and Udine is well served, with comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power. There is a small coworking presence helped by the University of Udine. The time zone is central European. The practical friction in Italy is bureaucracy rather than infrastructure: a codice fiscale is the gate to almost everything, banking is slow, and residency registration takes patience. Friuli Venezia Giulia is an autonomous region with some of its own administration, which occasionally helps and occasionally complicates. Anyone planning to stay should get a codice fiscale first, since it is required to open a bank account, sign a lease or buy a phone contract, and it is quick to obtain.
udine.gettingAround: Udine is flat and compact and works well on foot or by bicycle, with the Venetian-arcaded Piazza della Liberta at its centre and the castle on the hill above it. Buses cover the rest. Trains reach Venice in about two hours, Trieste in an hour and Vienna in around six, and the line north through Tarvisio into Austria is a genuinely scenic route. Trieste and Venice airports are both within reach, and Ljubljana is about two hours by road, which makes this a well positioned base. Anyone heading for the wine country should know that the Collio and Colli Orientali hills start about twenty kilometres east and run to the Slovenian border.
udine.visas: Italy is a member of the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit, registering with the comune once resident. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a permesso di soggiorno for longer ones. Italy introduced a digital nomad visa in 2024 for highly skilled remote workers meeting income and insurance thresholds, though the implementation has been slower and more inconsistent than the announcement suggested. The elective residency visa remains the more established route for those with passive income.
udine.bestTime: April to June and September to October are the best windows, warm at around twenty two degrees, with the Friulian hills at their best for the wine harvest in September. July and August are hot and humid at around thirty degrees. Winter from December to February is cold, often near freezing, with fog on the plain and the bora wind occasionally reaching down from Trieste. The Alps north of the city hold snow from December to March and the ski areas at Tarvisio and Piancavallo are within ninety minutes. Anyone here in autumn should look for the Friuli DOC food festival in September, which fills the arcaded squares with the region's producers for four days.
udine.prosCons: The case for Udine is a Venetian city that almost nobody outside Italy has heard of, with a Tiepolo-frescoed archbishop's palace, an arcaded main square modelled on St Mark's, and a position between the Alps, the Adriatic and the Slovenian border that puts three countries within two hours. Friulian food and wine are among the best in Italy and cost a fraction of Tuscany. The case against is the winter fog, an Italian bureaucracy that tests everyone, and limited English outside the university. Friulian is also a recognised minority language with around half a million speakers, and it appears on road signs alongside Italian throughout the region.
udine.whoFor: Udine suits anyone who wants northern Italy without the tourist economy, particularly people who take food and wine seriously, since Friuli is a serious wine region and San Daniele prosciutto comes from up the road. It suits skiers and hikers, given the Julian Alps. It suits anyone wanting a base within reach of Slovenia, Austria and Croatia. It does not suit anyone without some Italian, since the bureaucracy is unforgiving, and it does not suit anyone who needs an international community, because there is not one here. It also suits anyone drawn to the First World War, since the Isonzo front and the enormous ossuaries at Redipuglia and Caporetto are within an hour of the city.

sassari.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,150 a month, which makes Sassari one of the cheaper cities in Italy. A one-bedroom runs roughly $400 to $700, well below the Sardinian coast and a fraction of the Costa Smeralda an hour east. Market produce is cheap and Sardinian food is distinctive: pane carasau, pecorino sardo, bottarga and the island's own wines. Eating out is inexpensive. Utilities are moderate with summer cooling the main cost. Island logistics push some imported goods above mainland prices, and the ferry and flight costs to the mainland are a real annual line for anyone travelling often.
sassari.whereToWork: Connectivity is adequate. Fibre has reached Sassari and the main towns at reasonable speeds, mobile coverage is good along the developed coast and thins in the interior, and power is reliable. There is a small coworking presence helped by the University of Sassari, which was founded in 1562. The time zone is central European. Sardinia has actively courted remote workers through regional programmes, and several municipalities have offered incentives to people relocating, which is worth investigating for anyone considering a longer stay on the island. Anyone considering a longer move should look at the Sardinian regional relocation schemes, several of which offer grants towards property purchase in the interior villages.
sassari.gettingAround: Sassari is walkable in the historic centre and spread out beyond it, with buses covering the city and a light rail line. A car is close to essential for the island, since the coast, the nuraghe sites and the interior are not otherwise reachable. Alghero airport is about half an hour southwest with flights across Italy and to several European cities, and Porto Torres, twenty minutes north, has ferries to Genoa, Barcelona and Corsica. The road to the Costa Paradiso and the north coast beaches takes under an hour. Anyone driving inland should expect the roads to slow considerably once the coast is behind, since the interior is mountainous and the routes are narrow.
sassari.visas: Italy is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering with the comune once resident. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a permesso di soggiorno for longer ones. The 2024 digital nomad visa applies here as elsewhere in Italy for highly skilled remote workers meeting income and insurance thresholds. Sardinia's regional relocation incentives are separate from the visa question and generally require residency to be established first. Anyone using the Genoa or Barcelona ferries should book vehicle space well ahead in summer, since the crossings fill with Italian holiday traffic from June.
sassari.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, warm at around twenty four degrees with the sea swimmable from June to October and the beaches empty either side of the Italian holidays. July and August are hot at around thirty two degrees and are when the whole of Italy arrives, which changes the island completely. Winter is mild at around thirteen degrees and wet, and much of the coastal infrastructure closes. The mistral wind blows hard from the northwest through much of the year and is a genuine feature.
sassari.prosCons: The case for Sassari is Sardinia at Sardinian rather than resort prices: the island's second city, with a genuine old town, an excellent archaeological museum, and half an hour to Alghero's Catalan-speaking old quarter and to beaches at Stintino that are among the best in the Mediterranean. The nuraghe, Bronze Age stone towers of which the island has thousands, are unlike anything else in Europe. The case against is that Sassari itself is a working city rather than a beautiful one, and that everything requires a car. Sardinian is also a distinct Romance language rather than an Italian dialect, and it is spoken widely in the interior with several quite different regional forms.
sassari.whoFor: Sassari suits anyone who wants a Sardinian base that is not a resort, particularly people who will use the island properly: divers, walkers, and anyone drawn to the nuraghic sites, which are genuinely mysterious and largely unexcavated. It suits people who want Italian costs at the low end. It does not suit anyone without a car, anyone expecting a picturesque town centre, or anyone who needs to leave the island frequently, since ferries and flights are both a real expense and a real constraint. It also suits anyone drawn to the Alghero area half an hour southwest, where Catalan has been spoken since the fourteenth century and is still an official local language.

ancona.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,300 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $800, considerably cheaper than the Adriatic resorts to the north and a fraction of Bologna two hours inland. Market produce is good and cheap, and the Marche produces excellent wine, olive oil and the seafood that comes off the boats here daily. Eating out is inexpensive and the brodetto, the local fish stew, is the regional dish. Utilities are moderate. Ancona is a working port rather than a resort, which is the main reason the prices are what they are.
ancona.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Ancona at reasonable speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a small coworking presence helped by the Marche Polytechnic University. The time zone is central European. The practical friction is Italian administration rather than infrastructure: a codice fiscale gates everything, banking is slow and the permesso di soggiorno process for non-Europeans takes months. The port brings a certain amount of international business traffic, which means the city is more used to foreigners than its size suggests. Anyone planning a stay should get a codice fiscale on arrival, since it gates the bank account, the phone contract and the lease, and it is straightforward to obtain.
ancona.gettingAround: Ancona is built on a headland and is steep in parts, with the historic centre walkable and the outer districts spread along the coast. Buses cover the rest. The railway station is on the main Adriatic line, with Bologna about two hours away, Rome three and Bari four. Ancona Falconara airport is fifteen kilometres west with limited flights. The port is the real connection: ferries run to Split, Zadar, Igoumenitsa, Patras and Durres, which makes this one of the best places in Italy from which to reach the Balkans and Greece by sea.
ancona.visas: Italy is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here without a permit. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a permesso di soggiorno for longer ones, and Italy's 2024 digital nomad visa applies for highly skilled remote workers meeting income and insurance thresholds. Anyone using the ferries to Croatia, Greece or Albania should note that Croatia and Greece are in Schengen and Albania is not, so the crossings are treated differently. Anyone taking the Albania ferry should note that Albania is outside Schengen, so the crossing to Durres is an external border and the stamps matter for a Schengen count.
ancona.bestTime: May, June and September are the best months, warm at around twenty four degrees with the sea swimmable and the Conero coast at its best. July and August are hot and busy with Italian holidaymakers. Winter from December to February is cool at around eight degrees and wet, with the bora wind occasionally reaching down the Adriatic. The Conero regional park south of the city, where limestone cliffs drop into the sea, is walkable in every season and is the best thing within reach of Ancona. Anyone visiting the Conero beaches should know that Due Sorelle is reachable only by boat or a difficult descent, and that the boats run from Numana in summer.
ancona.prosCons: The case for Ancona is an underrated Adriatic city with a Roman arch on the quay, a Romanesque cathedral on the headland, and the Conero park just south where white cliffs fall into clear water at Portonovo and Due Sorelle. Ferry connections to Croatia, Greece and Albania make it an unusually good base for the eastern Mediterranean. Costs are low for Italy. The case against is that Ancona is a working port, heavily bombed in the war and rebuilt without much care, so the city itself is patchy rather than lovely.
ancona.whoFor: Ancona suits anyone who wants an Italian base with sea connections to the Balkans and Greece, which is a genuinely unusual combination, along with walkers and swimmers drawn to the Conero coast. It suits people who want Adriatic Italy at working prices rather than resort ones. It does not suit anyone expecting a beautiful Italian city, since the war took much of it, and it does not suit anyone without a car who wants to reach the Conero beaches regularly, because the bus service is seasonal. It also suits anyone drawn to Le Marche's hill towns, since Urbino, a Renaissance ducal capital and a UNESCO site, is about ninety minutes northwest by road.

pescara.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,250 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $800, with the seafront blocks at the top and the inland districts cheaper. Market produce is good and cheap, and Abruzzo produces excellent wine, particularly Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, along with saffron, lamb and arrosticini, the skewered mutton that is the regional obsession. Eating out is inexpensive. Utilities are moderate. Pescara is a domestic resort rather than an international one, which keeps the summer premium lower than the Adriatic towns further north. Anyone comparing with the coast further north should note that Rimini and the Romagna resorts run considerably higher in summer for a comparable flat near the sea.
pescara.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Pescara at reasonable speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a small coworking presence. The time zone is central European. Abruzzo has been among the more active Italian regions in trying to attract remote workers to its inland villages, several of which have offered relocation incentives, and while those are aimed at depopulating hill towns rather than at Pescara, the region is unusually receptive to the idea. Italian bureaucracy applies here as elsewhere. Anyone planning a stay should obtain a codice fiscale early, since Italian banks, landlords and phone companies all require it before anything else can proceed.
pescara.gettingAround: Pescara is flat and long, running sixteen kilometres along the beach, and cycling is genuinely the best way to move: the seafront cycle path runs the full length and connects to the Bike to Coast route that follows the whole Abruzzo shore. Buses cover the city. The railway station is central, with Rome about three and a half hours away and Bologna four. Abruzzo airport is a few kilometres inland with limited flights. The Gran Sasso and Majella national parks are both under ninety minutes by road. Anyone heading into the mountains should note that the Gran Sasso road tunnel and the passes both close in bad winter weather, sometimes at short notice.
pescara.visas: Italy is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering with the comune. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa or a permesso di soggiorno, and Italy's 2024 digital nomad visa applies for highly skilled remote workers meeting income and insurance thresholds. Anyone attracted by the inland relocation incentives that Abruzzo municipalities have offered should read the residency conditions carefully, since they generally require establishing residence in the specific village rather than the region. Anyone applying for the digital nomad visa should build in time, since Italian consulates have interpreted the 2024 rules inconsistently and processing has varied widely.
pescara.bestTime: May, June and September are the best months, warm at around twenty four degrees with the sea swimmable and the beaches manageable. July and August are hot and the Italian holiday crowd fills the whole coast. Winter from December to February is mild at around nine degrees on the coast and genuinely snowy in the mountains an hour inland, which is the point: Abruzzo is the only place in Italy where you can reasonably ski in the morning and be on the beach in the afternoon, and people do. Anyone here in winter should know that Campo Imperatore and Roccaraso are both within ninety minutes and hold snow reliably from January to March.
pescara.prosCons: The case for Pescara is sixteen kilometres of Adriatic beach with the Apennines directly behind, which means swimming and skiing in the same day, and the Gran Sasso and Majella national parks, two of the largest protected areas in Europe, within ninety minutes. Costs are low, the food is excellent and the city is flat and cyclable. The case against is that Pescara itself was almost entirely rebuilt after wartime bombing and has very little historic fabric, so it is a pleasant modern city rather than an Italian one in the postcard sense.
pescara.whoFor: Pescara suits anyone who wants beach and mountains in the same base, which very few places genuinely offer, along with cyclists, since the coastal route is excellent and the inland climbs are serious. It suits people who take food and wine seriously and want Abruzzo prices. It does not suit anyone looking for a historic Italian city, since the war removed it, and it does not suit anyone who needs an international scene, because Pescara's visitors are almost entirely Italian. It also suits anyone drawn to Abruzzo's wildlife, since the national parks hold the last Marsican brown bears, along with wolves and chamois, and sightings are genuinely possible.

logrono.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,250 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $800, well below Bilbao an hour north and a fraction of Madrid. Market produce is very good and cheap, since La Rioja is agricultural country, and the wine is the obvious point: good Rioja costs a few euros a bottle here. Eating out is where the city excels and it is inexpensive, with the pincho bars on Calle Laurel serving a small plate and a glass for a couple of euros. Utilities are moderate. Anyone comparing with the Basque country should note that San Sebastian, two hours north, costs roughly double for a comparable flat and considerably more to eat in.
logrono.whereToWork: Connectivity is very good. Spain has extensive fibre at high speeds and low prices, comprehensive mobile coverage and reliable power, and Logrono is well served. There is a small coworking presence and the University of La Rioja adds a young population. The time zone is central European, which in northern Spain is an hour ahead of solar time and produces the famously late Spanish day. Spain's digital nomad visa applies here as everywhere and has brought a substantial number of people to the country, though mostly to the larger cities.
logrono.gettingAround: Logrono is flat and compact and entirely walkable, with the old town, the cathedral and Calle Laurel within a few minutes of each other. Buses cover the rest and cycling is easy along the Ebro. Trains reach Zaragoza in two hours and Madrid in about four, and buses to Bilbao take under two hours, which makes Bilbao airport the practical international connection. The Camino de Santiago passes directly through the city, which means a steady stream of walkers through the centre from spring to autumn. Anyone walking the Camino should know that Logrono is the end of a long stage from Los Arcos and that the municipal albergue fills early in summer.
logrono.visas: Spain is in the European Union and the Schengen area, so European Union and EEA citizens may live and work here with no permit, registering for an NIE number and on the local padron. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa for short stays or a residence permit for longer ones. Spain operates a digital nomad visa under its 2023 startups law, valid up to a year initially and renewable to five, with an income threshold and a favourable tax regime for qualifying applicants, and it has become one of the most used schemes in Europe.
logrono.bestTime: May, June, September and October are the best months, warm at around twenty two degrees, with the grape harvest in September and October the region's busiest and most interesting period. July and August are hot at around thirty degrees. Winter is cold for Spain, often near freezing, with the Ebro valley catching fog and the Sierra de Cebollera holding snow. The San Mateo festival in September, which celebrates the harvest and includes the treading of the first grapes, fills the city for a week. Anyone visiting during the September harvest should book ahead, since the wineries run tours through it and the city fills for the San Mateo week.
logrono.prosCons: The case for Logrono is Calle Laurel, a single street with around forty pincho bars where each specialises in one thing and you move from bar to bar eating and drinking for a few euros at a time, which is a genuinely distinctive way to spend an evening and is why Spaniards come here. The Rioja vineyards are all around, several with architecturally serious wineries. The case against is a small city with limited cultural offer beyond food and wine, a cold winter for Spain, and very little English. La Rioja is also Spain's smallest autonomous community by population, which means the regional government is unusually accessible and the administration is quicker than in the larger regions.
logrono.whoFor: Logrono suits anyone who takes wine seriously, since this is the centre of Spain's best known region and the wineries are open and welcoming, along with walkers on the Camino, which passes through. It suits people who want Spanish quality of life at northern Spanish prices with a genuinely excellent food scene. It does not suit anyone without Spanish, since English is thin here, and it does not suit anyone who needs a city, because Logrono has about a hundred and fifty thousand people and behaves accordingly. It also suits anyone drawn to dinosaur tracks, since the Cameros hills south of the city hold thousands of preserved footprints and several marked trails between them.

swansea.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,250 a month, which makes Swansea one of the cheaper cities in Britain. A one-bedroom runs roughly $550 to $850, well below Cardiff and a fraction of Bristol across the water. Groceries are ordinary British prices. Eating out is inexpensive by British standards and the covered market, the largest in Wales, sells cockles and laverbread that are genuinely local specialities. Utilities run through a mild but wet winter. Council tax applies separately and catches people out when comparing with continental Europe, where the equivalent is often bundled into rent.
swansea.whereToWork: Connectivity is good. Fibre reaches most of Swansea at reasonable speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and power is reliable. There is a coworking scene helped by Swansea University, which has two campuses including one directly on the beach at Singleton, and by a small technology sector the Welsh Government has actively funded. The time zone is GMT with British summer time, which serves Europe and North America equally well. Welsh Government schemes for business support are available and are more generous than the English equivalents. Anyone comparing Welsh cities should note that Cardiff has the larger professional market and that Swansea's costs run roughly a third lower for a comparable flat.
swansea.gettingAround: Swansea is walkable in the centre and along the Maritime Quarter, with buses covering the rest and a good cycle route along Swansea Bay to Mumbles. A car is genuinely useful for Gower, since the bus service to the best beaches is limited and seasonal. The railway station has direct trains to Cardiff in an hour and London in about three. Cardiff Airport is around an hour by road. The bay path itself, running five miles along the sand to Mumbles pier, is the best thing about getting around here.
swansea.visas: The United Kingdom requires most non-visa nationals to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, and visa nationals need a standard visitor visa. Visitors may not work for a British employer, though remote work for an overseas employer during a visit is permitted within narrow limits that are worth reading carefully. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays require a sponsored work visa, the Global Talent route or the Graduate route, which is relevant here given the university, and the salary thresholds rose substantially in 2024. Anyone using the Graduate route should apply before the student visa expires, since the application must be made from inside the United Kingdom and cannot be filed late.
swansea.bestTime: May to September is the best window, with July around nineteen degrees and Gower at its finest, though south Wales is genuinely wet and rain is possible in every month. April and October are quieter and often clear. Winter from November to March is mild and very wet, with the Atlantic weather arriving directly. The surf on Gower is best in autumn and winter when the swells are larger, which is when the beaches empty of everyone except the people who came for that. Anyone visiting Rhossili at the western end of Gower should aim for low tide, when the Worm's Head causeway opens for a few hours and the whole bay is walkable.
swansea.prosCons: The case for Swansea is Gower, which in 1956 became the first designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Britain and holds Rhossili, Three Cliffs Bay and a run of beaches that would be famous anywhere with a better climate. The city has a five mile bay path, a covered market, a good university and very low costs. The case against is Swansea itself, which was heavily bombed in 1941 and rebuilt without much care, and which Dylan Thomas called an ugly lovely town in a phrase the city has never escaped.
swansea.whoFor: Swansea suits surfers, walkers and anyone whose priority is Gower, which is genuinely one of the best stretches of coast in Britain and is twenty minutes from the city centre. It suits students and academics, given the university. It suits anyone wanting a very cheap British base with good rail links. It does not suit anyone who needs a beautiful city, since the war took most of it, and it does not suit anyone who would find persistent Atlantic rain difficult, because south Wales gets a great deal of it.

hull.costOfLiving: Budget around $1,200 a month, which makes Hull the cheapest city on this site in the United Kingdom. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $800 and house prices here are among the lowest in England, which is the single most striking economic fact about the place. Groceries are ordinary British prices.
