constantine.whereToWork: Constantine has no coworking market to speak of, though the university, one of the largest in Algeria, has generated a small incubator scene. Practically, you work from a flat, so the fixed connection matters more than anything else: Algerie Telecom fibre reaches parts of the city at usable speeds for $15 to $30 a month, while the old copper lines are slow. Mobile 4G from Djezzy, Mobilis and Ooredoo is cheap and works well in the city, and tethering is a sensible backup. The recurring problem is international routing rather than local bandwidth, so calls to Europe can stutter at peak times even on a good line. Test before you commit to a month.
constantine.gettingAround: Constantine is built on a plateau split by the Rhummel gorge, so the topography does most of the work of deciding how you move. Seven bridges cross the chasm, including the Sidi M'Cid suspension bridge of 1912 and the modern Salah Bey viaduct, and walking between them is the best way to understand the city. A cable car runs from the centre across to the hospital side and is cheap and quick. A tram line serves the newer districts, buses cover the rest, and taxis cost a couple of dollars. Mohamed Boudiaf airport is 9km south with flights to Paris, Marseille, Istanbul and the Gulf. Algiers is about four hours by road.
constantine.visas: Algeria requires most nationalities to obtain a visa before travel from an embassy or consulate, supported by a hotel booking or an invitation, proof of funds and an itinerary. Processing takes weeks and refusals come without explanation. The visa on arrival introduced for tourism applies only to the Saharan south around Djanet and Tamanrasset and is of no use for Constantine. There is no digital nomad visa and no provision for remote work. Extensions go through the wilaya police and are slow. Practically, this is a destination you plan several months ahead, and the paperwork is a larger obstacle than anything you will meet once you arrive.
constantine.bestTime: Constantine sits at about 640m on the edge of the Tell Atlas, which gives it a genuinely continental climate rather than a Mediterranean one. April to June and September to October are the good months, with highs of 22C to 28C and clear air over the gorge. July and August are hot and dry at 33C to 35C, hotter than the coast because there is no sea breeze. Winter is the surprise: December to February brings highs of only 11C to 13C, cold nights, heavy rain and occasional snow, and older buildings are poorly heated. The gorge is at its most dramatic after winter rain, when the Rhummel actually runs.
constantine.prosCons: The case for Constantine is that there is nowhere else like it. A city of half a million built on a rock, cut off from the plateau by a gorge two hundred metres deep, crossed by seven bridges, continuously inhabited since it was Cirta and the Numidian capital. The Emir Abdelkader mosque, the Ahmed Bey palace and the malouf music tradition are all here, and it costs $650 a month. Against that: the visa is a major obstacle, winters are cold and wet in badly heated buildings, international internet is unreliable, there is no coworking and no foreign community, English is barely spoken, and card payments are largely unusable.
constantine.whoFor: Constantine suits a French or Arabic speaker with a specific interest in North African history, architecture or music, and the patience for Algerian bureaucracy. It is a spectacular place to spend a month if your work is self-contained and you do not depend on video calls. Photographers in particular will find few cities that reward walking as much. It does not suit anyone needing reliable international connectivity, anyone without French, anyone who wants other remote workers around, or anyone travelling on short notice. If North Africa is the goal and the visa is the obstacle, Tunisia and Morocco offer most of the same appeal on arrival.

sfax.costOfLiving: Sfax runs about $650 a month for one person, a little cheaper than Tunis and considerably cheaper than the coastal resort towns. A furnished one-bedroom apartment near the centre or in Sfax El Jadida is $200 to $350, and further out $130 to $220. Food is inexpensive: a plate of couscous or a bowl of lablabi is $2 to $4, a full restaurant meal $8 to $14, and the fish landed at the port is both excellent and cheap. There is a small coworking scene at $60 to $120 a month. Fixed internet is $15 to $30 for a usable connection. Louages and buses cost pennies and taxis a couple of dollars.
sfax.whereToWork: Sfax has a modest but genuine coworking sector, driven by the University of Sfax and a local software industry that is larger than the city's reputation suggests, with desks at $60 to $120 a month. Fixed internet from Tunisie Telecom, Ooredoo or Orange runs $15 to $30 monthly, with fibre available in parts of the city and ADSL elsewhere; ask which one an apartment actually has. Mobile 4G is cheap, widely available and a reasonable primary connection if you are staying a few weeks. International routing to Europe is decent, better than most of North Africa, and video calls generally hold. Cafes are plentiful but are social spaces first.
sfax.gettingAround: The medina at the centre of Sfax is compact, still enclosed by its walls, and walking is the only way to see it. Beyond that the city is spread out and you will use louages, the shared inter-city taxis, or the yellow city taxis which are metered and cheap at $1 to $3. A local rail line, the Metro du Sahel equivalent here being the Sfax suburban service, plus buses cover the suburbs. The ferry to the Kerkennah Islands leaves from the port and takes about an hour, and is the standard weekend escape. Sfax-Thyna airport is 6km out with limited flights; Tunis is three hours by train or road for wider connections.
sfax.visas: Tunisia is one of the easier North African countries to enter. Most European, North American, Japanese and several other nationalities get 90 days visa free on arrival, with no advance paperwork. Extensions beyond 90 days require an application to the local police and are not routinely granted, and overstaying carries a fine payable on departure. There is no digital nomad visa, though Tunisia has discussed one for several years. A long-stay residence permit, the carte de sejour, exists but is aimed at people with local employment, study or family ties. Most remote workers here simply use the 90 days and leave, which is straightforward given the flight connections to Europe.
sfax.bestTime: Sfax has a hot semi-arid climate, drier than Tunis and drier than most of the Tunisian coast. April, May, October and November are the best months, with highs of 22C to 28C and comfortable evenings. July and August are hot at 33C to 36C and humid near the water, and the city empties somewhat as people head to Kerkennah or the beaches. Winter from December to February is mild at 16C to 18C, with the year's modest rainfall arriving then in short bursts. The olive harvest runs from November into January and is the region's economic heartbeat, since Sfax sits at the centre of one of the largest olive-growing areas in the world.
sfax.prosCons: The case for Sfax is that it is a working Tunisian city rather than a resort, with a medina that is intact, walled and almost entirely free of tourists, a genuine software and university sector, excellent seafood, and a cost of living around $650 a month. The visa is free on arrival for most people, flights to Europe are short, and the Kerkennah Islands are an hour away by ferry. Against that: it is an industrial port and it looks like one in places, air quality near the phosphate plants is poor, summers are hot, the foreign community is small, English is limited so French helps enormously, and there is very little nightlife.
sfax.whoFor: Sfax suits somebody who wants North Africa without the tourist infrastructure, has some French, and values a real city over a pretty one. The combination of visa-free entry, low cost, short flights to Europe and a functioning local tech scene makes it a more practical base than its profile suggests. It is a good choice for a month or two in spring or autumn. It does not suit anyone who wants beaches on the doorstep, nightlife, an English-speaking environment, or a community of other remote workers. If Tunisia is the goal and company matters more than authenticity, Tunis and Hammamet are where the foreigners are.

portsaid.costOfLiving: Port Said runs about $600 a month for one person, which is cheap even by Egyptian standards for a coastal city. A furnished apartment near the corniche or in the centre is $150 to $300, and away from the water considerably less. Food costs very little: koshari is under a dollar, a plate of grilled fish from one of the port restaurants $4 to $8, and a full meal for two $10 to $16. There is no coworking market to budget for. Internet from Telecom Egypt or one of the mobile operators is $12 to $25 a month. Microbuses and the canal ferry cost pennies, and taxis a dollar or two.
portsaid.whereToWork: Port Said has no coworking sector, so this means an apartment with a working connection. Telecom Egypt's fixed lines cover the city and fibre has reached parts of it, giving 30 to 100 Mbps for $12 to $25 a month; older copper connections in the historic district are much slower and worth checking before you sign anything. Mobile data from Vodafone, Orange or Etisalat is cheap and 4G coverage is good, making tethering a sound backup. Egypt periodically throttles or blocks VoIP services, so test whichever calling platform your work depends on before committing to a stay. Cafes along the corniche have wifi but are places to sit rather than to work.
portsaid.gettingAround: Port Said is long and narrow, squeezed between the Mediterranean and the canal, so the centre is walkable and the corniche runs its full length. Microbuses cover the length of the city for pennies and are how most residents move. Taxis cost a dollar or two and app services operate patchily. The free ferry across the canal to Port Fouad runs constantly and takes a few minutes, and is worth doing simply to watch the shipping. Cairo is about three hours by road or bus, Ismailia an hour and a half south along the canal, and Damietta an hour west. There is no useful passenger airport; fly into Cairo.
portsaid.visas: Egypt issues a 30-day tourist visa on arrival to most Western nationalities for $25 in cash at the airport, or through an e-visa applied for online in advance, which is the smoother option. Extensions are handled at the Mogamma or a local passport office and are usually granted, though the process takes a morning and some patience. There is no digital nomad visa. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a tourist visa is not addressed in Egyptian law and is not enforced against, but it is not authorised either. Longer stays are normally built on repeat entries or on a residence permit tied to study, work or property.
portsaid.bestTime: Port Said sits on the Mediterranean and is milder than inland Egypt all year. April to June and September to November are the best months, with highs of 24C to 29C, sea breezes and warm water. July and August reach 31C to 33C with high humidity off the sea, uncomfortable but far easier than Cairo or Luxor at the same time. Winter from December to February is mild at 18C to 19C and is when the modest rainfall arrives, mostly in short showers. The city is busiest in summer when Egyptians come for the beaches. The Khamsin winds in spring can bring dust for a few days at a time.
portsaid.prosCons: The case for Port Said is that it is a Mediterranean city with an extraordinary setting, at the northern mouth of the Suez Canal, where you can sit on the corniche and watch container ships pass through the middle of town. The wooden-verandahed colonial houses along Sharia Palestine are unlike anything else in Egypt, the seafood is excellent, the beaches are within the city, and it costs $600 a month with easy visa entry. Against that: no coworking, no foreign community, patchy VoIP, limited English outside the tourist trade, a fairly conservative social atmosphere, and very little to do in the evening beyond eating and walking.
portsaid.whoFor: Port Said suits somebody who wants Egypt without Cairo's scale and noise, on a very low budget, and whose work is independent and does not hang on video calls. It is a good choice for a writer or a researcher, and a genuinely interesting one for anyone drawn to maritime history or twentieth-century politics, since the canal and the 1956 crisis are the city's whole story. It also makes a comfortable Mediterranean summer alternative to inland Egypt. It does not suit anyone needing a community, nightlife, reliable calling, or the kind of tourist infrastructure that Dahab and Hurghada provide for foreigners staying months.

kumasi.costOfLiving: Kumasi runs about $780 a month for one person, cheaper than Accra by a clear margin. A furnished one-bedroom in Ahodwo, Nhyiaeso or around KNUST is $250 to $450, and a room in a shared house $120 to $220. Local food is very cheap: a bowl of fufu with light soup is $2 to $3 and waakye under a dollar, while a western-style restaurant meal is $10 to $18. Coworking exists in a small way at $70 to $130 a month. Internet is the notable expense in Ghana, at $30 to $60 for a decent fixed connection. Trotros cost pennies and a taxi across town is $2 to $5.
kumasi.whereToWork: Kumasi's coworking scene is small but growing, largely tied to KNUST, one of the strongest engineering universities in West Africa, with spaces around the campus and in Nhyiaeso at $70 to $130 a month. Fixed internet comes from Vodafone, Surfline or fibre operators and costs $30 to $60, which is expensive relative to everything else here. MTN's 4G is widespread, reliable and often the better option, with generous data bundles; most people working remotely in Ghana tether. The real planning item is power: Ghana's supply has improved but outages still happen, and an inverter or a UPS is a normal precaution rather than an unusual one.
kumasi.gettingAround: Kumasi is built in concentric rings around Kejetia and the central market, and the traffic reflects it, so allow more time than the distance suggests. Trotros, the shared minibuses, run every route for pennies once you learn the calls and hand signals. Taxis are $2 to $5 across town, shared taxis cheaper, and Bolt and Uber both operate. The Kejetia market complex, one of the largest in West Africa, is the centre of gravity and is worth a morning. Kumasi airport has domestic flights to Accra, about 45 minutes, against five to six hours by road. Lake Bosomtwe, a meteorite crater lake, is 30km southeast.
kumasi.visas: Ghana requires a visa in advance for most nationalities, applied for at an embassy or through the online system, usually issued for 30 or 60 days single or multiple entry. Visa on arrival is available only in limited circumstances and should not be relied on. Extensions are handled by the Ghana Immigration Service in Accra or Kumasi and are generally granted for a fee. There is no digital nomad visa. Ghana has actively courted the African diaspora through initiatives like the Year of Return, and routes to longer residence and even citizenship exist for people of African descent, which is a genuinely distinctive feature of Ghanaian policy.
kumasi.bestTime: Kumasi sits in the forest belt and is wetter and greener than the Ghanaian coast. It has two rainy seasons: a heavy one from March to July and a second, lighter one in September and October. The dry window from November to February is the best time to be here, with highs around 32C and lower humidity, though December and January bring the Harmattan, the Saharan dust haze that drops visibility and air quality for weeks and is hard on anyone with a respiratory condition. August is a relatively dry break between the two wet seasons. Temperatures barely move across the year, sitting between 30C and 33C most days.
kumasi.prosCons: The case for Kumasi is that it is the heart of the Ashanti kingdom and one of the most culturally distinct cities in West Africa: the Manhyia Palace and the Asantehene's court, the Kejetia market, kente weaving at Bonwire, adinkra printing at Ntonso, and a major university keeping the city young. English is the official language, Ghana is politically stable and among the safest countries in the region, and it costs $780 a month. Against that: internet is expensive and power is not fully reliable, the traffic is heavy, the Harmattan months are genuinely unpleasant, there is little nomad community, and Accra has most of what infrastructure the country offers.
kumasi.whoFor: Kumasi suits somebody with a specific interest in West African history, textiles, craft or the Ashanti kingdom, or someone in the diaspora looking at Ghana as a longer-term base, for which the country's policies are unusually welcoming. English as the working language removes the barrier that Francophone West Africa presents. It works well for a month or two in the November to February dry window, budgeting for good mobile data and a UPS. It does not suit anyone who needs cheap fast internet, a coworking community, or a temperate climate. Accra is the easier Ghanaian landing point and has the small expatriate scene the country has.

townsville.costOfLiving: Townsville runs about $1,900 a month for one person, which is inexpensive for an Australian city but high against most of this site. A one-bedroom flat near the Strand or in North Ward is $850 to $1,150; a room in a share house is $450 to $650. Groceries are $400 to $500 a month and a pub meal $18 to $28. Coworking is available at $200 to $350 a month. Internet on the NBN costs $50 to $70. Running a car is roughly $200 a month including fuel at about $1.20 a litre, and air conditioning through the wet season pushes power bills to $80 to $140.
townsville.whereToWork: Townsville has a functioning coworking market for a city of its size, with spaces in the CBD and around the Flinders Street precinct at $200 to $350 a month, supported by James Cook University, the defence presence at Lavarack Barracks and a marine science sector built around AIMS and the reef research institutions. The NBN reaches the city with fibre or fibre-to-the-node depending on the street, at 50 to 250 Mbps for $50 to $70 a month; check which technology an address has, because the difference is large. Mobile coverage from Telstra, Optus and Vodafone is good in the city and thins quickly inland. Cafes along the Strand are pleasant for a morning.
townsville.gettingAround: Townsville is flat and spread out, and while the CBD and the Strand are walkable, most people drive. Sunbus runs the suburban network on weekdays with a reduced weekend service. Cycling works well given the terrain and the climate for most of the year. The Magnetic Island ferry from the terminal takes 25 minutes and runs frequently, which is what makes the island a genuine part of daily life here rather than an excursion. Castle Hill rises straight out of the centre and the walk up is the local morning ritual. The airport is 5km out with flights to Brisbane, Sydney, Cairns and Melbourne, and Cairns is four hours north by road.
townsville.visas: Australia's eVisitor and ETA cover most European, North American and several Asian nationalities for stays of up to three months per entry within a twelve-month validity, applied for online for little or no fee. Working holiday visas of twelve months, extendable to two or three years with specified regional work, are available to under-30s or under-35s depending on nationality, and northern Queensland is a common place to complete the regional requirement. There is no digital nomad visa. Working remotely for a foreign employer while on a visitor visa sits in a grey area Australia has not clarified, and tax residency starts to matter well before the visa does.
townsville.bestTime: Townsville is in the dry tropics rather than the wet tropics, which is why it gets roughly 300 sunny days a year while Cairns, four hours north, gets drenched. May to October is the dry season and the reason to be here: highs of 25C to 28C, low humidity, blue skies, and the best diving conditions on the Yongala wreck. November to April is the wet, with highs near 31C, oppressive humidity, and the cyclone season running formally from November to April. Stinger season overlaps it, so swimming outside netted enclosures is inadvisable from roughly November to May. The city has flooded badly in exceptional years, most recently in 2019.
townsville.prosCons: The case for Townsville is dry tropical winter sun, a beachfront promenade in the Strand, Magnetic Island 25 minutes offshore, the Yongala wreck which is regularly ranked among the best dives in the world, and Great Barrier Reef access without Cairns prices or crowds. It has a university, a hospital, an airport and coworking, and rents well below the Australian average. Against that: it is expensive by global standards, a car is close to essential, the November to April wet season is genuinely hard work, cyclone and flood risk are real rather than theoretical, and the city is functional rather than beautiful away from the waterfront.
townsville.whoFor: Townsville suits somebody who wants tropical Australia at a working city's prices rather than a resort's, and whose winter matters more than their summer: a May to October stay here is close to ideal. Divers have a specific reason to come, and marine scientists and defence contractors are why much of the professional population is here. It works well on a working holiday visa, particularly for anyone needing regional work. It does not suit a tight budget, anyone without a car, or anyone planning to sit out the wet season. If you want the reef with more company and more to do, Cairns is four hours north.

launceston.costOfLiving: Launceston runs about $1,850 a month for one person, cheaper than Hobart and well under the mainland capitals. A one-bedroom flat in the centre or in East Launceston is $750 to $1,050; a room in a share house is $400 to $600. Groceries are $380 to $480 a month and a pub meal $22 to $30, with the Tamar Valley wineries adding a pleasant but not cheap habit. Coworking is available at $200 to $320 a month. NBN internet is $50 to $70. Heating is the line that surprises visitors: Tasmanian winters are cold and older weatherboard houses are poorly insulated, so power can reach $150 in July.
launceston.whereToWork: Launceston has a small coworking market centred on the CBD and the Inveresk precinct, where the University of Tasmania moved its northern campus, with desks at $200 to $320 a month. The NBN covers the city, mostly on fibre-to-the-node with fibre upgrades progressing, delivering 50 to 250 Mbps for $50 to $70 monthly; the technology at a given address matters more than the plan you buy. Mobile coverage from Telstra is good in town and reliable on the main highways, less so in the highlands. Cafes around Charles Street and the Quadrant are genuinely good, this being a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, and several tolerate a laptop all morning.
launceston.gettingAround: Launceston is compact by Australian standards and the centre is walkable, with the Cataract Gorge reserve beginning about a kilometre from the main street, which is remarkable for a city of this size. Metro Tasmania runs the bus network, adequate on weekdays and thin at weekends. A car is the practical answer for anything beyond town: the Tamar Valley wine route runs north, Cradle Mountain is about two and a half hours west, the Bay of Fires three hours east and Hobart two and a half hours south on the Midland Highway. Launceston Airport is 15km southeast with direct flights to Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.
launceston.visas: Australia's eVisitor and ETA schemes cover most European, North American and several Asian nationalities for stays of up to three months per entry across a twelve-month validity, applied for online for little or no fee. Working holiday visas give twelve months to under-30s or under-35s depending on nationality, extendable with specified regional work, and Tasmania counts as a regional area throughout, which makes it a popular place to complete the requirement. There is no digital nomad visa. Remote work for a foreign employer on a visitor visa is not addressed in Australian policy, and tax residency becomes the more pressing question well before the visa does.
launceston.bestTime: Launceston has a cool temperate climate and four genuine seasons, which sets it apart from almost everywhere else on this site. December to February is summer: highs of 24C to 25C, long light evenings, and the best time for the gorge, the coast and the highlands. March and April are the pick for many, with settled weather and the Tamar Valley vintage. Winter from June to August is cold, with highs of 12C to 13C, frosts, and a temperature inversion that traps woodsmoke in the valley on still mornings, which is a real air quality problem in July. Spring is changeable. Rain is spread through the year rather than concentrated.
launceston.prosCons: The case for Launceston is that it is a Georgian and Victorian city of 90,000 with a river gorge inside its boundary, some of the best food and wine in Australia, a university campus, an airport with mainland flights, and rents a third below Sydney. Cradle Mountain, the Bay of Fires and the whole Tasmanian wilderness are within a few hours. It is safe, quiet and green. Against that: it is still expensive globally, a car is needed for most of the appeal, winter is genuinely cold in badly insulated housing, the winter woodsmoke inversion is unpleasant, and the remote-work community is close to non-existent.
launceston.whoFor: Launceston suits somebody who wants a cool climate rather than a warm one, which is unusual enough on this site to be the whole selling point. If you work better at 15C than at 30C, if you hike, cycle, fish or care about food and wine, and if you can absorb Australian prices, this is one of the most liveable small cities anywhere. It works well on a working holiday visa, where Tasmania's regional status is an advantage. It does not suit a tight budget, anyone wanting beaches and heat, anyone without a car, or anyone looking for a nomad scene. Hobart is livelier if you want a Tasmanian city with more going on.

maceio.costOfLiving: Maceio runs about $780 a month for one person, cheap for a Brazilian state capital with beaches this good. A furnished one-bedroom in Ponta Verde or Jatiuca, the two safest and most walkable beach neighbourhoods, is $280 to $500; further from the water it drops sharply. A prato feito lunch is $4 to $6, a churrascaria dinner $12 to $20, and a caipirinha on the beach $2 to $3. Coworking is available at $80 to $150 a month. Fibre internet is $20 to $35 for 200 to 500 Mbps. An Uber across town is $3 to $7, and air conditioning adds $30 to $60 to the power bill.
maceio.whereToWork: Maceio has a handful of coworking spaces, mostly in Jatiuca, Ponta Verde and Farol, priced at $80 to $150 a month, serving a local startup scene rather than visitors. Brazilian fibre is the real advantage: 200 to 500 Mbps costs $20 to $35 a month from Claro, Vivo or one of the many regional providers, and it is fast, cheap and widely available in the beach neighbourhoods. Mobile 4G and 5G are good and inexpensive. Cafes along the beachfront work for a couple of hours. Power is reliable. The practical constraint is choosing a neighbourhood you are comfortable walking home in after dark rather than anything technical.
maceio.gettingAround: Maceio stretches along the coast, and the beachfront avenue running through Pajucara, Ponta Verde and Jatiuca is the walkable spine where most visitors stay. Buses cover the city cheaply but are slow and crowded. Uber and 99 both work well and are the default for most people at $3 to $7 a trip. The jangada sailing rafts take you out to the natural pools on the reef at low tide, which is the classic Maceio outing. Zumbi dos Palmares airport is 25km north with flights across Brazil and some international routes. Praia do Frances is 25km south and the beaches of Sao Miguel dos Milagres about 100km north.
maceio.visas: Brazil gives most European nationalities 90 days visa free on arrival, extendable once by another 90 days through the Policia Federal, for a maximum of 180 days in any 12-month period. US, Canadian and Australian citizens now need an e-visa, applied for online, following the reintroduction of reciprocity. Brazil also operates a digital nomad visa, valid for one year and renewable once, requiring proof of remote employment with a foreign company and a minimum monthly income, currently set at $1,500 or savings of $18,000. It is applied for at a consulate or after arrival, and it is one of the more accessible nomad visas available.
maceio.bestTime: Maceio is nine degrees south and warm all year, with highs between 28C and 31C in every month. The distinction that matters is rain: the wet season runs from April to July and is genuinely heavy, with May and June the wettest, and it is when the sea gets churned up and the natural pools lose their clarity. September to February is the dry half, with lower humidity, calm water and the best conditions for the reef pools, which are only accessible at low tide so it is worth checking the tide tables before booking a jangada. Carnival in February fills the city. Sea temperature never drops below about 26C.
maceio.prosCons: The case for Maceio is the water. The sea here is a startling green over white sand, the reef creates natural pools you can walk out to at low tide, and the coast north and south of the city is among the best in Brazil. Costs are low, fibre is fast and cheap, and Brazil's digital nomad visa is one of the easier ones to obtain. Against that, and it is serious: Alagoas has among the highest homicide rates of any Brazilian state and Maceio requires real care about neighbourhoods and hours. Little English is spoken. The Pinheiro district was evacuated after salt mining collapsed the ground beneath it, and parts of the city are permanently emptied.
maceio.whoFor: Maceio suits somebody who already knows Brazil or speaks reasonable Portuguese, wants a beach base with fast cheap internet, and is comfortable exercising the ordinary caution that a Brazilian capital requires: stay in Ponta Verde or Jatiuca, use Uber after dark, do not walk the beach at night. On the digital nomad visa it can be a very good year. It does not suit a first trip to Latin America, a solo traveller who wants to wander freely at any hour, or anyone without any Portuguese. Florianopolis and Fortaleza offer Brazilian beach life with a larger foreign community and a calmer safety picture.

joaopessoa.costOfLiving: Joao Pessoa runs about $750 a month for one person. A furnished one-bedroom in Tambau, Cabo Branco or Manaira, the three beachfront neighbourhoods where most visitors stay, is $270 to $480; inland districts are considerably cheaper. A prato feito lunch is $4 to $6, a good restaurant dinner $12 to $20, and a beer on the beach a dollar. Coworking runs $80 to $150 a month. Fibre at 200 to 500 Mbps costs $20 to $35, which is among the best internet value anywhere on this site. An Uber across the city is $3 to $6. Air conditioning adds $30 to $55 to the monthly power bill.
joaopessoa.whereToWork: Joao Pessoa has a modest coworking scene concentrated in Tambau, Manaira and near the university, at $80 to $150 a month, with a local software sector larger than the city's size suggests. The stronger point is home internet: Brazilian fibre from Claro, Vivo, Oi or the regional providers delivers 200 to 500 Mbps for $20 to $35 a month across the beach neighbourhoods, which makes video calls and large uploads a non-issue. Mobile 4G and 5G are cheap and widespread. Beachfront cafes are workable for a morning. Power is reliable and outages are rare, so no backup setup is needed here.
joaopessoa.gettingAround: The city runs along a beachfront that is unusually green and low rise by Brazilian standards, with building height restricted so the beaches keep afternoon sun. The Tambau to Cabo Branco stretch is walkable and cycleable, with a beachfront path along most of it. Buses cover the city cheaply, and Uber and 99 handle everything else for $3 to $6. Ponta do Seixas, the easternmost point of the Americas, is 14km south below the Cabo Branco lighthouse. Praia do Jacare on the Paraiba river is 15km north, where boats gather at sunset. The airport is 11km out, and Recife is two hours south by road for wider connections.
joaopessoa.visas: Brazil admits most European nationalities visa free for 90 days, extendable once by a further 90 through the Policia Federal, capped at 180 days in any 12-month period. American, Canadian and Australian citizens require an e-visa obtained online in advance. Brazil's digital nomad visa gives one year, renewable for a second, and asks for proof of remote work for a company outside Brazil plus a minimum income of about $1,500 a month or savings of $18,000. It can be applied for at a consulate abroad or converted after arrival, and the paperwork burden is lighter than most European equivalents.
joaopessoa.bestTime: Joao Pessoa sits seven degrees south and its temperature barely moves, with highs of 29C to 31C all year and a constant sea breeze that makes it feel milder than the numbers. Rain is the variable: the wet season runs March to July, with April, May and June the heaviest, and while the showers are usually short they can be intense. September to February is the dry stretch, with lower humidity, calm seas and the best beach conditions. The city claims the first sunrise in the Americas at Ponta do Seixas, which is a genuine geographic fact and worth an early morning. Sea temperature stays around 27C throughout.
joaopessoa.prosCons: The case for Joao Pessoa is that it is the calmest of the northeastern Brazilian capitals: greener, lower rise, less crowded, with a beachfront where building height rules keep the sand in sunlight, a well-preserved colonial centre including the Sao Francisco church complex, and fast cheap fibre. It is generally regarded as safer than Recife, Salvador or Maceio, though it is still a Brazilian city and the usual precautions apply. Costs are low and the digital nomad visa is accessible. Against that: little English is spoken, the foreign community is small, nightlife is quiet compared with Recife or Natal, and the wet season from April to June is heavy.
joaopessoa.whoFor: Joao Pessoa suits somebody who wants northeastern Brazil at a slower pace: a beach city with real infrastructure, excellent internet and a low cost of living, where the trade-off for fewer people is less noise rather than less to do. Some Portuguese makes an enormous difference and is close to necessary. It is a strong candidate for a year on the digital nomad visa if you want warmth, water and a manageable city rather than a big one. It does not suit anyone who needs an English-speaking environment, a large foreign community, or serious nightlife. Recife is two hours south for all three, at a higher cost and a busier safety picture.
